I walked in on them kissing in an empty classroom one day. He was so upset when she was -you know - attacked. You won’t tease him, will you?’ she added anxiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: ‘Wouldn’t dream of it,’ said Fred, who was looking as if his birthday had come early.

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: ‘Definitely not,’ said George, sniggering.

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: The Hogwarts Express slowed and finally stopped.

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: Harry pulled out his quill and a bit of parchment and turned to Ron and Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: ‘This is called a telephone number,’ he told Ron, scribbling it twice, tearing the parchment in two and handing it to them. ‘I told your dad how to use a telephone last summer, he’ll know. Call me at the Dursleys, OK? I can’t stand another two months with only Dudley to talk to …’

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: ‘Your aunt and uncle will be proud, though, won’t they?’ said Hermione, as they got off the train and joined the crowd thronging towards the enchanted barrier. ‘When they hear what you did this year?’

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: ‘Proud?’ said Harry. ‘Are you mad? All those times I could’ve died, and I didn’t manage it? They’ll be furious …’

book: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (UK)
text_content: And together they walked back through the gateway to the Muggle world.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry Potter was a highly unusual boy in many ways. For one thing, he hated the summer holidays more than any other time of year. For another, he really wanted to do his homework, but was forced to do it in secret, in the dead of night. And he also happened to be a wizard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was nearly midnight, and he was lying on his front in bed, the blankets drawn right over his head like a tent, a torch in one hand and a large leather-bound book (A History of Magic, by Adalbert Waffling) propped open against the pillow. Harry moved the tip of his eagle-feather quill down the page, frowning as he looked for something that would help him write his essay, ‘Witch-Burning in the Fourteenth Century Was Completely Pointless – discuss’.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The quill paused at the top of a likely-looking paragraph. Harry pushed his round glasses up his nose, moved his torch closer to the book and read:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Non-magic people (more commonly known as Muggles) were particularly afraid of magic in medieval times, but not very good at recognising it. On the rare occasion that they did catch a real witch or wizard, burning had no effect whatsoever. The witch or wizard would perform a basic Flame-Freezing Charm and then pretend to shriek with pain while enjoying a gentle, tickling sensation. Indeed, Wendelin the Weird enjoyed being burnt so much that she allowed herself to be caught no fewer than forty-seven times in various disguises.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry put his quill between his teeth and reached underneath his pillow for his ink bottle and a roll of parchment. Slowly and very carefully he unscrewed the ink bottle, dipped his quill into it and began to write, pausing every now and then to listen, because if any of the Dursleys heard the scratching of his quill on their way to the bathroom, he’d probably find himself locked in the cupboard under the stairs for the rest of the summer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Dursley family of number four, Privet Drive, was the reason that Harry never enjoyed his summer holidays. Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia and their son, Dudley, were Harry’s only living relatives. They were Muggles, and they had a very medieval attitude towards magic. Harry’s dead parents, who had been a witch and wizard themselves, were never mentioned under the Dursleys’ roof. For years, Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon had hoped that if they kept Harry as downtrodden as possible, they would be able to squash the magic out of him. To their fury, they had been unsuccessful, and now lived in terror of anyone finding out that Harry had spent most of the last two years at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. The most the Dursleys could do these days was to lock away Harry’s spellbooks, wand, cauldron and broomstick at the start of the summer holidays, and forbid him to talk to the neighbours.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: This separation from his spellbooks had been a real problem for Harry, because his teachers at Hogwarts had given him a lot of holiday work. One of the essays, a particularly nasty one about Shrinking Potions, was for Harry’s least favourite teacher, Professor Snape, who would be delighted to have an excuse to give Harry detention for a month. Harry had therefore seized his chance in the first week of the holidays. Whilst Uncle Vernon, Aunt Petunia and Dudley had gone out into the front garden to admire Uncle Vernon’s new company car (in very loud voices, so that the rest of the street would notice it too), Harry had crept downstairs, picked the lock on the cupboard under the stairs, grabbed some of his books and hidden them in his bedroom. As long as he didn’t leave spots of ink on the sheets, the Dursleys need never know that he was studying magic by night.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was keen to avoid trouble with his aunt and uncle at the moment, as they were already in a bad mood with him, all because he’d received a telephone call from a fellow wizard one week into the school holidays.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron Weasley, who was one of Harry’s best friends at Hogwarts, came from a whole family of wizards. This meant that he knew a lot of things Harry didn’t, but had never used a telephone before. Most unluckily, it had been Uncle Vernon who had answered the call.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Vernon Dursley speaking.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, who happened to be in the room at the time, froze as he heard Ron’s voice answer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘HELLO? HELLO? CAN YOU HEAR ME? I – WANT – TO – TALK – TO – HARRY – POTTER!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron was yelling so loudly that Uncle Vernon jumped and held the receiver a foot away from his ear, staring at it with an expression of mingled fury and alarm.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘WHO IS THIS?’ he roared in the direction of the mouthpiece. ‘WHO ARE YOU?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘RON – WEASLEY!’ Ron bellowed back, as though he and Uncle Vernon were speaking from opposite ends of a football pitch. ‘I’M – A – FRIEND – OF – HARRY’S – FROM – SCHOOL –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Uncle Vernon’s small eyes swivelled around to Harry, who was rooted to the spot.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘THERE IS NO HARRY POTTER HERE!’ he roared, now holding the receiver at arm’s length, as though frightened it might explode. ‘I DON’T KNOW WHAT SCHOOL YOU’RE TALKING ABOUT! NEVER CONTACT ME AGAIN! DON’T YOU COME NEAR MY FAMILY!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And he threw the receiver back onto the telephone as if dropping a poisonous spider.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The row that had followed had been one of the worst ever.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘HOW DARE YOU GIVE THIS NUMBER TO PEOPLE LIKE – PEOPLE LIKE YOU!’ Uncle Vernon had roared, spraying Harry with spit.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron obviously realised that he’d got Harry into trouble, because he hadn’t called again. Harry’s other best friend from Hogwarts, Hermione Granger, hadn’t been in touch either. Harry suspected that Ron had warned Hermione not to call, which was a pity, because Hermione, the cleverest witch in Harry’s year, had Muggle parents, knew perfectly well how to use a telephone, and would probably have had enough sense not to say that she went to Hogwarts.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: So Harry had had no word from any of his wizarding friends for five long weeks, and this summer was turning out to be almost as bad as the last one. There was just one, very small improvement: after swearing that he wouldn’t use her to send letters to any of his friends, Harry had been allowed to let his owl, Hedwig, out at night. Uncle Vernon had given in because of the racket Hedwig made if she was locked in her cage all the time.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry finished writing about Wendelin the Weird and paused to listen again. The silence in the dark house was broken only by the distant, grunting snores of his enormous cousin, Dudley. It must be very late. Harry’s eyes were itching with tiredness. Perhaps he’d finish this essay tomorrow night …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He replaced the top of the ink bottle, pulled an old pillowcase from under his bed, put the torch, A History of Magic, his essay, quill and ink inside it, got out of bed and hid the lot under a loose floorboard under his bed. Then he stood up, stretched, and checked the time on the luminous alarm clock on his bedside table.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was one o’clock in the morning. Harry’s stomach gave a funny jolt. He had been thirteen years old, without realising it, for a whole hour.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Yet another unusual thing about Harry was how little he looked forward to his birthdays. He had never received a birthday card in his life. The Dursleys had completely ignored his last two birthdays, and he had no reason to suppose they would remember this one.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry walked across the dark room, past Hedwig’s large, empty cage, to the open window. He leaned on the sill, the cool night air pleasant on his face after a long time under the blankets. Hedwig had been absent for two nights now. Harry wasn’t worried about her – she’d been gone this long before – but he hoped she’d be back soon. She was the only living creature in this house who didn’t flinch at the sight of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, though still rather small and skinny for his age, had grown a few inches over the last year. His jet-black hair, however, was just as it always had been: stubbornly untidy, whatever he did to it. The eyes behind his glasses were bright green, and on his forehead, clearly visible through his hair, was a thin scar, shaped like a bolt of lightning.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Of all the unusual things about Harry, this scar was the most extraordinary of all. It was not, as the Dursleys had pretended for ten years, a souvenir of the car crash that had killed Harry’s parents, because Lily and James Potter had not died in a car crash. They had been murdered, murdered by the most feared Dark wizard for a hundred years, Lord Voldemort. Harry had escaped from the same attack with nothing more than a scar on his forehead, when Voldemort’s curse, instead of killing him, had rebounded upon its originator. Barely alive, Voldemort had fled …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Harry had come face to face with him since at Hogwarts. Remembering their last meeting as he stood at the dark window, Harry had to admit he was lucky even to have reached his thirteenth birthday.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He scanned the starry sky for a sign of Hedwig, perhaps soaring back to him with a dead mouse dangling from her beak, expecting praise. Gazing absently over the rooftops, it was a few seconds before Harry realised what he was seeing.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Silhouetted against the golden moon, and growing larger every moment, was a large, strangely lop-sided creature, and it was flapping in Harry’s direction. He stood quite still, watching it sink lower and lower. For a split second, he hesitated, his hand on the window-latch, wondering whether to slam it shut, but then the bizarre creature soared over one of the streetlamps of Privet Drive, and Harry, realising what it was, leapt aside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Through the window soared three owls, two of them holding up the third, which appeared to be unconscious. They landed with a soft flump on Harry’s bed, and the middle owl, which was large and grey, keeled right over and lay motionless. There was a large package tied to its legs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry recognised the unconscious owl at once – his name was Errol, and he belonged to the Weasley family. Harry dashed to the bed at once, untied the cords around Errol’s legs, took off the parcel and then carried Errol to Hedwig’s cage. Errol opened one bleary eye, gave a feeble hoot of thanks, and began to gulp some water.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry turned back to the remaining owls. One of them, the large snowy female, was his own Hedwig. She, too, was carrying a parcel, and looked extremely pleased with herself. She gave Harry an affectionate nip with her beak as he removed her burden, then flew across the room to join Errol.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t recognise the third owl, a handsome tawny one, but he knew at once where it had come from, because in addition to a third parcel, it was carrying a letter bearing the Hogwarts crest. When Harry relieved this owl of its post it ruffled its feathers importantly, stretched its wings and took off through the window into the night.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sat down on his bed, grabbed Errol’s package, ripped off the brown paper and discovered a present wrapped in gold, and his first ever birthday card. Fingers trembling slightly, he opened the envelope. Two pieces of paper fell out – a letter and a newspaper cutting.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The cutting had clearly come out of the wizarding newspaper, the Daily Prophet, because the people in the black and white picture were moving. Harry picked up the cutting, smoothed it out and read:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: MINISTRY OF MAGIC EMPLOYEE SCOOPS GRAND PRIZE

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Arthur Weasley, Head of the Misuse of Muggle Artefacts Office at the Ministry of Magic, has won the annual Daily Prophet Grand Prize Galleon Draw.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A delighted Mr Weasley told the Daily Prophet, ‘We will be spending the gold on a summer holiday in Egypt, where our eldest son, Bill, works as a curse breaker for Gringotts Wizarding Bank.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Weasley family will be spending a month in Egypt, returning for the start of the new school year at Hogwarts, which five of the Weasley children currently attend.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry scanned the moving photograph, and a grin spread across his face as he saw all nine of the Weasleys waving furiously at him, standing in front of a large pyramid. Plump little Mrs Weasley, tall, balding Mr Weasley, six sons and one daughter, all (though the black and white picture didn’t show it) with flaming red hair. Right in the middle of the picture was Ron, tall and gangling, with his pet rat Scabbers on his shoulder and his arm around his little sister, Ginny.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry couldn’t think of anyone who deserved to win a large pile of gold more than the Weasleys, who were very nice and extremely poor. He picked up Ron’s letter and unfolded it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dear Harry,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Happy birthday!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Look, I’m really sorry about that telephone call. I hope the Muggles didn’t give you a hard time. I asked Dad, and he reckons I shouldn’t have shouted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It’s brilliant here in Egypt. Bill’s taken us round all the tombs and you wouldn’t believe the curses those old Egyptian wizards put on them. Mum wouldn’t let Ginny come in the last one. There were all these mutant skeletons in there, of Muggles who’d broken in and grown extra heads and stuff.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: I couldn’t believe it when Dad won the Daily Prophet Draw. Seven hundred galleons! Most of it’s gone on this holiday, but they’re going to buy me a new wand for next year.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry remembered only too well the occasion when Ron’s old wand had snapped. It had happened when the car the two of them had been flying to Hogwarts had crashed into a tree in the school grounds.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: We’ll be back about a week before term starts and we’ll be going up to London to get my wand and our new books. Any chance of meeting you there?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Don’t let the Muggles get you down!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Try and come to London,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: PS: Percy’s Head Boy. He got the letter last week.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry glanced back at the photograph. Percy, who was in his seventh and final year at Hogwarts, was looking particularly smug. He had pinned his Head Boy badge to the fez perched jauntily on top of his neat hair, his horn-rimmed glasses flashing in the Egyptian sun.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry now turned to his present and unwrapped it. Inside was what looked like a miniature glass spinning top. There was another note from Ron beneath it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry – this is a Pocket Sneakoscope. If there’s someone untrustworthy around, it’s supposed to light up and spin. Bill says it’s rubbish sold for wizard tourists and isn’t reliable, because it kept lighting up at dinner last night. But he didn’t realise Fred and George had put beetles in his soup.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Bye – Ron

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry put the Pocket Sneakoscope on his bedside table, where it stood quite still, balanced on its point, reflecting the luminous hands of his clock. He looked at it happily for a few seconds, then picked up the parcel Hedwig had brought.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Inside this, too, there was a wrapped present, a card and a letter, this time from Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dear Harry,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron wrote to me and told me about his phone call to your Uncle Vernon. I do hope you’re all right.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: I’m on holiday in France at the moment and I didn’t know how I was going to send this to you – what if they’d opened it at Customs? – but then Hedwig turned up! I think she wanted to make sure you got something for your birthday for a change. I bought your present by owl-order; there was an advertisement in the Daily Prophet (I’ve been getting it delivered, it’s so good to keep up with what’s going on in the wizarding world). Did you see that picture of Ron and his family a week ago? I bet he’s learning loads, I’m really jealous – the ancient Egyptian wizards were fascinating.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There’s some interesting local history of witchcraft here, too. I’ve re-written my whole History of Magic essay to include some of the things I’ve found out. I hope it’s not too long, it’s two rolls of parchment more than Professor Binns asked for.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron says he’s going to be in London in the last week of the holidays. Can you make it? Will your aunt and uncle let you come? I really hope you can. If not, I’ll see you on the Hogwarts Express on September the first!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Love from

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: PS. Ron says Percy’s Head Boy. I’ll bet Percy’s really pleased. Ron doesn’t seem too happy about it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry laughed again as he put Hermione’s letter aside and picked up her present. It was very heavy. Knowing Hermione, he was sure it would be a large book full of very difficult spells – but it wasn’t. His heart gave a huge bound as he ripped back the paper and saw a sleek black leather case with silver words stamped across it: Broomstick Servicing Kit.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Wow, Hermione!’ Harry whispered, unzipping the case to look inside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a large jar of Fleetwood’s High-Finish Handle Polish, a pair of gleaming silver Tail-Twig Clippers, a tiny brass compass to clip onto your broom for long journeys, and a Handbook of Do-it-Yourself Broomcare.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Apart from his friends, the thing that Harry missed most about Hogwarts was Quidditch, the most popular sport in the magical world – highly dangerous, very exciting and played on broomsticks. Harry happened to be a very good Quidditch player; he had been the youngest person in a century to be picked for one of the Hogwarts house teams. One of Harry’s most prized possessions was his Nimbus Two Thousand racing broom.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry put the leather case aside and picked up his last parcel. He recognised the untidy scrawl on the brown paper at once: this was from Hagrid, the Hogwarts gamekeeper. He tore off the top layer of paper and glimpsed something green and leathery, but before he could unwrap it properly, the parcel gave a strange quiver, and whatever was inside it snapped loudly – as though it had jaws.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry froze. He knew that Hagrid would never send him anything dangerous on purpose, but then, Hagrid didn’t have a normal person’s view of what was dangerous. Hagrid had been known to befriend giant spiders, buy vicious, three-headed dogs from men in pubs and sneak illegal dragon eggs into his cabin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry poked the parcel nervously. It snapped loudly again. Harry reached for the lamp on his bedside table, gripped it firmly in one hand and raised it over his head, ready to strike. Then he seized the rest of the wrapping paper in his other hand and pulled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And out fell – a book. Harry just had time to register its handsome green cover, emblazoned with the golden title, The Monster Book of Monsters, before it flipped onto its edge and scuttled sideways along the bed like some weird crab.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Uh oh,’ Harry muttered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The book toppled off the bed with a loud clunk and shuffled rapidly across the room. Harry followed it stealthily. The book was hiding in the dark space under his desk. Praying that the Dursleys were still fast asleep, Harry got down on his hands and knees and reached towards it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ouch!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The book snapped shut on his hand and then flapped past him, still scuttling on its covers. Harry scrambled around, threw himself forward and managed to flatten it. Uncle Vernon gave a loud, sleepy grunt in the room next door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hedwig and Errol watched interestedly as Harry clamped the struggling book tightly in his arms, hurried to his chest of drawers and pulled out a belt, which he buckled tightly around it. The Monster Book shuddered angrily, but could no longer flap and snap, so Harry threw it down on the bed and reached for Hagrid’s card.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dear Harry,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Happy Birthday!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Think you might find this useful for next year. Won’t say no more here. Tell you when I see you.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hope the Muggles are treating you right.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: All the best,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It struck Harry as ominous that Hagrid thought a biting book would come in useful, but he put up Hagrid’s card next to Ron and Hermione’s, grinning more broadly than ever. Now there was only the letter from Hogwarts left.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Noticing that it was rather thicker than usual, Harry slit open the envelope, pulled out the first page of parchment within and read:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dear Mr Potter,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Please note that the new school year will begin on September the first. The Hogwarts Express will leave from King’s Cross Station, platform nine and three-quarters, at eleven o’clock.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Third-years are permitted to visit the village of Hogsmeade at certain weekends. Please give the enclosed permission form to your parent or guardian to sign.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A list of books for next year is enclosed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Yours sincerely,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor M. McGonagall

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Deputy Headmistress

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry pulled out the Hogsmeade permission form and looked at it, no longer grinning. It would be wonderful to visit Hogsmeade at weekends; he knew it was an entirely wizarding village, and he had never set foot there. But how on earth was he going to persuade Uncle Vernon or Aunt Petunia to sign the form?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He looked over at the alarm clock. It was now two o’clock in the morning.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Deciding that he’d worry about the Hogsmeade form when he woke up, Harry got back into bed and reached up to cross off another day on the chart he’d made for himself, counting down the days left until his return to Hogwarts. Then he took off his glasses and lay down, eyes open, facing his three birthday cards.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Extremely unusual though he was, at that moment Harry Potter felt just like everyone else: glad, for the first time in his life, that it was his birthday.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Harry went down to breakfast next morning to find the three Dursleys already sitting around the kitchen table. They were watching a brand-new television, a welcome-home-for-the-summer present for Dudley, who had been complaining loudly about the long walk between the fridge and the television in the living room. Dudley had spent most of the summer in the kitchen, his piggy little eyes fixed on the screen and his five chins wobbling as he ate continually.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Harry sat down between Dudley and Uncle Vernon, a large, beefy man with very little neck and a lot of moustache. Far from wishing Harry a happy birthday, none of the Dursleys gave any sign that they had noticed Harry enter the room, but Harry was far too used to this to care. He helped himself to a piece of toast and then looked up at the newsreader on the television, who was halfway through a report on an escaped convict.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘… the public is warned that Black is armed and extremely dangerous. A special hotline has been set up, and any sighting of Black should be reported immediately.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘No need to tell us he’s no good,’ snorted Uncle Vernon, staring over the top of his newspaper at the prisoner. ‘Look at the state of him, the filthy layabout! Look at his hair!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: He shot a nasty look sideways at Harry, whose untidy hair had always been a source of great annoyance to Uncle Vernon. Compared to the man on the television, however, whose gaunt face was surrounded by a matted, elbow-length tangle, Harry felt very well groomed indeed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: The newsreader had reappeared.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will announce today –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Hang on!’ barked Uncle Vernon, staring furiously at the newsreader. ‘You didn’t tell us where that maniac’s escaped from! What use is that? Lunatic could be coming up the street right now!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Aunt Petunia, who was bony and horse-faced, whipped around and peered intently out of the kitchen window. Harry knew Aunt Petunia would simply love to be the one to call the hotline number. She was the nosiest woman in the world and spent most of her life spying on her boring, law-abiding neighbours.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘When will they learn,’ said Uncle Vernon, pounding the table with his large purple fist, ‘that hanging’s the only way to deal with these people?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Very true,’ said Aunt Petunia, who was still squinting into next door’s runner-beans.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Uncle Vernon drained his teacup, glanced at his watch and added, ‘I’d better be off in a minute, Petunia, Marge’s train gets in at ten.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Harry, whose thoughts had been upstairs with the Broomstick Servicing Kit, was brought back to earth with an unpleasant bump.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Aunt Marge?’ he blurted out. ‘Sh-she’s not coming here, is she?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Aunt Marge was Uncle Vernon’s sister. Even though she was not a blood relative of Harry’s (whose mother had been Aunt Petunia’s sister), he had been forced to call her ‘Aunt’ all his life. Aunt Marge lived in the country, in a house with a large garden, where she bred bulldogs. She didn’t often stay in Privet Drive, because she couldn’t bear to leave her precious dogs, but each of her visits stood out horribly vividly in Harry’s mind.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: At Dudley’s fifth birthday party, Aunt Marge had whacked Harry around the shins with her walking stick to stop him beating Dudley at musical statues. A few years later, she had turned up at Christmas with a computerised robot for Dudley and a box of dog biscuits for Harry. On her last visit, the year before Harry had started at Hogwarts, Harry had accidentally trodden on the paw of her favourite dog. Ripper had chased Harry out into the garden and up a tree, and Aunt Marge had refused to call him off until past midnight. The memory of this incident still brought tears of laughter to Dudley’s eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Marge’ll be here for a week,’ Uncle Vernon snarled, ‘and while we’re on the subject,’ he pointed a fat finger threateningly at Harry, ‘we need to get a few things straight before I go and collect her.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Dudley smirked and withdrew his gaze from the television. Watching Harry being bullied by Uncle Vernon was Dudley’s favourite form of entertainment.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Firstly,’ growled Uncle Vernon, ‘you’ll keep a civil tongue in your head when you’re talking to Marge.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘All right,’ said Harry bitterly, ‘if she does when she’s talking to me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Secondly,’ said Uncle Vernon, acting as though he had not heard Harry’s reply, ‘as Marge doesn’t know anything about your abnormality, I don’t want any – any funny stuff while she’s here. You behave yourself, got me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘I will if she does,’ said Harry through gritted teeth.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘And thirdly,’ said Uncle Vernon, his mean little eyes now slits in his great purple face, ‘we’ve told Marge you attend St Brutus’s Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘What?’ Harry yelled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘And you’ll be sticking to that story, boy, or there’ll be trouble,’ spat Uncle Vernon.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Harry sat there, white-faced and furious, staring at Uncle Vernon, hardly able to believe it. Aunt Marge coming for a week-long visit – it was the worst birthday present the Dursleys had ever given him, including that pair of Uncle Vernon’s old socks.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Well, Petunia,’ said Uncle Vernon, getting heavily to his feet, ‘I’ll be off to the station, then. Want to come along for the ride, Dudders?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘No,’ said Dudley, whose attention had returned to the television now that Uncle Vernon had finished threatening Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: ‘Duddy’s got to make himself smart for his auntie,’ said Aunt Petunia, smoothing Dudley’s thick blond hair. ‘Mummy’s bought him a lovely new bow-tie.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake
text_content: Uncle Vernon clapped Dudley on his porky shoulder.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Two - Aunt Marge’s Big Mistake

And the worst of it was, he had just done serious magic, which meant that he was almost certainly expelled from Hogwarts. He had broken the Decree for the Restriction of Underage Wizardry so badly, he was surprised Ministry of Magic representatives weren’t swooping down on him where he sat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry shivered and looked up and down Magnolia Crescent. What was going to happen to him? Would he be arrested, or would he simply be outlawed from the wizarding world? He thought of Ron and Hermione, and his heart sank even lower. Harry was sure that, criminal or not, Ron and Hermione would want to help him now, but they were both abroad, and with Hedwig gone, he had no means of contacting them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He didn’t have any Muggle money, either. There was a little wizard gold in the moneybag at the bottom of his trunk, but the rest of the fortune his parents had left him was stored in a vault at Gringotts Wizarding Bank in London. He’d never be able to drag his trunk all the way to London. Unless …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He looked down at his wand, which he was still clutching in his hand. If he was already expelled (his heart was now thumping painfully fast), a bit more magic couldn’t hurt. He had the Invisibility Cloak he had inherited from his father – what if he bewitched the trunk to make it feather-light, tied it to his broomstick, covered himself in the Cloak and flew to London? Then he could get the rest of his money out of his vault and … begin his life as an outcast. It was a horrible prospect, but he couldn’t sit on this wall for ever or he’d find himself trying to explain to Muggle police why he was out in the dead of night with a trunkful of spellbooks and a broomstick.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry opened his trunk again and pushed the contents aside, looking for the Invisibility Cloak – but before he had found it, he straightened up suddenly, looking around him once more.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A funny prickling on the back of his neck had made Harry feel he was being watched, but the street appeared to be deserted, and no lights shone from any of the large square houses.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He bent over his trunk again, but almost immediately stood up once more, his hand clenched on his wand. He had sensed rather than heard it: someone or something was standing in the narrow gap between the garage and the fence behind him. Harry squinted at the black alleyway. If only it would move, then he’d know whether it was just a stray cat or – something else.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Lumos,’ Harry muttered, and a light appeared at the end of his wand, almost dazzling him. He held it high over his head, and the pebble-dashed walls of number two suddenly sparkled; the garage door gleamed, and between them, Harry saw, quite distinctly, the hulking outline of something very big, with wide, gleaming eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stepped backwards. His legs hit his trunk and he tripped. His wand flew out of his hand as he flung out an arm to break his fall, and he landed, hard, in the gutter.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a deafening BANG and Harry threw up his hands to shield his eyes against a sudden blinding light …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: With a yell, he rolled back onto the pavement, just in time. A second later, a gigantic pair of wheels and headlights had screeched to a halt exactly where Harry had just been lying. They belonged, as Harry saw when he raised his head, to a triple-decker, violently purple bus, which had appeared out of thin air. Gold lettering over the windscreen spelled The Knight Bus.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: For a split second, Harry wondered if he had been knocked silly by his fall. Then a conductor in a purple uniform leapt out of the bus and began to speak loudly to the night.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Welcome to the Knight Bus, emergency transport for the stranded witch or wizard. Just stick out your wand hand, step on board and we can take you anywhere you want to go. My name is Stan Shunpike, and I will be your conductor this eve –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The conductor stopped abruptly. He had just caught sight of Harry, who was still sitting on the ground. Harry snatched up his wand again and scrambled to his feet. Close to, he saw that Stan Shunpike was only a few years older than he was; eighteen or nineteen at most, with large, protruding ears and a fair few pimples.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What were you doin’ down there?’ said Stan, dropping his professional manner.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Fell over,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Choo fall over for?’ sniggered Stan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I didn’t do it on purpose,’ said Harry, annoyed. One of the knees in his jeans was torn, and the hand he had thrown out to break his fall was bleeding. He suddenly remembered why he had fallen over, and turned around quickly to stare at the alleyway between the garage and fence. The Knight Bus’s headlamps were flooding it with light, and it was empty.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Choo lookin’ at?’ said Stan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There was a big black thing,’ said Harry, pointing uncertainly into the gap. ‘Like a dog … but massive …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He looked around at Stan, whose mouth was slightly open. With a feeling of unease, Harry saw Stan’s eyes move to the scar on Harry’s forehead.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Woss that on your ’ead?’ said Stan abruptly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Nothing,’ said Harry quickly, flattening his hair over his scar. If the Ministry of Magic was looking for him, he didn’t want to make it too easy for them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Woss your name?’ Stan persisted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville Longbottom,’ said Harry, saying the first name that came into his head. ‘So – so this bus,’ he went on quickly, hoping to distract Stan, ‘did you say it goes anywhere?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yep,’ said Stan proudly, ‘anywhere you like, long’s it’s on land. Can’t do nuffink underwater. ’Ere,’ he said, looking suspicious again, ‘you did flag us down, dincha? Stuck out your wand ’and, dincha?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry quickly. ‘Listen, how much would it be to get to London?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Eleven Sickles,’ said Stan, ‘but for firteen you get ’ot chocolate, and for fifteen you get an ’ot-water bottle an’ a toofbrush in the colour of your choice.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry rummaged once more in his trunk, extracted his money bag and shoved some silver into Stan’s hand. He and Stan then lifted his trunk, with Hedwig’s cage balanced on top, up the steps of the bus.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There were no seats; instead, half-a-dozen brass bedsteads stood beside the curtained windows. Candles were burning in brackets beside each bed, illuminating the wood-panelled walls. A tiny wizard in a nightcap at the rear of the bus muttered, ‘Not now, thanks, I’m pickling some slugs,’ and rolled over in his sleep.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You ’ave this one,’ Stan whispered, shoving Harry’s trunk under the bed right behind the driver, who was sitting in an armchair in front of the steering wheel. ‘This is our driver, Ernie Prang. This is Neville Longbottom, Ern.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ernie Prang, an elderly wizard wearing very thick glasses, nodded to Harry, who nervously flattened his fringe again and sat down on his bed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Take ’er away, Ern,’ said Stan, sitting down in the armchair next to Ernie’s.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was another tremendous BANG, and next moment Harry found himself flat on his bed, thrown backwards by the speed of the Knight Bus. Pulling himself up, Harry stared out of the dark window and saw that they were now bowling along a completely different street. Stan was watching Harry’s stunned face with great enjoyment.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘This is where we was before you flagged us down,’ he said. ‘Where are we, Ern? Somewhere in Wales?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ar,’ said Ernie.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How come the Muggles don’t hear the bus?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Them!’ said Stan contemptuously. ‘Don’ listen properly, do they? Don’ look properly either. Never notice nuffink, they don’.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Best go wake up Madam Marsh, Stan,’ said Ern. ‘We’ll be in Abergavenny in a minute.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan passed Harry’s bed and disappeared up a narrow wooden staircase. Harry was still looking out of the window, feeling increasingly nervous. Ernie didn’t seem to have mastered the use of a steering wheel. The Knight Bus kept mounting the pavement, but it didn’t hit anything; lines of lamp posts, letter boxes and bins jumped out of its way as it approached and back into position once it had passed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan came back downstairs, followed by a faintly green witch wrapped in a travelling cloak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Ere you go, Madam Marsh,’ said Stan happily, as Ern stamped on the brake and the beds slid a foot or so towards the front of the bus. Madam Marsh clamped a handkerchief to her mouth and tottered down the steps. Stan threw her bag out after her and rammed the doors shut; there was another loud BANG, and they were thundering down a narrow country lane, trees leaping out of the way.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry wouldn’t have been able to sleep even if he had been travelling on a bus that didn’t keep banging loudly and jumping a hundred miles at a time. His stomach churned as he fell back to wondering what was going to happen to him, and whether the Dursleys had managed to get Aunt Marge off the ceiling yet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan had unfurled a copy of the Daily Prophet and was now reading with his tongue between his teeth. A large photograph of a sunken-faced man with long, matted hair blinked slowly at Harry from the front page. He looked strangely familiar.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That man!’ Harry said, forgetting his troubles for a moment. ‘He was on the Muggle news!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stanley turned to the front page and chuckled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sirius Black,’ he said, nodding. ‘’Course ’e was on the Muggle news, Neville. Where you been?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He gave a superior sort of chuckle at the blank look on Harry’s face, removed the front page and handed it to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You oughta read the papers more, Neville.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry held the paper up to the candlelight and read:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: BLACK STILL AT LARGE

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Sirius Black, possibly the most infamous prisoner ever to be held in Azkaban fortress, is still eluding capture, the Ministry of Magic confirmed today.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We are doing all we can to recapture Black,’ said the Minister for Magic, Cornelius Fudge, this morning, ‘and we beg the magical community to remain calm.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge has been criticised by some members of the International Federation of Warlocks for informing the Muggle Prime Minister of the crisis.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, really, I had to, don’t you know,’ said an irritable Fudge. ‘Black is mad. He’s a danger to anyone who crosses him, magic or Muggle. I have the Prime Minister’s assurance that he will not breathe a word of Black’s true identity to anyone. And let’s face it – who’d believe him if he did?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘While Muggles have been told that Black is carrying a gun (a kind of metal wand which Muggles use to kill each other), the magical community lives in fear of a massacre like that of twelve years ago, when Black murdered thirteen people with a single curse.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked into the shadowed eyes of Sirius Black, the only part of the sunken face that seemed alive. Harry had never met a vampire, but he had seen pictures of them in his Defence Against the Dark Arts classes, and Black, with his waxy white skin, looked just like one.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Scary-lookin’ fing, inee?’ said Stan, who had been watching Harry read.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He murdered thirteen people?’ said Harry, handing the page back to Stan, ‘with one curse?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yep,’ said Stan. ‘In front of witnesses an’ all. Broad daylight. Big trouble it caused, dinnit, Ern?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ar,’ said Ern darkly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan swivelled in his armchair, his hands on the back, the better to look at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Black woz a big supporter of You-Know-’Oo,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What, Voldemort?’ said Harry, without thinking.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Even Stan’s pimples went white; Ern jerked the steering wheel so hard that a whole farmhouse had to jump aside to avoid the bus.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You outta your tree?’ yelped Stan. ‘’Choo say ’is name for?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry,’ said Harry hastily. ‘Sorry, I – I forgot –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Forgot!’ said Stan weakly. ‘Blimey, my ’eart’s goin’ that fast …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So – so Black was a supporter of You-Know-Who?’ Harry prompted apologetically.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Stan, still rubbing his chest. ‘Yeah, that’s right. Very close to You-Know-’Oo, they say … anyway, when little ’Arry Potter put paid to You-Know-’Oo’ – Harry nervously flattened his fringe down again – ‘all You-Know-’Oo’s supporters was tracked down, wasn’t they, Ern? Most of ’em knew it was all over, wiv You-Know-’Oo gone, and they came quiet. But not Sirius Black. I ’eard he thought ’e’d be second-in-command once You-Know-’Oo ’ad taken over.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway, they cornered Black in the middle of a street full of Muggles an’ Black took out ’is wand and ’e blasted ’alf the street apart, an’ a wizard got it, an’ so did a dozen Muggles what got in the way. ’Orrible, eh? An’ you know what Black did then?’ Stan continued in a dramatic whisper.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Laughed,’ said Stan. ‘Jus’ stood there an’ laughed. An’ when reinforcements from the Ministry of Magic got there, ’e went wiv ’em quiet as anyfink, still laughing ’is ’ead off. ’Cos ’e’s mad, inee, Ern? Inee mad?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘If he weren’t when he went to Azkaban, he will be now,’ said Ern in his slow voice. ‘I’d blow meself up before I set foot in that place. Serves him right, mind … after what he did …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They ’ad a job coverin’ it up, din’ they, Ern?’ Stan said. ‘’Ole street blown up an’ all them Muggles dead. What was it they said ’ad ’appened, Ern?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Gas explosion,’ grunted Ernie.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘An’ now ’e’s out,’ said Stan, examining the newspaper picture of Black’s gaunt face again. ‘Never been a breakout from Azkaban before, ’as there, Ern? Beats me ’ow ’e did it. Frightenin’, eh? Mind, I don’t fancy ’is chances against them Azkaban guards, eh, Ern?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ernie suddenly shivered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Talk about summat else, Stan, there’s a good lad. Them Azkaban guards give me the collywobbles.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan put the paper away reluctantly and Harry leaned against the window of the Knight Bus, feeling worse than ever. He couldn’t help imagining what Stan might be telling his passengers in a few nights’ time.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Ear about that ’Arry Potter? Blew up ’is Aunt! We ’ad ’im ’ere on the Knight Bus, di’n’t we, Ern? ’E was tryin’ to run for it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He, Harry, had broken wizard law just like Sirius Black. Was inflating Aunt Marge bad enough to land him in Azkaban? Harry didn’t know anything about the wizard prison, though everyone he’d ever heard speak of it did so in the same fearful tone. Hagrid the Hogwarts gamekeeper had spend two months there only last year. Harry wouldn’t soon forget the look of terror on Hagrid’s face when he had been told where he was going, and Hagrid was one of the bravest people Harry knew.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Knight Bus rolled through the darkness, scattering bushes and bollards, telephone boxes and trees, and Harry lay, restless and miserable, on his feather bed. After a while, Stan remembered that Harry had paid for hot chocolate, but poured it all over Harry’s pillow when the bus moved abruptly from Anglesea to Aberdeen. One by one, wizards and witches in dressing gowns and slippers descended from the upper floors to leave the bus. They all looked very pleased to go.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Finally, Harry was the only passenger left.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Right then, Neville,’ said Stan, clapping his hands, ‘whereabouts in London?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Diagon Alley’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Righto,’ said Stan, ‘’old tight, then …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: BANG

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They were thundering along Charing Cross Road. Harry sat up and watched buildings and benches squeezing themselves out of the Knight Bus’s way. The sky was getting a little lighter. He would lie low for a couple of hours, go to Gringotts the moment it opened, then set off – where, he didn’t know.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ern slammed on the brakes and the Knight Bus skidded to a halt in front of a small and shabby-looking pub, the Leaky Cauldron, behind which lay the magical entrance to Diagon Alley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Thanks,’ Harry said to Ern.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He jumped down the steps and helped Stan lower his trunk and Hedwig’s cage onto the pavement.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Harry, ‘bye then!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Stan wasn’t paying attention. Still standing in the doorway to the bus, he was goggling at the shadowy entrance to the Leaky Cauldron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There you are, Harry’ said a voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Before Harry could turn, he felt a hand on his shoulder. At the same time, Stan shouted, ‘Blimey! Ern, come ’ere! Come ’ere!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked up at the owner of the hand on his shoulder and felt a bucketful of ice cascade into his stomach – he had walked right into Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Stan leapt onto the pavement beside them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What didja call Neville, Minister?’ he said excitedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge, a portly little man in a long, pinstriped cloak, looked cold and exhausted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville?’ he repeated, frowning. ‘This is Harry Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew it!’ Stan shouted gleefully. ‘Ern! Ern! Guess ’oo Neville is, Ern! ’E’s ’Arry Potter! I can see ’is scar!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Fudge testily. ‘Well, I’m very glad the Knight Bus picked Harry up, but he and I need to step inside the Leaky Cauldron now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge increased the pressure on Harry’s shoulder, and Harry found himself being steered inside the pub. A stooping figure bearing a lantern appeared through the door behind the bar. It was Tom, the wizened, toothless landlord.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’ve got him, Minister!’ said Tom. ‘Will you be wanting anything? Beer? Brandy?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Perhaps a pot of tea,’ said Fudge, who still hadn’t let go of Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a loud scraping and puffing from behind them, and Stan and Ern appeared, carrying Harry’s trunk and Hedwig’s cage and looking around excitedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Ow come you di’n’t tell us ’oo you are, eh, Neville?’ said Stan, beaming at Harry, while Ernie’s owlish face peered interestedly over Stan’s shoulder.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And a private parlour, please, Tom,’ said Fudge pointedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Bye,’ Harry said miserably to Stan and Ern, as Tom beckoned Fudge towards the passage that led from the bar.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Bye, Neville!’ called Stan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge marched Harry along the narrow passage after Tom’s lantern, and then into a small parlour. Tom clicked his fingers, a fire burst into life in the grate, and he bowed himself out of the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sit down, Harry,’ said Fudge, indicating a chair by the fire.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sat down, feeling goosebumps rising up his arms despite the glow of the fire. Fudge took off his pinstriped cloak and tossed it aside, then hitched up the trousers of his bottle-green suit and sat down opposite Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I am Cornelius Fudge, Harry. The Minister for Magic.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry already knew this, of course; he had seen Fudge once before, but as he had been wearing his father’s Invisibility Cloak at the time, Fudge wasn’t to know that.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Tom the innkeeper reappeared, wearing an apron over his nightshirt and bearing a tray of tea and crumpets. He placed the tray on a table between Fudge and Harry, and left the parlour, closing the door behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Harry,’ said Fudge, pouring out tea, ‘you’ve had us all in a right flap, I don’t mind telling you. Running away from your aunt and uncle’s house like that! I’d started to think … but you’re safe, and that’s what matters.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge buttered himself a crumpet and pushed the plate towards Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Eat, Harry, you look dead on your feet. Now then … You will be pleased to hear that we have dealt with the unfortunate blowing-up of Miss Marjorie Dursley. Two members of the Accidental Magic Reversal Department were dispatched to Privet Drive a few hours ago. Miss Dursley has been punctured and her memory has been modified. She has no recollection of the incident at all. So that’s that, and no harm done.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge smiled at Harry over the rim of his teacup, rather like an uncle surveying a favourite nephew. Harry, who couldn’t believe his ears, opened his mouth to speak, couldn’t think of anything to say, and closed it again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, you’re worrying about the reaction of your aunt and uncle?’ said Fudge. ‘Well, I won’t deny that they are extremely angry, Harry, but they are prepared to take you back next summer as long as you stay at Hogwarts for the Christmas and Easter holidays.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry unstuck his throat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I always stay at Hogwarts for the Christmas and Easter holidays,’ he said, ‘and I don’t ever want to go back to Privet Drive.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, now, I’m sure you’ll feel differently once you’ve calmed down,’ said Fudge in a worried tone. ‘They are your family, after all, and I’m sure you are fond of each other – er – very deep down.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It didn’t occur to Harry to put Fudge right. He was still waiting to hear what was going to happen to him now.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So all that remains,’ said Fudge, now buttering himself a second crumpet, ‘is to decide where you’re going to spend the last two weeks of your holidays. I suggest you take a room here at the Leaky Cauldron and –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hang on,’ blurted Harry, ‘what about my punishment?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge blinked.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Punishment?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I broke the law!’ Harry said. ‘The Decree for the Restriction of Underage Wizardry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, my dear boy, we’re not going to punish you for a little thing like that!’ cried Fudge, waving his crumpet impatiently. ‘It was an accident! We don’t send people to Azkaban just for blowing up their aunts!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But this didn’t tally at all with Harry’s past dealings with the Ministry of Magic.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Last year, I got an official warning just because a house-elf smashed a pudding in my uncle’s house!’ said Harry, frowning. ‘The Ministry of Magic said I’d be expelled from Hogwarts if there was any more magic there!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Unless Harry’s eyes were deceiving him, Fudge was suddenly looking awkward.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Circumstances change, Harry … we have to take into account … in the present climate … surely you don’t want to be expelled?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course I don’t,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well then, what’s all the fuss about?’ laughed Fudge airily. ‘Now, have a crumpet, Harry, while I go and see if Tom’s got a room for you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge strode out of the parlour and Harry stared after him. There was something extremely odd going on. Why had Fudge been waiting for him at the Leaky Cauldron, if not to punish him for what he’d done. And now Harry came to think of it, surely it wasn’t usual for the Minister for Magic himself to get involved in matters of underage magic?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge came back, accompanied by Tom the innkeeper.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Room eleven’s free, Harry,’ said Fudge. ‘I think you’ll be very comfortable. Just one thing, and I’m sure you’ll understand: I don’t want you wandering off into Muggle London, all right? Keep to Diagon Alley. And you’re to be back here before dark each night. Sure you’ll understand. Tom will be keeping an eye on you for me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OK,’ said Harry slowly, ‘but why –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t want to lose you again, do we?’ said Fudge with a hearty laugh. ‘No, no … best we know where you are … I mean …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge cleared his throat loudly and picked up his pinstriped cloak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’ll be off, plenty to do, you know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Have you had any luck with Black yet?’ Harry asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge’s fingers slipped on the silver fastenings of his cloak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s that? Oh, you’ve heard – well, no, not yet, but it’s only a matter of time. The Azkaban guards have never yet failed … and they are angrier than I’ve ever seen them.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge shuddered slightly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So, I’ll say goodbye.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He held out his hand and Harry, shaking it, had a sudden idea.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Er – Minister? Can I ask you something?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Certainly’ smiled Fudge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, third years at Hogwarts are allowed to visit Hogsmeade, but my aunt and uncle didn’t sign the permission form. D’you think you could?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge was looking uncomfortable.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ he said. ‘No. No, I’m very sorry, Harry, but as I’m not your parent or guardian –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But you’re the Minister for Magic,’ said Harry eagerly. ‘If you gave me permission –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I’m sorry, Harry, but rules are rules,’ said Fudge flatly. ‘Perhaps you’ll be able to visit Hogsmeade next year. In fact, I think it best if you don’t … yes … well, I’ll be off. Enjoy your stay, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And with a last smile and shake of Harry’s hand, Fudge left the room. Tom now moved forward, beaming at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘If you’ll follow me, Mr Potter,’ he said. ‘I’ve already taken your things up …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry followed Tom up a handsome wooden staircase to a door with a brass number eleven on it, which Tom unlocked and opened for him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Inside was a very comfortable-looking bed, some highly polished oak furniture, a cheerfully crackling fire and, perched on top of the wardrobe –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hedwig!’ Harry gasped.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The snowy owl clicked her break and fluttered down onto Harry’s arm.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Very smart owl you’ve got there,’ chuckled Tom. ‘Arrived about five minutes after you did. If there’s anything you need, Mr Potter, don’t hesitate to ask.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He gave another bow and left.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sat on his bed for a long time, absent-mindedly stroking Hedwig. The sky outside the window was changing rapidly from deep, velvety blue to cold, steely grey and then, slowly, to pink shot with gold. Harry could hardly believe that he’d only left Privet Drive a few hours ago, that he wasn’t expelled, and that he was now facing two completely Dursley-free weeks.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s been a very weird night, Hedwig,’ he yawned.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And without even removing his glasses, he slumped back onto his pillows and fell asleep.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It took Harry several days to get used to his strange new freedom. Never before had he been able to get up whenever he wanted or eat whatever he fancied. He could even go wherever he liked, as long as it was in Diagon Alley, and as this long cobbled street was packed with the most fascinating wizarding shops in the world, Harry felt no desire to break his word to Fudge and stray back into the Muggle world.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry ate breakfast each morning in the Leaky Cauldron, where he liked watching the other guests: funny little witches from the country, up for a day’s shopping; venerable-looking wizards arguing over the latest article in Transfiguration Today; wild-looking warlocks, raucous dwarfs and, once, what looked suspiciously like a hag, who ordered a plate of raw liver from behind a thick woollen balaclava.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: After breakfast Harry would go out into the back yard, take out his wand, tap the third brick from the left above the dustbin, and stand back as the archway into Diagon Alley opened in the wall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry spent the long sunny days exploring the shops and eating under the brightly coloured umbrellas outside cafes, where his fellow diners were showing each other their purchases (‘it’s a lunascope, old boy – no more messing around with moon charts, see?’) or else discussing the case of Sirius Black (‘personally I won’t let any of the children out alone until he’s back in Azkaban’). Harry didn’t have to do his homework under the blankets by torchlight any more; now he could sit in the bright sunshine outside Florean Fortescue’s Ice-Cream Parlour, finishing all his essays with occasional help from Florean Fortescue himself, who, apart from knowing a great deal about medieval witch-burnings, gave Harry free sundaes every half-hour.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Once Harry had refilled his money bag with gold Galleons, silver Sickles and bronze Knuts from his vault at Gringotts, he needed to exercise a lot of self-control not to spend the whole lot at once. He had to keep reminding himself that he had five years to go at Hogwarts, and how it would feel to ask the Dursleys for money for spellbooks, to stop himself buying a handsome set of solid gold Gobstones (a wizarding game rather like marbles, in which the stones squirted a nasty-smelling liquid into the other player’s face when they lost a point). He was sorely tempted, too, by the perfect, moving model of the galaxy in a large glass ball, which would have meant he never had to take another Astronomy lesson. But the thing that tested Harry’s resolution most appeared in his favourite shop, Quality Quidditch Supplies, a week after he’d arrived at the Leaky Cauldron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Curious to know what the crowd in the shop was staring at, Harry edged his way inside and squeezed in amongst the excited witches and wizards until he glimpsed a newly erected podium on which was mounted the most magnificent broom he had ever seen in his life.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Just come out … prototype …’ a square-jawed wizard was telling his companion.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s the fastest broom in the world, isn’t it, Dad?’ squeaked a boy younger than Harry, who was swinging off his father’s arm.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Irish International Side’s just put in an order for seven of these beauties!’ the proprietor of the shop told the crowd. ‘And they’re favourites for the World Cup!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A large witch in front of Harry moved, and he was able to read the sign next to the broom:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: THE FIREBOLT

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: This state-of-the-art racing broom sports a streamlined, superfine handle of ash, treated with a diamond-hard polish and hand-numbered with its own registration number. Each individually selected birch twig in the broomtail has been honed to aerodynamic perfection, giving the Firebolt unsurpassable balance and pinpoint precision. The Firebolt has an acceleration of 0-150 miles an hour in ten seconds and incorporates an unbreakable braking charm. Price on request.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Price on request … Harry didn’t like to think how much gold the Firebolt would cost. He had never wanted anything so much in his whole life – but he had never lost a Quidditch match on his Nimbus Two Thousand, and what was the point in emptying his Gringotts vault for the Firebolt, when he had a very good broom already? Harry didn’t ask for the price, but he returned, almost every day after that, just to look at the Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There were, however, things that Harry needed to buy. He went to the Apothecary to replenish his store of potions’ ingredients, and as his school robes were now several inches too short in the arm and leg, he visited Madam Malkin’s Robes for All Occasions and bought new ones. Most important of all, he had to buy his new school books, which would include those for his two new subjects, Care of Magical Creatures and Divination.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry got a surprise as he looked in at the bookshop window. Instead of the usual display of gold-embossed spellbooks the size of paving slabs, there was a large iron cage behind the glass which held about a hundred copies of The Monster Book of Monsters. Torn pages were flying everywhere as the books grappled with each other, locked together in furious wrestling matches and snapping aggressively.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
