text_content: Harry pulled his booklist out of his pocket and consulted it for the first time. The Monster Book of Monsters was listed as the set book for Care of Magical Creatures. Now Harry understood why Hagrid had said it would come in useful. He felt relieved; he had been wondering whether Hagrid wanted help with some terrifying new pet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As Harry entered Flourish and Blotts, the manager came hurrying towards him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hogwarts?’ he said abruptly. ‘Come to get your new books?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry. ‘I need –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Get out of the way,’ said the manager impatiently, brushing Harry aside. He drew on a pair of very thick gloves, picked up a large, knobbly walking stick and proceeded towards the door of the Monster books’ cage.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hang on,’ said Harry quickly, ‘I’ve already got one of those.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Have you?’ A look of enormous relief spread over the manager’s face. ‘Thank heavens for that, I’ve been bitten five times already this morning –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A loud ripping noise rent the air; two of the Monster books had seized a third and were pulling it apart.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Stop it! Stop it!’ cried the manager, poking the walking stick through the bars and knocking the books apart. ‘I’m never stocking them again, never! It’s been bedlam! I thought we’d seen the worst when we bought two hundred copies of The Invisible Book of Invisibility – cost a fortune, and we never found them … Well, is there anything else I can help you with?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry, looking down his booklist. ‘I need Unfogging the Future, by Cassandra Vablatsky.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, starting Divination, are you?’ said the manager stripping off his gloves and leading Harry into the back of the shop, where there was a corner devoted to fortune-telling. A small table was stacked with volumes such as Predicting the Unpredictable: Insulate Yourself against Shocks and Broken Balls: When Fortunes Turn Foul.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Here you are,’ said the manager, who had climbed a set of steps to take down a thick, black-bound book. ‘Unfogging the Future. Very good guide to all your basic fortune-telling methods – palmistry, crystal balls, bird entrails …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Harry wasn’t listening. His eyes had fallen on another book, which was among a display on a small table: Death Omens: What to Do When You Know the Worst is Coming.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I wouldn’t read that if I were you,’ said the assistant lightly, looking to see what Harry was staring at. ‘You’ll start seeing death omens everywhere, it’s enough to frighten anyone to death.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Harry continued to stare at the front cover of the book; it showed a black dog large as a bear, with gleaming eyes. It looked oddly familiar …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The assistant pressed Unfogging the Future into Harry’s hands.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Anything else?’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry, tearing his eyes away from the dog’s and dazedly consulting his booklist. ‘Er – I need Intermediate Transfiguration and The Standard Book of Spells, Grade Three.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry emerged from Flourish and Blotts ten minutes later with his new books under his arms, and made his way back to the Leaky Cauldron, hardly noticing where he was going and bumping into several people.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He tramped up the stairs to his room, went inside and tipped his books onto his bed. Somebody had been in to tidy; the windows were open and sun was pouring inside. Harry could hear the buses rolling by in the unseen Muggle street behind him, and the sound of the invisible crowd below in Diagon Alley. He caught sight of himself in the mirror over the basin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It can’t have been a death omen,’ he told his reflection defiantly. ‘I was panicking when I saw that thing in Magnolia Crescent. It was probably just a stray dog …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He raised his hand automatically and tried to make his hair lie flat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re fighting a losing battle there, dear,’ said his mirror in a wheezy voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As the days slipped by, Harry started looking wherever he went for a sign of Ron or Hermione. Plenty of Hogwarts students were arriving in Diagon Alley now, with the start of term so near. Harry met Seamus Finnigan and Dean Thomas, his fellow Gryffindors, in Quality Quidditch Supplies, where they, too, were ogling the Firebolt; he also ran into the real Neville Longbottom, a round-faced, forgetful boy, outside Flourish and Blotts. Harry didn’t stop to chat; Neville appeared to have mislaid his booklist, and was being told off by his very formidable-looking grandmother. Harry hoped she never found out that he’d pretended to be Neville while on the run from the Ministry of Magic.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry woke on the last day of the holidays, thinking that he would at least meet Ron and Hermione tomorrow, on the Hogwarts Express. He got up, dressed, went for a last look at the Firebolt, and was just wondering where he’d have lunch, when someone yelled his name and he turned.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry! HARRY!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They were there, both of them, sitting outside Florean Fortescue’s Ice-Cream Parlour; Ron looking incredibly freckly Hermione very brown, both waving frantically at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Finally!’ said Ron, grinning at Harry as he sat down. ‘We went to the Leaky Cauldron, but they said you’d left, and we went to Flourish and Blotts, and Madam Malkin’s, and –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I got all my school stuff last week,’ Harry explained. ‘And how come you know I’m staying at the Leaky Cauldron?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dad,’ said Ron simply.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley who worked at the Ministry of Magic, would of course have heard the whole story of what had happened to Aunt Marge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you really blow up your aunt, Harry?’ said Hermione in a very serious voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I didn’t mean to,’ said Harry, while Ron roared with laughter. ‘I just – lost control.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not funny, Ron,’ said Hermione sharply. ‘Honestly I’m amazed Harry wasn’t expelled.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So am I,’ admitted Harry. ‘Forget expelled, I thought I was going to be arrested.’ He looked at Ron. ‘Your dad doesn’t know why Fudge let me off, does he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Probably ’cause it’s you, isn’t it?’ shrugged Ron, still chuckling. ‘Famous Harry Potter and all that. I’d hate to see what the Ministry’d do to me if I blew up an aunt. Mind you, they’d have to dig me up first, because Mum would’ve killed me. Anyway, you can ask Dad yourself this evening. We’re staying at the Leaky Cauldron tonight, too! So you can come to King’s Cross with us tomorrow! Hermione’s there as well!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione nodded, beaming. ‘Mum and Dad dropped me off this morning with all my Hogwarts things.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Excellent!’ said Harry happily. ‘So, have you got all your new books and stuff?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Look at this,’ said Ron, pulling a long thin box out of a bag and opening it. ‘Brand-new wand. Fourteen inches, willow, containing one unicorn tail-hair. And we’ve got all our books’ – he pointed at a large bag under his chair. ‘What about those Monster books, eh? The assistant nearly cried when we said we wanted two.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s all that, Hermione?’ Harry asked, pointing at not one, but three, bulging bags in the chair next to her.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’m taking more new subjects than you, aren’t I?’ said Hermione. ‘Those are my books for Arithmancy, Care of Magical Creatures, Divination, the Study of Ancient Runes, Muggle Studies –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What are you doing Muggle Studies for?’ said Ron, rolling his eyes at Harry. ‘You’re Muggle-born! Your mum and dad are Muggles! You already know all about Muggles!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But it’ll be fascinating to study them from the wizarding point of view,’ said Hermione earnestly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you planning to eat or sleep at all this year, Hermione?’ asked Harry, while Ron sniggered. Hermione ignored them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve still got ten Galleons,’ she said, checking her purse. ‘It’s my birthday in September, and Mum and Dad gave me some money to get myself an early birthday present.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How about a nice book?’ said Ron innocently.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I don’t think so,’ said Hermione composedly. ‘I really want an owl. I mean, Harry’s got Hedwig and you’ve got Errol –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I haven’t,’ said Ron. ‘Errol’s a family owl. All I’ve got is Scabbers.’ He pulled his pet rat out of his pocket. ‘And I want to get him checked over,’ he added, placing Scabbers on the table in front of them. ‘I don’t think Egypt agreed with him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Scabbers was looking thinner than usual, and there was a definite droop to his whiskers.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s a magical-creature shop just over there,’ said Harry, who knew Diagon Alley very well by now. ‘You can see if they’ve got anything for Scabbers, and Hermione can get her owl.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: So they paid for their ice-creams and crossed the street to the Magical Menagerie.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There wasn’t much room inside. Every inch of wall was hidden by cages. It was smelly and very noisy because the occupants of these cages were all squeaking, squawking, jabbering or hissing. The witch behind the counter was already advising a wizard on the care of double-ended newts, so Harry, Ron and Hermione waited, examining the cages.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A pair of enormous purple toads sat gulping wetly and feasting on dead blowflies. A gigantic tortoise with a jewel-encrusted shell was glittering near the window. Poisonous orange snails were oozing slowly up the side of their glass tank, and a fat white rabbit kept changing into a silk top hat and back again with a loud popping noise. Then there were cats of every colour, a noisy cage of ravens, a basket of funny custard-coloured furballs that were humming loudly, and, on the counter, a vast cage of sleek black rats which were playing some sort of skipping game using their long bald tails.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The double-ended newt wizard left and Ron approached the counter.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s my rat,’ he told the witch. ‘He’s been a bit off-colour ever since I brought him back from Egypt.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Bang him on the counter,’ said the witch, pulling a pair of heavy black spectacles out of her pocket.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron lifted Scabbers out of his inside pocket and placed him next to the cage of his fellow rats, who stopped their skipping tricks and scuffled to the wire for a better look.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Like nearly everything Ron owned, Scabbers the rat was secondhand (he had once belonged to Ron’s brother Percy) and a bit battered. Next to the glossy rats in the cage, he looked especially woebegone.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hm,’ said the witch, picking Scabbers up. ‘How old is this rat?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dunno,’ said Ron. ‘Quite old. He used to belong to my brother.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What powers does he have?’ said the witch, examining Scabbers closely.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Er –’ said Ron. The truth was that Scabbers had never shown the faintest trace of interesting powers. The witch’s eyes moved from Scabbers’s tattered left ear to his front paw, which had a toe missing, and tutted loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s been through the mill, this one,’ she said.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He was like that when Percy gave him to me,’ said Ron defensively.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘An ordinary, common or garden rat like this can’t be expected to live longer than three years or so,’ said the witch. ‘Now, if you were looking for something a bit more hard-wearing, you might like one of these …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: She indicated the black rats, who promptly started skipping again. Ron muttered, ‘Show-offs.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, if you don’t want a replacement, you can try this Rat Tonic,’ said the witch, reaching under the counter and bringing out a small red bottle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OK,’ said Ron. ‘How much – OUCH!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron buckled as something huge and orange came soaring from the top of the highest cage, landed on his head and then propelled itself, spitting madly, at Scabbers.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘NO, CROOKSHANKS, NO!’ cried the witch, but Scabbers shot from between her hands like a bar of soap, landed splay-legged on the floor and then scarpered for the door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Scabbers!’ Ron shouted, haring out of the shop after him; Harry followed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It took them nearly ten minutes to find Scabbers, who had taken refuge under a wastepaper bin outside Quality Quidditch Supplies. Ron stuffed the trembling rat back into his pocket and straightened up, massaging his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What was that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It was either a very big cat or quite a small tiger,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Where’s Hermione?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Probably getting her owl.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They made their way back up the crowded street to the Magical Menagerie. As they reached it, Hermione came out, but she wasn’t carrying an owl. Her arms were clamped tightly around the enormous ginger cat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You bought that monster?’ said Ron, his mouth hanging open.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s gorgeous, isn’t he?’ said Hermione, glowing.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: That was a matter of opinion, thought Harry. The cat’s ginger fur was thick and fluffy, but it was definitely a bit bow-legged and its face looked grumpy and oddly squashed, as though it had run headlong into a brick wall. Now that Scabbers was out of sight, however, the cat was purring contentedly in Hermione’s arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione, that thing nearly scalped me!’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He didn’t mean to, did you, Crookshanks?’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And what about Scabbers?’ said Ron, pointing at the lump in his chest pocket. ‘He needs rest and relaxation! How’s he going to get it with that thing around?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That reminds me, you forgot your Rat Tonic,’ said Hermione, slapping the small red bottle into Ron’s hand. ‘And stop worrying, Crookshanks will be sleeping in my dormitory and Scabbers in yours. What’s the problem? Poor Crookshanks, that witch said he’d been in there for ages: no one wanted him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I wonder why,’ said Ron sarcastically, as they set off towards the Leaky Cauldron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They found Mr Weasley sitting in the bar, reading the Daily Prophet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ he said, smiling as he looked up. ‘How are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Fine, thanks,’ said Harry, as he, Ron and Hermione joined Mr Weasley with all their shopping.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley put down his paper, and Harry saw the now familiar picture of Sirius Black staring up at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They still haven’t caught him, then?’ he asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Mr Weasley, looking extremely grave. ‘They’ve pulled us all off our regular jobs at the Ministry to try and find him, but no luck so far.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Would we get a reward if we caught him?’ asked Ron. ‘It’d be good to get some more money –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be ridiculous, Ron,’ said Mr Weasley, who on closer inspection looked very strained. ‘Black’s not going to be caught by a thirteen-year-old wizard. It’s the Azkaban guards who’ll get him back, you mark my words.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: At that moment Mrs Weasley entered the bar, laden with shopping and followed by the twins, Fred and George, who were about to start their fifth year at Hogwarts, the newly elected Head Boy, Percy, and the Weasleys’ youngest child and only girl, Ginny.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ginny who had always been very taken with Harry, seemed even more heartily embarrassed than usual when she saw him, perhaps because he had saved her life during their last term at Hogwarts. She went very red and muttered ‘hello’ without looking at him. Percy, however, held out his hand solemnly as though he and Harry had never met and said, ‘Harry. How nice to see you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello, Percy,’ said Harry, trying not to laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I hope you’re well?’ said Percy pompously shaking hands. It was rather like being introduced to the mayor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Very well, thanks –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ said Fred, elbowing Percy out of the way and bowing deeply. ‘Simply splendid to see you, old boy –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Marvellous,’ said George, pushing Fred aside and seizing Harry’s hand in turn. ‘Absolutely spiffing.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Percy scowled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s enough, now,’ said Mrs Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mum!’ said Fred, as though he’d only just spotted her, and seized her hand, too. ‘How really corking to see you –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I said, that’s enough,’ said Mrs Weasley, depositing her shopping in an empty chair. ‘Hello, Harry, dear. I suppose you’ve heard our exciting news?’ She pointed at the brand-new silver badge on Percy’s chest. ‘Second Head Boy in the family!’ she said, swelling with pride.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And last,’ Fred muttered under his breath.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t doubt that,’ said Mrs Weasley, frowning suddenly. ‘I notice they haven’t made you two prefects.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What do we want to be prefects for?’ said George, looking revolted at the very idea. ‘It’d take all the fun out of life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ginny giggled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You want to set a better example to your sister!’ snapped Mrs Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ginny’s got other brothers to set her an example, Mother,’ said Percy loftily. ‘I’m going up to change for dinner …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He disappeared and George heaved a sigh.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We tried to shut him in a pyramid,’ he told Harry. ‘But Mum spotted us.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dinner that night was a very enjoyable affair. Tom the innkeeper put three tables together in the parlour and the seven Weasleys, Harry and Hermione ate their way through five delicious courses.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How’re we getting to King’s Cross tomorrow, Dad?’ asked Fred, as they tucked into a sumptuous chocolate pudding.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The Ministry’s providing a couple of cars,’ said Mr Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Everyone looked up at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Why?’ said Percy curiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s because of you, Perce,’ said George seriously. ‘And there’ll be little flags on the bonnets, with HB on them –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘– for Humungous Bighead,’ said Fred.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Everyone except Percy and Mrs Weasley snorted into their pudding.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Why are the Ministry providing cars, Father?’ Percy asked again, in a dignified voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, as we haven’t got one any more,’ said Mr Weasley, ‘and as I work there, they’re doing me a favour …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: His voice was casual, but Harry couldn’t help noticing that Mr Weasley’s ears had gone red, just like Ron’s did when he was under pressure.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Good job too,’ said Mrs Weasley briskly. ‘Do you realise how much luggage you’ve all got between you? A nice sight you’d be on the Muggle Underground … You are all packed, aren’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron hasn’t put all his new things in his trunk yet,’ said Percy, in a long-suffering voice. ‘He’s dumped them on my bed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’d better go and pack properly, Ron, because we won’t have much time in the morning,’ Mrs Weasley called down the table. Ron scowled at Percy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: After dinner everyone felt very full and sleepy. One by one they made their way upstairs to their rooms to check their things for the next day. Ron and Percy were next door to Harry. He had just closed and locked his own trunk when he heard angry voices through the wall, and went to see what was going on.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The door of number twelve was ajar and Percy was shouting.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It was here, on the bedside table, I took it off for polishing –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I haven’t touched it, all right?’ Ron roared back.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s up?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘My Head Boy badge has gone,’ said Percy, rounding on Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So’s Scabbers’ Rat Tonic,’ said Ron, throwing things out of his trunk to look. ‘I think I might’ve left it in the bar –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re not going anywhere till you’ve found my badge!’ yelled Percy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll get Scabbers’ stuff, I’m packed,’ Harry said to Ron, and he went downstairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was halfway along the passage to the bar, which was now very dark, when he heard another pair of angry voices coming from the parlour. A second later, he recognised them as Mr and Mrs Weasley’s. He hesitated, not wanting them to know he’d heard them rowing, when the sound of his own name made him stop, then move closer to the parlour door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘… makes no sense not to tell him,’ Mr Weasley was saying heatedly. ‘Harry’s got a right to know. I’ve tried to tell Fudge, but he insists on treating Harry like a child. He’s thirteen years old and –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Arthur, the truth would terrify him!’ said Mrs Weasley shrilly. ‘Do you really want to send Harry back to school with that hanging over him? For heaven’s sake, he’s happy not knowing!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t want to make him miserable, I want to put him on his guard!’ retorted Mr Weasley. ‘You know what Harry and Ron are like, wandering off by themselves – they’ve ended up in the Forbidden Forest twice! But Harry mustn’t do that this year! When I think what could have happened to him that night he ran away from home! If the Knight Bus hadn’t picked him up, I’m prepared to bet he would have been dead before the Ministry found him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But he’s not dead, he’s fine, so what’s the point –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Molly they say Sirius Black’s mad, and maybe he is, but he was clever enough to escape from Azkaban, and that’s supposed to be impossible. It’s been three weeks, and no one’s seen hide nor hair of him, and I don’t care what Fudge keeps telling the Daily Prophet, we’re no nearer catching Black than inventing self-spelling wands. The only thing we know for sure is what Black’s after –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But Harry will be perfectly safe at Hogwarts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We thought Azkaban was perfectly safe. If Black can break out of Azkaban, he can break into Hogwarts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But no one’s really sure that Black’s after Harry –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a thud on wood, and Harry was sure Mr Weasley had banged his fist on the table.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Molly, how many times do I have to tell you? They didn’t report it in the press because Fudge wanted it kept quiet, but Fudge went out to Azkaban the night Black escaped. The guards told Fudge that Black’s been talking in his sleep for a while now. Always the same words: ‘He’s at Hogwarts … he’s at Hogwarts.’ Black is deranged, Molly, and he wants Harry dead. If you ask me, he thinks murdering Harry will bring You-Know-Who back to power. Black lost everything the night Harry stopped You-Know-Who, and he’s had twelve years alone in Azkaban to brood on that …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a silence. Harry leaned still closer to the door, desperate to hear more.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Arthur, you must do what you think is right. But you’re forgetting Albus Dumbledore. I don’t think anything could hurt Harry at Hogwarts while Dumbledore’s Headmaster. I suppose he knows about all this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course he knows. We had to ask him if he minds the Azkaban guards stationing themselves around the entrances to the school grounds. He wasn’t happy about it, but he agreed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not happy? Why shouldn’t he be happy, if they’re there to catch Black?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore isn’t fond of the Azkaban guards,’ said Mr Weasley heavily. ‘Nor am I, if it comes to that … but when you’re dealing with a wizard like Black, you sometimes have to join forces with those you’d rather avoid.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘If they save Harry –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘– then I will never say another word against them,’ said Mr Weasley wearily. ‘It’s late, Molly, we’d better go up …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry heard chairs move. As quietly as he could, he hurried down the passage to the bar and out of sight. The parlour door opened, and a few seconds later footsteps told him that Mr and Mrs Weasley were climbing the stairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The bottle of rat tonic was lying under the table they had sat at earlier. Harry waited until he heard Mr and Mrs Weasley’s bedroom door close, then headed back upstairs with the bottle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fred and George were crouching in the shadows on the landing, heaving with laughter as they listened to Percy dismantling his and Ron’s room in the search for his badge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ve got it,’ Fred whispered to Harry. ‘We’ve been improving it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The badge now read Bighead Boy, Harry forced a laugh, went to give Ron the rat tonic, then shut himself in his room and lay down on his bed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: So Sirius Black was after him. That explained everything. Fudge had been lenient with him because he was so relieved to find him alive. He’d made Harry promise to stay in Diagon Alley where there were plenty of wizards to keep an eye on him. And he was sending two Ministry cars to take them all to the station tomorrow, so that the Weasleys could look after Harry until he was on the train.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry lay listening to the muffled shouting next door and wondered why he didn’t feel more scared. Sirius Black had murdered thirteen people with one curse; Mr and Mrs Weasley obviously thought Harry would be panic-stricken if he knew the truth. But Harry happened to agree whole-heartedly with Mrs Weasley that the safest place on earth was wherever Albus Dumbledore happened to be. Didn’t people always say that Dumbledore was the only person Lord Voldemort had ever been afraid of? Surely Black, as Voldemort’s right-hand man, would be just as frightened of him?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then there were these Azkaban guards everyone kept talking about. They seemed to scare most people senseless, and if they were stationed all around the school, Black’s chances of getting inside seemed very remote.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: No, all in all, the thing that bothered Harry most was the fact that his chances of visiting Hogsmeade now looked like zero. Nobody would want Harry to leave the safety of the castle until Black was caught; in fact, Harry suspected his every move would be carefully watched until the danger had passed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He scowled at the dark ceiling. Did they think he couldn’t look after himself? He’d escaped Lord Voldemort three times, he wasn’t completely useless …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Unbidden, the image of the beast in the shadows of Magnolia Crescent crossed his mind. What to do when you know the worst is coming …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not going to be murdered,’ Harry said out loud.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the spirit, dear,’ said his mirror sleepily.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Tom woke Harry next morning with his usual toothless grin and a cup of tea. Harry got dressed and was just persuading a disgruntled Hedwig to get back into her cage when Ron banged his way into the room, pulling a sweatshirt over his head and looking irritable.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The sooner we get on the train, the better,’ he said. ‘At least I can get away from Percy at Hogwarts. Now he’s accusing me of dripping tea on his photo of Penelope Clearwater. You know,’ Ron grimaced, ‘his girlfriend. She’s hidden her face under the frame because her nose has gone all blotchy …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve got something to tell you,’ Harry began, but they were interrupted by Fred and George, who had looked in to congratulate Ron on infuriating Percy again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They headed down to breakfast, where Mr Weasley was reading the front page of the Daily Prophet with a furrowed brow and Mrs Weasley was telling Hermione and Ginny about a Love Potion she’d made as a young girl. All three of them were rather giggly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What were you saying?’ Ron asked Harry, as they sat down.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Later,’ Harry muttered, as Percy stormed in.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had no chance to speak to Ron or Hermione in the chaos of leaving; they were too busy heaving all their trunks down the Leaky Cauldron’s narrow staircase and piling them up near the door, with Hedwig and Hermes, Percy’s screech owl, perched on top in their cages. A small wickerwork basket stood beside the heap of trunks, spitting loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s all right, Crookshanks,’ Hermione cooed through the wickerwork, ‘I’ll let you out on the train.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You won’t,’ snapped Ron. ‘What about poor Scabbers, eh?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He pointed at his chest, where a large lump indicated that Scabbers was curled up in his pocket.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley, who had been outside waiting for the Ministry cars, stuck his head inside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re here,’ he said. ‘Harry, come on.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley marched Harry across the short stretch of pavement towards the first of two old-fashioned dark green cars, each of which was driven by a furtive-looking wizard, wearing a suit of emerald velvet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘In you get, Harry,’ said Mr Weasley, glancing up and down the crowded street.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry got into the back of the car, and was shortly joined by Hermione, Ron and, to Ron’s disgust, Percy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The journey to King’s Cross was very uneventful compared to Harry’s trip on the Knight Bus. The Ministry of Magic cars seemed almost ordinary, though Harry noticed that they could slide through gaps that Uncle Vernon’s new company car certainly couldn’t have managed. They reached King’s Cross with twenty minutes to spare; the Ministry drivers found them trolleys, unloaded their trunks, touched their hats to Mr Weasley and drove away, somehow managing to jump to the head of an unmoving queue for the traffic lights.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley kept close to Harry’s elbow all the way into the station.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Right then,’ he said, glancing around them. ‘Let’s do this in pairs, as there are so many of us. I’ll go through first with Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley strolled towards the barrier between platforms nine and ten, pushing Harry’s trolley and apparently very interested in the InterCity 125 that had just arrived at platform nine. With a meaningful look at Harry, he leaned casually against the barrier. Harry imitated him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Next moment, they had fallen sideways through the solid metal onto platform nine and three-quarters and looked up to see the Hogwarts Express, a scarlet steam engine, puffing smoke over a platform packed with witches and wizards seeing their children onto the train.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Percy and Ginny suddenly appeared behind Harry. They were panting, and had apparently taken the barrier at a run.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, there’s Penelope!’ said Percy, smoothing his hair and going pink again. Ginny caught Harry’s eye and they both turned away to hide their laughter as Percy strode over to a girl with long, curly hair, walking with his chest thrown out so that she couldn’t miss his shiny badge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Once the remaining Weasleys and Hermione had joined them, Harry and Mr Weasley led the way to the end of the train, past packed compartments, to a carriage that looked quite empty. They loaded the trunks onto it, stowed Hedwig and Crookshanks in the luggage rack, then went back outside to say goodbye to Mr and Mrs Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mrs Weasley kissed all her children, then Hermione, and finally, Harry. He was embarrassed, but really quite pleased, when she gave him an extra hug.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Do take care, won’t you, Harry?’ she said as she straightened up, her eyes oddly bright. Then she opened her enormous handbag and said, ‘I’ve made you all sandwiches. Here you are, Ron … no, they’re not corned beef … Fred? Where’s Fred? Here you are, dear …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry,’ said Mr Weasley quietly, ‘come over here a moment.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He jerked his head towards a pillar, and Harry followed him behind it, leaving the others crowded around Mrs Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s something I’ve got to tell you before you leave –’ said Mr Weasley, in a tense voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s all right, Mr Weasley,’ said Harry, ‘I already know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You know? How could you know?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I – er – I heard you and Mrs Weasley talking last night. I couldn’t help hearing,’ Harry added quickly. ‘Sorry –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s not the way I’d have chosen for you to find out,’ said Mr Weasley, looking anxious.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No – honestly, it’s OK. This way, you haven’t broken your word to Fudge and I know what’s going on.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, you must be very scared –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not,’ said Harry sincerely. ‘Really,’ he added, because Mr Weasley was looking disbelieving. ‘I’m not trying to be a hero, but seriously, Sirius Black can’t be worse than Voldemort, can he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley flinched at the sound of the name, but overlooked it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, I knew you were, well, made of stronger stuff than Fudge seems to think, and I’m obviously pleased that you’re not scared, but –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Arthur!’ called Mrs Weasley, who was now shepherding the rest onto the train. ‘Arthur, what are you doing? It’s about to go!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s coming, Molly!’ said Mr Weasley, but he turned back to Harry and kept talking in a lower and more hurried voice. ‘Listen, I want you to give me your word –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘– that I’ll be a good boy and stay in the castle?’ said Harry gloomily.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not entirely’ said Mr Weasley, who looked more serious than Harry had ever seen him. ‘Harry, swear to me you won’t go looking for Black.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stared. ‘What?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a loud whistle. Guards were walking along the train, slamming all the doors shut.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘But Hogsmeade’s a very interesting place, isn’t it?’ Hermione pressed on eagerly. ‘In Sites of Historical Sorcery it says the inn was the headquarters for the 1612 goblin rebellion, and the Shrieking Shack’s supposed to be the most severely haunted building in Britain –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘– and massive sherbert balls that make you levitate a few inches off the ground while you’re sucking them,’ said Ron, who was plainly not listening to a word Hermione was saying.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked around at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Won’t it be nice to get out of school for a bit and explore Hogsmeade?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Spect it will,’ said Harry heavily. ‘You’ll have to tell me when you’ve found out.’

text_content: ‘What d’you mean?’ said Ron.

text_content: Ron looked horrified.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But if we’re with him,’ said Ron spiritedly to Hermione, ‘Black wouldn’t dare –’

text_content: ‘Oh, Ron, don’t talk rubbish,’ snapped Hermione. ‘Black’s already murdered a whole bunch of people in the middle of a crowded street, do you really think he’s going to worry about attacking Harry just because we’re there?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: She was fumbling with the straps of Crookshanks’ basket as she spoke.

text_content: ‘Get out of it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron was about to answer back when Professor Lupin stirred. They watched him apprehensively, but he simply turned his head the other way, mouth slightly open, and slept on.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Hogwarts Express moved steadily north and the scenery outside the window became wilder and darker while the clouds overhead thickened. People were chasing backwards and forwards past the door of their compartment. Crookshanks had now settled in an empty seat, his squashed face turned towards Ron, his yellow eyes on Ron’s top pocket.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: At one o’clock the plump witch with the food trolley arrived at the compartment door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you think we should wake him up?’ Ron asked awkwardly, nodding towards Professor Lupin. ‘He looks like he could do with some food.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione approached Professor Lupin cautiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Er – Professor?’ she said. ‘Excuse me – Professor?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He didn’t move.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t worry, dear,’ said the witch, as she handed Harry a large stack of cauldron cakes. ‘If he’s hungry when he wakes, I’ll be up front with the driver.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I suppose he is asleep?’ said Ron quietly, as the witch slid the compartment door closed. ‘I mean – he hasn’t died, has he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, no, he’s breathing,’ whispered Hermione, taking the cauldron cake Harry passed her.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He might not be very good company, but Professor Lupin’s presence in their compartment had its uses. Mid-afternoon, just as it had started to rain, blurring the rolling hills outside the window, they heard footsteps in the corridor again, and their three least favourite people appeared at the door: Draco Malfoy, flanked by his cronies, Vincent Crabbe and Gregory Goyle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Draco Malfoy and Harry had been enemies ever since they had met on their very first train journey to Hogwarts. Malfoy, who had a pale, pointed, sneering face, was in Slytherin house; he played Seeker on the Slytherin Quidditch team, the same position that Harry played on the Gryffindor team. Crabbe and Goyle seemed to exist to do Malfoy’s bidding. They were both wide and muscly; Crabbe was the taller, with a pudding-basin haircut and a very thick neck; Goyle had short, bristly hair and long, gorilla arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, look who it is,’ said Malfoy in his usual lazy drawl, pulling open the compartment door. ‘Potty and the Weasel.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle chuckled trollishly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I heard your father finally got his hands on some gold this summer, Weasley,’ said Malfoy. ‘Did your mother die of shock?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron stood up so quickly he knocked Crookshanks’ basket to the floor. Professor Lupin gave a snort.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Who’s that?’ said Malfoy, taking an automatic step backwards as he spotted Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘New teacher,’ said Harry, who had got to his feet, too, in case he needed to hold Ron back. ‘What were you saying, Malfoy?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy’s pale eyes narrowed; he wasn’t fool enough to pick a fight right under a teacher’s nose.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘C’mon,’ he muttered resentfully to Crabbe and Goyle, and they disappeared.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron sat down again, Ron massaging his knuckles.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not going to take any rubbish from Malfoy this year,’ he said angrily. ‘I mean it. If he makes one more crack about my family, I’m going to get hold of his head and –’

text_content: Ron made a violent gesture in mid-air.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron,’ hissed Hermione, pointing at Professor Lupin, ‘be careful …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Professor Lupin was still fast asleep.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

The train rattled, the rain hammered, the wind roared, but still, Professor Lupin slept.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The words had hardly left him when the train started to slow down.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So why’re we stopping?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, who was nearest the door, got up to look into the corridor. All along the carriage, heads were sticking curiously out of their compartments.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s going on?’ said Ron’s voice from behind Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry felt his way back to his seat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you think we’ve broken down?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dunno …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Who’s that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Who’s that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Stay where you are,’ he said, in the same hoarse voice, and he got slowly to his feet with his handful of fire held out in front of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But the door slid slowly open before Lupin could reach it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Standing in the doorway, illuminated by the shivering flames in Lupin’s hand, was a cloaked figure that towered to the ceiling. Its face was completely hidden beneath its hood. Harry’s eyes darted downwards, and what he saw made his stomach contract. There was a hand protruding from the cloak and it was glistening, greyish, slimy-looking and scabbed, like something dead that had decayed in water …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was visible only for a split second. As though the creature beneath the cloak sensed Harry’s gaze, the hand was suddenly withdrawn into the folds of the black material.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then the thing beneath the hood, whatever it was, drew a long, slow, rattling breath, as though it was trying to suck something more than air from its surroundings.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: An intense cold swept over them all. Harry felt his own breath catch in his chest. The cold went deeper than his skin. It was inside his chest, it was inside his very heart …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry’s eyes rolled up into his head. He couldn’t see. He was drowning in cold. There was a rushing in his ears as though of water. He was being dragged downwards, the roaring growing louder …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then, from far away, he heard screaming, terrible, terrified, pleading screams. He wanted to help whoever it was, he tried to move his arms, but couldn’t … a thick white fog was swirling around him, inside him –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry! Harry! Are you all right?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Someone was slapping his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘W-what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry opened his eyes. There were lanterns above him, and the floor was shaking – the Hogwarts Express was moving again and the lights had come back on. He seemed to have slid out of his seat onto the floor. Ron and Hermione were kneeling next to him, and above them he could see Neville and Professor Lupin watching. Harry felt very sick; when he put up his hand to push his glasses back on, he felt cold sweat on his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione heaved him back onto his seat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you OK?’ Ron asked nervously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, looking quickly towards the door. The hooded creature had vanished. ‘What happened? Where’s that – that thing? Who screamed?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No one screamed,’ said Ron, more nervously still.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around the bright compartment. Ginny and Neville looked back at him, both very pale.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But I heard screaming –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A loud snap made them all jump. Professor Lupin was breaking an enormous slab of chocolate into pieces.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What was that thing?’ he asked Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He strolled past Harry and disappeared into the corridor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you sure you’re OK, Harry?’ said Hermione, watching Harry anxiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t get it … what happened?’ said Harry, wiping more sweat off his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well – that thing – the Dementor – stood there and looked around (I mean, I think it did, I couldn’t see its face) – and you – you –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought you were having a fit or something,’ said Ron, who still looked scared. ‘You went sort of rigid and fell out of your seat and started twitching –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And Professor Lupin stepped over you, and walked towards the Dementor, and pulled out his wand,’ said Hermione. ‘And he said, ‘None of us is hiding Sirius Black under our cloaks. Go.’ But the Dementor didn’t move, so Lupin muttered something, and a silvery thing shot out of his wand at it, and it turned round and sort of glided away …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It was horrible,’ said Neville, in a higher voice than usual. ‘Did you feel how cold it went when it came in?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ginny, who was huddled in her corner looking nearly as bad as Harry felt, gave a small sob; Hermione went over and put a comforting arm around her.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But didn’t any of you – fall off your seats?’ said Harry awkwardly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Ron, looking anxiously at Harry again. ‘Ginny was shaking like mad, though …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t understand. He felt weak and shivery, as though he was recovering from a bad bout of flu; he also felt the beginnings of shame. Why had he gone to pieces like that, when no one else had?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor Lupin had come back. He paused as he entered, looked around and said, with a small smile, ‘I haven’t poisoned that chocolate, you know …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry took a bite and to his great surprise felt warmth spread suddenly to the tips of his fingers and toes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ll be at Hogwarts in ten minutes,’ said Professor Lupin. ‘Are you all right, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t ask how Professor Lupin knew his name.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Fine,’ he muttered, embarrassed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They didn’t talk much during the remainder of the journey. At long last, the train stopped at Hogsmeade station, and there was a great scramble to get out; owls hooted, cats miaowed, and Neville’s pet toad croaked loudly from under his hat. It was freezing on the tiny platform; rain was driving down in icy sheets.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Firs’ years this way!’ called a familiar voice. Harry, Ron and Hermione turned and saw the gigantic outline of Hagrid at the other end of the platform, beckoning the terrified-looking new students forward for their traditional journey across the lake.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘All righ’, you three?’ Hagrid yelled over the heads of the crowd. They waved at him, but had no chance to speak to him because the mass of people around them was shunting them away along the platform. Harry, Ron and Hermione followed the rest of the school out onto a rough mud track, where at least a hundred stagecoaches awaited the remaining students, each pulled, Harry could only assume, by an invisible horse, because when they climbed inside one and shut the door, the coach set off all by itself, bumping and swaying in procession.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The coach smelled faintly of mould and straw. Harry felt better since the chocolate, but still weak. Ron and Hermione kept looking at him sideways, as though frightened he might collapse again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As the carriage trundled towards a pair of magnificent wrought-iron gates, flanked with stone columns topped with winged boars, Harry saw two more towering, hooded Dementors, standing guard on either side. A wave of cold sickness threatened to engulf him again; he leaned back into the lumpy seat and closed his eyes until they had passed through the gates. The carriage picked up speed on the long, sloping drive up to the castle; Hermione was leaning out of the tiny window, watching the many turrets and towers draw nearer. At last, the carriage swayed to a halt, and Hermione and Ron got out.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As Harry stepped down, a drawling, delighted voice sounded in his ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You fainted, Potter? Is Longbottom telling the truth? You actually fainted?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy elbowed past Hermione to block Harry’s way up the stone steps to the castle, his face gleeful and his pale eyes glinting maliciously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Shove off, Malfoy’ said Ron, whose jaw was clenched.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you faint as well, Weasley?’ said Malfoy loudly. ‘Did the scary old Dementor frighten you, too, Weasley?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Is there a problem?’ said a mild voice. Professor Lupin had just got out of the next carriage.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy gave Professor Lupin an insolent stare, which took in the patches on his robes and the dilapidated suitcase. With a tiny hint of sarcasm in his voice, he said, ‘Oh, no – er – Professor,’ then he smirked at Crabbe and Goyle, and led them up the steps into the castle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione prodded Ron in the back to make him hurry, and the three of them joined the crowd swarming up the steps, through the giant oak front doors, and into the cavernous Entrance Hall, which was lit with flaming torches and housed a magnificent marble staircase which led to the upper floors.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The door into the Great Hall stood open at the right; Harry followed the crowd towards it, but had barely glimpsed the enchanted ceiling, which was black and cloudy tonight, when a voice called, ‘Potter! Granger! I want to see you both!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione turned around, surprised. Professor McGonagall, Transfiguration teacher and head of Gryffindor house, was calling over the heads of the crowd. She was a stern-looking witch who wore her hair in a tight bun; her sharp eyes were framed with square spectacles. Harry fought his way over to her with a feeling of foreboding; Professor McGonagall had a way of making him feel he must have done something wrong.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s no need to look so worried – I just want a word in my office,’ she told them. ‘Move along there, Weasley.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron stared as Professor McGonagall ushered Harry and Hermione away from the chattering crowd; they accompanied her across the Entrance Hall, up the marble staircase and along a corridor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Once they were in her office, a small room with a large, welcoming fire, Professor McGonagall motioned Harry and Hermione to sit down. She settled herself behind her desk and said abruptly, ‘Professor Lupin sent an owl ahead to say that you were taken ill on the train, Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Before Harry could reply, there was a soft knock on the door and Madam Pomfrey the matron, came bustling in.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry felt himself going red in the face. It was bad enough that he’d passed out, or whatever he had done, without everyone making all this fuss.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m fine,’ he said. ‘I don’t need anything –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, it’s you, is it?’ said Madam Pomfrey, ignoring this and bending down to stare closely at him. ‘I suppose you’ve been doing something dangerous again?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It was a Dementor, Poppy,’ said Professor McGonagall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They exchanged a dark look and Madam Pomfrey clucked disapprovingly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Setting Dementors around a school,’ she muttered, pushing Harry’s hair back and feeling his forehead. ‘He won’t be the first one who collapses. Yes, he’s all clammy. Terrible things, they are, and the effect they have on people who are already delicate –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not delicate!’ said Harry crossly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course you’re not,’ said Madam Pomfrey absent-mindedly, now taking his pulse.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What does he need?’ said Professor McGonagall crisply. ‘Bed rest? Should he perhaps spend tonight in the hospital wing?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m fine!’ said Harry, jumping up. The idea of what Draco Malfoy would say if he had to go to the hospital wing was torture.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, he should have some chocolate, at the very least,’ said Madam Pomfrey, who was now trying to peer into Harry’s eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve already had some,’ said Harry. ‘Professor Lupin gave me some. He gave it to all of us.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did he, now?’ said Madam Pomfrey approvingly. ‘So we’ve finally got a Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher who knows his remedies.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you sure you feel all right, Potter?’ said Professor McGonagall sharply.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Very well. Kindly wait outside while I have a quick word with Miss Granger about her timetable, then we can go down to the feast together.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry went back into the corridor with Madam Pomfrey who left for the hospital wing, muttering to herself. He only had to wait a few minutes; then Hermione emerged looking very happy about something, followed by Professor McGonagall, and the three of them made their way back down the marble staircase to the Great Hall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was a sea of pointed black hats; each of the long house tables was lined with students, their faces glimmering by the light of thousands of candles, which were floating over the tables in midair. Professor Flitwick, who was a tiny little wizard with a shock of white hair, was carrying an ancient hat and a three-legged stool out of the hall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh,’ said Hermione softly, ‘we’ve missed the Sorting!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: New students at Hogwarts were sorted into houses by trying on the Sorting Hat, which shouted out the house they were best suited to (Gryffindor, Ravenclaw, Hufflepuff or Slytherin). Professor McGonagall strode off towards her empty seat at the staff table, and Harry and Hermione set off in the other direction, as quietly as possible, towards the Gryffindor table. People looked around at them as they passed along the back of the hall, and a few of them pointed at Harry. Had the story of him collapsing in front of the Dementor travelled that fast?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He and Hermione sat down on either side of Ron, who had saved them seats.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What was all that about?’ he muttered to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry started to explain in a whisper, but at that moment the Headmaster stood up to speak, and he broke off.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor Dumbledore, though very old, always gave an impression of great energy. He had several feet of long silver hair and beard, half-moon spectacles and an extremely crooked nose. He was often described as the greatest wizard of the age, but that wasn’t why Harry respected him. You couldn’t help trusting Albus Dumbledore, and as Harry watched him beaming around at the students, he felt really calm for the first time since the Dementor had entered the train compartment.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Welcome!’ said Dumbledore, the candlelight shimmering on his beard. ‘Welcome to another year at Hogwarts! I have a few things to say to you all, and as one of them is very serious, I think it best to get it out of the way before you become befuddled by our excellent feast …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore cleared his throat and continued. ‘As you will all be aware after their search of the Hogwarts Express, our school is presently playing host to some of the Dementors of Azkaban, who are here on Ministry of Magic business.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He paused, and Harry remembered what Mr Weasley had said about Dumbledore not being happy with the Dementors guarding the school.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They are stationed at every entrance to the grounds,’ Dumbledore continued, ‘and while they are with us, I must make it plain that nobody is to leave school without permission. Dementors are not to be fooled by tricks or disguises – or even Invisibility Cloaks,’ he added blandly, and Harry and Ron glanced at each other. ‘It is not in the nature of a Dementor to understand pleading or excuses. I therefore warn each and every one of you to give them no reason to harm you. I look to the Prefects, and our new Head Boy and Girl, to make sure that no student runs foul of the Dementors.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Percy, who was sitting a few seats along from Harry, puffed out his chest again and stared around impressively. Dumbledore paused again; he looked very seriously around the hall, and nobody moved or made a sound.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘On a happier note,’ he continued, ‘I am pleased to welcome two new teachers to our ranks this year.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Firstly, Professor Lupin, who has kindly consented to fill the post of Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was some scattered, rather unenthusiastic, applause. Only those who had been in the compartment on the train with Professor Lupin clapped hard, Harry among them. Professor Lupin looked particularly shabby next to all the other teachers in their best robes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Look at Snape!’ Ron hissed in Harry’s ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor Snape, the Potions master, was staring along the staff table at Professor Lupin. It was common knowledge that Snape wanted the Defence Against the Dark Arts job, but even Harry, who hated Snape, was startled at the expression twisting his thin, sallow face. It was beyond anger: it was loathing. Harry knew that expression only too well; it was the look Snape wore every time he set eyes on Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘As to our second new appointment,’ Dumbledore continued, as the lukewarm applause for Professor Lupin died away, ‘well, I am sorry to tell you that Professor Kettleburn, our Care of Magical Creatures teacher, retired at the end of last year in order to enjoy more time with his remaining limbs. However, I am delighted to say that his place will be filled by none other than Rubeus Hagrid, who has agreed to take on this teaching job in addition to his gamekeeping duties.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione stared at each other, stunned. Then they joined in with the applause, which was tumultuous at the Gryffindor table in particular. Harry leaned forward to see Hagrid, who was ruby red in the face and staring down at his enormous hands, his wide grin hidden in the tangle of his black beard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We should’ve known!’ Ron roared, pounding the table. ‘Who else would have set us a biting book?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione were the last to stop clapping, and as Professor Dumbledore started speaking again, they saw that Hagrid was wiping his eyes on the tablecloth.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I think that’s everything of importance,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Let the feast begin!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The golden plates and goblets before them filled suddenly with food and drink. Harry, suddenly ravenous, helped himself to everything he could reach and began to eat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was a delicious feast; the Hall echoed with talk, laughter and the clatter of knives and forks. Harry, Ron and Hermione, however, were eager for it to finish so that they could talk to Hagrid. They knew how much being made a teacher would mean to him. Hagrid wasn’t a fully qualified wizard; he had been expelled from Hogwarts in his third year, for a crime he had not committed. It had been Harry, Ron and Hermione who had cleared Hagrid’s name last year.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: At long last, when the last morsels of pumpkin tart had melted from the golden platters, Dumbledore gave the word that it was time for them all to go to bed, and they got their chance.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Congratulations, Hagrid!’ Hermione squealed, as they reached the teachers’ table.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘All down ter you three,’ said Hagrid, wiping his shining face on his napkin as he looked up at them. ‘Can’ believe it … great man, Dumbledore … came straight down to me hut after Professor Kettleburn said he’d had enough … it’s what I always wanted …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Overcome with emotion, he buried his face in his napkin, and Professor McGonagall shooed them away.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione joined the Gryffindors streaming up the marble staircase and, very tired now, along more corridors, up more and more stairs, to the hidden entrance to Gryffindor Tower. A large portrait of a fat lady in a pink dress asked them, ‘Password?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Coming through, coming through!’ Percy called from behind the crowd. ‘The new password’s Fortuna Major!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh no,’ said Neville Longbottom sadly. He always had trouble remembering the passwords.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Through the portrait hole and across the common room, the girls and boys divided towards their separate staircases. Harry climbed the spiral stairs with no thought in his head except how glad he was to be back. They reached their familiar, circular dormitory with its five four-poster beds and Harry, looking around, felt he was home at last.

As they passed, Malfoy did a ridiculous impression of a swooning fit and there was a roar of laughter.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘Ignore him,’ said Hermione, who was right behind Harry. ‘Just ignore him, it’s not worth it …’

text_content: Harry dropped into a seat at the Gryffindor table, next to George Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Nearly wet himself,’ said Fred, with a contemptuous glance at Malfoy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘I wasn’t too happy myself,’ said George. ‘They’re horrible things, those Dementors …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Sort of freeze your insides, don’t they?’ said Fred.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘You didn’t pass out, though, did you?’ said Harry in a low voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Anyway, we’ll see how happy Malfoy looks after our first Quidditch match,’ said Fred. ‘Gryffindor versus Slytherin, first game of the season, remember?’

text_content: The only time Harry and Malfoy had faced each other in a Quidditch match, Malfoy had definitely come off worse. Feeling slightly more cheerful, Harry helped himself to sausages and fried tomatoes.

chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves

text_content: ‘Well, then –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘But –’
