text_content: Just then, Hagrid entered the Great Hall. He was wearing his long moleskin overcoat and was absent-mindedly swinging a dead polecat from one enormous hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: He grinned broadly at them and headed off to the staff table, still swinging the polecat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘Wonder what he’s been getting ready?’ said Ron, a note of anxiety in his voice. The Hall was starting to empty as people headed off towards their first lesson. Ron checked his timetable.

text_content: ‘I think it’s this way,’ said Hermione, peering down the empty passage to the right.

text_content: Harry was watching the painting. A fat, dapple-grey pony had just ambled onto the grass and was grazing nonchalantly. Harry was used to the subjects of Hogwarts paintings moving around and leaving their frames to visit each other, but he always enjoyed watching them. A moment later, a short, squat knight in a suit of armour had clanked into the picture after his pony. By the look of the grass stains on his metal knees, he had just fallen off.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘Aha!’ he yelled, seeing Harry, Ron and Hermione. ‘What villains are these that trespass upon my private lands! Come to scorn at my fall, perchance? Draw, you knaves, you dogs!’

text_content: They watched in astonishment as the little knight tugged his sword out of its scabbard and began brandishing it violently, hopping up and down in rage. But the sword was too long for him; a particularly wild swing made him overbalance, and he landed face down in the grass.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Are you all right?’ said Harry, moving closer to the picture.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Get back, you scurvy braggart! Back, you rogue!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: The knight seized his sword again and used it to push himself back up, but the blade sank deeply into the grass and, though he pulled with all his might, he couldn’t get it out again. Finally he had to flop back down onto the grass and push up his visor to mop his sweating face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Six - Talons and Tea Leaves
text_content: ‘Listen,’ said Harry, taking advantage of the knight’s exhaustion, ‘we’re looking for the North Tower. You don’t know the way, do you?’

Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The day before the match, the winds reached howling point and the rain fell harder than ever. It was so dark inside the corridors and classrooms that extra torches and lanterns were lit. The Slytherin team were looking very smug indeed, and none more so than Malfoy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, if only my arm was feeling a bit better!’ he sighed, as the gale outside pounded the windows.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry woke extremely early next morning; so early that it was still dark. For a moment he thought the roaring of the wind had woken him, then he felt a cold breeze on the back of his neck and sat bolt upright – Peeves the poltergeist had been floating next to him, blowing hard in his ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What did you do that for?’ said Harry furiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Peeves puffed out his cheeks, blew hard and zoomed backwards out of the room, cackling.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry fumbled for his alarm clock and looked at it. It was half past four. Cursing Peeves, he rolled over and tried to get back to sleep, but it was very difficult, now he was awake, to ignore the sounds of the thunder rumbling overhead, the pounding of the wind against the castle walls and the distant creaking of the trees in the Forbidden Forest. In a few hours he would be out on the Quidditch pitch, battling through that gale. Finally he gave up any thought of more sleep, got up, dressed, picked up his Nimbus Two Thousand and walked quietly out of the dormitory.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As Harry opened the door, something brushed against his leg. He bent down just in time to grab Crookshanks by the end of his bushy tail, and drag him outside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You know, I reckon Ron was right about you,’ Harry told Crookshanks suspiciously. ‘There are plenty of mice around this place, go and chase them. Go on,’ he added, nudging Crookshanks down the spiral staircase with his foot, ‘leave Scabbers alone.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The noise of the storm was even louder in the common room. Harry knew better than to think the match would be cancelled; Quidditch matches weren’t called off for trifles such as thunderstorms. Nevertheless, he was starting to feel very apprehensive. Wood had pointed out Cedric Diggory to him in the corridor; Diggory was a fifth year and a lot bigger than Harry. Seekers were usually light and speedy, but Diggory’s weight would be an advantage in this weather because he was less likely to be blown off course.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Stand and fight, you mangy cur!’ yelled Sir Cadogan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

Madam Hooch put her whistle to her lips and gave it a blast that sounded shrill and distant – they were off.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry rose fast, but his Nimbus was swerving slightly with the wind. He held it as steady as he could and turned, squinting into the rain.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

He flew backwards and forwards across the pitch, past blurred red and yellow shapes, with no idea of what was happening in the rest of the game. He couldn’t hear the commentary over the wind. The crowd was hidden beneath a sea of cloaks and battered umbrellas. Twice Harry came very close to being unseated by a Bludger; his vision was so clouded by the rain on his glasses he hadn’t seen them coming.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘What’s the score?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry’s numb hands slipped on the broom handle and his Nimbus dropped a few feet. Shaking his sodden fringe out of his eyes, he squinted back into the stands. The dog had vanished.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: With a jolt of panic, Harry threw himself flat to the broom handle and zoomed towards the Snitch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then a horribly familiar wave of cold swept over him, inside him, just as he became aware of something moving on the pitch below …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Before he’d had time to think, Harry had taken his eyes off the Snitch and looked down.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not Harry, not Harry, please not Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Stand aside, you silly girl … stand aside, now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not Harry, please no, take me, kill me instead –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Numbing, swirling white mist was filling Harry’s brain … What was he doing? Why was he flying? He needed to help her … she was going to die … she was going to be murdered …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He was falling, falling through the icy mist.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not Harry! Please … have mercy … have mercy …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A shrill voice was laughing, the woman was screaming, and Harry knew no more.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Lucky the ground was so soft.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought he was dead for sure.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That was the scariest thing I’ve ever seen in my life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But if they beat Ravenclaw …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No way, Ravenclaw are too good. But if Slytherin lose against Hufflepuff …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It all depends on the points – a margin of a hundred either way –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: After ten minutes or so, Madam Pomfrey came over to tell the team to leave him in peace.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ll come and see you later,’ Fred told him. ‘Don’t beat yourself up, Harry, you’re still the best Seeker we’ve ever had.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The team trooped out, trailing mud behind them. Madam Pomfrey shut the door behind them looking disapproving. Ron and Hermione moved nearer to Harry’s bed.

text_content: It took ages, but Harry had the thought of Honeydukes to sustain him. After what felt like an hour, the passage began to rise. Panting, Harry sped up, his face hot, his feet very cold.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ten minutes later, he came to the foot of some worn, stone steps which rose out of sight above him. Careful not to make any noise, Harry began to climb. A hundred steps, two hundred steps, he lost count as he climbed, watching his feet … then, without warning, his head hit something hard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It seemed to be a trapdoor. Harry stood there, massaging the top of his head, listening. He couldn’t hear any sounds above him. Very slowly, he pushed the trapdoor open and peered over the edge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He was in a cellar which was full of wooden crates and boxes. Harry climbed out of the trapdoor and replaced it – it blended so perfectly with the dusty floor that it was impossible to tell it was there. Harry crept slowly towards the wooden staircase that led upstairs. Now he could definitely hear voices, not to mention the tinkle of a bell and the opening and shutting of a door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Wondering what he ought to do, he suddenly heard a door open much closer at hand; somebody was about to come downstairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And get another box of Jelly Slugs, dear, they’ve nearly cleaned us out –’ said a woman’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A pair of feet was coming down the staircase. Harry leapt behind an enormous crate and waited for the footsteps to pass. He heard the man shifting boxes against the wall opposite. He might not get another chance –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Quickly and silently, Harry dodged out from his hiding place and climbed the stairs; looking back, he saw an enormous backside and a shiny bald head buried in a box. Harry reached the door at the top of the stairs, slipped through it, and found himself behind the counter of Honeydukes – he ducked, crept sideways and then straightened up.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Honeydukes was so crowded with Hogwarts students that no one looked twice at Harry. He edged amongst them, looking around, and suppressed a laugh as he imagined the look that would spread over Dudley’s piggy face if he could see where Harry was now.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There were shelves upon shelves of the most succulent-looking sweets imaginable. Creamy chunks of nougat, shimmering pink squares of coconut ice, fat, honey-coloured toffees; hundreds of different kinds of chocolate in neat rows; there was a large barrel of Every Flavour Beans, and another of Fizzing Whizzbees, the levitating sherbert balls that Ron had mentioned; along yet another wall were ‘Special Effects’ sweets: Droobles Best Blowing Gum (which filled a room with bluebell-coloured bubbles that refused to pop for days), the strange, splintery Toothflossing Stringmints, tiny black Pepper Imps (‘breathe fire for your friends!’), Ice Mice (‘hear your teeth chatter and squeak!’), peppermint creams shaped like toads (‘hop realistically in the stomach!’), fragile sugar-spun quills and exploding bonbons.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry squeezed himself through a crowd of sixth-years and saw a sign hanging in the furthest corner of the shop (‘Unusual Tastes’). Ron and Hermione were standing underneath it, examining a tray of blood-flavoured lollipops. Harry sneaked up behind them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Urgh, no, Harry won’t want one of those, they’re for vampires, I expect,’ Hermione was saying.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How about these?’ said Ron, shoving a jar of Cockroach Cluster under Hermione’s nose.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Definitely not,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron nearly dropped the jar.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ squealed Hermione. ‘What are you doing here? How – how did you –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Wow!’ said Ron, looking very impressed. ‘You’ve learned to Apparate!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘’Course I haven’t,’ said Harry. He dropped his voice so that none of the sixth-years could hear him and told them all about the Marauder’s Map.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How come Fred and George never gave it to me!’ said Ron, outraged. ‘I’m their brother!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But Harry isn’t going to keep it!’ said Hermione, as though the idea was ludicrous. ‘He’s going to hand it in to Professor McGonagall, aren’t you, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I’m not!’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you mad?’ said Ron, goggling at Hermione. ‘Hand in something that good?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘If I hand it in, I’ll have to say where I got it! Filch would know Fred and George nicked it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But what about Sirius Black?’ Hermione hissed. ‘He could be using one of the passages on that map to get into the castle! The teachers have got to know!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He can’t be getting in through a passage,’ said Harry quickly. ‘There are seven secret tunnels on the map, right? Fred and George reckon Filch already knows about four of them. And the other three – one of them’s caved in, so no one can get through it. One of them’s got the Whomping Willow planted over the entrance, so you can’t get out of it. And the one I just came through – well – it’s really hard to see the entrance to it down in the cellar – so unless he knew it was there –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry hesitated. What if Black did know the passage was there? Ron, however, cleared his throat significantly, and pointed to a notice pasted on the inside of the sweetshop door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: BY ORDER OF THE MINISTRY OF MAGIC

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Customers are reminded that until further notice, Dementors will be patrolling the streets of Hogsmeade every night after sundown. This measure has been put in place for the safety of Hogsmeade residents and will be lifted upon the recapture of Sirius Black. It is therefore advisable that you complete your shopping well before nightfall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Merry Christmas!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘See?’ said Ron quietly. ‘I’d like to see Black try and break into Honeydukes with Dementors swarming all over the village. Anyway, Hermione, the Honeydukes owners would hear a break in, wouldn’t they? They live over the shop!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, but – but –’ Hermione seemed to be struggling to find another problem. ‘Look, Harry still shouldn’t be coming into Hogsmeade, he hasn’t got a signed form! If anyone finds out, he’ll be in so much trouble! And it’s not nightfall yet – what if Sirius Black turns up today? Now?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’d have a job spotting Harry in this,’ said Ron, nodding through the mullioned windows at the thick, swirling snow.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come on, Hermione, it’s Christmas, Harry deserves a break.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione bit her lip, looking extremely worried.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you going to report me?’ Harry asked her, grinning.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh – of course not – but honestly, Harry –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Seen the Fizzing Whizzbees, Harry?’ said Ron, grabbing him and leading him over to their barrel. ‘And the Jelly Slugs? And the Acid Pops? Fred gave me one of those when I was seven – it burnt a hole right through my tongue. I remember Mum walloping him with her broomstick.’ Ron stared broodingly into the Acid Pop box. ‘Reckon Fred’d take a bit of Cockroach Cluster if I told him they were peanuts?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: When Ron and Hermione had paid for all their sweets, the three of them left Honeydukes for the blizzard outside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hogsmeade looked like a Christmas card; the little thatched cottages and shops were all covered in a layer of crisp snow; there were holly wreaths on the doors and strings of enchanted candles hanging in the trees.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry shivered; unlike the other two, he didn’t have his cloak. They headed up the street, heads bowed against the wind, Ron and Hermione shouting through their scarves.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the Post Office –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Zonko’s is up there –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We could go up to the Shrieking Shack –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell you what,’ said Ron, his teeth chattering, ‘shall we go for a Butterbeer in the Three Broomsticks?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was more than willing; the wind was fierce and his hands were freezing, so they crossed the road, and in a few minutes were entering the tiny inn.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was extremely crowded, noisy, warm and smoky. A curvy sort of woman with a pretty face was serving a bunch of rowdy warlocks up at the bar.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s Madam Rosmerta,’ said Ron. ‘I’ll get the drinks, shall I?’ he added, going slightly red.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione made their way to the back of the room, where there was a small, vacant table between the window and a handsome Christmas tree which stood next to the fireplace. Ron came back five minutes later, carrying three foaming tankards of hot Butterbeer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Happy Christmas!’ he said happily, raising his tankard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry drank deeply. It was the most delicious thing he’d ever tasted and seemed to heat every bit of him from the inside.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A sudden breeze ruffled his hair. The door of the Three Broomsticks had opened again. Harry looked over the rim of his tankard and choked.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professors McGonagall and Flitwick had just entered the pub in a flurry of snowflakes, shortly followed by Hagrid, who was deep in conversation with a portly man in a lime-green bowler hat and a pinstriped cloak: Cornelius Fudge, Minister for Magic.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: In an instant, Ron and Hermione had both placed hands on the top of Harry’s head and forced him off his stool and under the table. Dripping with Butterbeer and crouching out of sight, Harry clutched his empty tankard and watched the teachers’ and Fudge’s feet move towards the bar, pause, then turn and walk right towards him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Somewhere above him, Hermione whispered, ‘Mobiliarbus!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Christmas tree beside their table rose a few inches off the ground, drifted sideways and landed with a soft thump right in front of their table, hiding them from view. Staring through the dense lower branches, Harry saw four sets of chair legs move back from the table right beside theirs, then heard the grunts and sighs of the teachers and Minister as they sat down.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Next he saw another pair of feet, wearing sparkly turquoise high heels, and heard a woman’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘A small Gillywater –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mine,’ said Professor McGonagall’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Four pints of mulled mead –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ta, Rosmerta,’ said Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘A cherry syrup and soda with ice and umbrella –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mmm!’ said Professor Flitwick, smacking his lips.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So you’ll be the redcurrant rum, Minister.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you, Rosmerta, m’dear,’ said Fudge’s voice. ‘Lovely to see you again, I must say. Have one yourself, won’t you? Come and join us …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, thank you very much, Minister.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry watched the glittering heels march away and back again. His heart was pounding uncomfortably in his throat. Why hadn’t it occurred to him that this was the last weekend of term for the teachers, too? And how long were they going to sit there? He needed time to sneak back into Honeydukes if he wanted to return to school tonight … Hermione’s leg gave a nervous twitch next to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So, what brings you to this neck of the woods, Minister?’ came Madam Rosmerta’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry saw the lower part of Fudge’s thick body twist in his chair as though he was checking for eavesdroppers. Then he said in a quiet voice, ‘What else, m’dear, but Sirius Black? I daresay you heard what happened up at the school at Hallowe’en?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I did hear a rumour,’ admitted Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you tell the whole pub, Hagrid?’ said Professor McGonagall exasperatedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Do you think Black’s still in the area, Minister?’ whispered Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sure of it,’ said Fudge shortly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You know that the Dementors have searched my pub twice?’ said Madam Rosmerta, a slight edge to her voice. ‘Scared all my customers away … it’s very bad for business, Minister.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Rosmerta, m’dear, I don’t like them any more than you do,’ said Fudge uncomfortably. ‘Necessary precaution … unfortunate, but there you are … I’ve just met some of them. They’re in a fury against Dumbledore – he won’t let them inside the castle grounds.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I should think not,’ said Professor McGonagall sharply. ‘How are we supposed to teach with those horrors floating around?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hear, hear!’ squeaked tiny Professor Flitwick, whose feet were dangling a foot from the ground.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘All the same,’ demurred Fudge, ‘they are here to protect you all from something much worse … we all know what Black’s capable of …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Do you know, I still have trouble believing it,’ said Madam Rosmerta thoughtfully. ‘Of all the people to go over to the Dark side, Sirius Black was the last I’d have thought … I mean, I remember him when he was a boy at Hogwarts. If you’d told me then what he was going to become, I’d have said you’d had too much mead.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t know the half of it, Rosmerta,’ said Fudge gruffly. ‘The worst he did isn’t widely known.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The worst?’ said Madam Rosmerta, her voice alive with curiosity. ‘Worse than murdering all those poor people, you mean?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I certainly do,’ said Fudge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t believe that. What could possibly be worse?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You say you remember him at Hogwarts, Rosmerta,’ murmured Professor McGonagall. ‘Do you remember who his best friend was?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Naturally,’ said Madam Rosmerta, with a small laugh. ‘Never saw one without the other, did you? The number of times I had them in here – ooh, they used to make me laugh. Quite the double act, Sirius Black and James Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry dropped his tankard with a loud clunk. Ron kicked him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Precisely,’ said Professor McGonagall. ‘Black and Potter. Ringleaders of their little gang. Both very bright, of course – exceptionally bright, in fact – but I don’t think we’ve ever had such a pair of troublemakers –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I dunno,’ chuckled Hagrid. ‘Fred and George Weasley could give ’em a run fer their money’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’d have thought Black and Potter were brothers!’ chimed in Professor Flitwick. ‘Inseparable!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course they were,’ said Fudge. ‘Potter trusted Black beyond all his other friends. Nothing changed when they left school. Black was best man when James married Lily. Then they named him godfather to Harry. Harry has no idea, of course. You can imagine how the idea would torment him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Because Black turned out to be in league with You-Know-Who?’ whispered Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Worse even than that, m’dear …’ Fudge dropped his voice and proceeded in a sort of low rumble. ‘Not many people are aware that the Potters knew You-Know-Who was after them. Dumbledore, who was of course working tirelessly against You-Know-Who, had a number of useful spies. One of them tipped him off, and he alerted James and Lily at once. He advised them to go into hiding. Well, of course, You-Know-Who wasn’t an easy person to hide from. Dumbledore told them that their best chance was the Fidelius Charm.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How does that work?’ said Madam Rosmerta, breathless with interest. Professor Flitwick cleared his throat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘An immensely complex spell,’ he said squeakily, ‘involving the magical concealment of a secret inside a single, living soul. The information is hidden inside the chosen person, or Secret-Keeper, and is henceforth impossible to find – unless, of course, the Secret-Keeper chooses to divulge it. As long as the Secret-Keeper refused to speak, You-Know-Who could search the village where Lily and James were staying for years and never find them, not even if he had his nose pressed against their sitting-room window!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So Black was the Potters’ Secret-Keeper?’ whispered Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Naturally,’ said Professor McGonagall. ‘James Potter told Dumbledore that Black would die rather than tell where they were, that Black was planning to go into hiding himself … and yet, Dumbledore remained worried. I remember him offering to be the Potters’ Secret-Keeper himself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He suspected Black?’ gasped Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He was sure that somebody close to the Potters had been keeping You-Know-Who informed of their movements,’ said Professor McGonagall darkly. ‘Indeed, he had suspected for some time that someone on our side had turned traitor and was passing a lot of information to You-Know-Who.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But James Potter insisted on using Black?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He did,’ said Fudge heavily. ‘And then, barely a week after the Fidelius Charm had been performed –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Black betrayed them?’ breathed Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He did indeed. Black was tired of his double-agent role, he was ready to declare his support openly for You-Know-Who, and he seems to have planned this for the moment of the Potters’ death. But, as we all know, You-Know-Who met his downfall in little Harry Potter. Powers gone, horribly weakened, he fled. And this left Black in a very nasty position indeed. His Master had fallen at the very moment when he, Black, had shown his true colours as a traitor. He had no choice but to run for it –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Filthy, stinkin’ turncoat!’ Hagrid said, so loudly that half the bar went quiet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Shh!’ said Professor McGonagall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I met him!’ growled Hagrid. ‘I musta bin the last ter see him before he killed all them people! It was me what rescued Harry from Lily an’ James’ house after they was killed! Jus’ got him outta the ruins, poor little thing, with a great slash across his forehead, an’ his parents dead … an’ Sirius Black turns up, on that flyin’ motorbike he used ter ride. Never occurred ter me what he was doin’ there. I didn’ know he’d bin Lily an’ James’ Secret-Keeper. Thought he’d jus’ heard the news o’ You-Know-Who’s attack an’ come ter see what he could do. White an’ shakin’, he was. An’ yeh know what I did? I COMFORTED THE MURDERIN’ TRAITOR!’ Hagrid roared.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, please!’ said Professor McGonagall. ‘Keep your voice down!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How was I ter know he wasn’ upset abou’ Lily an’ James? It was You-Know-Who he cared abou’! An’ then he says, ‘Give Harry ter me, Hagrid, I’m his godfather, I’ll look after him –’ Ha! But I’d had me orders from Dumbledore, an’ I told Black no, Dumbledore said Harry was ter go ter his aunt an’ uncle’s. Black argued, but in the end he gave in. Told me ter take his motorbike ter get Harry there. ‘I won’ need it any more,’ he says.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I shoulda known there was somethin’ fishy goin’ on then. He loved that motorbike, what was he givin’ it ter me for? Why wouldn’ he need it any more? Fact was, it was too easy ter trace. Dumbledore knew he’d bin the Potters’ Secret-Keeper. Black knew he was goin’ ter have ter run fer it that night, knew it was a matter o’ hours before the Ministry was after him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But what if I’d given Harry to him, eh? I bet he’d’ve pitched him off the bike halfway out ter sea. His bes’ friend’s son! But when a wizard goes over ter the dark side, there’s nothin’ and no one that matters to ’em any more …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A long silence followed Hagrid’s story. Then Madam Rosmerta said with some satisfaction, ‘But he didn’t manage to disappear, did he? The Ministry of Magic caught up with him next day!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Alas, if only we had,’ said Fudge bitterly. ‘It was not we who found him. It was little Peter Pettigrew – another of the Potters’ friends. Maddened by grief, no doubt, and knowing that Black had been the Potters’ Secret-Keeper, he went after Black himself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Pettigrew … that fat little boy who was always tagging around after them at Hogwarts?’ said Madam Rosmerta.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hero-worshipped Black and Potter,’ said Professor McGonagall. ‘Never quite in their league, talent-wise. I was often rather sharp with him. You can imagine how I – how I regret that now …’ She sounded as though she had a sudden head cold.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There, now, Minerva,’ said Fudge kindly, ‘Pettigrew died a hero’s death. Eye-witnesses – Muggles, of course, we wiped their memories later – told us how Pettigrew cornered Black. They say he was sobbing. ‘Lily and James, Sirius! How could you!’ And then he went for his wand. Well, of course, Black was quicker. Blew Pettigrew to smithereens …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall blew her nose and said thickly, ‘Stupid boy … foolish boy … he was always hopeless at duelling … should have left it to the Ministry …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I tell yeh, if I’d got ter Black before little Pettigrew did, I wouldn’t’ve messed around with wands – I’d’ve ripped him limb – from – limb,’ Hagrid growled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t know what you’re talking about, Hagrid,’ said Fudge sharply. ‘Nobody but trained Hit Wizards from the Magical Law Enforcement Squad would have stood a chance against Black once he was cornered. I was Junior Minister in the Department of Magical Catastrophes at the time, and I was one of the first on the scene after Black murdered all those people. I – I will never forget it. I still dream about it sometimes. A crater in the middle of the street, so deep it had cracked the sewer below. Bodies everywhere. Muggles screaming. And Black standing there laughing, with what was left of Pettigrew in front of him … a heap of blood-stained robes and a few – a few fragments –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fudge’s voice stopped abruptly. There was the sound of five noses being blown.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, there you have it, Rosmerta,’ said Fudge thickly. ‘Black was taken away by twenty members of the Magical Law Enforcement Patrol and Pettigrew received the Order of Merlin, First Class, which I think was some comfort to his poor mother. Black’s been in Azkaban ever since.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Madam Rosmerta let out a long sigh.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Is it true he’s mad, Minister?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I wish I could say that he was,’ said Fudge slowly. ‘I certainly believe his master’s defeat unhinged him for a while. The murder of Pettigrew and all those Muggles was the action of a cornered and desperate man – cruel … pointless. Yet I met Black on my last inspection of Azkaban. You know, most of the prisoners in there sit muttering to themselves in the dark, there’s no sense in them … but I was shocked at how normal Black seemed. He spoke quite rationally to me. It was unnerving. You’d have thought he was merely bored – asked if I’d finished with my newspaper, cool as you please, said he missed doing the crossword. Yes, I was astounded at how little effect the Dementors seemed to be having on him – and he was one of the most heavily guarded in the place, you know. Dementors outside his door, day and night.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But what do you think he’s broken out to do?’ said Madam Rosmerta. ‘Good gracious, Minister, he isn’t trying to rejoin You-Know-Who, is he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I daresay that is his – er – eventual plan,’ said Fudge evasively. ‘But we hope to catch Black long before that. I must say, You-Know-Who alone and friendless is one thing … but give him back his most devoted servant, and I shudder to think how quickly he’ll rise again …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a small chink of glass on wood. Someone had set down their glass.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You know, Cornelius, if you’re dining with the Headmaster, we’d better head back up to the castle,’ said Professor McGonagall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: One by one, the pairs of feet in front of Harry took the weight of their owners once more; hems of cloaks swung into sight and Madam Rosmerta’s glittering heels disappeared behind the bar. book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione’s faces appeared under the table. They were both staring at him, lost for words.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t have a very clear idea of how he had managed to get back into the Honeydukes cellar, through the tunnel and into the castle once more. All he knew was that the return trip seemed to take no time at all, and that he hardly noticed what he was doing, because his head was still pounding with the conversation he had just heard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Why had nobody ever told him? Dumbledore, Hagrid, Mr Weasley, Cornelius Fudge … why hadn’t anyone ever mentioned the fact that Harry’s parents had died because their best friend had betrayed them?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione watched Harry nervously all through dinner, not daring to talk about what they’d overheard, because Percy was sitting close by them. When they went upstairs to the crowded common room, it was to find Fred and George had set off half-a-dozen Dungbombs in a fit of end-of-term high spirits. Harry, who didn’t want Fred and George asking him whether he’d reached Hogsmeade or not, sneaked quietly up to the empty dormitory, and headed straight for his bedside cabinet. He pushed his books aside and quickly found what he was looking for – the leather-bound photo album Hagrid had given him two years ago, which was full of wizard pictures of his mother and father. He sat down on his bed, drew the hangings around him, and started turning the pages, searching, until …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He stopped on a picture of his parents’ wedding day. There was his father waving up at him, beaming, the untidy black hair Harry had inherited standing up in all directions. There was his mother, alight with happiness, arm in arm with his Dad. And there … that must be him. Their best man … Harry had never given him a thought before.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: If he hadn’t known it was the same person, he would never have guessed it was Black in this old photograph. His face wasn’t sunken and waxy, but handsome, full of laughter. Had he already been working for Voldemort when this picture had been taken? Was he already planning the deaths of the two people next to him? Did he realise he was facing twelve years in Azkaban, twelve years which would make him unrecognisable?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But the Dementors don’t affect him, Harry thought, staring into the handsome, laughing face. He doesn’t have to hear my Mum screaming if they get too close –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry slammed the album shut, reached over and stuffed it back into his cabinet, took off his robes and glasses and got into bed, making sure the hangings were hiding him from view.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The dormitory door opened.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry?’ said Ron’s voice uncertainly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Harry lay still, pretending to be asleep. He heard Ron leave again, and rolled over on his back, his eyes wide open.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A hatred such as he had never known before was coursing through Harry like poison. He could see Black laughing at him through the darkness, as though somebody had pasted the picture from the album over his eyes. He watched, as though somebody was playing him a piece of film, Sirius Black blasting Peter Pettigrew (who resembled Neville Longbottom) into a thousand pieces. He could hear (though he had no idea what Black’s voice might sound like) a low, excited mutter. ‘It has happened, my Lord … the Potters have made me their Secret-Keeper …’ And then came another voice, laughing shrilly, the same laugh that Harry heard inside his head whenever the Dementors drew near …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry you – you look terrible.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

He had awoken to find the dormitory deserted, dressed and gone down the spiral staircase to a common room that was completely empty except for Ron, who was eating a Peppermint Toad and massaging his stomach, and Hermione, who had spread her homework over three tables.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Where is everyone?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Gone! It’s the first day of the holidays, remember?’ said Ron, watching Harry closely. ‘It’s nearly lunchtime, I was going to come and wake you up in a minute.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry slumped into a chair next to the fire. Snow was still falling outside the windows. Crookshanks was spread out in front of the fire like a large, ginger rug.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You really don’t look well, you know,’ Hermione said, peering anxiously into his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m fine,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, listen,’ said Hermione, exchanging a look with Ron, ‘you must be really upset about what we heard yesterday. But the thing is, you mustn’t go doing anything stupid.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Like what?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Like trying to go after Black,’ said Ron sharply.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry could tell they had rehearsed this conversation while he had been asleep. He didn’t say anything.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You won’t, will you, Harry?’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Because Black’s not worth dying for,’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked at them. They didn’t seem to understand at all.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you know what I see and hear every time a Dementor gets too near me?’ Ron and Hermione shook their heads, looking apprehensive. ‘I can hear my mum screaming and pleading with Voldemort. book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s nothing you can do!’ said Hermione, looking stricken. ‘The Dementors will catch Black and he’ll go back to Azkaban and – and serve him right!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You heard what Fudge said. Black isn’t affected by Azkaban like normal people are. It’s not a punishment for him like it is for the others.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So what are you saying?’ said Ron, looking very tense. ‘You want to – to kill Black or something?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be silly,’ said Hermione in a panicky voice. ‘Harry doesn’t want to kill anyone, do you, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Again, Harry didn’t answer. He didn’t know what he wanted to do. All he knew was that the idea of doing nothing, while Black was at liberty, was almost more than he could stand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Malfoy knows,’ he said abruptly. ‘Remember what he said to me in Potions? ‘If it was me, I’d hunt him down myself … I’d want revenge.’’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Malfoy’s dad must have told him,’ said Harry, ignoring Ron. ‘He was right in Voldemort’s inner circle –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Say You-Know-Who, will you?’ interjected Ron angrily.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘– so obviously, the Malfoys knew Black was working for Voldemort –’

text_content: ‘– and Malfoy’d love to see you blown into about a million pieces, like Pettigrew! Get a grip, Malfoy’s just hoping you’ll get yourself killed before he has to play you at Quidditch.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry please,’ said Hermione, her eyes now shining with tears, ‘please be sensible. Your mum and dad wouldn’t want you to get hurt, would they? They’d never want you to go looking for Black!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll never know what they’d have wanted because, thanks to Black, I’ve never spoken to them,’ said Harry shortly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a silence, in which Crookshanks stretched luxuriously, flexing his claws. Ron’s pocket quivered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Look,’ said Ron, obviously casting around for a change of subject, ‘it’s the holidays! It’s nearly Christmas! Let’s – let’s go down and see Hagrid. We haven’t visited him for ages!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ said Hermione quickly. ‘Harry isn’t supposed to leave the castle, Ron –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, let’s go,’ said Harry, sitting up, ‘and I can ask him how come he never mentioned Black when he told me all about my parents!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Further discussion of Sirius Black plainly wasn’t what Ron had had in mind.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Or we could have a game of chess,’ he said hastily, ‘or Gobstones. Percy left a set –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, let’s visit Hagrid,’ said Harry firmly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: So they got their cloaks from their dormitories and set off through the portrait hole (‘Stand and fight, you yellow-bellied mongrels!’), down through the empty castle and out through the oak front doors.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They made their way slowly down the lawn, making a shallow trench in the glittering, powdery snow, their socks and the hems of their cloaks soaked and freezing. The Forbidden Forest looked as though it had been enchanted, each tree smattered with silver, and Hagrid’s cabin looked like an iced cake.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron knocked, but there was no answer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s not out, is he?’ said Hermione, who was shivering under her cloak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron had his ear to the door.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s a weird noise,’ he said. ‘Listen – is that Fang?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione put their ears to the door, too. From inside the cabin came a series of low, throbbing moans.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Think we’d better go and get someone?’ said Ron nervously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid!’ called Harry, thumping the door. ‘Hagrid, are you in there?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a sound of heavy footsteps, then the door creaked open. Hagrid stood there with his eyes red and swollen; tears splashing down the front of his leather waistcoat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh’ve heard!’ he bellowed, and he flung himself onto Harry’s neck.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid being at least twice the size of a normal man, this was no laughing matter. Harry, about to collapse under Hagrid’s weight, was rescued by Ron and Hermione, who each seized Hagrid under an arm and heaved him, Harry helping, back into the cabin. Hagrid allowed himself to be steered into a chair and slumped over the table, sobbing uncontrollably, his face glazed with tears which dripped down into his tangled beard.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, what is it?’ said Hermione, aghast.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry spotted an official-looking letter lying open on the table.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s this, Hagrid?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid’s sobs redoubled, but he shoved the letter towards Harry, who picked it up and read aloud:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Dear Mr Hagrid,

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Further to our inquiry into the attack by a Hippogriff on a student in your class, we have accepted the assurances of Professor Dumbledore that you bear no responsibility for the regrettable incident.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, that’s OK, then, Hagrid!’ said Ron, clapping Hagrid on the shoulder. But Hagrid continued to sob, and waved one of his gigantic hands, inviting Harry to read on.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: However, we must register our concern about the Hippogriff in question. We have decided to uphold the official complaint of Mr Lucius Malfoy, and this matter will therefore be taken to the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures. The hearing will take place on April 20th, and we ask you to present yourself and your Hippogriff at the Committee’s offices in London on that date. In the meantime, the Hippogriff should be kept tethered and isolated.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Yours in fellowship …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There followed a list of the school governors.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh,’ said Ron. ‘But you said Buckbeak isn’t a bad Hippogriff, Hagrid. I bet he’ll get off –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh don’ know them gargoyles at the Committee fer the Disposal o’ Dangerous Creatures!’ choked Hagrid, wiping his eyes on his sleeve. ‘They’ve got it in fer interestin’ creatures!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A sudden sound from the corner of Hagrid’s cabin made Harry, Ron and Hermione whip around. Buckbeak the Hippogriff was lying in the corner, chomping on something that was oozing blood all over the floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I couldn’ leave him tied up out there in the snow!’ choked Hagrid. ‘All on his own! At Christmas!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione looked at each other. They had never seen eye to eye with Hagrid about what he called ‘interesting creatures’ and other people called ‘terrifying monsters’. On the other hand, there didn’t seem to be any particular harm in Buckbeak. In fact, by Hagrid’s usual standards, he was positively cute.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’ll have to put up a good strong defence, Hagrid,’ said Hermione, sitting down and laying a hand on Hagrid’s massive forearm. ‘I’m sure you can prove Buckbeak is safe.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Won’ make no diff’rence!’ sobbed Hagrid. ‘Them Disposal devils, they’re all in Lucius Malfoy’s pocket! Scared o’ him! An’ if I lose the case, Buckbeak –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid drew his finger swiftly across his throat, then gave a great wail and lurched forwards, his face in his arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What about Dumbledore, Hagrid?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s done more’n enough fer me already,’ groaned Hagrid. ‘Got enough on his plate what with keepin’ them Dementors outta the castle, an’ Sirius Black lurkin’ around –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione looked quickly at Harry, as though expecting him to start berating Hagrid for not telling him the truth about Black. But Harry couldn’t bring himself to do it, not now he saw Hagrid so miserable and scared.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Listen, Hagrid,’ he said, ‘you can’t give up. Hermione’s right, you just need a good defence. You can call us as witnesses –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sure I’ve read about a case of Hippogriff-baiting,’ said Hermione thoughtfully, ‘where the Hippogriff got off. I’ll look it up for you, Hagrid, and see exactly what happened.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid howled still more loudly. Harry and Hermione looked at Ron to help them.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Er – shall I make a cup of tea?’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stared at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s what my mum does whenever someone’s upset,’ Ron muttered, shrugging.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: At last, after many more assurances of help, with a steaming mug of tea in front of him, Hagrid blew his nose on a handkerchief the size of a tablecloth and said, ‘Yer right. I can’ afford to go ter pieces. Gotta pull meself together …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Fang the boarhound came timidly out from under the table and laid his head on Hagrid’s knee.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve not bin meself lately’ said Hagrid, stroking Fang with one hand and mopping his face with the other. ‘Worried abou’ Buckbeak, an’ no one likin’ me classes –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We do like them!’ lied Hermione at once.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, they’re great!’ said Ron, crossing his fingers under the table. ‘Er – how are the Flobberworms?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dead,’ said Hagrid gloomily. ‘Too much lettuce.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, no!’ said Ron, his lip twitching.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘An’ them Dementors make me feel ruddy terrible an’ all,’ said Hagrid, with a sudden shudder. ‘Gotta walk past ’em ev’ry time I want a drink in the Three Broomsticks. ’S like bein’ back in Azkaban –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He fell silent, gulping his tea. Harry, Ron and Hermione watched him breathlessly. They had never heard Hagrid talk about his brief spell in Azkaban before. After a brief pause, Hermione said timidly ‘Is it awful in there, Hagrid?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh’ve no idea,’ said Hagrid quietly. ‘Never bin anywhere like it. Thought I was goin’ mad. Kep’ goin’ over horrible stuff in me mind … the day I got expelled from Hogwarts … day me Dad died … day I had ter let Norbert go …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: His eyes filled with tears. Norbert was the baby dragon Hagrid had once won in a game of cards.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh can’ really remember who yeh are after a while. An’ yeh can’ see the point o’ livin’ at all. I used ter hope I’d jus’ die in me sleep … when they let me out, it was like bein’ born again, ev’ry-thin’ came floodin’ back, it was the bes’ feelin’ in the world. Mind, the Dementors weren’t keen on lettin’ me go.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘But you were innocent!’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid snorted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Think that matters to them? They don’ care. Long as they’ve got a couple o’ hundred humans stuck there with ’em, so they can leech all the happiness out of ’em, they don’ give a damn who’s guilty an’ who’s not.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid went quiet for a moment, staring into his tea. Then he said quietly, ‘Thought o’ jus’ letting Buckbeak go … tryin’ ter make him fly away … but how d’yeh explain ter a Hippogriff it’s gotta go inter hidin’? An’ – an’ I’m scared o’ breakin’ the law …’ He looked up at them, tears leaking down his face again. ‘I don’ ever want ter go back ter Azkaban.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The trip to Hagrid’s, though far from fun, had nevertheless had the effect Ron and Hermione had hoped. Though Harry had by no means forgotten about Black, he couldn’t brood constantly on revenge if he wanted to help Hagrid win his case against the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures. He, Ron and Hermione went to the library next day, and returned to the empty common room laden with books which might help prepare a defence for Buckbeak. The three of them sat in front of the roaring fire, slowly turning the pages of dusty volumes about famous cases of marauding beasts, speaking occasionally when they ran across something relevant.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Here’s something … there was a case in 1722 … but the Hippogriff was convicted – urgh, look what they did to it, that’s disgusting –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘This might help, look – a Manticore savaged someone in 1296, and they let the Manticore off – oh – no, that was only because everyone was too scared to go near it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Meanwhile, in the rest of the castle, the usual magnificent Christmas decorations had been put up, despite the fact that hardly any of the students remained to enjoy them. Thick streamers of holly and mistletoe were strung along the corridors, mysterious lights shone from inside every suit of armour and the Great Hall was filled with its usual twelve Christmas trees, glittering with golden stars. A powerful and delicious smell of cooking pervaded the corridors, and by Christmas Eve, it had grown so strong that even Scabbers poked his nose out of the shelter of Ron’s pocket to sniff hopefully at the air.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: On Christmas morning, Harry was woken by Ron throwing his pillow at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oy! Presents!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry reached for his glasses and put them on, squinting through the semi-darkness to the foot of his bed, where a small heap of parcels had appeared. Ron was already ripping the paper off his own presents.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Another jumper from Mum … maroon again … see if you’ve got one.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had. Mrs Weasley had sent him a scarlet jumper with the Gryffindor lion knitted on the front, also a dozen home-baked mince pies, some Christmas cake and a box of nut brittle. As he moved all these things aside, he saw a long, thin package lying underneath.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s that?’ said Ron, looking over, a freshly unwrapped pair of maroon socks in his hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Dunno …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry ripped the parcel open and gasped as a magnificent, gleaming broomstick rolled out onto his bedspread. Ron dropped his socks and jumped off his bed for a closer look.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t believe it,’ he said hoarsely.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was a Firebolt, identical to the dream broom Harry had gone to see every day in Diagon Alley. Its handle glittered as he picked it up. He could feel it vibrating, and let go; it hung in mid-air, unsupported, at exactly the right height for him to mount it. His eyes moved from the golden registration number at the top of the handle right down to the perfectly smooth, streamlined birch twigs that made up the tail.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Who sent it to you?’ said Ron in a hushed voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Look and see if there’s a card,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron ripped apart the Firebolt’s wrappings. ‘Nothing! Blimey, who’d spend that much on you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
