text_content: ‘So …’ Professor Lupin had taken out his own wand, and indicated that Harry should do the same. ‘The spell I am going to try and teach you is highly advanced magic, Harry – well beyond Ordinary Wizarding Level. It is called the Patronus Charm.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How does it work?’ said Harry nervously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, when it works correctly, it conjures up a Patronus,’ said Lupin, ‘which is a kind of Anti-Dementor – a guardian which acts as a shield between you and the Dementor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had a sudden vision of himself crouching behind a Hagrid-sized figure holding a large club. Professor Lupin continued, ‘The Patronus is a kind of positive force, a projection of the very things that the Dementor feeds upon – hope, happiness, the desire to survive – but it cannot feel despair, as real humans can, so the Dementors can’t hurt it. But I must warn you, Harry, that the Charm might be too advanced for you. Many qualified wizards have difficulty with it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What does a Patronus look like?’ said Harry curiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Each one is unique to the wizard who conjures it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And how do you conjure it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘With an incantation, which will work only if you are concentrating, with all your might, on a single, very happy memory.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry cast about for a happy memory. Certainly, nothing that had happened to him at the Dursleys’ was going to do. Finally, he settled on the moment when he had first ridden a broomstick.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Right,’ he said, trying to recall as exactly as possible the wonderful, soaring sensation in his stomach.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The incantation is this –’ Lupin cleared his throat, ‘expecto patronum!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Expecto patronum,’ Harry repeated under his breath, ‘expecto patronum.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Concentrating hard on your happy memory?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh – yeah –’ said Harry, quickly forcing his thoughts back to that first broom-ride. ‘Expecto patrono – no, patronum – sorry – expecto patronum, expecto patronum –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Something whooshed suddenly out of the end of his wand; it looked like a wisp of silvery gas.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you see that?’ said Harry excitedly. ‘Something happened!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Very good,’ said Lupin, smiling. ‘Right then – ready to try it on a Dementor?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ Harry said, gripping his wand very tightly, and moving into the middle of the deserted classroom. He tried to keep his mind on flying, but something else kept intruding … any second now, he might hear his mother again … but he shouldn’t think that, or he would hear her again, and he didn’t want to … or did he?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin grasped the lid of the packing case and pulled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A Dementor rose slowly from the box, its hooded face turned towards Harry, one glistening, scabbed hand gripping its cloak. The lamps around the classroom flickered and went out. The Dementor stepped from the box and started to sweep silently towards Harry, drawing a deep, rattling breath. A wave of piercing cold broke over him –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Expecto patronum!’ Harry yelled. ‘Expecto patronum! Expecto –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But the classroom and the Dementor were dissolving … Harry was falling again through thick white fog, and his mother’s voice was louder than ever, echoing inside his head – ‘Not Harry! Not Harry! Please – I’ll do anything –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Stand aside – stand aside, girl –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry jerked back to life. He was lying flat on his back on the floor. The classroom lamps were alight again. He didn’t have to ask what had happened.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry,’ he muttered, sitting up and feeling cold sweat trickling down behind his glasses.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you all right?’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes …’ Harry pulled himself up on one of the desks and leaned against it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Here –’ Lupin handed him a Chocolate Frog. ‘Eat this before we try again. I didn’t expect you to do it first time. In fact, I would have been astounded if you had.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s getting worse,’ Harry muttered, biting the Frog’s head off. ‘I could hear her louder that time – and him – Voldemort –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin looked paler than usual.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry if you don’t want to continue, I will more than understand –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I do!’ said Harry fiercely, stuffing the rest of the Chocolate Frog into his mouth. ‘I’ve got to! What if the Dementors turn up at our match against Ravenclaw? I can’t afford to fall off again. If we lose this game we’ve lost the Quidditch Cup!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘All right then …’ said Lupin. ‘You might want to select another memory, a happy memory, I mean, to concentrate on … that one doesn’t seem to have been strong enough …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry thought hard, and decided his feelings when Gryffindor had won the House Championship last year had definitely qualified as very happy. He gripped his wand tightly again, and took up his position in the middle of the classroom.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ready?’ said Lupin, gripping the box lid.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ready’ said Harry, trying hard to fill his head with happy thoughts about Gryffindor winning, and not dark thoughts about what was going to happen when the box opened.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Go!’ said Lupin, pulling off the lid. The room went icily cold and dark once more. The Dementor glided forwards, drawing its rattly breath; one rotting hand was extending towards Harry –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Expecto patronum!’ Harry yelled. ‘Expecto patronum! Expecto pat –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: White fog obscured his senses … big, blurred shapes were moving around him … then came a new voice, a man’s voice, shouting, panicking –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Lily, take Harry and go! It’s Him! Go! Run! I’ll hold him off –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The sounds of someone stumbling from a room – a door bursting open – a cackle of high-pitched laughter –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry! Harry … wake up …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin was tapping Harry hard on the face. This time it was a minute before Harry understood why he was lying on a dusty classroom floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I heard my dad,’ Harry mumbled. ‘That’s the first time I’ve ever heard him – he tried to take on Voldemort himself, to give my mum time to run for it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry suddenly realised that there were tears on his face mingling with the sweat. He bent his face low as possible, wiping them off on his robes, pretending to do up his shoelace, so that Lupin wouldn’t see.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You heard James?’ said Lupin, in a strange voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah …’ Face dry, Harry looked up. ‘Why – you didn’t know my dad, did you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I – I did, as a matter of fact,’ said Lupin. ‘We were friends at Hogwarts. Listen, Harry – perhaps we should leave it here for tonight. This charm is ridiculously advanced … I shouldn’t have suggested putting you through this …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ said Harry. He got up again. ‘I’ll have one more go! I’m not thinking of happy enough things, that’s what it is … hang on …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He racked his brains. A really, really happy memory … one that he could turn into a good, strong Patronus …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The moment when he’d first found out he was a wizard, and would be leaving the Dursleys for Hogwarts! If that wasn’t a happy memory, he didn’t know what was … concentrating very hard on how he had felt when he’d realised he’d be leaving Privet Drive, Harry got to his feet and faced the packing case once more.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ready?’ said Lupin, who looked as though he was doing this against his better judgement. ‘Concentrating hard? All right – go!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He pulled off the lid of the case for the third time, and the Dementor rose out of it; the room fell cold and dark –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘EXPECTO PATRONUM!’ Harry bellowed. ‘EXPECTO PATRONUM! EXPECTO PATRONUM!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The screaming inside Harry’s head had started again – except this time, it sounded as though it was coming from a badly tuned radio. Softer and louder and softer again … and he could still see the Dementor … it had halted … and then a huge, silver shadow came bursting out of the end of Harry’s wand, to hover between him and the Dementor, and though Harry’s legs felt like water, he was still on his feet … though for how much longer, he wasn’t sure …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Riddikulus!’ roared Lupin, springing forwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a loud crack, and Harry’s cloudy Patronus vanished along with the Dementor; he sank into a chair, feeling as exhausted as if he’d just run a mile, his legs shaking. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Professor Lupin forcing the Boggart back into the packing case with his wand; it had turned into a silvery orb again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Excellent!’ Lupin said, striding over to where Harry sat. ‘Excellent, Harry! That was definitely a start!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Can we have another go? Just one more go?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Not now,’ said Lupin firmly. ‘You’ve had enough for one night. Here –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He handed Harry a large bar of Honeydukes’ best chocolate.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Eat the lot, or Madam Pomfrey will be after my blood. Same time next week?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OK,’ said Harry. He took a bite of the chocolate and watched Lupin extinguishing the lamps that had rekindled with the disappearance of the Dementor. A thought had just occurred to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Lupin?’ he said. ‘If you knew my dad, you must’ve known Sirius Black as well.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin turned very quickly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What gives you that idea?’ he said sharply.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Nothing – I mean, I just knew they were friends at Hogwarts, too …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin’s face relaxed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I knew him,’ he said shortly. ‘Or I thought I did. You’d better get off, Harry, it’s getting late.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry left the classroom, walked along the corridor and around a corner, than took a detour behind a suit of armour and sank down on its plinth to finish his chocolate, wishing he hadn’t mentioned Black, as Lupin was obviously not keen on the subject. Then Harry’s thoughts wandered back to his mother and father …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He felt drained and strangely empty, even though he was so full of chocolate. Terrible though it was to hear his parents’ last moments replayed inside his head, these were the only times Harry had heard their voices since he was a very small child. But he’d never be able to produce a proper Patronus if he half-wanted to hear his parents again …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re dead,’ he told himself sternly. ‘They’re dead, and listening to echoes of them won’t bring them back. You’d better get a grip on yourself if you want that Quidditch Cup.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He stood up, crammed the last bit of chocolate into his mouth and headed back to Gryffindor Tower.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ravenclaw played Slytherin a week after the start of term. Slytherin won, though narrowly. According to Wood, this was good news for Gryffindor, who would take second place if they beat Ravenclaw too. He therefore increased the number of team practices to five a week. This meant that with Lupin’s Anti-Dementor classes, which in themselves were more draining than six Quidditch practices, Harry had just one night a week to do all his homework. Even so, he wasn’t showing the strain nearly as much as Hermione, whose immense workload finally seemed to be getting to her. Every night, without fail, Hermione was to be seen in a corner of the common room, several tables spread with books, Arithmancy charts, Rune dictionaries, diagrams of Muggles lifting heavy objects, and file upon file of extensive notes; she barely spoke to anybody, and snapped when she was interrupted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How’s she doing it?’ Ron muttered to Harry one evening, as Harry sat finishing a nasty essay on Undetectable Poisons for Snape. Harry looked up. Hermione was barely visible behind a tottering pile of books.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Doing what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Getting to all her classes!’ Ron said. ‘I heard her talking to Professor Vector, that Arithmancy witch, this morning. They were going on about yesterday’s lesson, but Hermione can’t’ve been there, because she was with us in Care of Magical Creatures! And Ernie McMillan told me she’s never missed a Muggle Studies class, but half of them are at the same time as Divination, and she’s never missed one of them, either!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t have time to fathom the mystery of Hermione’s impossible timetable at the moment; he really needed to get on with Snape’s essay. Two seconds later, however, he was interrupted again, this time by Wood.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Bad news, Harry. I’ve just been to see Professor McGonagall about the Firebolt. She – er – got a bit shirty with me. Told me I’d got my priorities wrong. Seemed to think I cared more about winning the Cup than I do about you staying alive. Just because I told her I didn’t care if it threw you off, as long as you caught the Snitch on it first.’ Wood shook his head in disbelief. ‘Honestly, the way she was yelling at me … you’d think I’d said something terrible. Then I asked her how much longer she was going to keep it …’ He screwed up his face and imitated Professor McGonagall’s severe voice, ‘‘As long as necessary, Wood’ … I reckon it’s time you ordered a new broom, Harry. There’s an order form at the back of Which Broomstick … you could get a Nimbus Two Thousand and One, like Malfoy’s got.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not buying anything Malfoy thinks is good,’ said Harry flatly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: January faded imperceptibly into February, with no change in the bitterly cold weather. The match against Ravenclaw was drawing nearer and nearer, but Harry still hadn’t ordered a new broom. He was now asking Professor McGonagall for news of the Firebolt after every Transfiguration lesson, Ron standing hopefully at his shoulder, Hermione rushing past with her face averted.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No, Potter, you can’t have it back yet,’ Professor McGonagall told him the twelfth time this happened, before he’d even opened his mouth. ‘We’ve checked for most of the usual curses, but Professor Flitwick believes the broom might be carrying a Hurling Hex. I shall tell you once we’ve finished checking it. Now, please stop badgering me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: To make matters even worse, Harry’s Anti-Dementor lessons were not going nearly as well as he had hoped. Several sessions on, he was able to produce an indistinct, silvery shadow every time the Boggart-Dementor approached him, but his Patronus was too feeble to drive the Dementor away. All it did was hover, like a semi-transparent cloud, draining Harry of energy as he fought to keep it there. Harry felt angry with himself, guilty about his secret desire to hear his parents’ voices again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re expecting too much of yourself,’ said Professor Lupin sternly, in their fourth week of practice. ‘For a thirteen-year-old wizard, even an indistinct Patronus is a huge achievement. You aren’t passing out any more, are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought a Patronus would – charge the Dementors down or something,’ said Harry dispiritedly. ‘Make them disappear –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The true Patronus does do that,’ said Lupin. ‘But you’ve achieved a great deal in a very short space of time. If the Dementors put in an appearance at your next Quidditch match, you will be able to keep them at bay long enough to get back to the ground.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You said it’s harder if there are loads of them,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I have complete confidence in you,’ said Lupin, smiling. ‘Here – you’ve earned a drink. Something from the Three Broomsticks, you won’t have tried it before –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He pulled two bottles out of his briefcase.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Butterbeer!’ said Harry, without thinking. ‘Yeah, I like that stuff!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin raised an eyebrow.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh – Ron and Hermione brought me some back from Hogsmeade,’ Harry lied quickly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I see,’ said Lupin, though he still looked slightly suspicious. ‘Well – let’s drink to a Gryffindor victory against Ravenclaw! Not that I’m supposed to take sides, as a teacher …’ he added hastily.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They drank the Butterbeer in silence, until Harry voiced something he’d been wondering for a while.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s under a Dementor’s hood?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor Lupin lowered his bottle thoughtfully.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hmmm … well, the only people who really know are in no condition to tell us. You see, the Dementor only lowers its hood to use its last and worst weapon.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They call it the Dementors’ Kiss,’ said Lupin, with a slightly twisted smile. ‘It’s what Dementors do to those they wish to destroy utterly. I suppose there must be some kind of mouth under there, because they clamp their jaws upon the mouth of the victim and – and suck out his soul.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry accidentally spat out a bit of Butterbeer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What – they kill –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, no,’ said Lupin. ‘Much worse than that. You can exist without your soul, you know, as long as your brain and heart are still working. But you’ll have no sense of self any more, no memory, no … anything. There’s no chance at all of recovery. You’ll just – exist. As an empty shell. And your soul is gone for ever … lost.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin drank a little more Butterbeer, then said, ‘It’s the fate that awaits Sirius Black. It was in the Daily Prophet this morning. The Ministry have given the Dementors permission to perform it if they find him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sat stunned for a moment at the idea of someone having their soul sucked out through their mouth. But then he thought of Black.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He deserves it,’ he said suddenly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You think so?’ said Lupin lightly. ‘Do you really think anyone deserves that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry defiantly. ‘For … for some things …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He would have liked to have told Lupin about the conversation he’d overheard about Black in the Three Broomsticks, about Black betraying his mother and father, but it would have involved revealing that he’d gone to Hogsmeade without permission, and he knew Lupin wouldn’t be very impressed by that. So he finished his Butterbeer, thanked Lupin, and left the History of Magic classroom.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry half-wished that he hadn’t asked what was under a Dementor’s hood, the answer had been so horrible, and he was so lost in unpleasant thoughts of what it would feel like to have your soul sucked out of you, that he walked headlong into Professor McGonagall halfway up the stairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Do watch where you’re going, Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry, Professor –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve just been looking for you in the Gryffindor common room. Well, here it is, we’ve done everything we could think of, and there doesn’t seem to be anything wrong with it at all – you’ve got a very good friend somewhere, Potter …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry’s jaw dropped. She was holding out his Firebolt, and it looked as magnificent as ever.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I can have it back?’ Harry said weakly. ‘Seriously?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Seriously,’ said Professor McGonagall, and she was actually smiling. ‘I daresay you’ll need to get the feel of it before Saturday’s match, won’t you? And Potter – do try and win, won’t you? Or we’ll be out of the running for the eighth year in a row, as Professor Snape was kind enough to remind me only last night …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Speechless, Harry carried the Firebolt back upstairs towards Gryffindor Tower. As he turned a corner, he saw Ron dashing towards him, grinning from ear to ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘She gave it to you? Excellent! Listen, can I still have a go on it? Tomorrow?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah … anything …’ said Harry, his heart lighter than it had been in a month. ‘You know what – we should make it up with Hermione. She was only trying to help …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, all right,’ said Ron. ‘She’s in the common room now – working, for a change.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They turned into the corridor to Gryffindor Tower and saw Neville Longbottom, pleading with Sir Cadogan, who seemed to be refusing him entrance.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I wrote them down,’ Neville was saying tearfully, ‘but I must’ve dropped them somewhere!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘A likely tale!’ roared Sir Cadogan. Then, spotting Harry and Ron, ‘Good even, my fine young yeomen! Come clap this loon in irons, he is trying to force entry to the chambers within!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, shut up,’ said Ron, as he and Harry drew level with Neville.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve lost the passwords!’ Neville told them miserably. ‘I made him tell me what passwords he was going to use this week, because he keeps changing them, and now I don’t know what I’ve done with them!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oddsbodikins,’ said Harry to Sir Cadogan, who looked extremely disappointed and reluctantly swung forwards to let them into the common room. There was a sudden, excited murmur as every head turned and the next moment, Harry was surrounded by people exclaiming over his Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Where’d you get it, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Will you let me have a go?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Have you ridden it yet, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ravenclaw’ll have no chance, they’re all on Cleansweep Sevens!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Can I just hold it, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: After ten minutes or so, during which the Firebolt was passed around and admired from every angle, the crowd dispersed and Harry and Ron had a clear view of Hermione, the only person who hadn’t rushed over to them, bent over her work, and carefully avoiding their eyes. Harry and Ron approached her table and at last, she looked up.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I got it back,’ said Harry, grinning at her and holding up the Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘See, Hermione? There wasn’t anything wrong with it!’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well – there might have been!’ said Hermione. ‘I mean, at least you know now that it’s safe!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I suppose so,’ said Harry. ‘I’d better put it upstairs –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll take it!’ said Ron eagerly. ‘I’ve got to give Scabbers his Rat Tonic.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He took the Firebolt, and, holding it as if it were made of glass, carried it away up the boys’ staircase.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Can I sit down, then?’ Harry asked Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I suppose so,’ said Hermione, moving a great stack of parchment off a chair.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around at the cluttered table, at the long Arithmancy essay on which the ink was still glistening, at the even longer Muggle Studies essay (‘Explain why Muggles Need Electricity’) and at the Rune translation Hermione was now poring over.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How are you getting through all this stuff?’ Harry asked her.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, well – you know – working hard,’ said Hermione. Close to, Harry saw that she looked almost as tired as Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Why don’t you just drop a couple of subjects?’ Harry asked, watching her lifting books as she searched for her Rune dictionary.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I couldn’t do that!’ said Hermione, looking scandalised.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Arithmancy looks terrible,’ said Harry, picking up a very complicated-looking number chart.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, no, it’s wonderful!’ said Hermione earnestly. ‘It’s my favourite subject! It’s –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But exactly what was wonderful about Arithmancy, Harry never found out. At that precise moment, a strangled yell echoed down the boys’ staircase. The whole common room fell silent, staring, petrified, at the entrance. There came hurried footsteps, growing louder and louder – and then, Ron came leaping into view, dragging with him a bedsheet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘LOOK!’ he bellowed, striding over to Hermione’s table. ‘LOOK!’ he yelled, shaking the sheets in her face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron, what –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘SCABBERS! LOOK! SCABBERS!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione was leaning away from Ron, looking utterly bewildered. Harry looked down at the sheet Ron was holding. There was something red on it. Something that looked horribly like –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘BLOOD!’ Ron yelled into the stunned silence. ‘HE’S GONE! AND YOU KNOW WHAT WAS ON THE FLOOR?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘N-no,’ said Hermione, in a trembling voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron threw something down onto Hermione’s Rune translation. Hermione and Harry leaned forward. Lying on top of the weird, spiky shapes were several long, ginger cat hairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It looked like the end of Ron and Hermione’s friendship. Each was so angry with the other that Harry couldn’t see how they’d ever make it up.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron was enraged that Hermione had never taken Crookshanks’s attempts to eat Scabbers seriously, hadn’t bothered to keep a close enough watch on him and was still trying to pretend that Crookshanks was innocent by suggesting Ron look for Scabbers under all the boys’ beds. Hermione, meanwhile, maintained fiercely that Ron had no proof that Crookshanks had eaten Scabbers, that the ginger hairs might have been there since Christmas, and that Ron had been prejudiced against her cat ever since Crookshanks had landed on Ron’s head in the Magical Menagerie.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Personally, Harry was sure that Crookshanks had eaten Scabbers, and when he tried to point out to Hermione that the evidence all pointed that way, she lost her temper with Harry, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OK, side with Ron, I knew you would!’ she said shrilly. ‘First the Firebolt, now Scabbers, everything’s my fault, isn’t it! Just leave me alone, Harry, I’ve got a lot of work to do!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron had taken the loss of his rat very hard indeed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come on, Ron, you were always saying how boring Scabbers was,’ said Fred bracingly. ‘And he’s been off colour for ages, he was wasting away. It was probably better for him to snuff it quickly. One swallow – he probably didn’t feel a thing.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Fred!’ said Ginny indignantly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘All he did was eat and sleep, Ron, you said it yourself,’ said George.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He bit Goyle for us once!’ Ron said miserably. ‘Remember, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, that’s true,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘His finest hour,’ said Fred, unable to keep a straight face. ‘Let the scar on Goyle’s finger stand as a lasting tribute to his memory. Oh, come on, Ron, get yourself down to Hogsmeade and buy a new rat. What’s the point of moaning?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: In a last-ditch attempt to cheer Ron up, Harry persuaded him to come along to the Gryffindor team’s final practice before the Ravenclaw match, so that he could have a go on the Firebolt after they’d finished. This did seem to take Ron’s mind off Scabbers for a moment (‘Brilliant! Can I try and shoot a few goals on it?’) so they set off for the Quidditch pitch together.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Madam Hooch, who was still overseeing Gryffindor practices to keep an eye on Harry was just as impressed with the Firebolt as everyone else had been. She took it in her hands before take-off and gave them the benefit of her professional opinion.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Look at the balance on it! If the Nimbus series has a fault, it’s a slight list to the tail-end – you often find they develop a drag after a few years. They’ve updated the handle, too, a bit slimmer than the Cleansweeps, reminds me of the old Silver Arrows – a pity they’ve stopped making them, I learned to fly on one, and a very fine old broom it was too …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: She continued in this vein for some time, until Wood said, ‘Er – Madam Hooch? Is it OK if Harry has the Firebolt back? Only we need to practise …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh – right – here you are, then, Potter,’ said Madam Hooch. ‘I’ll sit over here with Weasley …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: She and Ron left the pitch to sit in the stadium, and the Gryffindor team gathered around Wood for his final instructions for tomorrow’s match.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, I’ve just found out who Ravenclaw are playing as Seeker. It’s Cho Chang. She’s a fourth-year, and she’s pretty good … I really hoped she wouldn’t be fit, she’s had some problems with injuries …’ Wood scowled his displeasure that Cho Chang had made a full recovery, then said, ‘On the other hand, she rides a Comet Two Sixty, which is going to look like a joke next to the Firebolt.’ He gave Harry’s broom a look of fervent admiration, then said, ‘OK, everyone, let’s go –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And at long last, Harry mounted his Firebolt, and kicked off from the ground.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was better than he’d ever dreamed. The Firebolt turned with the lightest touch; it seemed to obey his thoughts rather than his grip. It sped across the pitch at such speed that the stadium turned into a green and grey blur; Harry turned it so sharply that Alicia Spinnet screamed, then he went into a perfectly controlled dive, brushing the grassy pitch with his toes before rising thirty, forty, fifty feet into the air again –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, I’m letting the Snitch out!’ Wood called.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry turned and raced a Bludger towards the goalposts; he outstripped it easily, saw the Snitch dart out from behind Wood and within ten seconds had caught it tightly in his hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The team cheered madly. Harry let the Snitch go again, gave it a minute’s head start, then tore after it, weaving in and out of the others; he spotted it lurking near Katie Bell’s knee, looped her easily, and caught it again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was the best practice ever; the team, inspired by the presence of the Firebolt in their midst, performed their best moves faultlessly, and by the time they hit the ground again, Wood didn’t have a single criticism to make, which, as George Weasley pointed out, was a first.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t see what’s going to stop us tomorrow!’ said Wood. ‘Not unless – Harry, you’ve sorted your Dementor problem, haven’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, thinking of his feeble Patronus and wishing it was stronger.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dementors won’t turn up again, Oliver, Dumbledore’d do his nut,’ said Fred confidently.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, let’s hope not,’ said Wood. ‘Anyway – good work, everyone. Let’s get back to the Tower – turn in early …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m staying out for a bit, Ron wants a go on the Firebolt,’ Harry told Wood, and while the rest of the team headed off to the changing rooms, Harry strode over to Ron, who vaulted the barrier to the stands and came to meet him. Madam Hooch had fallen asleep in her seat.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Here you go,’ said Harry, handing Ron the Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron, an expression of ecstasy on his face, mounted the broom and zoomed off into the gathering darkness while Harry walked around the edge of the pitch, watching him. Night had fallen before Madam Hooch awoke with a start, told Harry and Ron off for not waking her, and insisted that they go back to the castle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry shouldered the Firebolt and he and Ron walked out of the shadowy stadium, discussing the Firebolt’s superbly smooth action, its phenomenal acceleration and its pinpoint turning.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They were halfway towards the castle when Harry, glancing to his left, saw something that made his heart turn over – a pair of eyes, gleaming out of the darkness.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stopped dead, his heart banging against his ribs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s the matter?’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry pointed. Ron pulled out his wand and muttered, ‘Lumos!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: A beam of light fell across the grass, hit the bottom of a tree and illuminated its branches; there, crouching amongst the budding leaves, was Crookshanks.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Get out of it!’ Ron roared, and he stooped down and seized a stone lying on the grass, but before he could do anything else, Crookshanks had vanished with one swish of his long ginger tail.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘See?’ Ron said furiously, chucking the stone down again. ‘She’s still letting him wander about wherever he wants – probably washing down Scabbers with a couple of birds now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t say anything. He took a deep breath as relief seeped through him; he had been sure for a moment that those eyes had belonged to the Grim. They set off for the castle once more. Slightly ashamed of his moment of panic, Harry didn’t say anything to Ron – nor did he look left or right until they had reached the well lit Entrance Hall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry went down to breakfast next morning with the rest of the boys in his dormitory, all of whom seemed to think the Firebolt deserved a sort of guard of honour. As Harry entered the Great Hall, heads turned in the direction of the Firebolt, and there was a good deal of excited muttering. Harry saw, with enormous satisfaction, that the Slytherin team were all looking thunderstruck.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you see his face?’ said Ron gleefully, looking back at Malfoy. ‘He can’t believe it! This is brilliant!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Wood, too, was basking in the reflected glory of the Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Put it here, Harry,’ he said, laying the broom in the middle of the table and carefully turning it so that its name faced upwards. People from the Ravenclaw and Hufflepuff tables were soon coming over to look. Cedric Diggory came over to congratulate Harry on having acquired such a superb replacement for his Nimbus, and Percy’s Ravenclaw girlfriend, Penelope Clearwater, asked if she could actually hold the Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, now, Penny, no sabotage!’ said Percy heartily, as she examined the Firebolt closely. ‘Penelope and I have got a bet on,’ he told the team. ‘Ten Galleons on the outcome of the match!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Penelope put the Firebolt down again, thanked Harry and went back to her table.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry – make sure you win,’ said Percy, in an urgent whisper. ‘I haven’t got ten Galleons. Yes, I’m coming, Penny!’ And he bustled off to join her in a piece of toast.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sure you can manage that broom, Potter?’ said a cold, drawling voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Draco Malfoy had arrived for a closer look, Crabbe and Goyle right behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, reckon so,’ said Harry casually.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Got plenty of special features, hasn’t it?’ said Malfoy, eyes glittering maliciously. ‘Shame it doesn’t come with a parachute – in case you get too near a Dementor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle sniggered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Pity you can’t attach an extra arm to yours, Malfoy,’ said Harry. ‘Then it could catch the Snitch for you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Gryffindor team laughed loudly. Malfoy’s pale eyes narrowed, and he stalked away. They watched him rejoin the rest of the Slytherin team, who put their heads together, no doubt asking Malfoy whether Harry’s broom really was a Firebolt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: At a quarter to eleven, the Gryffindor team set off for the changing rooms. The weather couldn’t have been more different from their match against Hufflepuff. It was a clear, cool day, with a very light breeze; there would be no visibility problems this time, and Harry, though nervous, was starting to feel the excitement only a Quidditch match could bring. They could hear the rest of the school moving into the stadium beyond. Harry took off his black school robes, removed his wand from his pocket, and stuck it inside the T-shirt he was going to wear under his Quidditch robes. He only hoped he wouldn’t need it. He wondered suddenly whether Professor Lupin was in the crowd, watching.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You know what we’ve got to do,’ said Wood, as they prepared to leave the changing rooms. ‘If we lose this match, we’re out of the running. Just – just fly like you did in practice yesterday, and we’ll be OK!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They walked out onto the pitch to tumultuous applause. The Ravenclaw team, dressed in blue, were already standing in the middle of the pitch. Their Seeker, Cho Chang, was the only girl in their team. She was shorter than Harry by about a head, and Harry couldn’t help noticing, nervous as he was, that she was extremely pretty. She smiled at Harry as the teams faced each other behind their captains, and he felt a slight jolt in the region of his stomach that he didn’t think had anything to do with nerves.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Wood, Davies, shake hands,’ Madam Hooch said briskly, and Wood shook hands with the Ravenclaw captain.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mount your brooms … on my whistle … three – two – one –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry kicked off into the air and the Firebolt zoomed higher and faster than any other broom; he soared around the stadium and began squinting around for the Snitch, listening all the while to the commentary, which was being provided by the Weasley twins’ friend, Lee Jordan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re off, and the big excitement this match is the Firebolt which Harry Potter is flying for Gryffindor. According to Which Broomstick, the Firebolt’s going to be the broom of choice for the national teams at this year’s World Championship –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Jordan, would you mind telling us what’s going on in the match?’ interrupted Professor McGonagall’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Right you are, Professor – just giving a bit of background information. The Firebolt, incidentally, has a built-in auto-brake and –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Jordan!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OK, OK, Gryffindor in possession, Katie Bell of Gryffindor heading for goal …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry streaked past Katie in the opposite direction, gazing around for a glint of gold and noticing that Cho Chang was tailing him closely. She was undoubtedly a very good flier – she kept cutting across him, forcing him to change direction.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Show her your acceleration, Harry!’ Fred yelled, as he whooshed past in pursuit of a Bludger that was aiming for Alicia.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry urged the Firebolt forward as they rounded the Ravenclaw goalposts and Cho fell behind. Just as Katie succeeded in scoring the first goal of the match, and the Gryffindor end of the pitch went wild, he saw it – the Snitch was close to the ground, flitting near one of the barriers.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry dived; Cho saw what he was doing and tore after him. Harry was speeding up, excitement flooding him; dives were his speciality. He was ten feet away –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Then a Bludger, hit by one of the Ravenclaw Beaters, came pelting out of nowhere; Harry veered off course, avoiding it by an inch, and in those few, crucial seconds, the Snitch had vanished.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a great ‘Ooooooh’ of disappointment from the Gryffindor supporters, but much applause for their Beater from the Ravenclaw end. George Weasley vented his feelings by hitting the second Bludger directly at the offending Beater, who was forced to roll right over in mid-air to avoid it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Gryffindor lead by eighty points to zero, and look at that Firebolt go! Potter’s really putting it through its paces now. See it turn – Chang’s Comet is just no match for it. The Firebolt’s precision-balance is really noticeable in these long –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘JORDAN! ARE YOU BEING PAID TO ADVERTISE FIREBOLTS? GET ON WITH THE COMMENTARY!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ravenclaw were pulling back; they had now scored three goals, which put Gryffindor only fifty points ahead – if Cho got the Snitch before him, Ravenclaw would win. Harry dropped lower, narrowly avoiding a Ravenclaw Chaser, scanning the pitch frantically. A glint of gold, a flutter of tiny wings – the Snitch was circling the Gryffindor goalpost …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry accelerated, eyes fixed on the speck of gold ahead – but next second, Cho had appeared out of thin air, blocking him –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘HARRY, THIS IS NO TIME TO BE A GENTLEMAN!’ Wood roared, as Harry swerved to avoid a collision. ‘KNOCK HER OFF HER BROOM IF YOU HAVE TO!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry turned and caught sight of Cho; she was grinning. The Snitch had vanished again. Harry turned his Firebolt upwards and was soon twenty feet above the game. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Cho following him … she’d decided to mark him rather than search for the Snitch herself. Right then … if she wanted to tail him, she’d have to take the consequences …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He dived again, and Cho, thinking he’d seen the Snitch, tried to follow. Harry pulled out of the dive very sharply, she hurtled downwards; he rose fast as a bullet once more, and then saw it, for the third time: the Snitch was glittering way above the pitch at the Ravenclaw end.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He accelerated; so, many feet below, did Cho. He was winning, gaining on the Snitch with every second – then –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh!’ screamed Cho, pointing.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Distracted, Harry looked down.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Three Dementors, three tall, black, hooded Dementors, were looking up at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He didn’t stop to think. Plunging a hand down the neck of his robes, he whipped out his wand and roared, ‘Expecto patronum!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Something silver white, something enormous, erupted from the end of his wand. He knew it had shot directly at the Dementors but didn’t pause to watch; his mind still miraculously clear, he looked ahead – he was nearly there. He stretched out the hand still grasping his wand and just managed to close his fingers over the small, struggling Snitch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Madam Hooch’s whistle sounded, Harry turned around in midair and saw six scarlet blurs bearing down on him. Next moment, the whole team were hugging him so hard he was nearly pulled off his broom. Down below he could hear the roars of the Gryffindors in the crowd.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s my boy!’ Wood kept yelling. Alicia, Angelina and Katie had all kissed Harry, and Fred had him in a grip so tight Harry felt as though his head would come off. In complete disarray, the team managed to make its way back to the ground. Harry got off his broom and looked up to see a gaggle of Gryffindor supporters sprinting onto the pitch, Ron in the lead. Before he knew it, he had been engulfed by the cheering crowd.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes!’ Ron yelled, yanking Harry’s arm into the air. ‘Yes! Yes!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well done, Harry!’ said Percy, looking delighted. ‘Ten Galleons to me! Must find Penelope, excuse me –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Good on you, Harry!’ roared Seamus Finnigan.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ruddy brilliant!’ boomed Hagrid over the heads of the milling Gryffindors.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That was quite some Patronus,’ said a voice in Harry’s ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry turned around to see Professor Lupin, who looked both shaken and pleased.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dementors didn’t affect me at all!’ Harry said excitedly. ‘I didn’t feel a thing!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That would be because they – er – weren’t Dementors,’ said Professor Lupin. ‘Come and see –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He led Harry out of the crowd until they were able to see the edge of the pitch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You gave Mr Malfoy quite a fright,’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stared. Lying in a crumpled heap on the ground were Malfoy, Crabbe, Goyle and Marcus Flint, the Slytherin team captain, all struggling to remove themselves from long, black, hooded robes. It looked as though Malfoy had been standing on Goyle’s shoulders. Standing over them, with an expression of the utmost fury on her face, was Professor McGonagall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘An unworthy trick!’ she was shouting. ‘A low and cowardly attempt to sabotage the Gryffindor Seeker! Detention for all of you, and fifty points from Slytherin! I shall be speaking to Professor Dumbledore about this, make no mistake! Ah, here he comes now!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: If anything could have set the seal on Gryffindor’s victory, it was this. Ron, who had fought his way through to Harry’s side, doubled up with laughter as they watched Malfoy fighting to extricate himself from the robe, Goyle’s head still stuck inside it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come on, Harry!’ said George, fighting his way over. ‘Party! Gryffindor common room, now!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Right,’ said Harry, and feeling happier than he had done in ages, he and the rest of the team led the way, still in their scarlet robes, out of the stadium and back up to the castle.

text_content: ‘Are you sure you weren’t dreaming, Ron?’

text_content: No one in Gryffindor Tower slept that night. They knew that the castle was being searched again, and the whole house stayed awake in the common room, waiting to hear whether Black had been caught. Professor McGongall came back at dawn, to tell them that he had again escaped.

text_content: Everywhere they went next day they saw signs of tighter security; Professor Flitwick could be seen teaching the front doors to recognise a large picture of Sirius Black; Filch was suddenly bustling up and down the corridors, boarding up everything from tiny cracks in the walls to mouse holes. Sir Cadogan had been sacked. His portrait had been taken back to its lonely landing on the seventh floor, and the Fat Lady was back. She had been expertly restored, but was still extremely nervous, and had only agreed to return to her job on condition that she was given extra protection. A bunch of surly security trolls had been hired to guard her. They paced the corridor in a menacing group, talking in grunts and comparing the size of their clubs.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you reckon we should tell someone?’ Harry asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

For the first time in his life, people were paying more attention to him than to Harry, and it was clear that Ron was rather enjoying the experience. Though still severely shaken by the night’s events, he was happy to tell anyone who asked, what had happened, with a wealth of detail.

text_content: ‘ was asleep, and I heard this ripping noise, and I thought it was in my dream, you know? book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Why, though?’ Ron added to Harry, as the group of second-year girls who had been listening to his chilling tale departed. ‘Why did he scarper?’

text_content: Harry had been wondering the same thing. Why had Black, having got the wrong bed, not silenced Ron and proceeded to Harry? Black had proved twelve years ago that he didn’t mind murdering innocent people, and this time he had been facing five unarmed boys, four of whom were asleep.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He must’ve known he’d have a job getting back out of the castle once you’d yelled and woken people up,’ said Harry thoughtfully. ‘He’d’ve had to kill the whole house to get back through the portrait hole … then he would’ve met the teachers …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Neville was in total disgrace. Professor McGonagall was so furious with him she had banned him from all future Hogsmeade visits, given him a detention and forbidden anyone to give him the password into the Tower. Poor Neville was forced to wait outside the common room every night for somebody to let him in, while the security trolls leered unpleasantly at him. None of these punishments, however, came close to matching the one his grandmother had in store for him. Two days after Black’s break-in, she sent Neville the very worst thing a Hogwarts student could receive over breakfast – a Howler.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The school owls swooped into the Great Hall, carrying the post as usual, and Neville choked as a huge barn owl landed in front of him, a scarlet envelope clutched in its beak. book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

He seized the envelope and, holding it before him like a bomb, sprinted out of the Hall, while the Slytherin table exploded with laughter at the sight of him. They heard the Howler go off in the Entrance Hall – Neville’s grandmother’s voice, magically magnified to a hundred times its usual volume, shrieking about how he had brought shame on the whole family.
