book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, completely hidden beneath the Invisibility Cloak, emerged into the sunlight outside Honeydukes and prodded Ron in the back.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s me,’ he muttered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What kept you?’ Ron hissed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Snape was hanging around …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They set off up the High Street.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Where are you?’ Ron kept muttering out of the corner of his mouth. ‘Are you still there? This feels weird …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They went to the Post Office; Ron pretended to be checking the price of an owl to Bill in Egypt so that Harry could have a good look around. The owls sat hooting softly down at him, at least three hundred of them; from Great Greys right down to tiny little Scops owls (‘Local Deliveries Only’) which were so small they could have sat in the palm of Harry’s hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Then they visited Zonko’s, which was so packed with students Harry had to exercise great care not to tread on anyone and cause a panic. There were jokes and tricks to fulfil even Fred and George’s wildest dreams; Harry gave Ron whispered orders and passed him some gold from under the Cloak. They left Zonko’s with their money bags considerably lighter than they had been on entering, but their pockets bulging with Dungbombs, Hiccough Sweets, Frog Spawn Soap and a Nose-Biting Teacup apiece.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The day was fine and breezy, and neither of them felt like staying indoors, so they walked past the Three Broomsticks and climbed a slope to visit the Shrieking Shack, the most haunted dwelling in Britain. It stood a little way above the rest of the village, and even in daylight was slightly creepy, with its boarded windows and dank overgrown garden.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Even the Hogwarts ghosts avoid it,’ said Ron, as they leaned on the fence, looking up at it. ‘I asked Nearly Headless Nick … he says he’s heard a very rough crowd live here. No one can get in. Fred and George tried, obviously, but all the entrances are sealed shut …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, feeling hot from their climb, was just considering taking off the Cloak for a few minutes, when they heard voices nearby. Someone was climbing towards the house from the other side of the hill; moments later, Malfoy had appeared, followed closely by Crabbe and Goyle. Malfoy was speaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘… should have an owl from Father any time now. He had to go to the hearing to tell them about my arm … about how I couldn’t use it for three months …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle sniggered.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I really wish I could hear that great hairy moron trying to defend himself … ‘There’s no ’arm in ’im , ’onest –’ … that Hippogriff’s as good as dead –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy suddenly caught sight of Ron. His pale face split in a malevolent grin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What are you doing, Weasley?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy looked up at the crumbling house behind Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Suppose you’d love to live here, wouldn’t you, Weasley? Dreaming about having your own bedroom? I heard your family all sleep in one room – is that true?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry seized the back of Ron’s robes to stop him leaping on Malfoy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Leave him to me,’ he hissed in Ron’s ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The opportunity was too perfect to miss. Harry crept silently around behind Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle, bent down and scooped a large handful of mud out of the path.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We were just discussing your friend Hagrid,’ Malfoy said to Ron. ‘Just trying to imagine what he’s saying to the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures. D’you think he’ll cry when they cut off his Hippogriff’s –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: SPLAT!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy’s head jerked forwards as the mud hit him; his silver-blond hair was suddenly dripping in muck.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What the –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Ron had to hold onto the fence to keep himself standing, he was laughing so hard. Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle spun stupidly on the spot, staring wildly around, Malfoy trying to wipe his hair clean.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What was that? Who did that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Very haunted up here, isn’t it?’ said Ron, with the air of one commenting on the weather.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle were looking scared. Their bulging muscles were no use against ghosts. Malfoy was staring madly around at the deserted landscape.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sneaked along the path, where a particularly sloppy puddle yielded some foul-smelling, green sludge.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: SPLATTER!

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle caught some this time. Goyle hopped furiously on the spot, trying to rub it out of his small, dull eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It came from over there!’ said Malfoy, wiping his face, and staring at a spot some six feet to the left of Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Crabbe blundered forwards, his long arms outstretched like a zombie. Harry dodged around him, picked up a stick, and lobbed it at Crabbe’s back. Harry doubled up with silent laughter as Crabbe did a kind of pirouette in mid-air, trying to see who had thrown it. As Ron was the only person Crabbe could see, it was Ron he started towards, but Harry stuck out his leg. Crabbe stumbled – and his huge, flat foot caught the hem of Harry’s Cloak. Harry felt a great tug, then the Cloak slid off his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: For a split second, Malfoy stared at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘AAARGH!’ he yelled, pointing at Harry’s head. Then he turned tail and ran, at breakneck speed, back down the hill, Crabbe and Goyle behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry tugged the Cloak up again, but the damage was done.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ Ron said, stumbling forward and staring hopelessly at the point where Harry had disappeared, ‘you’d better run for it! If Malfoy tells anyone – you’d better get back to the castle, quick –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘See you later,’ said Harry, and without another word, he tore back down the path towards Hogsmeade.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Would Malfoy believe what he had seen? Would anyone believe Malfoy? Nobody knew about the Invisibility Cloak – nobody except Dumbledore. Harry’s stomach turned over – Dumbledore would know exactly what had happened, if Malfoy said anything –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Back into Honeydukes, back down the cellar steps, across the stone floor, through the trapdoor – Harry pulled off the Cloak, tucked it under his arm, and ran, flat out, along the passage …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Malfoy would get back first … how long would it take him to find a teacher? Panting, a sharp pain in his side, Harry didn’t slow down until he reached the stone slide. He would have to leave the Cloak where it was, it was too much of a giveaway if Malfoy had tipped off a teacher. He hid it in a shadowy corner, then started to climb, fast as he could, his sweaty hands slipping on the sides of the chute. He reached the inside of the witch’s hump, tapped it with his wand, stuck his head through and hoisted himself out; the hump closed, and just as Harry jumped out from behind the statue, he heard quick footsteps approaching.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was Snape. He approached Harry at a swift walk, his black robes swishing, then stopped in front of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a look of suppressed triumph about him. Harry tried to look innocent, all too aware of his sweaty face and his muddy hands, which he quickly hid in his pockets.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come with me, Potter,’ said Snape.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry followed him downstairs, trying to wipe his hands clean on the inside of his robes without Snape noticing. They walked down the stairs to the dungeons and then into Snape’s office.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had only been in here once before, and he had been in very serious trouble then, too. Snape had aquired a few more horrible slimy things in jars since last time, all standing on shelves behind his desk, glinting in the firelight and adding to the threatening atmosphere.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sit,’ said Snape.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry sat. Snape, however, remained standing.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Malfoy has just been to see me with a strange story, Potter,’ said Snape.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t say anything.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘He tells me that he was up by the Shrieking Shack when he ran into Weasley – apparently alone.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Still, Harry didn’t speak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Malfoy states that he was standing talking to Weasley, when a large amount of mud hit him in the back of the head. How do you think that could have happened?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry tried to look mildly surprised.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know, Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape’s eyes were boring into Harry’s. It was exactly like trying to stare out a Hippogriff. Harry tried hard not to blink.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Malfoy then saw an extraordinary apparition. Can you imagine what it might have been, Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry, now trying to sound innocently curious.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It was your head, Potter. Floating in mid-air.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: There was a long silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Maybe he’d better go to Madam Pomfrey,’ said Harry. ‘If he’s seeing things like –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What would your head have been doing in Hogsmeade, Potter?’ said Snape softly. ‘Your head is not allowed in Hogsmeade. No part of your body has permission to be in Hogsmeade.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I know that,’ said Harry, striving to keep his face free of guilt or fear. ‘It sounds like Malfoy’s having hallucin–’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Malfoy is not having hallucinations,’ snarled Snape, and he bent down, a hand on each arm of Harry’s chair, so that their faces were a foot apart. ‘If your head was in Hogsmeade, so was the rest of you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve been up in Gryffindor Tower,’ said Harry. ‘Like you told –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Can anyone confirm that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t say anything. Snape’s thin mouth curled into a horrible smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So,’ he said, straightening up again. ‘Everyone from the Minister for Magic downwards has been trying to keep famous Harry Potter safe from Sirius Black. But famous Harry Potter is a law unto himself. Let the ordinary people worry about his safety! Famous Harry Potter goes where he wants to, with no thought for the consequences.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry stayed silent. Snape was trying to provoke him into telling the truth. He wasn’t going to do it. Snape had no proof – yet.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘How extraordinarily like your father you are, Potter,’ Snape said suddenly, his eyes glinting. ‘He, too, was exceedingly arrogant. A small amount of talent on the Quidditch pitch made him think he was a cut above the rest of us, too. Strutting around the place with his friends and admirers … the resemblance between you is uncanny.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘My dad didn’t strut,’ said Harry, before he could stop himself. ‘And nor do I.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Your father didn’t set much store by rules, either,’ Snape went on, pressing his advantage, his thin face full of malice. ‘Rules were for lesser mortals, not Quidditch Cup-winners. His head was so swollen –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘SHUT UP!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was suddenly on his feet. Rage such as he had not felt since his last night in Privet Drive was thundering through him. He didn’t care that Snape’s face had gone rigid, the black eyes flashing dangerously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What did you say to me, Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I told you to shut up about my dad!’ Harry yelled. ‘I know the truth, all right? He saved your life! Dumbledore told me! You wouldn’t even be here if it weren’t for my dad!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape’s sallow skin had gone the colour of sour milk.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And did the Headmaster tell you the circumstances in which your father saved my life?’ he whispered. ‘Or did he consider the details too unpleasant for precious Potter’s delicate ears?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry bit his lip. He didn’t know what had happened and didn’t want to admit it – but Snape seemed to have guessed the truth.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I would hate you to run away with a false idea of your father, Potter,’ he said, a terrible grin twisting his face. ‘Have you been imagining some act of glorious heroism? Then let me correct you – your saintly father and his friends played a highly amusing joke on me that would have resulted in my death if your father hadn’t got cold feet at the last moment. There was nothing brave about what he did. He was saving his own skin as much as mine. Had their joke succeeded, he would have been expelled from Hogwarts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape’s uneven, yellowish teeth were bared.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Turn out your pockets, Potter!’ he spat suddenly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t move. There was a pounding in his ears.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Turn out your pockets, or we go straight to the Headmaster! Pull them out, Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Cold with dread, Harry slowly pulled out the bag of Zonko’s tricks and the Marauder’s Map.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape picked up the Zonko’s bag.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron gave them to me,’ said Harry, praying he’d get a chance to tip Ron off before Snape saw him. ‘He – brought them back from Hogsmeade last time –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Indeed? And you’ve been carrying them round ever since? How very touching … and what is this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape had picked up the map. Harry tried with all his might to keep his face impassive.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Spare bit of parchment,’ he shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape turned it over, his eyes on Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Surely you don’t need such a very old piece of parchment?’ he said. ‘Why don’t I just – throw this away?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: His hand moved towards the fire.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ Harry said quickly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So!’ said Snape, his long nostrils quivering. ‘Is this another treasured gift from Mr Weasley? Or is it – something else? A letter, perhaps, written in invisible ink? Or – instructions to get into Hogsmeade without passing the Dementors?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry blinked. Snape’s eyes gleamed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Let me see, let me see …’ he muttered, taking out his wand and smoothing the map out on his desk. ‘Reveal your secret!’ he said, touching the wand to the parchment.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Nothing happened. Harry clenched his hands to stop them shaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Show yourself!’ Snape said, tapping the map sharply.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It stayed blank. Harry was taking deep, calming breaths.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Severus Snape, master of this school, commands you to yield the information you conceal!’ Snape said, hitting the map with his wand.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: As though an invisible hand was writing upon it, words appeared on the smooth surface of the map.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Moony presents his compliments to Professor Snape, and begs him to keep his abnormally large nose out of other people’s business.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape froze. Harry stared, dumbstruck, at the message. But the map didn’t stop there. More writing was appearing beneath the first.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Prongs agrees with Mr Moony, and would like to add that Professor Snape is an ugly git.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It would have been very funny if the situation hadn’t been so serious. And there was more …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Padfoot would like to register his astonishment that an idiot like that ever became a Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry closed his eyes in horror. When he’d opened them, the map had had its last word.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Wormtail bids Professor Snape good day, and advises him to wash his hair, the slimeball.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry waited for the blow to fall.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘So …’ said Snape softly. ‘We’ll see about this …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He strode across to his fire, seized a fistful of glittering powder from a jar on the fireplace, and threw it into the flames.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Lupin!’ Snape called into the fire. ‘I want a word!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Utterly bewildered, Harry stared at the fire. A large shape had appeared in it, revolving very fast. Seconds later, Professor Lupin was clambering out of the fireplace, brushing ash off his shabby robes.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You called, Severus?’ said Lupin mildly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I certainly did,’ said Snape, his face contorted with fury as he strode back to his desk. ‘I have just asked Potter to empty his pockets. He was carrying this.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Snape pointed at the parchment, on which the words of Messrs Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs were still shining. An odd, closed expression appeared on Lupin’s face.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well?’ said Snape.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin continued to stare at the map. Harry had the impression that Lupin was doing some very quick thinking.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well?’ said Snape again. ‘This parchment is plainly full of Dark Magic. This is supposed to be your area of expertise, Lupin. Where do you imagine Potter got such a thing?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lupin looked up and, by the merest half-glance in Harry’s direction, warned him not to interrupt.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Full of Dark Magic?’ he repeated mildly. ‘Do you really think so, Severus? It looks to me as though it is merely a piece of parchment that insults anybody who tries to read it. Childish, but surely not dangerous? I imagine Harry got it from a joke-shop –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Indeed?’ said Snape. His jaw had gone rigid with anger. ‘You think a joke-shop could supply him with such a thing? You don’t think it more likely that he got it directly from the manufacturers?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t understand what Snape was talking about. Nor, apparently, did Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You mean, from Mr Wormtail or one of these people?’ he said. ‘Harry, do you know any of these men?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry quickly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You see, Severus?’ said Lupin, turning back to Snape. ‘It looks like a Zonko product to me –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Right on cue, Ron came bursting into the office. He was completely out of breath, and stopped just short of Snape’s desk, clutching the stitch in his chest and trying to speak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I – gave – Harry – that – stuff,’ he choked. ‘Bought – it – in Zonkos – ages – ago …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Well!’ said Lupin, clapping his hands together and looking around cheerfully. ‘That seems to clear that up! Severus, I’ll take this back, shall I?’ He folded the map and tucked it inside his robes. ‘Harry, Ron, come with me, I need a word about my vampire essay. Excuse us, Severus.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry didn’t dare look at Snape as they left his office. He, Ron and Lupin walked all the way back into the Entrance Hall before speaking. Then Harry turned to Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor, I –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t want to hear explanations,’ said Lupin shortly. He glanced around the empty Entrance Hall and lowered his voice. ‘I happen to know that this map was confiscated by Mr Filch many years ago. Yes, I know it’s a map,’ he said, as Harry and Ron looked amazed. ‘I don’t want to know how it fell into your possession. I am, however, astounded that you didn’t hand it in. Particularly after what happened the last time a student left information about the castle lying around. And I can’t let you have it back, Harry’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had expected that, and was too keen for explanations to protest.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Why did Snape think I’d got it from the manufacturers?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Because …’ Lupin hesitated, ‘because these mapmakers would have wanted to lure you out of school. They’d think it extremely entertaining.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Do you know them?’ said Harry, impressed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ve met,’ he said shortly. He was looking at Harry more seriously than ever before.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t expect me to cover up for you again, Harry. I cannot make you take Sirius Black seriously. But I would have thought that what you have heard when the Dementors draw near you would have had more of an effect on you. Your parents gave their lives to keep you alive, Harry. A poor way to repay them – gambling their sacrifice for a bag of magic tricks.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He walked away, leaving Harry feeling worse by far than he had at any point in Snape’s office. Slowly, he and Ron mounted the marble staircase. As Harry passed the one-eyed witch, he remembered the Invisibility Cloak – it was still down there, but he didn’t dare go and get it.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s my fault,’ said Ron abruptly. ‘I persuaded you to go. Lupin’s right, it was stupid, we shouldn’t’ve done it –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He broke off; they had reached the corridor where the security trolls were pacing, and Hermione was walking towards them. One look at her face convinced Harry that she had heard what had happened. His heart plummeted – had she told Professor McGonagall?

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come to have a good gloat?’ said Ron savagely, as she stopped in front of them. ‘Or have you just been to tell on us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Hermione. She was holding a letter in her hands and her lip was trembling. ‘I just thought you ought to know … Hagrid lost his case. Buckbeak is going to be executed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: None of them spoke as they changed into their scarlet robes. Harry wondered if they were feeling like he was: as though he’d eaten something extremely wriggly for breakfast. In what seemed like no time at all, Wood was saying, ‘OK, it’s time, let’s go …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They walked out onto the pitch to a tidal wave of noise. Three-quarters of the crowd were wearing scarlet rosettes, waving scarlet flags with the Gryffindor lion upon them or brandishing banners with slogans such as ‘GO GRYFFINDOR!’ and ‘LIONS FOR THE CUP!’. Behind the Slytherin goalposts, however, two hundred people were wearing green; the silver serpent of Slytherin glittered on their flags, and Professor Snape sat in the very front row, wearing green like everyone else, and a very grim smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And here are the Gryffindors!’ yelled Lee Jordan, who was acting as commentator as usual. ‘Potter, Bell, Johnson, Spinnet, Weasley, Weasley and Wood. Widely acknowledged as the best side Hogwarts has seen in a good few years –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lee’s comments were drowned by a tide of ‘boos’ from the Slytherin end.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And here come the Slytherin team, led by captain Flint. He’s made some changes in the line-up and seems to be going for size rather than skill –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: More boos from the Slytherin crowd. Harry, however, thought Lee had a point. Malfoy was easily the smallest person on the Slytherin team; the rest of them were enormous.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Captains, shake hands!’ said Madam Hooch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Flint and Wood approached each other and grasped each other’s hands very tightly; it looked as though each was trying to break the other’s fingers.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mount your brooms!’ said Madam Hooch. ‘Three … two … one …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The sound of her whistle was lost in the roar from the crowd as fourteen brooms rose into the air. Harry felt his hair fly back off his forehead; his nerves left him in the thrill of the flight; he glanced around, saw Malfoy on his tail, and sped off in search of the Snitch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And it’s Gryffindor in possession, Alicia Spinnet of Gryffindor with the Quaffle, heading straight for the Slytherin goalposts, looking good, Alicia! Argh, no – Quaffle intercepted by Warrington, Warrington of Slytherin tearing up the pitch – WHAM! – nice Bludger work there by George Weasley, Warrington drops the Quaffle, it’s caught by – Johnson, Gryffindor back in possession, come on, Angelina – nice swerve round Montague – duck, Angelina, that’s a Bludger! – SHE SCORES! TEN–ZERO TO GRYFFINDOR!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Angelina punched the air as she soared round the end of the pitch; the sea of scarlet below was screaming its delight –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘OUCH!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Angelina was nearly thrown from her broom as Marcus Flint went smashing into her.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry!’ said Flint, as the crowd below booed. ‘Sorry didn’t see her!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Next moment, Fred Weasley had chucked his Beater’s club at the back of Flint’s head. Flint’s nose smashed into the handle of his broom and began to bleed.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That will do!’ shrieked Madam Hooch, zooming between them. ‘Penalty to Gryffindor for an unprovoked attack on their Chaser! Penalty to Slytherin for deliberate damage to their Chaser!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come off it, Miss!’ howled Fred, but Madam Hooch blew her whistle and Alicia flew forward to take the penalty.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Come on, Alicia!’ yelled Lee into the silence that had descended on the crowd. ‘YES! SHE’S BEATEN THE KEEPER! TWENTY–ZERO TO GRYFFINDOR!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry turned the Firebolt sharply to watch Flint, still bleeding freely, fly forwards to take the Slytherin penalty. Wood was hovering in front of the Gryffindor goalposts, his jaw clenched.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Course, Wood’s a superb Keeper!’ Lee Jordan told the crowd, as Flint waited for Madam Hooch’s whistle. ‘Superb! Very difficult to pass – very difficult indeed – YES! I DON’T BELIEVE IT! HE’S SAVED IT!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Relieved, Harry zoomed away, gazing around for the Snitch, but still making sure he caught every word of Lee’s commentary. It was essential that he hold Malfoy off the Snitch until Gryffindor was more than fifty points up …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Gryffindor in possession, no, Slytherin in possession – no! – Gryffindor back in possession and it’s Katie Bell, Katie Bell for Gryffindor with the Quaffle, she’s streaking up the pitch – THAT WAS DELIBERATE!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Montague, a Slytherin Chaser, had swerved in front of Katie, and instead of seizing the Quaffle, had grabbed her head. Katie cartwheeled in the air, managed to stay on her broom but dropped the Quaffle.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Madam Hooch’s whistle rang out again as she soared over to Montague and began shouting at him. A minute later, Katie had put another penalty past the Slytherin Keeper.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘THIRTY–ZERO! TAKE THAT, YOU DIRTY, CHEATING –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Jordan, if you can’t commentate in an unbiased way –!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m telling it like it is, Professor!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry felt a huge jolt of excitement. He had seen the Snitch – it was shimmering at the foot of one of the Gryffindor goalposts – but he mustn’t catch it yet. And if Malfoy saw it …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Faking a look of sudden concentration, Harry pulled his Firebolt round and sped off towards the Slytherin end. It worked. Malfoy went haring after him, clearly thinking Harry had seen the Snitch there …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: WHOOSH.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: One of the Bludgers came streaking past Harry’s right ear, hit by the gigantic Slytherin Beater, Derrick. Next moment –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: WHOOSH.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The second Bludger had grazed Harry’s elbow. The other Beater, Bole, was closing in.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry had a fleeting glimpse of Bole and Derrick zooming towards him, clubs raised –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He turned the Firebolt upwards at the last second, and Bole and Derrick collided with a sickening crunch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Ha haaa!’ yelled Lee Jordan, as the Slytherin Beaters lurched away from each other, clutching their heads. ‘Too bad, boys! You’ll need to get up earlier than that to beat a Firebolt! And it’s Gryffindor in possession again, as Johnson takes the Quaffle – Flint alongside her – poke him in the eye, Angelina! – it was a joke, Professor, it was a joke – oh, no – Flint in possession, Flint flying towards the Gryffindor goalposts, come on, now, Wood, save –!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Flint had scored; there was an eruption of cheers from the Slytherin end and Lee swore so badly that Professor McGonagall tried to tug the magical megaphone away from him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry, Professor, sorry! Won’t happen again! So, Gryffindor in the lead, thirty points to ten, and Gryffindor in possession –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It was turning into the dirtiest match Harry had ever played in. Enraged that Gryffindor had taken such an early lead, the Slytherins were rapidly resorting to any means to take the Quaffle. Bole hit Alicia with his club and tried to say he’d thought she was a Bludger. George Weasley elbowed Bole in the face in retaliation. Madam Hooch awarded both teams penalties, and Wood pulled off another spectacular save, making the score forty-ten to Gryffindor.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Snitch had disappeared again. Malfoy was still keeping close to Harry as he soared over the match, looking around for it – once Gryffindor were fifty points ahead …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Katie scored. Fifty–ten. Fred and George Weasley were swooping around her, clubs raised, in case any of the Slytherins were thinking of revenge. Bole and Derrick took advantage of Fred and George’s absence to aim both Bludgers at Wood; they caught him in the stomach, one after the other, and he rolled over in the air, clutching his broom, completely winded.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Madam Hooch was beside herself.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You do not attack the Keeper unless the Quaffle is within the scoring area!’ she shrieked at Bole and Derrick. ‘Gryffindor penalty!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And Angelina scored. Sixty–ten. Moments later, Fred Weasley pelted a Bludger at Warrington, knocking the Quaffle out of his hands; Alicia seized it and put it through the Slytherin goal: seventy–ten.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: The Gryffindor crowd below were screaming themselves hoarse – Gryffindor were sixty points in the lead, and if Harry caught the Snitch now, the Cup was theirs. Harry could almost feel hundreds of eyes following him as he soared around the pitch, high above the rest of the game, with Malfoy speeding along behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then he saw it. The Snitch was sparkling twenty feet above him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry put on a huge burst of speed, the wind roaring in his ears; he stretched out his hand, but suddenly, the Firebolt was slowing down –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Horrified, he looked around. Malfoy had thrown himself forward, grabbed hold of the Firebolt’s tail and was pulling it back.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘You –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was angry enough to hit Malfoy, but he couldn’t reach. Malfoy was panting with the effort of holding onto the Firebolt, but his eyes were sparkling maliciously. He had achieved what he’d wanted – the Snitch had disappeared again.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Penalty! Penalty to Gryffindor! I’ve never seen such tactics!’ Madam Hooch screeched, shooting up to where Malfoy was sliding back onto his Nimbus Two Thousand and One.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘YOU CHEATING SCUM!’ Lee Jordan was howling into the megaphone, dancing out of Professor McGonagall’s reach. ‘YOU FILTHY, CHEATING B –’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall didn’t even bother to tell him off. She was actually shaking her fist in Malfoy’s direction; her hat had fallen off, and she, too, was shouting furiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Alicia took Gryffindor’s penalty, but she was so angry she missed by several feet. The Gryffindor team was losing concentration and the Slytherins, delighted by Malfoy’s foul on Harry, were being spurred on to greater heights.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Slytherin in possession, Slytherin heading for goal – Montague scores –’ Lee groaned. ‘Seventy–twenty to Gryffindor …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry was now marking Malfoy so closely their knees kept hitting each other. Harry wasn’t going to let Malfoy anywhere near the Snitch …

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Get out of it, Potter!’ Malfoy yelled in frustration, as he tried to turn and found Harry blocking him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Angelina Johnson gets the Quaffle for Gryffindor, come on, Angelina, COME ON!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry looked round. Every single Slytherin player apart from Malfoy, even the Slytherin Keeper, was streaking up the pitch towards Angelina – they were all going to block her –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry wheeled the Firebolt about, bent so low he was lying flat along the handle and kicked it forwards. Like a bullet, he shot towards the Slytherins.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘AAAAAAARRRGH!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They scattered as the Firebolt zoomed towards them; Angelina’s way was clear.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘SHE SCORES! SHE SCORES! Gryffindor lead by eighty points to twenty!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry, who had almost pelted headlong into the stands, skidded to a halt in mid-air, reversed and zoomed back into the middle of the pitch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: And then he saw something to make his heart stand still. Malfoy was diving, a look of triumph on his face – there, a few feet above the grass below, was a tiny, golden glimmer.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry urged the Firebolt downwards but Malfoy was miles ahead.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Go! Go! Go!’ Harry urged his broom. They were gaining on Malfoy … Harry flattened himself to the broom handle as Bole sent a Bludger at him … he was at Malfoy’s ankles … he was level –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry threw himself forwards, taking both hands off his broom. He knocked Malfoy’s arm out of the way and –

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘YES!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He pulled out of his dive, his hand in the air, and the stadium exploded. Harry soared above the crowd, an odd ringing in his ears. The tiny golden ball was held tight in his fist, beating its wings hopelessly against his fingers.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Then Wood was speeding towards him, half-blinded by tears; he seized Harry around the neck and sobbed unrestrainedly into his shoulder. Harry felt two large thumps as Fred and George hit them; then Angelina, Alicia and Katie’s voices, ‘We’ve won the Cup! We’ve won the Cup!’ Tangled together in a many-armed hug, the Gryffindor team sank, yelling hoarsely, back to earth.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Wave upon wave of crimson supporters was pouring over the barriers onto the pitch. Hands were raining down on their backs. Harry had a confused impression of noise and bodies pressing in on him. Then he, and the rest of the team, were hoisted onto the shoulders of the crowd. Thrust into the light, he saw Hagrid, plastered with crimson rosettes – ‘Yeh beat ’em, Harry, yeh beat ’em! Wait till I tell Buckbeak!’ There was Percy, jumping up and down like a maniac, all dignity forgotten. Professor McGonagall was sobbing harder even than Wood, wiping her eyes with an enormous Gryffindor flag; and there, fighting their way towards Harry, were Ron and Hermione. Words failed them. They simply beamed, as Harry was borne towards the stands, where Dumbledore stood waiting with the enormous Quidditch Cup.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: If only there had been a Dementor around … As a sobbing Wood passed Harry the Cup, as he lifted it into the air, Harry felt he could have produced the world’s best Patronus.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry’s euphoria at finally winning the Quidditch Cup lasted at least a week. Even the weather seemed to be celebrating; as June approached, the days became cloudless and sultry, and all anybody felt like doing was strolling into the grounds and flopping down on the grass with several pints of iced pumpkin juice, perhaps playing a casual game of Gobstones or watching the giant squid propel itself dreamily across the surface of the lake.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But they couldn’t. The exams were nearly upon them, and instead of lazing around outside, the students were forced to remain inside the castle, trying to bully their brains into concentrating while enticing wafts of summer air drifted in through the windows. Even Fred and George Weasley had been spotted working; they were about to take their OWLs (Ordinary Wizarding Levels). Percy was getting ready to sit his NEWTs (Nastily Exhausting Wizarding Tests), the highest qualification Hogwarts offered. As Percy hoped to enter the Ministry of Magic, he needed top grades. He was becoming increasingly edgy, and gave very severe punishments to anybody who disturbed the quiet of the common room in the evenings. In fact, the only person who seemed more anxious than Percy was Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron had given up asking her how she was managing to attend several classes at once, but they couldn’t restrain themselves when they saw the exam timetable she had drawn up for herself. The first column read:

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: MONDAY

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: 9 o’clock, Arithmancy

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: 9 o’clock, Transfiguration

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Lunch

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: 1 o’clock, Charms

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: 1 o’clock, Ancient Runes

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione?’ Ron said cautiously, because she was liable to explode when interrupted these days. ‘Er – are you sure you’ve copied down these times right?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ snapped Hermione, picking up the exam timetable and examining it. ‘Yes, of course I have.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Is there any point asking how you’re going to sit two exams at once?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Hermione shortly. ‘Has either of you seen my copy of Numerology and Grammatica?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yeah, I borrowed it for a bit of bedtime reading,’ said Ron, but very quietly. Hermione started shifting heaps of parchment around on her table, looking for the book. Just then, there was a rustle at the window and Hedwig fluttered through it, a note clutched tightly in her beak.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s from Hagrid,’ said Harry, ripping the note open. ‘Buckbeak’s appeal – it’s set for the sixth.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the day we finish our exams,’ said Hermione, still looking everywhere for her Arithmancy book.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘And they’re coming up here to do it,’ said Harry, still reading from the letter. ‘Someone from the Ministry of Magic and – and an executioner.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked up, startled.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re bringing the executioner to the appeal! But that sounds as though they’ve already decided!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, it does,’ said Harry slowly.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘They can’t!’ Ron howled. ‘I’ve spent ages reading up stuff for him, they can’t just ignore it all!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: But Harry had a horrible feeling that the Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures had had its mind made up for it by Mr Malfoy. Draco, who had been noticeably subdued since Gryffindor’s triumph in the Quidditch final, seemed to regain some of his old swagger over the next few days. From sneering comments Harry overheard, Malfoy was certain Buckbeak was going to be killed, and seemed thoroughly pleased with himself for bringing it about. It was all Harry could do to stop himself imitating Hermione and hitting Malfoy in the face on these occasions. And the worst thing of all was that they had no time or opportunity to go and see Hagrid, because the strict new security measures had not been lifted, and Harry didn’t dare retrieve his Invisibility Cloak from below the one-eyed witch.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Exam week began and an unnatural hush fell over the castle. The third-years emerged from Transfiguration at lunchtime on Monday limp and ashen-faced, comparing results and bemoaning the difficulty of the tasks they had been set, which had included turning a teapot into a tortoise. Hermione irritated the rest by fussing about how her tortoise had looked more like a turtle, which was the least of everyone else’s worries.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Mine still had a spout for a tail, what a nightmare …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Were the tortoises supposed to breathe steam?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘It still had a willow-patterned shell, d’you think that’ll count against me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Then, after a hasty lunch, it was straight back upstairs for the Charms exam. Hermione had been right; Professor Flitwick did indeed test them on Cheering Charms. Harry slightly overdid his out of nerves and Ron, who was partnering him, ended up in fits of hysterical laughter and had to be led away to a quiet room for an hour before he was ready to perform the Charm himself. After dinner, the students hurried back to their common rooms, not to relax, but to start revising for Care of Magical Creatures, Potions and Astronomy.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Hagrid presided over the Care of Magical Creatures exam the following morning with a very preoccupied air indeed; his heart didn’t seem to be in it at all. He had provided a large tub of fresh Flobberworms for the class, and told them that, to pass the test, their Flobberworm had to still be alive at the end of one hour. As Flobberworms flourished best if left to their own devices, it was the easiest exam any of them had ever sat, and also gave Harry, Ron and Hermione plenty of opportunity to speak to Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Beaky’s gettin’ a bit depressed,’ Hagrid told them, bending low on the pretence of checking that Harry’s Flobberworm was still alive. ‘Bin cooped up too long. But still … we’ll know day after tomorrow – one way or the other.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: They had Potions that afternoon, which was an unqualified disaster. Try as Harry might, he couldn’t get his Confusing Concoction to thicken, and Snape, standing watching with an air of vindictive pleasure, scribbled something that looked suspiciously like a zero onto his notes before moving away.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Then came Astronomy at midnight, up on the tallest tower; History of Magic on Wednesday morning, in which Harry scribbled everything Florean Fortescue had ever told him about medieval witch hunts, while wishing he could have had one of Fortescue’s choco-nut sundaes with him in the stifling classroom. Wednesday afternoon meant Herbology in the greenhouses under a baking hot sun; then back to the common room once more, with the backs of their necks sunburnt, thinking longingly of this time next day, when it would all be over.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Their second from last exam, on Thursday morning, was Defence Against the Dark Arts. Professor Lupin had compiled the most unusual exam any of them had ever taken; a sort of obstacle course outside in the sun, where they had to wade across a deep paddling pool containing a Grindylow, cross a series of potholes full of Red Caps, squish their way across a patch of marsh, ignoring the misleading directions from a Hinkypunk, then climb into an old trunk and battle with a new Boggart.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Excellent, Harry,’ Lupin muttered, as Harry climbed out of the trunk, grinning. ‘Full marks.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Flushed with his success, Harry hung around to watch Ron and Hermione. Ron did very well until he reached the Hinkypunk, which successfully confused him into sinking waist-high into the quagmire. Hermione did everything perfectly until she reached the trunk with the Boggart in it. After about a minute inside it, she burst out again, screaming.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione!’ said Lupin, startled. ‘What’s the matter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘P-P-Professor McGonagall!’ Hermione gasped, pointing into the trunk. ‘Sh-she said I’d failed everything!’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: It took a little while to calm Hermione down. When at last she had regained a grip on herself, she, Harry and Ron went back to the castle. Ron was still slightly inclined to laugh at Hermione’s Boggart, but an argument was averted by the sight that met them on the top of the steps.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: Cornelius Fudge, sweating slightly in his pinstriped cloak, was standing there staring out at the grounds. He started at the sight of Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello there, Harry!’ he said. ‘Just had an exam, I expect? Nearly finished?’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry. Hermione and Ron, not being on speaking terms with the Minister for Magic, hovered awkwardly in the background.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Lovely day,’ said Fudge, casting an eye over the lake. ‘Pity … pity …’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: He sighed deeply and looked down at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m here on an unpleasant mission, Harry. The Committee for the Disposal of Dangerous Creatures required a witness to the execution of a mad Hippogriff. As I needed to visit Hogwarts to check on the Black situation, I was asked to step in.’

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
text_content: ‘Does that mean the appeal’s already happened?’ Ron interrupted, stepping forwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)

text_content: ‘He can go to Azkaban,’ Harry repeated. ‘If anyone deserves that place, he does …’

text_content: Pettigrew was still wheezing behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort

chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort
text_content: Harry stepped out of the way. Thin cords shot from Lupin’s wand this time, and next moment, Pettigrew was wriggling on the floor, bound and gagged.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort
text_content: ‘But if you transform, Peter,’ growled Black, his own wand pointing at Pettigrew, too, ‘we will kill you. You agree, Harry?’

chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort
text_content: Harry looked down at the pitiful figure on the floor, and nodded so that Pettigrew could see him.

book: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (UK)
chapter: Chapter Nineteen - The Servant of Lord Voldemort
text_content: ‘Right,’ said Lupin, suddenly business-like. ‘Ron, I can’t mend bones nearly as well as Madam Pomfrey, so I think it’s best if we just strap your leg up until we can get you to the hospital wing.’
