text_content: ‘Dumbledore, I’m afraid I don’t see the connection, don’t see it at all!’ It was the voice of the Minister for Magic, Cornelius Fudge. ‘Ludo says Bertha’s perfectly capable of getting herself lost. I agree we would have expected to have found her by now, but all the same, we’ve no evidence of foul play, Dumbledore, none at all. As for her disappearance being linked with Barty Crouch’s!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘And what do you think’s happened to Barty Crouch, Minister?’ said Moody’s growling voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I see two possibilities, Alastor,’ said Fudge. ‘Either Crouch has finally cracked - more than likely, I’m sure you’ll agree, given his personal history - lost his mind, and gone wandering off somewhere -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘He wandered extremely quickly, if that is the case, Cornelius,’ said Dumbledore calmly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Or else - well …’ Fudge sounded embarrassed. ‘Well, I’ll reserve judgement until after I’ve seen the place where he was found, but you say it was just past the Beauxbatons carriage? Dumbledore, you know what that woman is?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I consider her to be a very able Headmistress - and an excellent dancer,’ said Dumbledore quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore, come!’ said Fudge angrily. ‘Don’t you think you might be prejudiced in her favour because of Hagrid? They don’t all turn out harmless - if, indeed, you can call Hagrid harmless, with that monster fixation he’s got -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I no more suspect Madame Maxime than Hagrid,’ said Dumbledore, just as calmly. ‘I think it possible that it is you who are prejudiced, Cornelius.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Can we wrap up this discussion?’ growled Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, yes, let’s go down into the grounds, then,’ said Cornelius impatiently.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No, it’s not that,’ said Moody, ‘it’s just that Potter wants a word with you, Dumbledore. He’s just outside the door.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The door of the office opened.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello, Potter,’ said Moody. ‘Come in, then.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry walked inside. He had been inside Dumbledore’s office once before; it was a very beautiful, circular room, lined with pictures of previous Headmasters and mistresses of Hogwarts, all of whom were fast asleep, their chests rising and falling gently.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Cornelius Fudge was standing beside Dumbledore’s desk, wearing his usual pinstriped cloak and holding his lime-green bowler hat.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ said Fudge jovially, moving forwards. ‘How are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Fine,’ Harry lied.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘We were just talking about the night when Mr Crouch turned up in the grounds,’ said Fudge. ‘It was you who found him, was it not?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry. Then, feeling it was pointless to pretend that he hadn’t overheard what they had been saying, he added, ‘I didn’t see Madame Maxime anywhere, though, and she’d have a job hiding, wouldn’t she?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled at Harry behind Fudge’s back, his eyes twinkling.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, well,’ said Fudge, looking embarrassed, ‘we’re about to go for a short walk in the grounds, Harry, if you’ll excuse us … perhaps if you just go back to your class -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I wanted to talk to you, Professor,’ Harry said quickly, looking at Dumbledore, who gave him a swift, searching look.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Wait here for me, Harry,’ he said. ‘Our examination of the grounds will not take long.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: They trooped out in silence past him, and closed the door. After a minute or so, Harry heard the clunks of Moody’s wooden leg growing fainter in the corridor below. He looked around.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello, Fawkes,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Fawkes, Professor Dumbledore’s phoenix, was standing on his golden perch beside the door. The size of a swan, with magnificent scarlet and gold plumage, he swished his long tail and blinked benignly at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry sat down in a chair in front of Dumbledore’s desk. For several minutes, he sat and watched the old Headmasters and mistresses snoozing in their frames, thinking about what he had just heard, and running his fingers over his scar. It had stopped hurting now.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He felt much calmer, somehow, now he was in Dumbledore’s office, knowing he would shortly be telling him about the dream. Harry looked up at the walls behind the desk. The patched and ragged Sorting Hat was standing on a shelf. A glass case next to it held a magnificent silver sword, with large rubies set into the hilt, which Harry recognised as the one he himself had pulled out of the Sorting Hat in his second year. The sword had once belonged to Godric Gryffindor, founder of Harry’s house. He was gazing at it, remembering how it had come to his aid when he had thought all hope was lost, when he noticed a patch of silvery light, dancing and shimmering on the glass case. He looked around for the source of the light, and saw a sliver of silver white shining brightly from within a black cabinet behind him, whose door had not been closed properly. Harry hesitated, glanced at Fawkes, then got up, walked across the office, and pulled the cabinet door open.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: A shallow stone basin lay there, with odd carvings around the edge; runes and symbols that Harry did not recognise. The silvery light was coming from the basin’s contents, which were like nothing Harry had ever seen before. He could not tell whether the substance was liquid or gas. It was a bright, whitish silver, and it was moving ceaselessly; the surface of it became ruffled like water beneath wind, and then, like clouds, separated and swirled smoothly. It looked like light made liquid - or like wind made solid - Harry couldn’t make up his mind.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He wanted to touch it, to find out what it felt like, but nearly four years’ experience of the magical world told him that sticking his hand into a bowl full of some unknown substance was a very stupid thing to do. He therefore pulled his wand out of the inside of his robes, cast a nervous look around the office, looked back at the contents of the basin, and prodded them. The surface of the silvery stuff inside the basin began to swirl very fast.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry bent closer, his head right inside the cabinet. The silvery substance had become transparent; it looked like glass. He looked down into it, expecting to see the stone bottom of the basin - and saw instead an enormous room below the surface of the mysterious substance, a room into which he seemed to be looking through a circular window in the ceiling.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The room was dimly lit; he thought it might even be underground, for there were no windows, merely torches in brackets such as the ones that illuminated the walls of Hogwarts. Lowering his face so that his nose was a mere inch away from the glassy substance, Harry saw that rows and rows of witches and wizards were sat around every wall on what seemed to be benches rising in levels. An empty chair stood in the very centre of the room. There was something about the chair that gave Harry an ominous feeling. Chains encircled the arms of it, as though its occupants were usually tied to it.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Where was this place? It surely wasn’t Hogwarts; he had never seen a room like that here in the castle. Moreover, the crowd in the mysterious room at the bottom of the basin was composed of adults, and Harry knew there were not nearly that many teachers at Hogwarts. They seemed, he thought, to be waiting for something; even though he could only see the tops of their pointed hats, they all seemed to be facing in one direction, and nobody was talking to anybody else.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The basin being circular, and the room he was observing square, Harry could not make out what was going on in the corners of it. He leant even closer, tilting his head, trying to see …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The tip of his nose touched the strange substance into which he was staring.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore’s office gave an almighty lurch - Harry was thrown forwards and pitched headfirst into the substance inside the basin -

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But his head did not hit the stone bottom. He was falling through something icy cold and black; it was like being sucked into a dark whirlpool -

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: And suddenly, he found himself sitting on a bench at the end of the room inside the basin, a bench raised high above the others. He looked up at the high stone ceiling, expecting to see the circular window through which he had just been staring, but there was nothing there but dark, solid stone.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Breathing hard and fast, Harry looked around him. Not one of the witches and wizards in the room (and there were at least two hundred of them) was looking at him. Not one of them seemed to have noticed that a fourteen-year-old boy had just dropped from the ceiling into their midst. Harry turned to the wizard next to him on the bench, and uttered a loud cry of surprise that reverberated around the silent room.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He was sitting right next to Albus Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor!’ Harry said, in a kind of strangled whisper. ‘I’m sorry - I didn’t mean to - I was just looking at that basin in your cabinet - I - where are we?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But Dumbledore didn’t move or speak. He ignored Harry completely. Like every other wizard on the benches, he was staring into the far corner of the room, where there was a door.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry gazed, nonplussed, at Dumbledore, then around at the silently watchful crowd, then back at Dumbledore. And then it dawned on him …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Once before, Harry had found himself a place where nobody could see or hear him. That time, he had fallen through a page in an enchanted diary, right into somebody else’s memory … and unless he was very much mistaken, something of the sort had happened again …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry raised his right hand, hesitated, and then waved it energetically in front of Dumbledore’s face. Dumbledore did not blink, look around at Harry, or indeed move at all. And that, in Harry’s opinion, settled the matter. Dumbledore wouldn’t ignore him like that. He was inside a memory, and this was not the present-day Dumbledore. Yet it couldn’t be that long ago … the Dumbledore sitting next to him now was silver-haired, just like the present-day Dumbledore. But what was this place? What were all these wizards waiting for?

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around more carefully. The room, as he had suspected when observing it from above, was almost certainly underground - more of a dungeon than a room, he thought. There was a bleak and forbidding air about the place; there were no pictures on the walls, no decorations at all; just these serried rows of benches, rising in levels all around the room, all positioned so that they had a clear view of that chair with the chains on its arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Before Harry could reach any conclusions about the place in which they were, he heard footsteps. The door in the corner of the dungeon opened, and three people entered - or at least, one man, flanked by two Dementors.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry’s insides went cold. The Dementors, tall, hooded creatures whose faces were concealed, were gliding slowly towards the chair in the centre of the room, each grasping one of the man’s arms with their dead and rotten-looking hands. The man between them looked as though he was about to faint, and Harry couldn’t blame him … he knew the Dementors could not touch him inside a memory, but Harry remembered their power only too well. The watching crowd recoiled slightly as the Dementors placed the man in the chained chair and glided back out of the room. The door swung shut behind them.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry looked down at the man now sitting in the chair, and saw that it was Karkaroff.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Unlike Dumbledore, Karkaroff looked much younger; his hair and goatee were black. He was not dressed in sleek furs, but in thin and ragged robes. He was shaking. Even as Harry watched, the chains on the arms of the chair glowed suddenly gold, and snaked their way up his arms, binding him there.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Igor Karkaroff,’ said a curt voice to Harry’s left. Harry looked around, and saw Mr Crouch standing up in the middle of the bench beside him. Crouch’s hair was dark, his face was much less lined, he looked fit and alert. ‘You have been brought from Azkaban to give evidence to the Ministry of Magic. You have given us to understand that you have important information for us.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Karkaroff straightened himself as best he could, tightly bound to the chair.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I have, sir,’ he said, and although his voice was very scared, Harry could still hear the familiar unctuous note in it. ‘I wish to be of use to the Ministry. I wish to help. I - I know that the Ministry is trying to - to round up the last of the Dark Lord’s supporters. I am eager to assist in any way I can …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: There was a murmur around the benches. Some of the wizards and witches were surveying Karkaroff with interest, others with pronounced mistrust. Then Harry heard, quite distinctly, from Dumbledore’s other side, a familiar, growling voice saying, ‘Filth.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry leant forwards so that he could see past Dumbledore. Mad-Eye Moody was sitting there - though there was a very noticeable difference in his appearance. He did not have his magical eye, but two normal ones. Both were looking down upon Karkaroff, and both were narrowed in intense dislike.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Crouch is going to let him out,’ Moody breathed quietly to Dumbledore. ‘He’s done a deal with him. Took me six months to track him down, and Crouch is going to let him go if he’s got enough new names. Let’s hear his information, I say, and throw him straight back to the Dementors.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore made a small noise of dissent through his long, crooked nose.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, I was forgetting … you don’t like the Dementors, do you, Albus?’ said Moody, with a sardonic smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Dumbledore calmly, ‘I’m afraid I don’t. I have long felt the Ministry is wrong to ally itself with such creatures.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘But for filth like this …’ Moody said softly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You say you have names for us, Karkaroff,’ said Mr Crouch. ‘Let us hear them, please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You must understand,’ said Karkaroff hurriedly, ‘that He Who Must Not Be Named operated always in the greatest secrecy … he preferred that we -I mean to say, his supporters - and I regret now, very deeply, that I ever counted myself among them -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Get on with it,’ sneered Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘- we never knew the names of every one of our fellows - he alone knew exactly who we all were -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Which was a wise move, wasn’t it, as it prevented someone like you, Karkaroff, turning all of them in,’ muttered Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yet you say you have some names for us?’ said Mr Crouch.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I - I do,’ said Karkaroff breathlessly. ‘And these were important supporters, mark you. People I saw with my own eyes doing his bidding. I give this information as a sign that I fully and totally renounce him, and am filled with a remorse so deep I can barely -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘These names are?’ said Mr Crouch sharply.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Karkaroff drew a deep breath.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘There was Antonin Dolohov,’ he said. ‘I - I saw him torture countless Muggles and - and non-supporters of the Dark Lord.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘And helped him do it,’ murmured Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘We have already apprehended Dolohov,’ said Crouch. ‘He was caught shortly after yourself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Indeed?’ said Karkaroff, his eyes widening. ‘I - I am delighted to hear it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But he didn’t look it. Harry could tell that this news had come as a real blow to him. One of his names was worthless.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Any others?’ said Crouch coldly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Why, yes … there was Rosier,’ said Karkaroff hurriedly. ‘Evan Rosier.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Rosier is dead,’ said Crouch. ‘He was caught shortly after you were, too. He preferred to fight rather than coming quietly, and was killed in the struggle.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Took a bit of me with him, though,’ whispered Moody to Harry’s right. Harry looked around at him once more, and saw him indicating the large chunk out of his nose to Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No - no more than Rosier deserved!’ said Karkaroff, a real note of panic in his voice now. Harry could see that he was starting to worry that none of his information would be any use to the Ministry. Karkaroff’s eyes darted towards the door in the corner, behind which the Dementors undoubtedly still stood, waiting.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Any more?’ said Crouch.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes!’ said Karkaroff. ‘There was Travers - he helped murder the McKinnons! Mulciber - he specialised in the Imperius Curse, forced countless people to do horrific things! Rookwood, who was a spy, and passed He Who Must Not Be Named useful information from inside the Ministry itself!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry could tell that, this time, Karkaroff had struck gold. The watching crowd were all murmuring together.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Rookwood?’ said Mr Crouch, nodding to a witch sitting in front of him, who began scribbling upon her piece of parchment. ‘Augustus Rookwood of the Department of Mysteries?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘The very same,’ said Karkaroff eagerly. ‘I believe he used a network of well-placed wizards, both inside the Ministry and out, to collect information -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘But Travers and Mulciber, we have,’ said Mr Crouch. ‘Very well, Karkaroff, if that is all, you will be returned to Azkaban while we decide -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Not yet!’ cried Karkaroff, looking quite desperate. ‘Wait, I have more!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry could see him sweating in the torchlight, his white skin contrasting strongly with the black of his hair and beard.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Snape!’ he shouted. ‘Severus Snape!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Snape has been cleared by this council,’ said Crouch coldly. ‘He has been vouched for by Albus Dumbledore.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ shouted Karkaroff, straining at the chains which bound him to the chair. ‘I assure you! Severus Snape is a Death Eater!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore had got to his feet. ‘I have given evidence already on this matter,’ he said calmly. ‘Severus Snape was indeed a Death Eater. However, he rejoined our side before Lord Voldemort’s downfall and turned spy for us, at great personal risk. He is now no more a Death Eater than I am.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry turned to look at Mad-Eye Moody. He was wearing a look of deep scepticism behind Dumbledore’s back.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Very well, Karkaroff,’ Crouch said coldly, ‘you have been of assistance. I shall review your case. You will return to Azkaban in the meantime …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Mr Crouch’s voice faded. Harry looked around; the dungeon was dissolving as though it was made of smoke; everything was fading, he could see only his own body, all else was swirling darkness …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: And then, the dungeon returned. Harry was sitting in a different seat; still on the highest bench, but now to the left side of Mr Crouch. The atmosphere seemed quite different; relaxed, even cheerful. The witches and wizards all around the walls were talking to each other, almost as though they were at some sort of sporting event. A witch halfway up the rows of benches opposite caught Harry’s eye. She had short blonde hair, was wearing magenta robes, and was sucking the end of an acid-green quill. It was, unmistakeably, a younger Rita Skeeter. Harry looked around; Dumbledore was sitting beside him again, wearing different robes. Mr Crouch looked tireder and somehow fiercer, gaunter … Harry understood. It was a different memory, a different day … a different trial.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The door in the corner opened, and Ludo Bagman walked into the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: This was not, however, a Ludo Bagman gone to seed, but a Ludo Bagman who was clearly at the height of his Quidditch-playing fitness. His nose wasn’t broken now; he was tall and lean and muscly. Bagman looked nervous as he sat down in the chained chair, but it did not bind him there, as it had bound Karkaroff, and Bagman, perhaps taking heart from this, glanced around at the watching crowd, waved at a couple of them, and managed a small smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Ludo Bagman, you have been brought here in front of the Council of Magical Law to answer charges relating to the activities of the Death Eaters,’ said Mr Crouch. ‘We have heard the evidence against you, and are about to reach our verdict. Do you have anything to add to your testimony before we pronounce judgement?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry couldn’t believe his ears. Ludo Bagman, a Death Eater?

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Only,’ said Bagman, smiling awkwardly, ‘well - I know I’ve been a bit of an idiot -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: One or two wizards and witches in the surrounding seats smiled indulgently. Mr Crouch did not appear to share their feelings. He was staring down at Ludo Bagman with an expression of the utmost severity and dislike.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You never spoke a truer word, boy,’ someone muttered drily to Dumbledore behind Harry. He looked around, and saw Moody sitting there again. ‘If I didn’t know he’d always been dim, I’d have said some of those Bludgers had permanently affected his brain …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Ludovic Bagman, you were caught passing information to Lord Voldemort’s supporters,’ said Mr Crouch. ‘For this, I suggest a term of imprisonment in Azkaban lasting no less than -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But there was an angry outcry from the surrounding benches. Several of the witches and wizards around the walls stood up, shaking their heads, and even their fists, at Mr Crouch.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘But I’ve told you, I had no idea!’ Bagman called earnestly over the crowd’s babble, his round blue eyes widening. ‘None at all! Old Rookwood was a friend of my dad’s … never crossed my mind he was in with You-Know-Who! I thought I was collecting information for our side! And Rookwood kept talking about getting me a job in the Ministry later on … once my Quidditch days are over, you know … I mean, I can’t keep getting hit by Bludgers for the rest of my life, can I?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: There were titters from the crowd.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘It will be put to the vote,’ said Mr Crouch coldly. He turned to the right-hand side of the dungeon. ‘The jury will please raise their hands … those in favour of imprisonment …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry looked towards the right-hand side of the dungeon. Not one person raised their hand. Many of the witches and wizards around the walls began to clap. One of the witches on the jury stood up.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes?’ barked Crouch.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘We’d just like to congratulate Mr Bagman on his splendid performance for England in the Quidditch match against Turkey last Saturday,’ the witch said breathlessly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Mr Crouch looked furious. The dungeon was ringing with applause now. Bagman got to his feet and bowed, beaming.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Despicable,’ Mr Crouch spat at Dumbledore, sitting down as Bagman walked out of the dungeon. ‘Rookwood get him a job indeed … the day Ludo Bagman joins us will be a very sad day for the Ministry …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: And the dungeon dissolved again. When it had returned, Harry looked around. He and Dumbledore were still sitting beside Mr Crouch, but the atmosphere could not have been more different. There was total silence, broken only by the dry sobs of a frail, wispy-looking witch in the seat next to Mr Crouch. She was clutching a handkerchief to her mouth with trembling hands. Harry looked up at Crouch, and saw that he looked gaunter, and greyer than ever before. A nerve was twitching in his temple.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Bring them in,’ he said, and his voice echoed through the silent dungeon.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The door in the corner opened yet again. Six Dementors entered this time, flanking a group of four people. Harry saw the people in the crowd turn to look up at Mr Crouch. A few of them whispered to each other.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The Dementors placed each of the four people in the four chairs with chained arms which now stood on the dungeon floor. There was a thickset man who stared blankly up at Crouch, a thinner and more nervous-looking man, whose eyes were darting around the crowd, a woman, with thick, shining dark hair, and heavily hooded eyes, who was sitting in the chained chair as though it were a throne, and a boy in his late teens, who looked nothing short of petrified. He was shivering, his straw-coloured hair all over his face, his freckled skin milk-white. The wispy little witch beside Crouch began to rock backwards and forwards in her seat, whimpering into her handkerchief.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Crouch stood up. He looked down upon the four in front of him, and there was pure hatred in his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You have been brought here before the Council of Magical Law,’ he said clearly, ‘so that we may pass judgement on you, for a crime so heinous -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Father,’ said the boy with the straw-coloured hair. ‘Father … please …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘- that we have rarely heard the like of it within this court,’ said Crouch, speaking more loudly, drowning out his son’s voice. ‘We have heard the evidence against you. The four of you stand accused of capturing an Auror -Frank Longbottom - and subjecting him to the Cruciatus Curse, believing him to have knowledge of the present whereabouts of your exiled master, He Who Must Not Be Named -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Father, I didn’t!’ shrieked the boy in chains below. ‘I didn’t, I swear it, Father, don’t send me back to the Dementors -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You are further accused,’ bellowed Mr Crouch, ‘of using the Cruciatus Curse on Frank Longbottom’s wife, when he would not give you information. You planned to restore He Who Must Not Be Named to power, and to resume the lives of violence you presumably led while he was strong. I now ask the jury -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Mother!’ screamed the boy below, and the wispy little witch beside Crouch began to sob, rocking backwards and forwards. ‘Mother, stop him, Mother, I didn’t do it, it wasn’t me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I now ask the jury,’ shouted Mr Crouch, ‘to raise their hands if they believe, as I do, that these crimes deserve a life sentence in Azkaban.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: In unison, the witches and wizards along the right-hand side of the dungeon raised their hands. The crowd around the walls began to clap as it had for Bagman, their faces full of savage triumph. The boy began to scream.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No! Mother, no! I didn’t do it, I didn’t do it, I didn’t know! Don’t send me there, don’t let him!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The Dementors were gliding back into the room. The boy’s three companions rose quietly from their seats; the woman with the heavy-lidded eyes looked up at Crouch and called, ‘The Dark Lord will rise again, Crouch! Throw us into Azkaban, we will wait! He will rise again and will come for us, he will reward us beyond any of his other supporters! We alone were faithful! We alone tried to find him!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But the boy was trying to fight the Dementors off, even though Harry could see their cold, draining power starting to affect him. The crowd were jeering, some of them on their feet, as the woman swept out of the dungeon, and the boy continued to struggle.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m your son!’ he screamed up at Crouch. ‘I’m your son!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You are no son of mine!’ bellowed Mr Crouch, his eyes bulging suddenly. ‘I have no son!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The wispy witch beside him gave a great gasp, and slumped in her seat. She had fainted. Crouch appeared not to have noticed.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Take them away!’ Crouch roared at the Dementors, spit flying from his mouth. ‘Take them away, and may they rot there!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Father! Father, I wasn’t involved! No! No! Father, please!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I think, Harry, it is time to return to my office,’ said a quiet voice in Harry’s ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry started. He looked around. Then he looked on his other side.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: There was an Albus Dumbledore sitting on his right, watching Crouch’s son being dragged away by the Dementors - and there was an Albus Dumbledore on his left, looking right at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Come,’ said the Dumbledore on his left, and he put his hand under Harry’s elbow. Harry felt himself rising into the air; the dungeon dissolved around him; for a moment, all was blackness, and then he felt as though he had done a slow-motion somersault, suddenly landing flat on his feet, in what seemed like the dazzling light of Dumbledore’s sunlit office. The stone basin was shimmering in the cabinet in front of him, and Albus Dumbledore was standing beside him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor,’ Harry gasped, ‘I know I shouldn’t’ve - I didn’t mean - the cabinet door was sort of open and -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I quite understand,’ said Dumbledore. He lifted the basin, carried it over to his desk, placed it upon the polished top, and sat down in the chair behind it. He motioned Harry to sit down opposite him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry did so, staring at the stone basin. The contents had returned to their original, silvery white state, swirling and rippling beneath his gaze.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘What is it?’ Harry asked shakily.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘This? It is called a Pensieve,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I sometimes find, and I am sure you know the feeling, that I simply have too many thoughts and memories crammed into my mind.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Er,’ said Harry, who couldn’t truthfully say that he had ever felt anything of the sort.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘At these times,’ said Dumbledore, indicating the stone basin, ‘I use the Pensieve. One simply siphons the excess thoughts from one’s mind, pours them into the basin, and examines them at one’s leisure. It becomes easier to spot patterns and links, you understand, when they are in this form.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You mean … that stuff’s your thoughts?’ Harry said, staring at the swirling white substance in the basin.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Certainly,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Let me show you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore drew his wand out of the inside of his robes, and placed the tip into his own silvery hair, near his temple. When he took the wand away, hair seemed to be clinging to it - but then Harry saw that it was in fact a glistening strand of the same strange, silvery white substance that filled the Pensieve. Dumbledore added this fresh thought to the basin, and Harry, astonished, saw his own face swimming around the surface of the bowl.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore placed his long hands on either side of the Pensieve and swirled it, rather as a gold prospector would swirl for fragments of gold … and Harry saw his own face change smoothly into Snape’s, who opened his mouth, and spoke to the ceiling, his voice echoing slightly. ‘It’s coming back … Karkaroff’s too … stronger and clearer than ever …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘A connection I could have made without assistance,’ Dumbledore sighed, ‘but never mind.’ He peered over the top of his half-moon spectacles at Harry, who was gaping at Snape’s face, which was continuing to swirl around the bowl. ‘I was using the Pensieve when Mr Fudge arrived for our meeting, and put it away rather hastily. Undoubtedly I did not fasten the cabinet door properly. Naturally, it would have attracted your attention.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry,’ Harry mumbled.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore shook his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Curiosity is not a sin,’ he said. ‘But we should exercise caution with our curiosity … yes, indeed …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Frowning slightly, he prodded the thoughts within the basin with the tip of his wand. Instantly, a figure rose out of it, a plump, scowling girl of around sixteen, who began to revolve slowly, with her feet still in the basin. She took no notice whatsoever of Harry or Professor Dumbledore. When she spoke, her voice echoed as Snape’s had done, as though it was coming from the depths of the stone basin: ‘He put a hex on me, Professor Dumbledore, and I was only teasing him, sir, I only said I’d seen him kissing Florence behind the greenhouses last Thursday …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘But why, Bertha,’ said Dumbledore sadly, looking up at the now silently revolving girl, ‘why did you have to follow him in the first place?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Bertha?’ Harry whispered, looking up at her. ‘Is that - was that Bertha Jorkins?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Dumbledore, prodding the thoughts in the basin again; Bertha sank back into them, and they became silvery and opaque once more. ‘That was Bertha as I remember her at school.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The silvery light from the Pensieve illuminated Dumbledore’s face, and it struck Harry suddenly how very old he was looking. He knew, of course, that Dumbledore was getting on in years, but somehow he never really thought of Dumbledore as an old man.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘So, Harry,’ said Dumbledore quietly. ‘Before you got lost in my thoughts, you wanted to tell me something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry. ‘Professor - I was in Divination just now, and - er - I fell asleep.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He hesitated here, wondering if a reprimand was coming, but Dumbledore merely said, ‘Quite understandable. Continue.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I had a dream,’ said Harry. ‘A dream about Lord Voldemort. He was torturing Wormtail … you know who Wormtail -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I do know,’ said Dumbledore, promptly. ‘Please continue.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort got a letter from an owl. He said something like, Wormtail’s blunder had been repaired. He said someone was dead. Then he said, Wormtail wouldn’t be fed to the snake - there was a snake beside his chair. He said - he said he’d be feeding me to it, instead. Then he did the Cruciatus Curse on Wormtail - and my scar hurt,’ Harry said. ‘It woke me up, it hurt so badly.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore merely looked at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Er - that’s all,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I see,’ said Dumbledore quietly. ‘I see. Now, has your scar hurt at any other time this year, excepting the time it woke you up over the summer?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I - how did you know it woke me up over the summer?’ said Harry, astonished.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You are not Sirius’ only correspondent,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I have also been in contact with him ever since he left Hogwarts last year. It was I who suggested the mountainside cave as the safest place for him to stay.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore got up, and began walking up and down behind his desk. Every now and then, he placed his wand tip to his temple, removed another shining silver thought, and added it to the Pensieve. The thoughts inside began to swirl so fast that Harry couldn’t make out anything clearly; it was merely a blur of colour.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor?’ he said quietly, after a couple of minutes.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore stopped pacing, and looked at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘My apologies,’ he said quietly. He sat back down at his desk.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you - d’you know why my scar’s hurting me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore looked very intently at Harry for a moment, and then said, ‘I have a theory, no more than that … It is my belief that your scar hurts both when Lord Voldemort is near you, and when he is feeling a particularly strong surge of hatred.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘But … why?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Because you and he are connected by the curse that failed,’ said Dumbledore. ‘That is no ordinary scar.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘So you think … that dream … did it really happen?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘It is possible,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I would say - probable. Harry - did you see Voldemort?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry. ‘Just the back of his chair. But - there wouldn’t have been anything to see, would there? I mean, he hasn’t got a body, has he? But … but then how could he have held the wand?’ Harry said slowly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘How indeed?’ muttered Dumbledore. ‘How indeed …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Neither Dumbledore nor Harry spoke for a while. Dumbledore was gazing across the room, every now and then placing his wand tip to his temple, and adding another shining, silver thought to the seething mass within the Pensieve.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor,’ Harry said at last, ‘do you think he’s getting stronger?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort?’ said Dumbledore, looking at Harry over the Pensieve. It was the characteristic, piercing look Dumbledore had given him on other occasions, and always made Harry feel as though Dumbledore was seeing right through him, in a way that even Moody’s magical eye could not. ‘Once again, Harry, I can only give you my suspicions.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore sighed again, and he looked older, and wearier, than ever.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘The years of Voldemort’s ascent to power,’ he said, ‘were marked with disappearances. Bertha Jorkins has vanished without trace in the place where Voldemort was certainly known to be last. Mr Crouch, too, has disappeared … within these very grounds. And there was a third disappearance, one which the Ministry, I regret to say, does not consider of any importance, for it concerns a Muggle. His name was Frank Bryce, he lived in the village where Voldemort’s father grew up, and he has not been seen since last August. You see, I read the Muggle newspapers, unlike most of my Ministry friends.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore looked very seriously at Harry. ‘These disappearances seem to me to be linked. The Ministry disagrees - as you may have heard, while waiting outside my office.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry nodded. Silence fell between them again, Dumbledore extracting thoughts every now and then. Harry felt as though he ought to go, but his curiosity held him in his chair.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor?’ he said again.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Harry?’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Er … could I ask you about … that court thing I was in … in the Pensieve?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You could,’ said Dumbledore heavily. ‘I attended it many times, but some trials come back to me more clearly than others… particularly now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You know - you know the trial you found me in? The one with Crouch’s son? Well … were they talking about Neville’s parents?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore gave Harry a very sharp look.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Has Neville never told you why he has been brought up by his grandmother?’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry shook his head, wondering, as he did so, how he could have failed to ask Neville this, in almost four years of knowing him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, they were talking about Neville’s parents,’ said Dumbledore. ‘His father, Frank, was an Auror just like Professor Moody. He and his wife were tortured for information about Voldemort’s whereabouts after he lost his powers, as you heard.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘So they’re dead?’ said Harry quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Dumbledore, his voice full of a bitterness Harry had never heard there before, ‘they are insane. They are both in St Mungo’s Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries. I believe Neville visits them, with his grandmother, during the holidays. They do not recognise him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry sat there, horror-struck. He had never known … never, in four years, bothered to find out …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘The Longbottoms were very popular,’ said Dumbledore. ‘The attacks on them came after Voldemort’s fall from power, just when everyone thought they were safe. Those attacks caused a wave of fury such as I have never known. The Ministry was under great pressure to catch those who had done it. Unfortunately, the Longbottoms’ evidence was - given their condition -none too reliable.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Then Mr Crouch’s son might not have been involved?’ said Harry slowly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore shook his head. ‘As to that, I have no idea.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry sat in silence once more, watching the contents of the Pensieve swirl. There were two more questions he was burning to ask … but they concerned the guilt of living people …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Er,’ he said, ‘Mr Bagman …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘… has never been accused of any Dark activity since,’ said Dumbledore calmly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Right,’ said Harry hastily, staring at the contents of the Pensieve again, which were swirling more slowly now that Dumbledore had stopped adding thoughts. ‘And … er …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But the Pensieve seemed to be asking his question for him. Snape’s face was swimming on the surface again. Dumbledore glanced down into it, and then up at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No more has Professor Snape,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry looked into Dumbledore’s light-blue eyes, and the thing he really wanted to know spilled out of his mouth before he could stop it. ‘What made you think he’d really stopped supporting Voldemort, Professor?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore held Harry’s gaze for a few seconds, and then said, ‘That, Harry, is a matter between Professor Snape and myself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry knew that the interview was over; Dumbledore did not look angry, yet there was a finality in his tone that told Harry it was time to go. He stood up, and so did Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry,’ he said, as Harry reached the door. ‘Please do not speak about Neville’s parents to anybody else. He has the right to let people know, when he is ready.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Professor,’ said Harry, turning to go.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘And -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry looked back.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore was standing over the Pensieve, his face lit from beneath by its silvery spots of light, looking older than ever. He stared at Harry for a moment, and then said, ‘Good luck with the third task.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore reckons You-Know-Who’s getting stronger again as well?’ Ron whispered.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Everything Harry had seen in the Pensieve, nearly everything Dumbledore had told and shown him afterwards, he had now shared with Ron and Hermione - and, of course, with Sirius, to whom Harry had sent an owl the moment he had left Dumbledore’s office. Harry, Ron and Hermione sat up late in the common room once again that night, talking it all over until Harry’s mind was reeling, until he understood what Dumbledore had meant about a head becoming so full of thoughts that it would have been a relief to siphon them off.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Ron stared into the common-room fire. Harry thought he saw Ron shiver slightly, even though the evening was warm.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘And he trusts Snape?’ Ron said. ‘He really trusts Snape, even though he knows he was a Death Eater?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Hermione had not spoken for ten minutes. She was sitting with her forehead in her hands, staring at her knees. Harry thought she, too, looked as though she could have done with a Pensieve.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Rita Skeeter,’ she muttered finally.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘How can you be worrying about her now?’ said Ron, indisbelief.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not worrying about her,’ Hermione said to her knees. ‘I’m just thinking … remember what she said to me in the Three Broomsticks? “I know things about Ludo Bagman that would make your hair curl.” This is what she meant, isn’t it? She reported his trial, she knew he’d passed information to the Death Eaters. And Winky, too, remember … “Mr Bagman is a bad wizard.” Mr Crouch would have been furious he got off, he would have talked about it at home.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, but Bagman didn’t pass information on purpose, did he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Hermione shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘And Fudge reckons Madame Maxime attacked Crouch?’ Ron said, turning back to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, ‘but he’s only saying that because Crouch disappeared near the Beauxbatons carriage.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘We never thought of her, did we?’ said Ron, slowly. ‘Mind you, she’s definitely got giant blood, and she doesn’t want to admit it -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course she doesn’t,’ said Hermione sharply, looking up. ‘Look what happened to Hagrid when Rita found out about his mother. Look at Fudge, jumping to conclusions about her, just because she’s part giant. Who needs that sort of prejudice? I’d probably say I had big bones if I knew that’s what I’d get for telling the truth.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked at her watch.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘We haven’t done any practising!’ she said, looking shocked. ‘We were going to do the Impediment Jinx! We’ll have to really get down to it tomorrow! Come on, Harry, you need to get some sleep.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron went slowly upstairs to their dormitory. As Harry pulled on his pyjamas, he looked over at Neville’s bed. True to his word to Dumbledore, he had not told Ron and Hermione about Neville’s parents. As Harry took off his glasses and climbed into his four-poster, he imagined how it must feel to have parents still living, but unable to recognise you. He often got sympathy from strangers for being an orphan, but as he listened to Neville’s snores, he thought that Neville deserved it more than he did. Lying in the darkness, Harry felt a rush of anger and hate towards the people who had tortured Mr and Mrs Longbottom … he remembered the jeers of the crowd as Crouch’s son and his companions had been dragged from the court by the Dementors … he understood how they had felt … then he remembered the milk-white face of the screaming boy, and realised with a jolt that he had died a year later …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: It was Voldemort, Harry thought, staring up at the canopy of his bed in the darkness, it all came back to Voldemort … he was the one who had torn these families apart, who had ruined all these lives …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione were supposed to be revising for their exams, which would finish on the day of the third task, but they were putting most of their efforts into helping Harry prepare.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t worry about it,’ Hermione said shortly, when Harry pointed this out to them, and said he didn’t mind practising on his own for a while. ‘At least we’ll get top marks in Defence Against the Dark Arts, we’d never have found out about all these hexes in class.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Good training for when we’re all Aurors,’ said Ron excitedly, attempting the Impediment Jinx on a wasp that had buzzed into the room, and making it stop dead in mid-air.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The mood in the castle as they entered June became excited and tense again. Everyone was looking forward to the third task, which would take place a week before the end of term. Harry was practising hexes in every available moment. He felt more confident about this task than either of the others. Difficult and dangerous though it would undoubtedly be, Moody was right: Harry had managed to find his way past monstrous creatures and enchanted barriers before now, and this time he had some notice, some chance to prepare himself for what lay ahead.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Tired of walking in on them all over the school, Professor McGonagall had given Harry permission to use the empty Transfiguration classroom at lunchtimes. He had soon mastered the Impediment Jinx, a spell to slow down and obstruct attackers, the Reductor curse, which would enable him to blast solid objects out of his way, and the Four-Point Spell, a useful discovery of Hermione’s which would make his wand point due north, therefore enabling him to check whether he was going in the right direction within the maze. He was still having trouble with the Shield Charm, though. This was supposed to cast a temporary, invisible wall around himself that deflected minor curses; Hermione managed to shatter it with a well-placed Jelly-Legs Jinx. Harry wobbled around the room for ten minutes afterwards before she had looked up the counter-jinx.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re still doing really well, though,’ Hermione said encouragingly, looking down her list, and crossing off those spells they had already learnt. ‘Some of these are bound to come in handy.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Come and look at this,’ said Ron, who was standing by the window. He was staring down into the grounds. ‘What’s Malfoy doing?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione went to see. Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle were standing in the shadow of a tree below. Crabbe and Goyle seemed to be keeping a look out; both were smirking. Malfoy was holding his hand up to his mouth, and speaking into it.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘He looks like he’s using a walkie-talkie,’ said Harry curiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)

Krum slouched off to join them shortly afterwards. Harry stayed where he was. He really didn’t want to go into the chamber. He had no family - no family who would turn up to see him risk his life, anyway. But just as he was getting up, thinking that he might as well go up to the library and do a spot more hex revision, the door of the side chamber opened, and Cedric stuck his head out.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)

text_content: The path ahead was empty, too, and when Harry reached a right turn and took it, he again found his way unblocked. Harry didn’t know why, but the lack of obstacles was unnerving him. Surely he should have met something by now? It felt as though the maze was luring him into a false sense of security. Then he heard movement right behind him. He held out his wand, ready to attack, but its beam fell only upon Cedric, who had just hurried out of a path on the right-hand side. Cedric looked severely shaken. The sleeve of his robes was smoking.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid’s Blast-Ended Skrewts!’ he hissed. ‘They’re enormous - I only just got away!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He shook his head, and dived out of sight, along another path. Keen to put plenty of distance between himself and the Skrewts, Harry hurried off again. Then, as he turned a corner, he saw -

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: A Dementor was gliding towards him. Twelve feet tall, its face hidden by its hood, its rotting, scabbed hands outstretched, it advanced, sensing its way blindly towards him. Harry could hear its rattling breath; he felt clammy coldness stealing over him, but knew what he had to do …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He summoned the happiest thought he could, concentrated with all his might on the thought of getting out of the maze and celebrating with Ron and Hermione, raised his wand and cried, ‘Expecto Patronum!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: A silver stag erupted from the end of Harry’s wand and galloped towards the Dementor, which fell back, and tripped over the hem of its robes … Harry had never seen a Dementor stumble.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Hang on!’ he shouted, advancing in the wake of his silver Patronus, ‘you’re a Boggart! Riddikulus!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: There was a loud crack, and the shape-shifter exploded in a wisp of smoke. The silver stag faded from sight. Harry wished it could have stayed, he could have used some company … but he moved on as quickly and quietly as possible, listening hard, his wand held high once more.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Left … right … left again … twice he found himself facing dead ends. He did the Four-Point Spell again, and found that he was going too far east. He turned back, took a right turn, and saw an odd golden mist floating ahead of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry approached it cautiously, pointing the wand’s beam at it. This looked like some kind of enchantment. He wondered whether he might be able to blast it out of the way.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Reducto!’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The spell shot straight through the mist, leaving it intact. He supposed he should have known better; the Reductor curse was for solid objects. What would happen if he walked through the mist? Was it worth chancing it, or should he double back?

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He was still hesitating, when a scream shattered the silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Fleur?’ Harry yelled.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: There was silence. He stared all around him. What had happened to her? Her scream seemed to have come from somewhere ahead. He took a deep breath, and ran through the enchanted mist.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The world turned upside-down. Harry was hanging from the ground, with his hair on end, his glasses dangling off his nose, threatening to fall into the bottomless sky. He clutched them to the end of his nose and hung there, terrified. It felt as though his feet were glued to the grass, which had now become the ceiling. Below him the dark, star-spangled heavens stretched endlessly. He felt as though if he tried to move one of his feet, he would fall away from the earth completely.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Think, he told himself, as all the blood rushed to his head, think …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: But not one of the spells he had practised had been designed to combat a sudden reversal of ground and sky. Did he dare move his foot? He could hear the blood pounding in his ears. He had two choices - try and move, or send up red sparks, and get rescued and disqualified from the task.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He shut his eyes, so he wouldn’t be able to see the view of endless space below him, and pulled his right foot as hard as he could, away from the grassy ceiling.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Immediately, the world righted itself. Harry fell forwards onto his knees on the wonderfully solid ground. He felt temporarily limp with shock. He took a deep, steadying breath, then got up again, and hurried forwards, looking back over his shoulder as he ran out of the golden mist, which twinkled innocently at him in the moonlight.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He paused at a junction of two paths and looked around for some sign of Fleur. He was sure it had been she who had screamed. What had she met? Was she all right? There was no sign of red sparks - did that mean she had got herself out of trouble, or was she in such trouble that she couldn’t reach her wand? Harry took the right fork with a feeling of increasing unease … but at the same time, he couldn’t help thinking, one champion down …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The Cup was somewhere close by, and it sounded as though Fleur was no longer in the running. He’d got this far, hadn’t he? What if he actually managed to win? Fleetingly, and for the first time since he’d found himself champion, he saw again that image of himself, raising the Triwizard Cup in front of the rest of the school …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He met nothing for ten minutes, except dead ends. Twice he took the same wrong turning. Finally he found a new route, and started to jog along it, his wand-light waving, making his shadow flicker and distort on the hedge walls. Then he rounded another corner, and found himself facing a Blast-Ended Skrewt.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Cedric was right - it was enormous. Ten feet long, it looked more like a giant scorpion than anything. Its long sting was curled over its back. Its thick armour glinted in the light from Harry’s wand, which he pointed at it.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Stupefy!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The spell hit the Skrewt’s armour, and rebounded; Harry ducked just in time, but could smell burning hair; it had singed the top of his head. The Skrewt issued a blast of fire from its end, and flew forwards towards him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Impedimenta!’ Harry yelled. The spell hit the Skrewt’s armour again and ricocheted off; Harry staggered back a few paces and fell over. ‘IMPEDIMENTA!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The Skrewt was inches from him when it froze - he had managed to hit it on its fleshy, shell-less underside. Panting, Harry pushed himself away from it and ran, hard, in the opposite direction - the Impediment Jinx was not permanent, the Skrewt would be regaining the use of its legs at any moment.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He took a left path, and hit a dead end, a right, and hit another: forcing himself to stop, heart hammering, he performed the Four-Point Spell again, backtracked, and chose a path that would take him north-west.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He had been hurrying along the new path for a few minutes, when he heard something in the path running parallel to his own which made him stop dead.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘What are you doing?’ yelled Cedric’s voice. ‘What the hell d’you think you’re doing?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: And then Harry heard Krum’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Crucio!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The air was suddenly full of Cedric’s yells. Horrified, Harry began sprinting up his path, trying to find a way into Cedric’s. When none appeared, he tried the Reductor curse again. It wasn’t very effective, but it burnt a small hole in the hedge, through which Harry forced his leg, kicking at the thick brambles and branches until they broke and made an opening; he struggled through it, tearing his robes and, looking to his right, saw Cedric jerking and twitching on the ground, Krum standing over him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry pulled himself up and pointed his wand at Krum just as Krum looked up. Krum turned and began to run.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Stupefy!’ Harry yelled.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The spell hit Krum in the back; he stopped dead in his tracks, fell forwards and lay motionless, face down in the grass. Harry dashed over to Cedric, who had stopped twitching, and was lying there panting, his hands over his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you all right?’ Harry said roughly, grabbing Cedric’s arm.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ panted Cedric. ‘Yeah … I don’t believe it … he crept up behind me … I heard him, I turned round, and he had his wand on me …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Cedric got up. He was still shaking. He and Harry looked down at Krum.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t believe this … I thought he was all right,’ Harry said, staring at Krum.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘So did I,’ said Cedric.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you hear Fleur scream earlier?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Cedric. ‘You don’t think Krum got her, too?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know,’ said Harry slowly.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Should we leave him here?’ Cedric muttered.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry. ‘I reckon we should send up red sparks. Someone’ll come and collect him … otherwise he’ll probably be eaten by a Skrewt.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘He’d deserve it,’ Cedric muttered, but all the same, he raised his wand and shot a shower of red sparks into the air, which hovered high above Krum, marking the spot where he lay.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry and Cedric stood there in the darkness for a moment, looking around them. Then Cedric said, ‘Well … I s’pose we’d better go on …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Harry. ‘Oh … yeah … right …’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: It was an odd moment. He and Cedric had been briefly united against Krum - now the fact that they were opponents came back to them both. They proceeded up the dark path without speaking, then Harry turned left, and Cedric right. Cedric’s footsteps soon died away.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry moved on, continuing to use the Four-Point Spell, making sure he was moving in the right direction. It was between him and Cedric now. His desire to reach the Cup first was now burning stronger than ever, but he could hardly believe what he’d just seen Krum do. The use of an Unforgivable Curse on a fellow human being meant a life term in Azkaban, that was what Moody had told them. Krum surely couldn’t have wanted the Triwizard Cup that badly … Harry sped up.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Every so often he hit more dead ends, but the increasing darkness made him feel sure he was getting near the heart of the maze. Then, as he strode down a long, straight path, he saw movement once again, and his beam of wand-light hit an extraordinary creature, one which he had only seen in picture form, in his Monster Book of Monsters.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: It was a sphinx. It had the body of an overlarge lion; great clawed paws, and a long yellowish tail ending in a brown tuft. Its head, however, was that of a woman. She turned her long, almond-shaped eyes upon Harry as he approached. He raised his wand, hesitating. She was not crouching as if to spring, but pacing from side to side of the path, blocking his progress.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Then she spoke, in a deep, hoarse voice. ‘You are very near your goal. The quickest way is past me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘So … so will you move, please?’ said Harry, knowing what the answer was going to be.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ she said, continuing to pace. ‘Not unless you can answer my riddle. Answer on your first guess - I let you pass. Answer wrongly - I attack. Remain silent - I will let you walk away from me, unscathed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Harry’s stomach slipped several notches. It was Hermione who was good at this sort of thing, not him. He weighed his chances. If the riddle was too hard, he could keep silent, get away from her unharmed, and try and find an alternative route to the centre.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘OK,’ he said. ‘Can I hear the riddle?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The sphinx sat down upon her hind legs, in the very centre of the path, and recited:

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘First think of the person who lives in disguise,

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Who deals in secrets and tells naught but lies.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Next, tell me what’s always the last thing to mend,

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The middle of middle and end of the end?

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: And finally give me the sound often heard

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: During the search for a hard-to-find word.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Now string them together, and answer me this,

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Which creature would you be unwilling to kiss?’ Harry gaped at her.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Could I have it again … more slowly?’ he asked tentatively.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: She blinked at him, smiled, and repeated the poem.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘All the clues add up to a creature I wouldn’t want to kiss?’ Harry asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: She merely smiled her mysterious smile. Harry took that for a ‘yes’. Harry cast his mind around. There were plenty of animals he wouldn’t want to kiss; his immediate thought was a Blast-Ended Skrewt, but something told him that wasn’t the answer. He’d have to try and work out the clues …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘A person in disguise,’ Harry muttered, staring at her, ‘who lies … er … that’d be a - an impostor. No, that’s not my guess! A - a spy? I’ll come back to that … could you give me the next clue again, please?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: She repeated the next lines of the poem.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘The last thing to mend,’ Harry repeated. ‘Er … no idea … middle of middle … could I have the last bit again?’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: She gave him the last four lines.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘A sound often heard in the search for a hard-to-find word,’ said Harry. ‘Er … that’d be … er … hang on - “er”! “Er“‘s a sound!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The sphinx smiled at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Spy … er … spy … er …’ said Harry, pacing up and down himself. ‘A creature I wouldn’t want to kiss … a spider!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The sphinx smiled more broadly. She got up, stretched her front legs, and then moved aside for him to pass.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Thanks!’ said Harry, and, amazed at his own brilliance, he dashed forwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He had to be close now, he had to be … his wand was telling him he was bang on course; as long as he didn’t meet anything too horrible, he might be in with a chance …

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: He had a choice of paths up ahead. ‘Point me!’ he whispered again to his wand, and it spun around and pointed him to the right-hand one. He dashed up this one, and saw light ahead.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: The Triwizard Cup was gleaming on a plinth a hundred yards away. Harry had just broken into a run, when a dark figure hurtled out onto the path in front of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Cedric was going to get there first. Cedric was sprinting as fast as he could towards the Cup, and Harry knew he would never catch up, Cedric was much taller, had much longer legs -

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Then Harry saw something immense over a hedge to his left, moving quickly along a path that intersected with his own; it was moving so fast Cedric was about to run into it, and Cedric, his eyes on the Cup, had not seen it -

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Cedric!’ Harry bellowed. ‘On your left!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: Cedric looked around just in time to hurl himself past the thing and avoid colliding with it but, in his haste, he tripped. Harry saw Cedric’s wand fly out of his hand, as a gigantic spider stepped into the path, and began to bear down upon Cedric.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Stupefy!’ Harry yelled again; the spell hit the spider’s gigantic, hairy black body but, for all the good it did, he might as well have thrown a stone at it; the spider jerked, scuttled around, and ran at Harry instead.

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
text_content: ‘Stupefy! Impedimenta! Stupefy!’

book: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (UK)
