book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yeah,’ said Ron. ‘Bound to be, isn’t it? O.W.L.s are really important, affect the jobs you can apply for and everything. We get career advice, too, later this year, Bill told me. So you can choose what N.E.W.T.s you want to do next year.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you know what you want to do after Hogwarts?’ Harry asked the other two, as they left the Great Hall shortly afterwards and set off towards their History of Magic classroom.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Not really,’ said Ron slowly. ‘Except … well …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He looked slightly sheepish.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ Harry urged him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, it’d be cool to be an Auror,’ said Ron in an off-hand voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, it would,’ said Harry fervently.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But they’re, like, the elite,’ said Ron. ‘You’ve got to be really good. What about you, Hermione?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know,’ she said. ‘I think I’d like to do something really worthwhile.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘An Auror’s worthwhile!’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, it is, but it’s not the only worthwhile thing,’ said Hermione thoughtfully, ‘I mean, if I could take S.P.E.W. further …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron carefully avoided looking at each other.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: History of Magic was by common consent the most boring subject ever devised by wizardkind. Professor Binns, their ghost teacher, had a wheezy, droning voice that was almost guaranteed to cause severe drowsiness within ten minutes, five in warm weather. He never varied the form of their lessons, but lectured them without pausing while they took notes, or rather, gazed sleepily into space. Harry and Ron had so far managed to scrape passes in this subject only by copying Hermione’s notes before exams; she alone seemed able to resist the soporific power of Binns’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Today, they suffered three quarters of an hour’s droning on the subject of giant wars. Harry heard just enough within the first ten minutes to appreciate dimly that in another teacher’s hands this subject might have been mildly interesting, but then his brain disengaged, and he spent the remaining thirty-five minutes playing hangman on a corner of his parchment with Ron, while Hermione shot them filthy looks out of the corner of her eye.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘How would it be,’ she asked them coldly, as they left the classroom for break (Binns drifting away through the blackboard), ‘if I refused to lend you my notes this year?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We’d fail our O.W.L.,’ said Ron. ‘If you want that on your conscience, Hermione …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, you’d deserve it,’ she snapped. ‘You don’t even try to listen to him, do you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We do try,’ said Ron. ‘We just haven’t got your brains or your memory or your concentration - you’re just cleverer than we are - is it nice to rub it in?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, don’t give me that rubbish,’ said Hermione, but she looked slightly mollified as she led the way out into the damp courtyard.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: A fine misty drizzle was falling, so that the people standing in huddles around the yard looked blurred at the edges. Harry, Ron and Hermione chose a secluded corner under a heavily dripping balcony, turning up the collars of their robes against the chilly September air and talking about what Snape was likely to set them in the first lesson of the year. They had got as far as agreeing that it was likely to be something extremely difficult, just to catch them off guard after a two-month holiday, when someone walked around the corner towards them.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello, Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: It was Cho Chang and, what was more, she was on her own again. This was most unusual: Cho was almost always surrounded by a gang of giggling girls; Harry remembered the agony of trying to get her by herself to ask her to the Yule Ball.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hi,’ said Harry, feeling his face grow hot. At least you’re not covered in Stinksap this time, he told himself. Cho seemed to be thinking along the same lines.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You got that stuff off, then?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, trying to grin as though the memory of their last meeting was funny as opposed to mortifying. ‘So, did you … er … have a good summer?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The moment he had said this he wished he hadn’t - Cedric had been Cho’s boyfriend and the memory of his death must have affected her holiday almost as badly as it had affected Harry’s. Something seemed to tauten in her face, but she said, ‘Oh, it was all right, you know …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Is that a Tornados badge?’ Ron demanded suddenly, pointing to the front of Cho’s robes, where a sky-blue badge emblazoned with a double gold ‘T’ was pinned. ‘You don’t support them, do you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I do,’ said Cho.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Have you always supported them, or just since they started winning the league?’ said Ron, in what Harry considered an unnecessarily accusatory tone of voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve supported them since I was six,’ said Cho coolly. ‘Anyway … see you, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She walked away. Hermione waited until Cho was halfway across the courtyard before rounding on Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You are so tactless!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What? I only asked her if -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Couldn’t you tell she wanted to talk to Harry on her own?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So? She could’ve done, I wasn’t stopping -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Why on earth were you attacking her about her Quidditch team?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Attacking? I wasn’t attacking her, I was only -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Who cares if she supports the Tornados?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, come on, half the people you see wearing those badges only bought them last season -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But what does it matter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It means they’re not real fans, they’re just jumping on the bandwagon -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the bell,’ said Harry listlessly, because Ron and Hermione were bickering too loudly to hear it. They did not stop arguing all the way down to Snape’s dungeon, which gave Harry plenty of time to reflect that between Neville and Ron he would be lucky ever to have two minutes of conversation with Cho that he could look back on without wanting to leave the country.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: And yet, he thought, as they joined the queue lining up outside Snape’s classroom door, she had chosen to come and talk to him, hadn’t she? She had been Cedric’s girlfriend; she could easily have hated Harry for coming out of the Triwizard maze alive when Cedric had died, yet she was talking to him in a perfectly friendly way, not as though she thought him mad, or a liar, or in some horrible way responsible for Cedric’s death … yes, she had definitely chosen to come and talk to him, and that made the second time in two days … and at this thought, Harry’s spirits rose. Even the ominous sound of Snape’s dungeon door creaking open did not puncture the small, hopeful bubble that seemed to have swelled in his chest. He filed into the classroom behind Ron and Hermione and followed them to their usual table at the back, ignoring the huffy, irritable noises now issuing from both of them.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Settle down,’ said Snape coldly, shutting the door behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There was no real need for the call to order; the moment the class had heard the door close, quiet had fallen and all fidgeting stopped. Snape’s mere presence was usually enough to ensure a class’s silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Before we begin today’s lesson,’ said Snape, sweeping over to his desk and staring around at them all, ‘I think it appropriate to remind you that next June you will be sitting an important examination, during which you will prove how much you have learned about the composition and use of magical potions. Moronic though some of this class undoubtedly are, I expect you to scrape an “Acceptable” in your O.W.L., or suffer my … displeasure.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: His gaze lingered this time on Neville, who gulped.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘After this year, of course, many of you will cease studying with me,’ Snape went on. ‘I take only the very best into my N.E.W.T. Potions class, which means that some of us will certainly be saying goodbye.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: His eyes rested on Harry and his lip curled. Harry glared back, feeling a grim pleasure at the idea that he would be able to give up Potions after fifth year.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But we have another year to go before that happy moment of farewell,’ said Snape softly, ‘so, whether or not you are intending to attempt N.E.W.T., I advise all of you to concentrate your efforts upon maintaining the high pass level I have come to expect from my O.W.L. students.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Today we will be mixing a potion that often comes up at Ordinary Wizarding Level: the Draught of Peace, a potion to calm anxiety and soothe agitation. Be warned: if you are too heavy-handed with the ingredients you will put the drinker into a heavy and sometimes irreversible sleep, so you will need to pay close attention to what you are doing.’ On Harry’s left, Hermione sat up a little straighter, her expression one of utmost attention. ‘The ingredients and method -‘ Snape flicked his wand ‘- are on the blackboard -‘ (they appeared there) ‘- you will find everything you need -‘ he flicked his wand again ‘- in the store cupboard -‘ (the door of the said cupboard sprang open) ‘- you have an hour and a half … start.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Just as Harry, Ron and Hermione had predicted, Snape could hardly have set them a more difficult, fiddly potion. The ingredients had to be added to the cauldron in precisely the right order and quantities; the mixture had to be stirred exactly the right number of times, firstly in clockwise, then in anti-clockwise directions; the heat of the flames on which it was simmering had to be lowered to exactly the right level for a specific number of minutes before the final ingredient was added.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘A light silver vapour should now be rising from your potion,’ called Snape, with ten minutes left to go.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry, who was sweating profusely, looked desperately around the dungeon. His own cauldron was issuing copious amounts of dark grey steam; Ron’s was spitting green sparks. Seamus was feverishly prodding the flames at the base of his cauldron with the tip of his wand, as they seemed to be going out. The surface of Hermione’s potion, however, was a shimmering mist of silver vapour, and as Snape swept by he looked down his hooked nose at it without comment, which meant he could find nothing to criticise. At Harry’s cauldron, however, Snape stopped, and looked down at it with a horrible smirk on his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Potter, what is this supposed to be?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The Slytherins at the front of the class all looked up eagerly; they loved hearing Snape taunt Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘The Draught of Peace,’ said Harry tensely.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell me, Potter,’ said Snape softly, ‘can you read?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Draco Malfoy laughed.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I can,’ said Harry, his fingers clenched tightly around his wand.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Read the third line of the instructions for me, Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry squinted at the blackboard; it was not easy to make out the instructions through the haze of multi-coloured steam now filling the dungeon.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘“Add powdered moonstone, stir three times counter-clockwise, allow to simmer for seven minutes then add two drops of syrup of hellebore.”’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: His heart sank. He had not added syrup of hellebore, but had proceeded straight to the fourth line of the instructions after allowing his potion to simmer for seven minutes.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you do everything on the third line, Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry very quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I beg your pardon?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry, more loudly. ‘I forgot the hellebore.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I know you did, Potter, which means that this mess is utterly worthless. Evanesco.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The contents of Harry’s potion vanished; he was left standing foolishly beside an empty cauldron.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Those of you who have managed to read the instructions, fill one flagon with a sample of your potion, label it clearly with your name and bring it up to my desk for testing,’ said Snape. ‘Homework: twelve inches of parchment on the properties of moonstone and its uses in potion-making, to be handed in on Thursday.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: While everyone around him filled their flagons, Harry cleared away his things, seething. His potion had been no worse than Ron’s, which was now giving off a foul odour of bad eggs; or Neville’s, which had achieved the consistency of just-mixed cement and which Neville was now having to gouge out of his cauldron; yet it was he, Harry, who would be receiving zero marks for the day’s work. He stuffed his wand back into his bag and slumped down on to his seat, watching everyone else march up to Snape’s desk with filled and corked flagons. When at long last the bell rang, Harry was first out of the dungeon and had already started his lunch by the time Ron and Hermione joined him in the Great Hall. The ceiling had turned an even murkier grey during the morning. Rain was lashing the high windows.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘That was really unfair,’ said Hermione consolingly, sitting down next to Harry and helping herself to shepherd’s pie. ‘Your potion wasn’t nearly as bad as Goyle’s; when he put it in his flagon the whole thing shattered and set his robes on fire.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well,’ said Harry, glowering at his plate, ‘since when has Snape ever been fair to me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Neither of the others answered; all three of them knew that Snape and Harry’s mutual enmity had been absolute from the moment Harry had set foot in Hogwarts.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I did think he might be a bit better this year,’ said Hermione in a disappointed voice. ‘I mean … you know …’ she looked around carefully; there were half a dozen empty seats on either side of them and nobody was passing the table ‘… now he’s in the Order and everything.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Poisonous toadstools don’t change their spots,’ said Ron sagely. ‘Anyway, I’ve always thought Dumbledore was cracked to trust Snape. Where’s the evidence he ever really stopped working for You-Know-Who?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I think Dumbledore’s probably got plenty of evidence, even if he doesn’t share it with you, Ron,’ snapped Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, shut up, the pair of you,’ said Harry heavily, as Ron opened his mouth to argue back. Hermione and Ron both froze, looking angry and offended. ‘Can’t you give it a rest?’ said Harry. ‘You’re always having a go at each other, it’s driving me mad.’ And abandoning his shepherd’s pie, he swung his schoolbag back over his shoulder and left them sitting there.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He walked up the marble staircase two steps at a time, past the many students hurrying towards lunch. The anger that had just flared so unexpectedly still blazed inside him, and the vision of Ron and Hermione’s shocked faces afforded him a sense of deep satisfaction. Serve them right, he thought, why can’t they give it a rest … bickering all the time … it’s enough to drive anyone up the wall …

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He passed the large picture of Sir Cadogan the knight on a landing; Sir Cadogan drew his sword and brandished it fiercely at Harry, who ignored him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Come back, you scurvy dog! Stand fast and fight!’ yelled Sir Cadogan in a muffled voice from behind his visor, but Harry merely walked on and when Sir Cadogan attempted to follow him by running into a neighbouring picture, he was rebuffed by its inhabitant, a large and angry-looking wolfhound.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry spent the rest of the lunch hour sitting alone underneath the trapdoor at the top of North Tower. Consequently, he was the first to ascend the silver ladder that led to Sybill Trelawney’s classroom when the bell rang.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: After Potions, Divination was Harry’s least favourite class, which was due mainly to Professor Trelawney’s habit of predicting his premature death every few lessons. A thin woman, heavily draped in shawls and glittering with strings of beads, she always reminded Harry of some kind of insect, with her glasses hugely magnifying her eyes. She was busy putting copies of battered leather-bound books on each of the spindly little tables with which her room was littered when Harry entered the room, but the light cast by the lamps covered by scarves and the low-burning, sickly-scented fire was so dim she appeared not to notice him as he took a seat in the shadows. The rest of the class arrived over the next five minutes. Ron emerged from the trapdoor, looked around carefully, spotted Harry and made directly for him, or as directly as he could while having to wend his way between tables, chairs and overstuffed pouffes.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione and me have stopped arguing,’ he said, sitting down beside Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ grunted Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But Hermione says she thinks it would be nice if you stopped taking out your temper on us,’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m just passing on the message,’ said Ron, talking over him. ‘But I reckon she’s right. It’s not our fault how Seamus and Snape treat you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I never said it -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good-day,’ said Professor Trelawney in her usual misty, dreamy voice, and Harry broke off, again feeling both annoyed and slightly ashamed of himself. ‘And welcome back to Divination. I have, of course, been following your fortunes most carefully over the holidays, and am delighted to see that you have all returned to Hogwarts safely - as, of course, I knew you would.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You will find on the tables before you copies of The Dream Oracle, by Inigo Imago. Dream interpretation is a most important means of divining the future and one that may very probably be tested in your O.W.L. Not, of course, that I believe examination passes or failures are of the remotest importance when it comes to the sacred art of divination. If you have the Seeing Eye, certificates and grades matter very little. However, the Headmaster likes you to sit the examination, so …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Her voice trailed away delicately, leaving them all in no doubt that Professor Trelawney considered her subject above such sordid matters as examinations.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Turn, please, to the introduction and read what Imago has to say on the matter of dream interpretation. Then, divide into pairs. Use The Dream Oracle to interpret each other’s most recent dreams. Carry on.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The one good thing to be said for this lesson was that it was not a double period. By the time they had all finished reading the introduction of the book, they had barely ten minutes left for dream interpretation. At the table next to Harry and Ron, Dean had paired up with Neville, who immediately embarked on a long-winded explanation of a nightmare involving a pair of giant scissors wearing his grandmother’s best hat; Harry and Ron merely looked at each other glumly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I never remember my dreams,’ said Ron, ‘you say one.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You must remember one of them,’ said Harry impatiently.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He was not going to share his dreams with anyone. He knew perfectly well what his regular nightmare about a graveyard meant, he did not need Ron or Professor Trelawney or the stupid Dream Oracle to tell him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I dreamed I was playing Quidditch the other night,’ said Ron, screwing up his face in an effort to remember. ‘What d’you reckon that means?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Probably that you’re going to be eaten by a giant marshmallow or something,’ said Harry, turning the pages of The Dream Oracle without interest. It was very dull work looking up bits of dreams in the Oracle and Harry was not cheered up when Professor Trelawney set them the task of keeping a dream diary for a month as homework. When the bell went, he and Ron led the way back down the ladder, Ron grumbling loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you realise how much homework we’ve got already? Binns set us a foot-and-a-half-long essay on giant wars, Snape wants a foot on the use of moonstones, and now we’ve got a month’s dream diary from Trelawney! Fred and George weren’t wrong about O.W.L. year, were they? That Umbridge woman had better not give us any …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: When they entered the Defence Against the Dark Arts classroom they found Professor Umbridge already seated at the teacher’s desk, wearing the fluffy pink cardigan of the night before and the black velvet bow on top of her head. Harry was again reminded forcibly of a large fly perched unwisely on top of an even larger toad.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The class was quiet as it entered the room; Professor Umbridge was, as yet, an unknown quantity and nobody knew how strict a disciplinarian she was likely to be.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, good afternoon!’ she said, when finally the whole class had sat down.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: A few people mumbled ‘good afternoon’ in reply.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Tut, tut,’ said Professor Umbridge. ‘That won’t do, now, will it? I should like you, please, to reply “Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge”. One more time, please. Good afternoon, class!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good afternoon, Professor Umbridge,’ they chanted back at her.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘There, now,’ said Professor Umbridge sweetly. ‘That wasn’t too difficult, was it? Wands away and quills out, please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Many of the class exchanged gloomy looks; the order ‘wands away’ had never yet been followed by a lesson they had found interesting. Harry shoved his wand back inside his bag and pulled out quill, ink and parchment. Professor Umbridge opened her handbag, extracted her own wand, which was an unusually short one, and tapped the blackboard sharply with it; words appeared on the board at once:

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Defence Against the Dark Arts A Return to Basic Principles

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well now, your teaching in this subject has been rather disrupted and fragmented, hasn’t it?’ stated Professor Umbridge, turning to face the class with her hands clasped neatly in front of her. ‘The constant changing of teachers, many of whom do not seem to have followed any Ministry-approved curriculum, has unfortunately resulted in your being far below the standard we would expect to see in your O.W.L. year.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You will be pleased to know, however, that these problems are now to be rectified. We will be following a carefully structured, theory-centred, Ministry-approved course of defensive magic this year. Copy down the following, please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She rapped the blackboard again; the first message vanished and was replaced by the ‘Course Aims’.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: 1. Understanding the principles underlying defensive magic.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: 2. Learning to recognise situations in which defensive magic can

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: legally be used.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: 3. Placing the use of defensive magic in a context for practical use. For a couple of minutes the room was full of the sound of scratching quills on parchment. When everyone had copied down Professor Umbridge’s three course aims she asked, ‘Has everybody got a copy of Defensive Magical Theory by Wilbert Slinkhard?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There was a dull murmur of assent throughout the class.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I think we’ll try that again,’ said Professor Umbridge. ‘When I ask you a question, I should like you to reply, “Yes, Professor Umbridge”, or “No, Professor Umbridge”. So: has everyone got a copy of Defensive Magical Theory by Wilbert Slinkhard?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Professor Umbridge,’ rang through the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ said Professor Umbridge. ‘I should like you to turn to page five and read “Chapter One, Basics for Beginners”. There will be no need to talk.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge left the blackboard and settled herself in the chair behind the teacher’s desk, observing them all with those pouchy toad’s eyes. Harry turned to page five of his copy of Defensive Magical Theory and started to read.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: It was desperately dull, quite as bad as listening to Professor Binns. He felt his concentration sliding away from him; he had soon read the same line half a dozen times without taking in more than the first few words. Several silent minutes passed. Next to him, Ron was absent-mindedly turning his quill over and over in his fingers, staring at the same spot on the page. Harry looked right and received a surprise to shake him out of his torpor. Hermione had not even opened her copy of Defensive Magical Theory. She was staring fixedly at Professor Umbridge with her hand in the air.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry could not remember Hermione ever neglecting to read when instructed to, or indeed resisting the temptation to open any book that came under her nose. He looked at her enquiringly, but she merely shook her head slightly to indicate that she was not about to answer questions, and continued to stare at Professor Umbridge, who was looking just as resolutely in another direction.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: After several more minutes had passed, however, Harry was not the only one watching Hermione. The chapter they had been instructed to read was so tedious that more and more people were choosing to watch Hermione’s mute attempt to catch Professor Umbridge’s eye rather than struggle on with ‘Basics for Beginners’.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: When more than half the class were staring at Hermione rather than at their books, Professor Umbridge seemed to decide that she could ignore the situation no longer.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Did you want to ask something about the chapter, dear?’ she asked Hermione, as though she had only just noticed her.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Not about the chapter, no,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, we’re reading just now,’ said Professor Umbridge, showing her small pointed teeth. ‘If you have other queries we can deal with them at the end of class.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve got a query about your course aims,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge raised her eyebrows.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And your name is?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione Granger,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Miss Granger, I think the course aims are perfectly clear if you read them through carefully,’ said Professor Umbridge in a voice of determined sweetness.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I don’t,’ said Hermione bluntly. ‘There’s nothing written up there about using defensive spells.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There was a short silence in which many members of the class turned their heads to frown at the three course aims still written on the blackboard.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Using defensive spells?’ Professor Umbridge repeated with a little laugh. ‘Why, I can’t imagine any situation arising in my classroom that would require you to use a defensive spell, Miss Granger. You surely aren’t expecting to be attacked during class?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re not going to use magic?’ Ron exclaimed loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Students raise their hands when they wish to speak in my class, Mr -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Weasley,’ said Ron, thrusting his hand into the air.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge, smiling still more widely, turned her back on him. Harry and Hermione immediately raised their hands too. Professor Umbridge’s pouchy eyes lingered on Harry for a moment before she addressed Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Miss Granger? You wanted to ask something else?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Hermione. ‘Surely the whole point of Defence Against the Dark Arts is to practise defensive spells?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you a Ministry-trained educational expert, Miss Granger?’ asked Professor Umbridge, in her falsely sweet voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, but -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well then, I’m afraid you are not qualified to decide what the “whole point” of any class is. Wizards much older and cleverer than you have devised our new programme of study. You will be learning about defensive spells in a secure, risk-free way -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What use is that?’ said Harry loudly. ‘If we’re going to be attacked, it won’t be in a -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hand, Mr Potter!’ sang Professor Umbridge.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry thrust his fist in the air. Again, Professor Umbridge promptly turned away from him, but now several other people had their hands up, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And your name is?’ Professor Umbridge said to Dean.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Dean Thomas.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Mr Thomas?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, it’s like Harry said, isn’t it?’ said Dean. ‘If we’re going to be attacked, it won’t be risk free.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I repeat,’ said Professor Umbridge, smiling in a very irritating fashion at Dean, ‘do you expect to be attacked during my classes?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, but -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge talked over him. ‘I do not wish to criticise the way things have been run in this school,’ she said, an unconvincing smile stretching her wide mouth, ‘but you have been exposed to some very irresponsible wizards in this class, very irresponsible indeed - not to mention,’ she gave a nasty little laugh, ‘extremely dangerous half-breeds.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘If you mean Professor Lupin,’ piped up Dean angrily, ‘he was the best we ever -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hand, Mr Thomas! As I was saying - you have been introduced to spells that have been complex, inappropriate to your age group and potentially lethal. You have been frightened into believing that you are likely to meet Dark attacks every other day -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No we haven’t,’ Hermione said, ‘we just -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Your hand is not up, Miss Granger!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Hermione put up her hand. Professor Umbridge turned away from her.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It is my understanding that my predecessor not only performed illegal curses in front of you, he actually performed them on you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, he turned out to be a maniac, didn’t he?’ said Dean hotly. ‘Mind you, we still learned loads.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Your hand is not up, Mr Thomas!’ trilled Professor Umbridge. ‘Now, it is the view of the Ministry that a theoretical knowledge will be more than sufficient to get you through your examination, which, after all, is what school is all about. And your name is?’ she added, staring at Parvati, whose hand had just shot up.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Parvati Patil, and isn’t there a practical bit in our Defence Against the Dark Arts O.W.L.? Aren’t we supposed to show that we can actually do the counter-curses and things?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘As long as you have studied the theory hard enough, there is no reason why you should not be able to perform the spells under carefully controlled examination conditions,’ said Professor Umbridge dismissively.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Without ever practising them beforehand?’ said Parvati incredulously. ‘Are you telling us that the first time we’ll get to do the spells will be during our exam?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I repeat, as long as you have studied the theory hard enough -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And what good’s theory going to be in the real world?’ said Harry loudly, his fist in the air again.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge looked up.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘This is school, Mr Potter, not the real world,’ she said softly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So we’re not supposed to be prepared for what’s waiting for us out there?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘There is nothing waiting out there, Mr Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yeah?’ said Harry. His temper, which seemed to have been bubbling just beneath the surface all day, was reaching boiling point.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Who do you imagine wants to attack children like yourselves?’ enquired Professor Umbridge in a horribly honeyed voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hmm, let’s think …’ said Harry in a mock thoughtful voice. ‘Maybe … Lord Voldemort?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Ron gasped; Lavender Brown uttered a little scream; Neville slipped sideways off his stool. Professor Umbridge, however, did not flinch. She was staring at Harry with a grimly satisfied expression on her face.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Ten points from Gryffindor, Mr Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The classroom was silent and still. Everyone was staring at either Umbridge or Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, let me make a few things quite plain.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge stood up and leaned towards them, her stubby-fingered hands splayed on her desk.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You have been told that a certain Dark wizard has returned from the dead -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He wasn’t dead,’ said Harry angrily, ‘but yeah, he’s returned!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr-Potter-you-have-already-lost-your-house-ten-points-do-not-make-matters-worse-for-yourself,’ said Professor Umbridge in one breath without looking at him. ‘As I was saying, you have been informed that a certain Dark wizard is at large once again. This is a lie.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It is NOT a lie!’ said Harry. ‘I saw him, I fought him!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Detention, Mr Potter!’ said Professor Umbridge triumphantly. ‘Tomorrow evening. Five o’clock. My office. I repeat, this is a lie. The Ministry of Magic guarantees that you are not in danger from any Dark wizard. If you are still worried, by all means come and see me outside class hours. If someone is alarming you with fibs about reborn Dark wizards, I would like to hear about it. I am here to help. I am your friend. And now, you will kindly continue your reading. Page five, “Basics for Beginners”.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge sat down behind her desk. Harry, however, stood up. Everyone was staring at him; Seamus looked half-scared, half-fascinated.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, no!’ Hermione whispered in a warning voice, tugging at his sleeve, but Harry jerked his arm out of her reach.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So, according to you, Cedric Diggory dropped dead of his own accord, did he?’ Harry asked, his voice shaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There was a collective intake of breath from the class, for none of them, apart from Ron and Hermione, had ever heard Harry talk about what had happened on the night Cedric had died. They stared avidly from Harry to Professor Umbridge, who had raised her eyes and was staring at him without a trace of a fake smile on her face.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Cedric Diggory’s death was a tragic accident,’ she said coldly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It was murder,’ said Harry. He could feel himself shaking. He had hardly spoken to anyone about this, least of all thirty eagerly listening classmates. ‘Voldemort killed him and you know it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge’s face was quite blank. For a moment, Harry thought she was going to scream at him. Then she said, in her softest, most sweetly girlish voice, ‘Come here, Mr Potter, dear.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He kicked his chair aside, strode around Ron and Hermione and up to the teacher’s desk. He could feel the rest of the class holding its breath. He felt so angry he did not care what happened next.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor Umbridge pulled a small roll of pink parchment out of her handbag, stretched it out on the desk, dipped her quill into a bottle of ink and started scribbling, hunched over so that Harry could not see what she was writing. Nobody spoke. After a minute or so she rolled up the parchment and tapped it with her wand; it sealed itself seamlessly so that he could not open it.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Take this to Professor McGonagall, dear,’ said Professor Umbridge, holding out the note to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He took it from her without saying a word and left the room, not even looking back at Ron and Hermione, slamming the classroom door shut behind him. He walked very fast along the corridor, the note to McGonagall clutched tight in his hand, and turning a corner walked slap into Peeves the poltergeist, a wide-mouthed little man floating on his back in midair, juggling several inkwells.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Why, it’s Potty Wee Potter!’ cackled Peeves, allowing two of the inkwells to fall to the ground where they smashed and spattered the walls with ink; Harry jumped backwards out of the way with a snarl.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Get out of it, Peeves.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oooh, Crackpot’s feeling cranky,’ said Peeves, pursuing Harry along the corridor, leering as he zoomed along above him. ‘What is it this time, my fine Potty friend? Hearing voices? Seeing visions? Speaking in -‘ Peeves blew a gigantic raspberry ‘- tongues?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I said, leave me ALONE!’ Harry shouted, running down the nearest flight of stairs, but Peeves merely slid down the banister on his back beside him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, most think he’s barking, the potty wee lad,

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But some are more kindly and think he’s just sad,

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But Peevesy knows better and says that he’s mad -‘ ‘SHUT UP!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: A door to his left flew open and Professor McGonagall emerged from her office looking grim and slightly harassed.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What on earth are you shouting about, Potter?’ she snapped, as Peeves cackled gleefully and zoomed out of sight. ‘Why aren’t you in class?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve been sent to see you,’ said Harry stiffly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Sent? What do you mean, sent?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He held out the note from Professor Umbridge. Professor McGonagall took it from him, frowning, slit it open with a tap of her wand, stretched it out and began to read. Her eyes zoomed from side to side behind their square spectacles as she read what Umbridge had written, and with each line they became narrower.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Come in here, Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He followed her inside her study. The door closed automatically behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well?’ said Professor McGonagall, rounding on him. ‘Is this true?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Is what true?’ Harry asked, rather more aggressively than he had intended. ‘Professor?’ he added, in an attempt to sound more polite.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Is it true that you shouted at Professor Umbridge?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You called her a liar?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You told her He Who Must Not Be Named is back?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall sat down behind her desk, frowning at Harry. Then she said, ‘Have a biscuit, Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Have - what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Have a biscuit,’ she repeated impatiently, indicating a tartan tin lying on top of one of the piles of papers on her desk. ‘And sit down.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There had been a previous occasion when Harry, expecting to be caned by Professor McGonagall, had instead been appointed by her to the Gryffindor Quidditch team. He sank into a chair opposite her and helped himself to a Ginger Newt, feeling just as confused and wrong-footed as he had done on that occasion.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall set down Professor Umbridge’s note and looked very seriously at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Potter, you need to be careful.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry swallowed his mouthful of Ginger Newt and stared at her. Her tone of voice was not at all what he was used to; it was not brisk, crisp and stern; it was low and anxious and somehow much more human than usual.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Misbehaviour in Dolores Umbridge’s class could cost you much more than house points and a detention.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What do you -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Potter, use your common sense,’ snapped Professor McGonagall, with an abrupt return to her usual manner. ‘You know where she comes from, you must know to whom she is reporting.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The bell rang for the end of the lesson. Overhead and all around came the elephantine sounds of hundreds of students on the move.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It says here she’s given you detention every evening this week, starting tomorrow,’ Professor McGonagall said, looking down at Umbridge’s note again.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Every evening this week!’ Harry repeated, horrified. ‘But, Professor, couldn’t you -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I couldn’t,’ said Professor McGonagall flatly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘She is your teacher and has every right to give you detention. You will go to her room at five o’clock tomorrow for the first one. Just remember: tread carefully around Dolores Umbridge.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But I was telling the truth!’ said Harry, outraged. ‘Voldemort is back, you know he is; Professor Dumbledore knows he is -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘For heaven’s sake, Potter!’ said Professor McGonagall, straightening her glasses angrily (she had winced horribly when he had used Voldemort’s name). ‘Do you really think this is about truth or lies? It’s about keeping your head down and your temper under control!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She stood up, nostrils wide and mouth very thin, and Harry stood up, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Have another biscuit,’ she said irritably, thrusting the tin at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, thanks,’ said Harry coldly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be ridiculous,’ she snapped.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He took one.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Thanks,’ he said grudgingly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Didn’t you listen to Dolores Umbridge’s speech at the start-ofterm feast, Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry. ‘Yeah … she said … progress will be prohibited or … well, it meant that … that the Ministry of Magic is trying to interfere at Hogwarts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall eyed him for a moment, then sniffed, walked around her desk and held open the door for him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’m glad you listen to Hermione Granger at any rate,’ she said, pointing him out of her office.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Dinner in the Great Hall that night was not a pleasant experience for Harry. The news about his shouting match with Umbridge had travelled exceptionally fast even by Hogwarts’ standards. He heard whispers all around him as he sat eating between Ron and Hermione. The funny thing was that none of the whisperers seemed to mind him overhearing what they were saying about him. On the contrary, it was as though they were hoping he would get angry and start shouting again, so that they could hear his story firsthand.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He says he saw Cedric Diggory murdered …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He reckons he duelled with You-Know-Who …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Come off it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Who does he think he’s kidding?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Pur-lease …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What I don’t get,’ said Harry in a shaking voice, laying down his knife and fork (his hands were trembling too much to hold them steady), ‘is why they all believed the story two months ago when Dumbledore told them …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘The thing is, Harry, I’m not sure they did,’ said Hermione grimly. ‘Oh, let’s get out of here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She slammed down her own knife and fork; Ron looked longingly at his half-finished apple pie but followed suit. People stared at them all the way out of the Hall.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What d’you mean, you’re not sure they believed Dumbledore?’ Harry asked Hermione when they reached the first-floor landing.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Look, you don’t understand what it was like after it happened,’ said Hermione quietly. ‘You arrived back in the middle of the lawn clutching Cedric’s dead body … none of us saw what happened in the maze … we just had Dumbledore’s word for it that You-Know-Who had come back and killed Cedric and fought you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Which is the truth!’ said Harry loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I know it is, Harry, so will you please stop biting my head off?’ said Hermione wearily. ‘It’s just that before the truth could sink in, everyone went home for the summer, where they spent two months reading about how you’re a nutcase and Dumbledore’s going senile!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Rain pounded on the windowpanes as they strode along the empty corridors back to Gryffindor Tower. Harry felt as though his first day had lasted a week, but he still had a mountain of homework to do before bed. A dull pounding pain was developing over his right eye. He glanced out of a rain-washed window at the dark grounds as they turned into the Fat Lady’s corridor. There was still no light in Hagrid’s cabin.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Mimbulus mimbletonia,’ said Hermione, before the Fat Lady could ask. The portrait swung open to reveal the hole behind it and the three of them scrambled through it.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The common room was almost empty; nearly everyone was still down at dinner. Crookshanks uncoiled himself from an armchair and trotted to meet them, purring loudly, and when Harry, Ron and Hermione took their three favourite chairs at the fireside he leapt lightly on to Hermione’s lap and curled up there like a furry ginger cushion. Harry gazed into the flames, feeling drained and exhausted.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘How can Dumbledore have let this happen?’ Hermione cried suddenly, making Harry and Ron jump; Crookshanks leapt off her, looking affronted. She pounded the arms of her chair in fury, so that bits of stuffing leaked out of the holes. ‘How can he let that terrible woman teach us? And in our O.W.L. year, too!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, we’ve never had great Defence Against the Dark Arts teachers, have we?’ said Harry. ‘You know what it’s like, Hagrid told us, nobody wants the job; they say it’s jinxed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, but to employ someone who’s actually refusing to let us do magic! What’s Dumbledore playing at?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And she’s trying to get people to spy for her,’ said Ron darkly. ‘Remember when she said she wanted us to come and tell her if we hear anyone saying You-Know-Who’s back?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course she’s here to spy on us all, that’s obvious, why else would Fudge have wanted her to come?’ snapped Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t start arguing again,’ said Harry wearily, as Ron opened his mouth to retaliate. ‘Can’t we just … let’s just do that homework, get it out of the way …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: They collected their schoolbags from a corner and returned to the chairs by the fire. People were coming back from dinner now. Harry kept his face averted from the portrait hole, but could still sense the stares he was attracting.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Shall we do Snape’s stuff first?’ said Ron, dipping his quill into his ink. ’”The properties … of moonstone … and its uses … in potion-making …”‘ he muttered, writing the words across the top of his parchment as he spoke them. ‘There.’ He underlined the title, then looked up expectantly at Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So, what are the properties of moonstone and its uses in potion-making?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But Hermione was not listening; she was squinting over into the far corner of the room, where Fred, George and Lee Jordan were now sitting at the centre of a knot of innocent-looking first-years, all of whom were chewing something that seemed to have come out of a large paper bag that Fred was holding.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I’m sorry, they’ve gone too far,’ she said, standing up and looking positively furious. ‘Come on, Ron.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I - what?’ said Ron, plainly playing for time. ‘No - come on, Hermione - we can’t tell them off for giving out sweets.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You know perfectly well that those are bits of Nosebleed Nougat or - or Puking Pastilles or -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Fainting Fancies?’ Harry suggested quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: It was the same, if not worse, in Transfiguration.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Now panicking slightly about the amount of homework they had to do, Harry and Ron spent their lunch hour in the library looking up the uses of moonstones in potion-making. book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The day had become cool and breezy, and as they walked down the sloping lawn towards Hagrid’s cabin on the edge of the Forbidden Forest, they felt the occasional drop of rain on their faces. As Harry and Ron reached her, a loud shout of laughter sounded behind them; turning, they saw Draco Malfoy striding towards them, surrounded by his usual gang of Slytherin cronies. He had clearly just said something highly amusing, because Crabbe, Goyle, Pansy Parkinson and the rest continued to snigger heartily as they gathered around the trestle table and, judging by the way they all kept looking over at Harry, he was able to guess the subject of the joke without too much difficulty.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She indicated the heap of twigs in front of her. Hermione’s hand shot into the air. book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

text_content: ‘Good girl, take another five points. book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What now?’ he muttered wearily, turning to face Angelina Johnson, who looked as though she was in a towering temper.

text_content: ‘Well, you can just go straight to her and ask her to let you off on Friday,’ said Angelina fiercely, ‘and I don’t care how you do it. Tell her You-Know-Who’s a figment of your imagination if you like, just make sure you’re there!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: She stormed away.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Ron moaned and for some reason glanced up at the ceiling.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s that got to do with our homework?’ said Hermione, her eyebrows raised.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: At five to five Harry bade the other two goodbye and set off for Umbridge’s office on the third floor. When he knocked on the door she called, ‘Come in,’ in a sugary voice. He entered cautiously, looking around.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He had known this office under three of its previous occupants. In the days when Gilderoy Lockhart had lived here it had been plastered in beaming portraits of himself. When Lupin had occupied it, it was likely you would meet some fascinating Dark creature in a cage or tank if you came to call. In the impostor Moody’s days it had been packed with various instruments and artefacts for the detection of wrongdoing and concealment.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Now, however, it looked totally unrecognisable. The surfaces had all been draped in lacy covers and cloths. There were several vases full of dried flowers, each one residing on its own doily, and on one of the walls was a collection of ornamental plates, each decorated with a large technicoloured kitten wearing a different bow around its neck. These were so foul that Harry stared at them, transfixed, until Professor Umbridge spoke again.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good evening, Mr Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry started and looked around. He had not noticed her at first because she was wearing a luridly flowered set of robes that blended only too well with the tablecloth on the desk behind her.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Evening, Professor Umbridge,’ Harry said stiffly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, sit down,’ she said, pointing towards a small table draped in lace beside which she had drawn up a straight-backed chair. A piece of blank parchment lay on the table, apparently waiting for him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Er,’ said Harry, without moving. ‘Professor Umbridge. Er - before we start, I - I wanted to ask you a … a favour.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Her bulging eyes narrowed.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

He had known Percy for four years, had stayed in his house during the summer holidays, shared a tent with him during the Quidditch World Cup, had even been awarded full marks by him in the second task of the Triwizard Tournament last year, yet now, Percy thought him unbalanced and possibly violent.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

text_content: Hagrid grunted in amusement.
