text_content: ‘Well,’ said Lupin slowly, ‘Snape was a special case. I mean, he never lost an opportunity to curse James so you couldn’t really expect James to take that lying down, could you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And my mum was OK with that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘She didn’t know too much about it, to tell you the truth,’ said Sirius. ‘I mean, James didn’t take Snape on dates with her and jinx him in front of her, did he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Sirius frowned at Harry, who was still looking unconvinced.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Look,’ he said, ‘your father was the best friend I ever had and he was a good person. A lot of people are idiots at the age of fifteen. He grew out of it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, OK,’ said Harry heavily. ‘I just never thought I’d feel sorry for Snape.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Now you mention it,’ said Lupin, a faint crease between his eyebrows, ‘how did Snape react when he found you’d seen all this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He told me he’d never teach me Occlumency again,’ said Harry indifferently, ‘like that’s a big disappoint—’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He WHAT?’ shouted Sirius, causing Harry to jump and inhale a mouthful of ashes.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you serious, Harry?’ said Lupin quickly. ‘He’s stopped giving you lessons?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, surprised at what he considered a great overreaction. ‘But it’s OK, I don’t care, it’s a bit of a relief to tell you the -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m coming up there to have a word with Snape!’ said Sirius forcefully, and he actually made to stand up, but Lupin wrenched him back down again.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘If anyone’s going to tell Snape it will be me!’ he said firmly. ‘But Harry, first of all, you’re to go back to Snape and tell him that on no account is he to stop giving you lessons - when Dumbledore hears -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t tell him that, he’d kill me!’ said Harry, outraged. ‘You didn’t see him when we got out of the Pensieve.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, there is nothing so important as you learning Occlumency!’ said Lupin sternly. ‘Do you understand me? Nothing!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘OK, OK,’ said Harry, thoroughly discomposed, not to mention annoyed. ‘I’ll … I’ll try and say something to him … but it won’t be -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He fell silent. He could hear distant footsteps.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Is that Kreacher coming downstairs?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Sirius, glancing behind him. ‘It must be somebody your end.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry’s heart skipped several beats.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’d better go!’ he said hastily and pulled his head backwards out of the Grimmauld Place fire. For a moment his head seemed to be revolving on his shoulders, then he found himself kneeling in front of Umbridge’s fire with it firmly back on and watching the emerald flames flicker and die.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Quickly, quickly!’ he heard a wheezy voice mutter right outside the office door. ‘Ah, she’s left it open -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry dived for the Invisibility Cloak and had just managed to pull it back over himself when Filch burst into the office. He looked absolutely delighted about something and was talking to himself feverishly as he crossed the room, pulled open a drawer in Umbridge’s desk and began rifling through the papers inside it.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Approval for Whipping … Approval for Whipping … I can do it at last … they’ve had it coming to them for years …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He pulled out a piece of parchment, kissed it, then shuffled rapidly back out of the door, clutching it to his chest.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry leapt to his feet and, making sure he had his bag and that the Invisibility Cloak was completely covering him, he wrenched open the door and hurried out of the office after Filch, who was hobbling along faster than Harry had ever seen him go.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: One landing down from Umbridge’s office, Harry thought it was safe to become visible again. He pulled off the Cloak, shoved it in his bag and hurried onwards. There was a great deal of shouting and movement coming from the Entrance Hall. He ran down the marble staircase and found what looked like most of the school assembled there.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: It was just like the night when Trelawney had been sacked. Students were standing all around the walls in a great ring (some of them, Harry noticed, covered in a substance that looked very like Stinksap); teachers and ghosts were also in the crowd. Prominent among the onlookers were members of the Inquisitorial Squad, who were all looking exceptionally pleased with themselves, and Peeves, who was bobbing overhead, gazed down at Fred and George who stood in the middle of the floor with the unmistakeable look of two people who had just been cornered.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So!’ said Umbridge triumphantly. Harry realised she was standing just a few stairs in front of him, once more looking down upon her prey. ‘So - you think it amusing to turn a school corridor into a swamp, do you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Pretty amusing, yeah,’ said Fred, looking up at her without the slightest sign of fear.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Filch elbowed his way closer to Umbridge, almost crying with happiness.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve got the form, Headmistress,’ he said hoarsely, waving the piece of parchment Harry had just seen him take from her desk. ‘I’ve got the form and I’ve got the whips waiting … oh, let me do it now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Very good, Argus,’ she said. ‘You two,’ she went on, gazing down at Fred and George, ‘are about to learn what happens to wrongdoers in my school.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You know what?’ said Fred. ‘I don’t think we are.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He turned to his twin.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘George,’ said Fred, ‘I think we’ve outgrown full-time education.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I’ve been feeling that way myself,’ said George lightly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Time to test our talents in the real world, d’you reckon?’ asked Fred.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Definitely,’ said George.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: And before Umbridge could say a word, they raised their wands and said together:

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Accio brooms!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry heard a loud crash somewhere in the distance. Looking to his left, he ducked just in time. Fred and George’s broomsticks, one still trailing the heavy chain and iron peg with which Umbridge had fastened them to the wall, were hurtling along the corridor towards their owners; they turned left, streaked down the stairs and stopped sharply in front of the twins, the chain clattering loudly on the flagged stone floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We won’t be seeing you,’ Fred told Professor Umbridge, swinging his leg over his broomstick.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, don’t bother to keep in touch,’ said George, mounting his own.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Fred looked around at the assembled students, at the silent, watchful crowd.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘If anyone fancies buying a Portable Swamp, as demonstrated upstairs, come to number ninety-three, Diagon Alley - Weasleys’ Wizard Wheezes,’ he said in a loud voice. ‘Our new premises!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Special discounts to Hogwarts students who swear they’re going to use our products to get rid of this old bat,’ added George, pointing at Professor Umbridge.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘STOP THEM!’ shrieked Umbridge, but it was too late. As the Inquisitorial Squad closed in, Fred and George kicked off from the floor, shooting fifteen feet into the air, the iron peg swinging dangerously below. Fred looked across the hall at the poltergeist bobbing on his level above the crowd.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Give her hell from us, Peeves.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: And Peeves, who Harry had never seen take an order from a student before, swept his belled hat from his head and sprang to a salute as Fred and George wheeled about to tumultuous applause from the students below and sped out of the open front doors into the glorious sunset.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The story of Fred and George’s flight to freedom was retold so often over the next few days that Harry could tell it would soon become the stuff of Hogwarts legend: within a week, even those who had been eye-witnesses were half-convinced they had seen the twins dive-bomb Umbridge on their brooms and pelt her with Dungbombs before zooming out of the doors. In the immediate aftermath of their departure there was a great wave of talk about copying them. Harry frequently heard students saying things like, ‘Honestly, some days I just feel like jumping on my broom and leaving this place,’ or else, ‘One more lesson like that and I might just do a Weasley.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Fred and George had made sure nobody was likely to forget them too soon. For one thing, they had not left instructions on how to remove the swamp that now filled the corridor on the fifth floor of the east wing. Umbridge and Filch had been observed trying different means of removing it but without success. Eventually, the area was roped off and Filch, gnashing his teeth furiously, was given the task of punting students across it to their classrooms. Harry was certain that teachers like McGonagall or Flitwick could have removed the swamp in an instant but, just as in the case of Fred and George’s Wildfire Whiz-bangs, they seemed to prefer to watch Umbridge struggle.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Then there were the two large broom-shaped holes in Umbridge’s office door, through which Fred and George’s Cleansweeps had smashed to rejoin their masters. Filch fitted a new door and removed Harry’s Firebolt to the dungeons where, it was rumoured, Umbridge had set an armed security troll to guard it. However, her troubles were far from over.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Inspired by Fred and George’s example, a great number of students were now vying for the newly vacant positions of Troublemakers-in-Chief. In spite of the new door, somebody managed to slip a hairy-snouted Niffler into Umbridge’s office, which promptly tore the place apart in its search for shiny objects, leapt on Umbridge when she entered and tried to gnaw the rings off her stubby fingers. Dungbombs and Stink Pellets were dropped so frequently in the corridors that it became the new fashion for students to perform Bubble-Head Charms on themselves before leaving lessons, which ensured them a supply of fresh air, even though it gave them all the peculiar appearance of wearing upside-down goldfish bowls on their heads.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Filch prowled the corridors with a horsewhip ready in his hands, desperate to catch miscreants, but the problem was that there were now so many of them he never knew which way to turn. The Inquisitorial Squad was attempting to help him, but odd things kept happening to its members. Warrington of the Slytherin Quidditch team reported to the hospital wing with a horrible skin complaint that made him look as though he had been coated in cornflakes; Pansy Parkinson, to Hermione’s delight, missed all her lessons the following day as she had sprouted antlers.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Meanwhile, it became clear just how many Skiving Snackboxes Fred and George had managed to sell before leaving Hogwarts. Umbridge only had to enter her classroom for the students assembled there to faint, vomit, develop dangerous fevers or else spout blood from both nostrils. Shrieking with rage and frustration, she attempted to trace the mysterious symptoms to their source, but the students told her stubbornly they were suffering from ‘Umbridgeitis’. After putting four successive classes in detention and failing to discover their secret, she was forced to give up and allow the bleeding, swooning, sweating and vomiting students to leave her classes in droves.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But not even the users of the Snackboxes could compete with that master of chaos, Peeves, who seemed to have taken Fred’s parting words deeply to heart. Cackling madly, he soared through the school, upending tables, bursting out of blackboards, toppling statues and vases; twice he shut Mrs Norris inside a suit of armour, from which she was rescued, yowling loudly, by the furious caretaker. Peeves smashed lanterns and snuffed out candles, juggled burning torches over the heads of screaming students, caused neatly stacked piles of parchment to topple into fires or out of windows; flooded the second floor when he pulled off all the taps in the bathrooms, dropped a bag of tarantulas in the middle of the Great Hall during breakfast and, whenever he fancied a break, spent hours at a time floating along after Umbridge and blowing loud raspberries every time she spoke.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: None of the staff but Filch seemed to be stirring themselves to help her. Indeed, a week after Fred and George’s departure Harry witnessed Professor McGonagall walking right past Peeves, who was determinedly loosening a crystal chandelier, and could have sworn he heard her tell the poltergeist out of the corner of her mouth, ‘It unscrews the other way.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: To cap matters, Montague had still not recovered from his sojourn in the toilet; he remained confused and disorientated and his parents were to be observed one Tuesday morning striding up the front drive, looking extremely angry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Should we say something?’ said Hermione in a worried voice, pressing her cheek against the Charms window so that she could see Mr and Mrs Montague marching inside. ‘About what happened to him? In case it helps Madam Pomfrey cure him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Course not, he’ll recover,’ said Ron indifferently.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway, more trouble for Umbridge, isn’t it?’ said Harry in a satisfied voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He and Ron both tapped the teacups they were supposed to be charming with their wands. Harry’s spouted four very short legs that could not reach the desk and wriggled pointlessly in midair. Ron’s grew four very thin spindly legs that hoisted the cup off the desk with great difficulty, trembled for a few seconds, then folded, causing the cup to crack into two.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Reparo,’ said Hermione quickly, mending Ron’s cup with a wave of her wand. ‘That’s all very well, but what if Montague’s permanently injured?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Who cares?’ said Ron irritably, while his teacup stood up drunkenly again, trembling violently at the knees. ‘Montague shouldn’t have tried to take all those points from Gryffindor, should he? If you want to worry about anyone, Hermione, worry about me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You?’ she said, catching her teacup as it scampered happily away across the desk on four sturdy little willow-patterned legs, and replacing it in front of her. ‘Why should I be worried about you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘When Mum’s next letter finally gets through Umbridge’s screening process,’ said Ron bitterly, now holding his cup up while its frail legs tried feebly to support its weight, ‘I’m going to be in deep trouble. I wouldn’t be surprised if she’s sent another Howler.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It’ll be my fault Fred and George left, you wait,’ said Ron darkly. ‘She’ll say I should’ve stopped them leaving, I should’ve grabbed the ends of their brooms and hung on or something … yeah, it’ll be all my fault.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, if she does say that it’ll be very unfair, you couldn’t have done anything! But I’m sure she won’t, I mean, if it’s really true they’ve got premises in Diagon Alley, they must have been planning this for ages.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, but that’s another thing, how did they get premises?’ said Ron, hitting his teacup so hard with his wand that its legs collapsed again and it lay twitching before him. ‘It’s a bit dodgy, isn’t it? They’ll need loads of Galleons to afford the rent on a place in Diagon Alley. She’ll want to know what they’ve been up to, to get their hands on that sort of gold.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, yes, that occurred to me, too,’ said Hermione, allowing her teacup to jog in neat little circles around Harry’s, whose stubby little legs were still unable to touch the desktop, ‘I’ve been wondering whether Mundungus has persuaded them to sell stolen goods or something awful.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He hasn’t,’ said Harry curtly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘How do you know?’ said Ron and Hermione together.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Because -‘ Harry hesitated, but the moment to confess finally seemed to have come. There was no good to be gained in keeping silent if it meant anyone suspected that Fred and George were criminals. ‘Because they got the gold from me. I gave them my Triwizard winnings last June.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: There was a shocked silence, then Hermione’s teacup jogged right over the edge of the desk and smashed on the floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Harry, you didn’t!’ she said.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I did,’ said Harry mutinously. ‘And I don’t regret it, either. I didn’t need the gold and they’ll be great at running a joke shop.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But this is excellent!’ said Ron, looking thrilled. ‘It’s all your fault, Harry - Mum can’t blame me at all! Can I tell her?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I suppose you’d better,’ said Harry dully, ”specially if she thinks they’re receiving stolen cauldrons or something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Hermione said nothing at all for the rest of the lesson, but Harry had a shrewd suspicion that her self-restraint was bound to crack before long. Sure enough, once they had left the castle for break and were standing around in the weak May sunshine, she fixed Harry with a beady eye and opened her mouth with a determined air.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry interrupted her before she had even started.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s no good nagging me, it’s done,’ he said firmly. ‘Fred and George have got the gold - spent a good bit of it, too, by the sounds of it - and I can’t get it back from them and I don’t want to. So save your breath, Hermione.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I wasn’t going to say anything about Fred and George!’ she said in an injured voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Ron snorted disbelievingly and Hermione threw him a very dirty look.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I wasn’t!’ she said angrily. ‘As a matter of fact, I was going to ask Harry when he’s going to go back to Snape and ask for more Occlumency lessons!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry’s heart sank. Once they had exhausted the subject of Fred and George’s dramatic departure, which admittedly had taken many hours, Ron and Hermione had wanted to hear news of Sirius. As Harry had not confided in them the reason he had wanted to talk to Sirius in the first place, it had been hard to think of what to tell them; he had ended up saying, truthfully, that Sirius wanted Harry to resume Occlumency lessons. He had been regretting this ever since; Hermione would not let the subject drop and kept reverting to it when Harry least expected it.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You can’t tell me you’ve stopped having funny dreams,’ Hermione said now, ‘because Ron told me you were muttering in your sleep again last night.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry threw Ron a furious look. Ron had the grace to look ashamed of himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You were only muttering a bit,’ he mumbled apologetically. ‘Something about “just a bit further”.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I dreamed I was watching you lot play Quidditch,’ Harry lied brutally. ‘I was trying to get you to stretch out a bit further to grab the Quaffle.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Ron’s ears went red. Harry felt a kind of vindictive pleasure; he had not, of course, dreamed anything of the sort.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Last night, he had once again made the journey along the Department of Mysteries corridor. He had passed through the circular room, then the room full of clicking and dancing light, until he found himself again inside that cavernous room full of shelves on which were ranged dusty glass spheres.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He had hurried straight towards row number ninety-seven, turned left and run along it … it had probably been then that he had spoken aloud … just a bit further … for he felt his conscious self struggling to wake … and before he had reached the end of the row, he had found himself lying in bed again, gazing up at the canopy of his four-poster.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You are trying to block your mind, aren’t you?’ said Hermione, looking beadily at Harry. ‘You are keeping going with your Occlumency?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course I am,’ said Harry, trying to sound as though this question was insulting, but not quite meeting her eye. The truth was he was so intensely curious about what was hidden in that room full of dusty orbs, that he was quite keen for the dreams to continue.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The problem was that with just under a month to go until the exams and every free moment devoted to revision, his mind seemed so saturated with information when he went to bed he found it very difficult to get to sleep at all; and when he did, his overwrought brain presented him most nights with stupid dreams about the exams. He also suspected that part of his mind - the part that often spoke in Hermione’s voice - now felt guilty on the occasions it strayed down that corridor ending in the black door, and sought to wake him before he could reach the journey’s end.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You know,’ said Ron, whose ears were still flaming red, ‘if Montague doesn’t recover before Slytherin play Hufflepuff, we might be in with a chance of winning the Cup.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I s’pose so,’ said Harry, glad of a change of subject.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I mean, we’ve won one, lost one - if Slytherin lose to Hufflepuff next Saturday -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, that’s right,’ said Harry, losing track of what he was agreeing to. Cho Chang had just walked across the courtyard, determinedly not looking at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The final match of the Quidditch season, Gryffindor versus Ravenclaw, was to take place on the last weekend of May. Although Slytherin had been narrowly defeated by Hufflepuff in their last match, Gryffindor were not daring to hope for victory, due mainly (though of course nobody said it to him) to Ron’s abysmal goal-keeping record. He, however, seemed to have found a new optimism.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I mean, I can’t get any worse, can I?’ he told Harry and Hermione grimly over breakfast on the morning of the match. ‘Nothing to lose now, is there?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You know,’ said Hermione, as she and Harry walked down to the pitch a little later in the midst of a very excitable crowd, ‘I think Ron might do better without Fred and George around. They never exactly gave him a lot of confidence.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Luna Lovegood overtook them with what appeared to be a live eagle perched on top of her head.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, gosh, I forgot!’ said Hermione, watching the eagle flapping its wings as Luna walked serenely past a group of cackling and pointing Slytherins. ‘Cho will be playing, won’t she?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry, who had not forgotten this, merely grunted.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: They found seats in the second topmost row of the stands. It was a fine, clear day; Ron could not wish for better, and Harry found himself hoping against hope that Ron would not give the Slytherins cause for more rousing choruses of ‘Weasley is our King’.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Lee Jordan, who had been very dispirited since Fred and George had left, was commentating as usual. As the teams zoomed out on to the pitch he named the players with something less than his usual gusto.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘… Bradley … Davies … Chang,’ he said, and Harry felt his stomach perform, less of a back flip, more a feeble lurch as Cho walked out on to the pitch, her shiny black hair rippling in the slight breeze. He was not sure what he wanted to happen any more, except that he could not stand any more rows. Even the sight of her chatting animatedly to Roger Davies as they prepared to mount their brooms caused him only a slight twinge of jealousy.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And they’re off!’ said Lee. ‘And Davies takes the Quaffle immediately, Ravenclaw Captain Davies with the Quaffle, he dodges Johnson, he dodges Bell, he dodges Spinnet as well … he’s going straight for goal! He’s going to shoot - and - and -‘ Lee swore very loudly. ‘And he’s scored.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione groaned with the rest of the Gryffindors. Predictably, horribly, the Slytherins on the other side of the stands began to sing:

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Weasley cannot save a thing

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He cannot block a single ring …’ ‘Harry,’ said a hoarse voice in Harry’s ear. ‘Hermione …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry looked round and saw Hagrid’s enormous bearded face sticking between the seats. Apparently, he had squeezed his way all along the row behind, for the first- and second-years he had just passed had a ruffled, flattened look about them. For some reason, Hagrid was bent double as though anxious not to be seen, though he was still at least four feet taller than everybody else.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Listen,’ he whispered, ‘can yeh come with me? Now? While ev’ryone’s watchin’ the match?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Er … can’t it wait, Hagrid?’ asked Harry. ‘Till the match is over?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Hagrid. ‘No, Harry, it’s gotta be now … while ev’ryone’s lookin’ the other way … please?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Hagrid’s nose was gently dripping blood. His eyes were both blackened. Harry had not seen him this close-up since his return to the school; he looked utterly woebegone.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Course,’ said Harry at once, ‘course we’ll come.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He and Hermione edged back along their row of seats, causing much grumbling among the students who had to stand up for them. The people in Hagrid’s row were not complaining, merely attempting to make themselves as small as possible.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I ‘ppreciate this, you two, I really do,’ said Hagrid as they reached the stairs. He kept looking around nervously as they descended towards the lawn below. ‘I jus’ hope she doesn’ notice us goin’.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You mean Umbridge?’ said Harry. ‘She won’t, she’s got her whole Inquisitorial Squad sitting with her, didn’t you see? She must be expecting trouble at the match.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, a bit o’ trouble wouldn’ hurt,’ said Hagrid, pausing to peer around the edge of the stands to make sure the stretch of lawn between there and his cabin was deserted. ‘Give us more time.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What is it, Hagrid?’ said Hermione, looking up at him with a concerned expression on her face as they hurried across the grass towards the edge of the Forest.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh - yeh’ll see in a mo’,’ said Hagrid, looking over his shoulder as a great roar rose from the stands behind them. ‘Hey - did someone jus’ score?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It’ll be Ravenclaw,’ said Harry heavily.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good … good …’ said Hagrid distractedly. ‘Tha’s good …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: They had to jog to keep up with him as he strode across the lawn, looking around with every other step. When they reached his cabin, Hermione turned automatically left towards the front door. Hagrid, however, walked straight past it into the shade of the trees on the outermost edge of the Forest, where he picked up a crossbow that was leaning against a tree. When he realised they were no longer with him, he turned.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re goin’ in here,’ he said, jerking his shaggy head behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Into the Forest?’ said Hermione, perplexed.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Hagrid. ‘C’mon now, quick, before we’re spotted!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione looked at each other, then ducked into the cover of the trees behind Hagrid, who was already striding away from them into the green gloom, his crossbow over his arm. Harry and Hermione ran to catch up with him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, why are you armed?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Jus’ a precaution,’ said Hagrid, shrugging his massive shoulders.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You didn’t bring your crossbow the day you showed us the Thestrals,’ said Hermione timidly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Nah, well, we weren’ goin’ in so far then,’ said Hagrid. ‘An’ anyway, tha’ was before Firenze left the Forest, wasn’ it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Why does Firenze leaving make a difference?’ asked Hermione curiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ”Cause the other centaurs are good an’ riled at me, tha’s why,’ said Hagrid quietly, glancing around. ‘They used ter be - well, yeh couldn’ call ‘em friendly - but we got on all righ’. Kept ‘emselves to ‘emselves, bu’ always turned up if I wanted a word. Not any more.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He sighed deeply.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Firenze said they’re angry because he went to work for Dumbledore,’ Harry said, tripping on a protruding root because he was busy watching Hagrid’s profile.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Hagrid heavily. ‘Well, angry doesn’ cover it. Ruddy livid. If I hadn’ stepped in, I reckon they’d’ve kicked Firenze ter death -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘They attacked him?’ said Hermione, sounding shocked.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yep,’ said Hagrid gruffly, forcing his way through several low-hanging branches. ‘He had half the herd on to him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And you stopped it?’ said Harry, amazed and impressed. ‘By yourself?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Course I did, couldn’t stand by an’ watch ‘em kill ‘im, could I?’ said Hagrid. ‘Lucky I was passin’, really … an’ I’d’ve thought Firenze mighta remembered tha’ before he started sendin’ me stupid warnin’s!’ he added hotly and unexpectedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione looked at each other, startled, but Hagrid, scowling, did not elaborate.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway,’ he said, breathing a little more heavily than usual, ‘since then the other centaurs’ve bin livid with me, an’ the trouble is they’ve got a lot of influence in the Forest … cleverest creatures in here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Is that why we’re here, Hagrid?’ asked Hermione. ‘The centaurs?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, no,’ said Hagrid, shaking his head dismissively, ‘no, it’s not them. Well, o’ course, they could complicate the problem, yeah … but yeh’ll see what I mean in a bit.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: On this incomprehensible note he fell silent and forged a little ahead, taking one stride for every three of theirs, so that they had great trouble keeping up with him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The path was becoming increasingly overgrown and the trees grew so closely together as they walked further and further into the Forest that it was as dark as dusk. They were soon a long way past the clearing where Hagrid had shown them the Thestrals, but Harry felt no sense of unease until Hagrid stepped unexpectedly off the path and began wending his way in and out of trees towards the dark heart of the Forest.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid!’ said Harry, fighting his way through thickly knotted brambles, over which Hagrid had stepped with ease, and remembering very vividly what had happened to him on the other occasion he had stepped off the Forest path. ‘Where are we going?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Bit further,’ said Hagrid over his shoulder. ‘C’mon, Harry … we need ter keep together now.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: It was a great struggle to keep up with Hagrid, what with branches and thickets of thorn through which Hagrid marched as easily as if they were cobwebs, but which snagged Harry and Hermione’s robes, frequently entangling them so severely that they had to stop for minutes at a time to free themselves. Harry’s arms and legs were soon covered in small cuts and scratches. They were so deep in the Forest now that sometimes all Harry could see of Hagrid in the gloom was a massive dark shape ahead of him. Any sound seemed threatening in the muffled silence. The breaking of a twig echoed loudly and the tiniest rustle of movement, even though it might have been made by an innocent sparrow, caused Harry to peer through the gloom for a culprit. It occurred to him that he had never managed to get this far into the Forest without meeting some kind of creature; their absence struck him as rather ominous.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, would it be all right if we lit our wands?’ said Hermione quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Er … all righ’,’ Hagrid whispered back. ‘In fact -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He stopped suddenly and turned around; Hermione walked right into him and was knocked over backwards. Harry caught her just before she hit the Forest floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Maybe we bes’ jus’ stop fer a momen’, so I can … fill yeh in,’ said Hagrid. ‘Before we ge’ there, like.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Good!’ said Hermione, as Harry set her back on her feet. They both murmured ‘Lumos!’ and their wand-tips ignited. Hagrid’s face swam through the gloom by the light of the two wavering beams and Harry saw again that he looked nervous and sad.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Righ’,’ said Hagrid. ‘Well … see … the thing is …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He took a great breath.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, there’s a good chance I’m goin’ ter be gettin’ the sack any day now,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione looked at each other, then back at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But you’ve lasted this long -‘ Hermione said tentatively. ‘What makes you think -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Umbridge reckons it was me that put tha’ Niffler in her office.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘And was it?’ said Harry, before he could stop himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘No, it ruddy well wasn’!’ said Hagrid indignantly. ‘On’y anythin’ ter do with magical creatures an’ she thinks it’s got somethin’ ter do with me. Yeh know she’s bin lookin’ fer a chance ter get rid of me ever since I got back. I don’ wan’ ter go, o’ course, but if it wasn’ fer … well … the special circumstances I’m abou’ ter explain to yeh, I’d leave righ’ now, before she’s go’ the chance ter do it in front o’ the whole school, like she did with Trelawney.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione both made noises of protest, but Hagrid overrode them with a wave of one of his enormous hands.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not the end o’ the world, I’ll be able ter help Dumbledore once I’m outta here, I can be useful ter the Order. An’ you lot’ll have Grubbly-Plank, yeh’ll - yeh’ll get through yer exams fine …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: His voice trembled and broke.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’ worry abou’ me,’ he said hastily, as Hermione made to pat his arm. He pulled his enormous spotted handkerchief from the pocket of his waistcoat and mopped his eyes with it. ‘Look, I wouldn’ be tellin’ yer this at all if I didn’ have ter. See, if I go … well, I can’ leave withou’ … withou’ tellin’ someone … because I’ll - I’ll need you two ter help me. An’ Ron, if he’s willin’.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course we’ll help you,’ said Harry at once. ‘What do you want us to do?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Hagrid gave a great sniff and patted Harry wordlessly on the shoulder with such force Harry was knocked sideways into a tree.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew yeh’d say yes,’ said Hagrid into his handkerchief, ‘but I won’ … never … forget … well … c’mon … jus’ a little bit further through here … watch yerselves, now, there’s nettles …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: They walked on in silence for another fifteen minutes; Harry had opened his mouth to ask how much further they had to go when Hagrid threw out his right arm to signal that they should stop.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Really easy,’ he said softly. ‘Very quiet, now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: They crept forwards and Harry saw that they were facing a large, smooth mound of earth nearly as tall as Hagrid that he thought, with a jolt of dread, was sure to be the lair of some enormous animal. Trees had been ripped up at the roots all around the mound, so that it stood on a bare patch of ground surrounded by heaps of trunks and boughs that formed a kind of fence or barricade, behind which Harry, Hermione and Hagrid now stood.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Sleepin’,’ breathed Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Sure enough, Harry could hear a distant, rhythmic rumbling that sounded like a pair of enormous lungs at work. He glanced sideways at Hermione, who was gazing at the mound with her mouth slightly open. She looked utterly terrified.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid,’ she said in a whisper barely audible over the sound of the sleeping creature, ‘who is he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry found this an odd question … ‘What is it?’ was the one he had been planning on asking.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, you told us -‘ said Hermione, her wand now shaking in her hand, ‘you told us none of them wanted to come!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry looked from her to Hagrid and then, as realisation hit him, he looked back at the mound with a small gasp of horror.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The great mound of earth, on which he, Hermione and Hagrid could easily have stood, was moving slowly up and down in time with the deep, grunting breathing. It was not a mound at all. It was the curved back of what was clearly -

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well - no - he didn’ want ter come,’ said Hagrid, sounding desperate. ‘But I had ter bring him, Hermione, I had ter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘But why?’ asked Hermione, who sounded as though she wanted to cry. ‘Why - what - oh, Hagrid!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew if I jus’ got him back,’ said Hagrid, sounding close to tears himself, ‘an’ - an’ taught him a few manners - I’d be able ter take him outside an’ show ev’ryone he’s harmless!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Harmless!’ said Hermione shrilly, and Hagrid made frantic hushing noises with his hands as the enormous creature before them grunted loudly and shifted in its sleep. ‘He’s been hurting you all this time, hasn’t he? That’s why you’ve had all these injuries!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He don’ know his own strength!’ said Hagrid earnestly. ‘An’ he’s gettin’ better, he’s not fightin’ so much any more -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So, this is why it took you two months to get home!’ said Hermione distractedly. ‘Oh, Hagrid, why did you bring him back if he didn’t want to come? Wouldn’t he have been happier with his own people?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘They were all bullyin’ him, Hermione, ‘cause he’s so small!’ said Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Small?’ said Hermione. ‘Small?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione, I couldn’ leave him,’ said Hagrid, tears now trickling down his bruised face into his beard. ‘See - he’s my brother!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Hermione simply stared at him, her mouth open.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, when you say “brother”,’ said Harry slowly, ‘do you mean -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well - half-brother,’ amended Hagrid. ‘Turns out me mother took up with another giant when she left me dad, an’ she went an’ had Grawp here -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Grawp?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah … well, tha’s what it sounds like when he says his name,’ said Hagrid anxiously. ‘He don’ speak a lot of English … I’ve bin tryin’ ter teach him … anyway, she don’ seem ter have liked him much more’n she liked me. See, with giantesses, what counts is producin’ good big kids, and he’s always been a bit on the runty side fer a giant - on’y sixteen foot -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes, tiny!’ said Hermione, with a kind of hysterical sarcasm. ‘Absolutely minuscule!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘He was bein’ kicked aroun’ by all o’ them - I jus’ couldn’ leave him -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Did Madame Maxime want to bring him back?’ asked Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘She - well, she could see it was right importan’ ter me,’ said Hagrid, twisting his enormous hands. ‘Bu’ - bu’ she got a bit tired o’ him after a while, I must admit … so we split up on the journey home … she promised not ter tell anyone, though …’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘How on earth did you get him back without anyone noticing?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, tha’s why it took so long, see,’ said Hagrid. ‘Could on’y travel by nigh’ an’ through wild country an’ stuff. Course, he covers the ground pretty well when he wants ter, but he kep’ wantin’ ter go back.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Hagrid, why on earth didn’t you let him!’ said Hermione, flopping down on to a ripped up tree and burying her face in her hands. ‘What do you think you’re going to do with a violent giant who doesn’t even want to be here!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, now - “violent” - tha’s a bit harsh,’ said Hagrid, still twisting his hands agitatedly. ‘I’ll admit he mighta taken a couple o’ swings at me when he’s bin in a bad mood, but he’s gettin’ better, loads better, settlin’ down well.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What are those ropes for, then?’ Harry asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: He had just noticed ropes thick as saplings stretching from around the trunks of the largest nearby trees towards the place where Grawp lay curled on the ground with his back to them.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You have to keep him tied up?’ said Hermione faintly.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Well … yeah …’ said Hagrid, looking anxious. ‘See - it’s like I say - he doesn’ really know ‘is own strength.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry understood now why there had been such a suspicious lack of any other living creature in this part of the Forest.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘So, what is it you want Harry and Ron and me to do?’ Hermione asked apprehensively.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Look after him,’ said Hagrid croakily. ‘After I’m gone.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione exchanged miserable looks, Harry uncomfortably aware that he had already promised Hagrid that he would do whatever he asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘What - what does that involve, exactly?’ Hermione enquired.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Not food or anythin’!’ said Hagrid eagerly. ‘He can get his own food, no problem. Birds an’ deer an’ stuff … no, it’s company he needs. If I jus’ knew someone was carryin’ on tryin’ ter help him a bit … teachin’ him, yeh know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry said nothing, but turned to look back at the gigantic form lying asleep on the ground in front of them. Unlike Hagrid, who simply looked like an oversized human, Grawp looked strangely misshapen. What Harry had taken to be a vast mossy boulder to the left of the great earthen mound he now recognised as Grawp’s head. It was much larger in proportion to the body than a human head, and was almost perfectly round and covered with tightly curling, close-growing hair the colour of bracken. The rim of a single large, fleshy ear was visible on top of the head, which seemed to sit, rather like Uncle Vernon’s, directly upon the shoulders with little or no neck in between. The back, under what looked like a dirty brownish smock comprised of animal skins sewn roughly together, was very broad; and as Grawp slept, it seemed to strain a little at the rough seams of the skins. The legs were curled up under the body. Harry could see the soles of enormous, filthy, bare feet, large as sledges, resting one on top of the other on the earthy Forest floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘You want us to teach him,’ Harry said in a hollow voice. He now understood what Firenze’s warning had meant. His attempt is not working. He would do better to abandon it. Of course, the other creatures who lived in the Forest would have heard Hagrid’s fruitless attempts to teach Grawp English.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah - even if yeh jus’ talk ter him a bit,’ said Hagrid hopefully. ”Cause I reckon, if he can talk ter people, he’ll understand more that we all like ‘im really, an’ want ‘im ter stay.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry looked at Hermione, who peered back at him from between the fingers over her face.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Kind of makes you wish we had Norbert back, doesn’t it?’ he said, and she gave a very shaky laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeh’ll do it, then?’ said Hagrid, who did not seem to have caught what Harry had just said.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ll …’ said Harry, already bound by his promise. ‘We’ll try, Hagrid.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew I could count on yeh, Harry,’ Hagrid said, beaming in a very watery way and dabbing at his face with his handkerchief again. ‘An’ I don’ wan’ yeh ter put yerself out too much, like … I know yeh’ve got exams … if yeh could jus’ nip down here in yer Invisibility Cloak maybe once a week an’ have a little chat with ‘im. I’ll wake ‘im up, then - introduce yeh -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Wha— no!’ said Hermione, jumping up. ‘Hagrid, no, don’t wake him, really, we don’t need -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But Hagrid had already stepped over the great tree trunk in front of them and was proceeding towards Grawp. When he was about ten feet away, he lifted a long, broken bough from the ground, smiled reassuringly over his shoulder at Harry and Hermione, then poked Grawp hard in the middle of the back with the end of the bough.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The giant gave a roar that echoed around the silent Forest; birds in the treetops overhead rose twittering from their perches and soared away. In front of Harry and Hermione, meanwhile, the gigantic Grawp was rising from the ground, which shuddered as he placed an enormous hand upon it to push himself on to his knees. He turned his head to see who and what had disturbed him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘All righ’, Grawpy?’ said Hagrid, in a would-be cheery voice, backing away with the long bough raised, ready to poke Grawp again. ‘Had a nice sleep, eh?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: Harry and Hermione retreated as far as they could while still keeping the giant within their sights. Grawp knelt between two trees he had not yet uprooted. They looked up into his startlingly huge face that resembled a grey full moon swimming in the gloom of the clearing. It was as though the features had been hewn on to a great stone ball. The nose was stubby and shapeless, the mouth lopsided and full of misshapen yellow teeth the size of half-bricks; the eyes, small by giant standards, were a muddy greenish-brown and just now were half-gummed together with sleep. Grawp raised dirty knuckles, each as big as a cricket ball, to his eyes, rubbed vigorously, then, without warning, pushed himself to his feet with surprising speed and agility.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh my!’ Harry heard Hermione squeal, terrified, beside him.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The trees to which the other ends of the ropes around Grawp’s wrists and ankles were attached creaked ominously. He was, as Hagrid had said, at least sixteen feet tall. Gazing blearily around, Grawp reached out a hand the size of a beach umbrella, seized a bird’s nest from the upper branches of a towering pine and turned it upside-down with a roar of apparent displeasure that there was no bird in it; eggs fell like grenades towards the ground and Hagrid threw his arms over his head to protect himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway, Grawpy,’ shouted Hagrid, looking up apprehensively in case of further falling eggs, ‘I’ve brought some friends ter meet yeh. Remember, I told yeh I might? Remember, when I said I might have ter go on a little trip an’ leave them ter look after yeh fer a bit? Remember that, Grawpy?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: But Grawp merely gave another low roar; it was hard to say whether he was listening to Hagrid or whether he even recognised the sounds Hagrid was making as speech. He had now seized the top of the pine tree and was pulling it towards him, evidently for the simple pleasure of seeing how far it would spring back when he let go.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, Grawpy, don’ do that!’ shouted Hagrid. ‘Tha’s how you ended up pullin’ up the others -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: And sure enough, Harry could see the earth around the tree’s roots beginning to crack.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘I got company for yeh!’ Hagrid shouted. ‘Company, see! Look down, yeh big buffoon, I brought yeh some friends!’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Hagrid, don’t,’ moaned Hermione, but Hagrid had already raised the bough again and gave Grawp’s knee a sharp poke.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The giant let go of the top of the tree, which swayed alarmingly and deluged Hagrid with a rain of pine needles, and looked down.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘This,’ said Hagrid, hastening over to where Harry and Hermione stood, ‘is Harry, Grawp! Harry Potter! He migh’ be comin’ ter visit yeh if I have ter go away, understand?’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: The giant had only just realised that Harry and Hermione were there. They watched, in great trepidation, as he lowered his huge boulder of a head so that he could peer blearily at them.

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)
text_content: ‘An’ this is Hermione, see? Her—’ Hagrid hesitated. Turning to Hermione, he said, ‘Would yeh mind if he called yeh Hermy, Hermione? On’y it’s a difficult name fer him ter remember.’

book: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (UK)

Every year, I am afraid to say, seems to harbour at least one student who thinks that he or she can get around the Wizarding Examinations Authority’s rules.
