Particular care should be taken during the hours of darkness. Wherever possible, arrange to complete journeys before night has fallen. 3. Review the security arrangements around your house, making sure that all family members are aware of emergency measures such as Shield and Disillusionment Charms and, in the case of under-age family members, Side-Along-Apparition. 4. Agree security questions with close friends and family so as to detect Death Eaters masquerading as others by use of Polyjuice Potion (see page 2). 5. Should you feel that a family member, colleague, friend or neighbour is acting in a strange manner, contact the Magical Law Enforcement Squad at once. They may have been put under the Imperius Curse (see page 4). 6. Should the Dark Mark appear over any dwelling place or other building, DO NOT ENTER, but contact the Auror Office immediately. 7. Unconfirmed sightings suggest that the Death Eaters may now be using Inferi (see page 10). Any sighting of an Inferius, or encounter with same, should be reported to the Ministry IMMEDIATELY.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry grunted in his sleep and his face slid down the window an inch or so, making his glasses still more lopsided, but he did not wake up. An alarm clock, repaired by Harry several years ago, ticked loudly on the sill, showing one minute to eleven. Beside it, held in place by Harry’s relaxed hand, was a piece of parchment covered in thin, slanting writing. Harry had read this letter so often since its arrival three days ago that, although it had been delivered in a tightly furled scroll, it now lay quite flat.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dear Harry, If it is convenient to you, I shall call at number four, Privet Drive this coming Friday at eleven p.m. to escort you to The Burrow, where you have been invited to spend the remainder of your school holidays. If you are agreeable, I should also be glad of your assistance in a matter to which I hope to attend on the way to The Burrow. I shall explain this more fully when I see you. Kindly send your answer by return of this owl. Hoping to see you this Friday, I am, yours most sincerely Albus Dumbledore

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Though he already knew it by heart, Harry had been stealing glances at this missive every few minutes since seven o’clock that evening, when he had first taken up his position beside his bedroom window, which had a reasonable view of both ends of Privet Drive. He knew it was pointless to keep rereading Dumbledore’s words; Harry had sent back his ‘yes’ with the delivering owl, as requested, and all he could do now was wait: either Dumbledore was going to come, or he was not.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But Harry had not packed. It just seemed too good to be true that he was going to be rescued from the Dursleys after a mere fortnight of their company. He could not shrug off the feeling that something was going to go wrong – his reply to Dumbledore’s letter might have gone astray; Dumbledore could be prevented from collecting him; the letter might turn out not to be from Dumbledore at all, but a trick or joke or trap. Harry had not been able to face packing and then being let down and having to unpack again. The only gesture he had made to the possibility of a journey was to shut his snowy owl, Hedwig, safely in her cage.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The minute hand on the alarm clock reached the number twelve, and at that precise moment, the streetlamp outside the window went out.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry awoke as though the sudden darkness was an alarm. Hastily straightening his glasses and unsticking his cheek from the glass, he pressed his nose against the window instead and squinted down at the pavement. A tall figure in a long, billowing cloak was walking up the garden path.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry jumped up as though he had received an electric shock, knocked over his chair, and started snatching anything and everything within reach from the floor and throwing it into the trunk. Even as he lobbed a set of robes, two spell-books and a packet of crisps across the room, the doorbell rang.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Downstairs in the living room his Uncle Vernon shouted, ‘Who the blazes is calling at this time of night?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry froze with a brass telescope in one hand and a pair of trainers in the other. He had completely forgotten to warn the Dursleys that Dumbledore might be coming. Feeling both panicky and close to laughter, he clambered over the trunk and wrenched open his bedroom door in time to hear a deep voice say, ‘Good evening. You must be Mr Dursley. I daresay Harry has told you I would be coming for him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry ran down the stairs two at a time, coming to an abrupt halt several steps from the bottom, as long experience had taught him to remain out of arm’s reach of his uncle whenever possible. There in the doorway stood a tall, thin man with waist-length silver hair and beard. Half-moon spectacles were perched on his crooked nose and he was wearing a long black travelling cloak and a pointed hat. Vernon Dursley, whose moustache was quite as bushy as Dumbledore’s, though black, and who was wearing a puce dressing-gown, was staring at the visitor as though he could not believe his tiny eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Judging by your look of stunned disbelief, Harry did not warn you that I was coming,’ said Dumbledore pleasantly. ‘However, let us assume that you have invited me warmly into your house. It is unwise to linger overlong on doorsteps in these troubled times.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He stepped smartly over the threshold and closed the front door behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It is a long time since my last visit,’ said Dumbledore, peering down his crooked nose at Uncle Vernon. ‘I must say, your agapanthuses are flourishing.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Vernon Dursley said nothing at all. Harry did not doubt that speech would return to him, and soon – the vein pulsing in his uncle’s temple was reaching danger point – but something about Dumbledore seemed to have robbed him temporarily of breath. It might have been the blatant wizardishness of his appearance, but it might, too, have been that even Uncle Vernon could sense that here was a man whom it would be very difficult to bully.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, good evening, Harry,’ said Dumbledore, looking up at him through his half-moon glasses with a most satisfied expression. ‘Excellent, excellent.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: These words seemed to rouse Uncle Vernon. It was clear that as far as he was concerned, any man who could look at Harry and say ‘excellent’ was a man with whom he could never see eye to eye.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t mean to be rude –’ he began, in a tone that threatened rudeness in every syllable.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– yet, sadly, accidental rudeness occurs alarmingly often,’ Dumbledore finished the sentence gravely. ‘Best to say nothing at all, my dear man. Ah, and this must be Petunia.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The kitchen door had opened, and there stood Harry’s aunt, wearing rubber gloves and a housecoat over her nightdress, clearly halfway through her usual pre-bedtime wipe-down of all the kitchen surfaces. Her rather horsy face registered nothing but shock.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Albus Dumbledore,’ said Dumbledore, when Uncle Vernon failed to effect an introduction. ‘We have corresponded, of course.’ Harry thought this an odd way of reminding Aunt Petunia that he had once sent her an exploding letter, but Aunt Petunia did not challenge the term. ‘And this must be your son Dudley?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dudley had that moment peered round the living-room door. His large, blond head rising out of the stripy collar of his pyjamas looked oddly disembodied, his mouth gaping in astonishment and fear. Dumbledore waited a moment or two, apparently to see whether any of the Dursleys were going to say anything, but as the silence stretched on he smiled.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Shall we assume that you have invited me into your sitting room?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dudley scrambled out of the way as Dumbledore passed him. Harry, still clutching the telescope and trainers, jumped the last few stairs and followed Dumbledore, who had settled himself in the armchair nearest the fire and was taking in the surroundings with an expression of benign interest. He looked quite extraordinarily out of place.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Aren’t – aren’t we leaving, sir?’ Harry asked anxiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, indeed we are, but there are a few matters we need to discuss first,’ said Dumbledore. ‘And I would prefer not to do so in the open. We shall trespass upon your aunt and uncle’s hospitality only a little longer.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You will, will you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Vernon Dursley had entered the room, Petunia at his shoulder and Dudley skulking behind them both.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Dumbledore simply, ‘I shall.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He drew his wand so rapidly that Harry barely saw it; with a casual flick, the sofa zoomed forwards and knocked the knees out from under all three of the Dursleys so that they collapsed upon it in a heap. Another flick of the wand and the sofa zoomed back to its original position.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘We may as well be comfortable,’ said Dumbledore pleasantly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: As he replaced his wand in his pocket, Harry saw that his hand was blackened and shrivelled; it looked as though his flesh had been burned away.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sir – what happened to your –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Later, Harry,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Please sit down.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry took the remaining armchair, choosing not to look at the Dursleys, who seemed stunned into silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I would assume that you were going to offer me refreshment,’ Dumbledore said to Uncle Vernon, ‘but the evidence so far suggests that that would be optimistic to the point of foolishness.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A third twitch of the wand and a dusty bottle and five glasses appeared in midair. The bottle tipped and poured a generous measure of honey-coloured liquid into each of the glasses, which then floated to each person in the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Madam Rosmerta’s finest, oak-matured mead,’ said Dumbledore, raising his glass to Harry, who caught hold of his own and sipped. He had never tasted anything like it before, but enjoyed it immensely. The Dursleys, after quick, scared looks at each other, tried to ignore their glasses completely, a difficult feat, as they were nudging them gently on the sides of their heads. Harry could not suppress a suspicion that Dumbledore was rather enjoying himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Harry,’ said Dumbledore, turning towards him, ‘a difficulty has arisen which I hope you will be able to solve for us. By us, I mean the Order of the Phoenix. But first of all I must tell you that Sirius’s will was discovered a week ago and that he left you everything he owned.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Over on the sofa, Uncle Vernon’s head turned, but Harry did not look at him, nor could he think of anything to say except, ‘Oh. Right.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘This is, in the main, fairly straightforward,’ Dumbledore went on. ‘You add a reasonable amount of gold to your account at Gringotts and you inherit all of Sirius’s personal possessions. The slightly problematic part of the legacy –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘His godfather’s dead?’ said Uncle Vernon loudly from the sofa. Dumbledore and Harry both turned to look at him. The glass of mead was now knocking quite insistently on the side of Vernon’s head; he attempted to beat it away. ‘He’s dead? His godfather?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Dumbledore. He did not ask Harry why he had not confided in the Dursleys. ‘Our problem,’ he continued to Harry, as if there had been no interruption, ‘is that Sirius also left you number twelve, Grimmauld Place.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s been left a house?’ said Uncle Vernon greedily, his small eyes narrowing, but nobody answered him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You can keep using it as Headquarters,’ said Harry. ‘I don’t care. You can have it, I don’t really want it.’ Harry never wanted to set foot in number twelve, Grimmauld Place again if he could help it. He thought he would be haunted for ever by the memory of Sirius prowling its dark musty rooms alone, imprisoned within the place he had wanted so desperately to leave.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That is generous,’ said Dumbledore. ‘We have, however, vacated the building temporarily.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Why?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Dumbledore, ignoring the mutterings of Uncle Vernon, who was now being rapped smartly over the head by the persistent glass of mead, ‘Black family tradition decreed that the house was handed down the direct line, to the next male with the name of Black. Sirius was the very last of the line as his younger brother, Regulus, predeceased him and both were childless. While his will makes it perfectly plain that he wants you to have the house, it is nevertheless possible that some spell or enchantment has been set upon the place to ensure that it cannot be owned by anyone other than a pure-blood.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A vivid image of the shrieking, spitting portrait of Sirius’s mother that hung in the hall of number twelve, Grimmauld Place flashed into Harry’s mind. ‘I bet there has,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Quite,’ said Dumbledore. ‘And if such an enchantment exists, then the ownership of the house is most likely to pass to the eldest of Sirius’s living relatives, which would mean his cousin, Bellatrix Lestrange.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Without realising what he was doing, Harry sprang to his feet; the telescope and trainers in his lap rolled across the floor. Bellatrix Lestrange, Sirius’s killer, inherit his house?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, obviously we would prefer that she didn’t get it, either,’ said Dumbledore calmly. ‘The situation is fraught with complications. We do not know whether the enchantments we ourselves have placed upon it, for example, making it unplottable, will hold now that ownership has passed from Sirius’s hands. It might be that Bellatrix will arrive on the doorstep at any moment. Naturally we had to move out until such time as we have clarified the position.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But how are you going to find out if I’m allowed to own it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Fortunately,’ said Dumbledore, ‘there is a simple test.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He placed his empty glass on a small table beside his chair, but before he could do anything else, Uncle Vernon shouted, ‘Will you get these ruddy things off us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry looked round; all three of the Dursleys were cowering with their arms over their heads as their glasses bounced up and down on their skulls, the contents flying everywhere.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I’m so sorry,’ said Dumbledore politely, and he raised his wand again. All three glasses vanished. ‘But it would have been better manners to drink it, you know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It looked as though Uncle Vernon was bursting with any number of unpleasant retorts, but he merely shrank back into the cushions with Aunt Petunia and Dudley and said nothing, keeping his small piggy eyes on Dumbledore’s wand.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You see,’ Dumbledore said, turning back to Harry and again speaking as though Uncle Vernon had not uttered, ‘if you have indeed inherited the house, you have also inherited –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He flicked his wand for a fifth time. There was a loud crack and a house-elf appeared, with a snout for a nose, giant bat’s ears and enormous bloodshot eyes, crouching on the Dursleys’ shagpile carpet and covered in grimy rags. Aunt Petunia let out a hair-raising shriek: nothing this filthy had entered her house in living memory; Dudley drew his large bare pink feet off the floor and sat with them raised almost above his head, as though he thought the creature might run up his pyjama trousers, and Uncle Vernon bellowed, ‘What the hell is that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher,’ finished Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher won’t, Kreacher won’t, Kreacher won’t!’ croaked the house-elf, quite as loudly as Uncle Vernon, stamping his long gnarled feet and pulling his ears. ‘Kreacher belongs to Miss Bellatrix, oh, yes, Kreacher belongs to the Blacks, Kreacher wants his new mistress, Kreacher won’t go to the Potter brat, Kreacher won’t, won’t, won’t –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘As you can see, Harry,’ said Dumbledore loudly, over Kreacher’s continued croaks of ‘won’t, won’t, won’t’, ‘Kreacher is showing a certain reluctance to pass into your ownership.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t care,’ said Harry again, looking with disgust at the writhing, stamping house-elf. ‘I don’t want him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Won’t, won’t, won’t, won’t –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You would prefer him to pass into the ownership of Bellatrix Lestrange? Bearing in mind that he has lived at the Headquarters of the Order of the Phoenix for the past year?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Won’t, won’t, won’t, won’t –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry stared at Dumbledore. He knew that Kreacher could not be permitted to go and live with Bellatrix Lestrange, but the idea of owning him, of having responsibility for the creature that had betrayed Sirius, was repugnant.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Give him an order,’ said Dumbledore. ‘If he has passed into your ownership, he will have to obey. If not, then we shall have to think of some other means of keeping him from his rightful mistress.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Won’t, won’t, won’t, WON’T!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Kreacher’s voice had risen to a scream. Harry could think of nothing to say, except, ‘Kreacher, shut up!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It looked for a moment as though Kreacher was going to choke. He grabbed his throat, his mouth still working furiously, his eyes bulging. After a few seconds of frantic gulping, he threw himself face forwards on to the carpet (Aunt Petunia whimpered) and beat the floor with his hands and feet, giving himself over to a violent, but entirely silent, tantrum.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, that simplifies matters,’ said Dumbledore cheerfully. ‘It seems that Sirius knew what he was doing. You are the rightful owner of number twelve, Grimmauld Place, and of Kreacher.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Do I – do I have to keep him with me?’ Harry asked, aghast, as Kreacher thrashed around at his feet.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not if you don’t want to,’ said Dumbledore. ‘If I might make a suggestion, you could send him to Hogwarts to work in the kitchen there. In that way, the other house-elves could keep an eye on him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry in relief, ‘yeah, I’ll do that. Er – Kreacher – I want you to go to Hogwarts and work in the kitchens there with the other house-elves.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Kreacher, who was now lying flat on his back with his arms and legs in the air, gave Harry one upside-down look of deepest loathing and, with another loud crack, vanished.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ said Dumbledore. ‘There is also the matter of the Hippogriff, Buckbeak. Hagrid has been looking after him since Sirius died, but Buckbeak is yours now, so if you would prefer to make different arrangements –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry at once, ‘he can stay with Hagrid. I think Buckbeak would prefer that.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid will be delighted,’ said Dumbledore, smiling. ‘He was thrilled to see Buckbeak again. Incidentally, we have decided, in the interests of Buckbeak’s safety, to rechristen him Witherwings for the time being, though I doubt that the Ministry would ever guess he is the Hippogriff they once sentenced to death. Now, Harry, is your trunk packed?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Erm …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Doubtful that I would turn up?’ Dumbledore suggested shrewdly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll just go and – er – finish off,’ said Harry hastily, hurrying to pick up his fallen telescope and trainers.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It took him a little over ten minutes to track down everything he needed; at last he had managed to extract his Invisibility Cloak from under the bed, screwed the top back on his jar of Colour-Change Ink and forced the lid of his trunk shut on his cauldron. Then, heaving his trunk in one hand and holding Hedwig’s cage in the other, he made his way back downstairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He was disappointed to discover that Dumbledore was not waiting in the hall, which meant that he had to return to the living room.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Nobody was talking. Dumbledore was humming quietly, apparently quite at his ease, but the atmosphere was thicker than cold custard and Harry did not dare look at the Dursleys as he said, ‘Professor – I’m ready now.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Just one last thing, then.’ And he turned to speak to the Dursleys once more. ‘As you will no doubt be aware, Harry comes of age in a year’s time –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Aunt Petunia, speaking for the first time since Dumbledore’s arrival.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry?’ said Dumbledore politely.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, he doesn’t. He’s a month younger than Dudley, and Dudders doesn’t turn eighteen until the year after next.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ said Dumbledore pleasantly, ‘but in the wizarding world, we come of age at seventeen.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Uncle Vernon muttered ‘preposterous’, but Dumbledore ignored him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, as you already know, the wizard called Lord Voldemort has returned to this country. The wizarding community is currently in a state of open warfare. Harry, whom Lord Voldemort has already attempted to kill on a number of occasions, is in even greater danger now than the day when I left him upon your doorstep fifteen years ago, with a letter explaining about his parents’ murder and expressing the hope that you would care for him as though he were your own.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore paused, and although his voice remained light and calm, and he gave no obvious sign of anger, Harry felt a kind of chill emanating from him and noticed that the Dursleys drew very slightly closer together.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You did not do as I asked. You have never treated Harry as a son. He has known nothing but neglect and often cruelty at your hands. The best that can be said is that he has at least escaped the appalling damage you have inflicted upon the unfortunate boy sitting between you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Both Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon looked around instinctively, as though expecting to see someone other than Dudley squeezed between them.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Us – mistreat Dudders? What d’you –?’ began Uncle Vernon furiously, but Dumbledore raised his finger for silence, a silence which fell as though he had struck Uncle Vernon dumb.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The magic I evoked fifteen years ago means that Harry has powerful protection while he can still call this house home. However miserable he has been here, however unwelcome, however badly treated, you have at least, grudgingly, allowed him houseroom. This magic will cease to operate the moment that Harry turns seventeen; in other words, the moment he becomes a man. I ask only this: that you allow Harry to return, once more, to this house, before his seventeenth birthday, which will ensure that the protection continues until that time.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: None of the Dursleys said anything. Dudley was frowning slightly, as though he was still trying to work out when he had ever been mistreated. Uncle Vernon looked as though he had something stuck in his throat; Aunt Petunia, however, was oddly flushed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Harry … time for us to be off,’ said Dumbledore at last, standing up and straightening his long black cloak. ‘Until we meet again,’ he said to the Dursleys, who looked as though that moment could wait for ever as far as they were concerned, and after doffing his hat, he swept from the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Bye,’ said Harry hastily to the Dursleys, and followed Dumbledore, who paused beside Harry’s trunk, upon which Hedwig’s cage was perched.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘We do not want to be encumbered by these just now,’ he said, pulling out his wand again. ‘I shall send them to The Burrow to await us there. However, I would like you to bring your Invisibility Cloak … just in case.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry extracted his Cloak from his trunk with some difficulty, trying not to show Dumbledore the mess within. When he had stuffed it into an inside pocket of his jacket, Dumbledore waved his wand and the trunk, cage and Hedwig vanished. Dumbledore then waved his wand again and the front door opened on to cool, misty darkness.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And now, Harry, let us step out into the night and pursue that flighty temptress, adventure.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Despite the fact that he had spent every waking moment of the past few days hoping desperately that Dumbledore would indeed come to fetch him, Harry felt distinctly awkward as they set off down Privet Drive together. He had never had a proper conversation with his headmaster outside Hogwarts before; there was usually a desk between them. The memory of their last face-to-face encounter kept intruding, too, and it rather heightened Harry’s sense of embarrassment; he had shouted a lot on that occasion, not to mention doing his best to smash several of Dumbledore’s most prized possessions.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore, however, seemed completely relaxed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Keep your wand at the ready, Harry,’ he said brightly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But I thought I’m not allowed to use magic outside school, sir?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘If there is an attack,’ said Dumbledore, ‘I give you permission to use any counter-jinx or -curse that might occur to you. However, I do not think you need worry about being attacked tonight.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Why not, sir?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You are with me,’ said Dumbledore simply. ‘This will do, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He came to an abrupt halt at the end of Privet Drive.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You have not, of course, passed your Apparition test?’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry. ‘I thought you had to be seventeen?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You do,’ said Dumbledore. ‘So you will need to hold on to my arm very tightly. My left, if you don’t mind – as you have noticed, my wand arm is a little fragile at the moment.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry gripped Dumbledore’s proffered forearm.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Very good,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Well, here we go.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry felt Dumbledore’s arm twist away from him and redoubled his grip: the next thing he knew, everything went black; he was being pressed very hard from all directions; he could not breathe, there were iron bands tightening around his chest; his eyeballs were being forced back into his head; his eardrums were being pushed deeper into his skull, and then –

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He gulped great lungfuls of cold night air and opened his streaming eyes. He felt as though he had just been forced through a very tight rubber tube. It was a few seconds before he realised that Privet Drive had vanished. He and Dumbledore were now standing in what appeared to be a deserted village square, in the centre of which stood an old war memorial and a few benches. His comprehension catching up with his senses, Harry realised that he had just Apparated for the first time in his life.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you all right?’ asked Dumbledore, looking down at him solicitously. ‘The sensation does take some getting used to.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m fine,’ said Harry, rubbing his ears, which felt as though they had left Privet Drive rather reluctantly. ‘But I think I might prefer brooms.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled, drew his travelling cloak a little more tightly around his neck and said, ‘This way.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He set off at a brisk pace, past an empty inn and a few houses. According to a clock on a nearby church, it was almost midnight.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So tell me, Harry,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Your scar … has it been hurting at all?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry raised a hand unconsciously to his forehead and rubbed the lightning-shaped mark.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ he said, ‘and I’ve been wondering about that. I thought it would be burning all the time now Voldemort’s getting so powerful again.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He glanced up at Dumbledore and saw that he was wearing a satisfied expression.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I, on the other hand, thought otherwise,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Lord Voldemort has finally realised the dangerous access to his thoughts and feelings you have been enjoying. It appears that he is now employing Occlumency against you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’m not complaining,’ said Harry, who missed neither the disturbing dreams nor the startling flashes of insight into Voldemort’s mind.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They turned a corner, passing a telephone box and a bus shelter. Harry looked sideways at Dumbledore again.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Er – where exactly are we?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘This, Harry, is the charming village of Budleigh Babberton.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And what are we doing here?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, yes, of course, I haven’t told you,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Well, I have lost count of the number of times I have said this in recent years, but we are, once again, one member of staff short. We are here to persuade an old colleague of mine to come out of retirement and return to Hogwarts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘How can I help with that, sir?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I think we’ll find a use for you,’ said Dumbledore vaguely. ‘Left here, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They proceeded up a steep, narrow street lined with houses. All the windows were dark. The odd chill that had lain over Privet Drive for two weeks persisted here, too. Thinking of Dementors, Harry cast a look over his shoulder and grasped his wand reassuringly in his pocket.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor, why couldn’t we just Apparate directly into your old colleague’s house?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Because it would be quite as rude as kicking down the front door,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Courtesy dictates that we offer fellow wizards the opportunity of denying us entry. In any case, most wizarding dwellings are magically protected from unwanted Apparators. At Hogwarts, for instance –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– you can’t Apparate anywhere inside the buildings or grounds,’ said Harry quickly. ‘Hermione Granger told me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And she is quite right. We turn left again.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The church clock chimed midnight behind them. Harry wondered why Dumbledore did not consider it rude to call on his old colleague so late, but now that conversation had been established, he had more pressing questions to ask.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sir, I saw in the Daily Prophet that Fudge has been sacked …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Correct,’ said Dumbledore, now turning up a steep side-street. ‘He has been replaced, as I am sure you also saw, by Rufus Scrimgeour, who used to be Head of the Auror Office.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Is he … do you think he’s good?’ asked Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘An interesting question,’ said Dumbledore. ‘He is able, certainly. A more decisive and forceful personality than Cornelius.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, but I meant –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I know what you meant. Rufus is a man of action and, having fought Dark wizards for most of his working life, does not underestimate Lord Voldemort.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry waited, but Dumbledore did not say anything about the disagreement with Scrimgeour that the Daily Prophet had reported, and he did not have the nerve to pursue the subject, so he changed it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And … sir … I saw about Madam Bones.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Dumbledore quietly. ‘A terrible loss. She was a great witch. Just up here, I think – ouch.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He had pointed with his injured hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor, what happened to your –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I have no time to explain now,’ said Dumbledore. ‘It is a thrilling tale, I wish to do it justice.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He smiled at Harry, who understood that he was not being snubbed, and that he had permission to keep asking questions.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sir – I got a Ministry of Magic leaflet by owl, about security measures we should all take against the Death Eaters …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I received one myself,’ said Dumbledore, still smiling. ‘Did you find it useful?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not really.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I thought not. You have not asked me, for instance, what is my favourite flavour of jam, to check that I am indeed Professor Dumbledore, and not an impostor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I didn’t …’ Harry began, not entirely sure whether he was being reprimanded or not.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘For future reference, Harry, it is raspberry … although of course, if I were a Death Eater, I would have been sure to research my own jam-preferences before impersonating myself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Er … right,’ said Harry. ‘Well, on that leaflet, it said something about Inferi. What exactly are they? The leaflet wasn’t very clear.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘They are corpses,’ said Dumbledore calmly. ‘Dead bodies that have been bewitched to do a Dark wizard’s bidding. Inferi have not been seen for a long time, however, not since Voldemort was last powerful … he killed enough people to make an army of them, of course. This is the place, Harry, just here …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They were nearing a small, neat stone house set in its own garden. Harry was too busy digesting the horrible idea of Inferi to have much attention left for anything else, but as they reached the front gate Dumbledore stopped dead and Harry walked into him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh dear. Oh dear, dear, dear.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry followed his gaze up the carefully tended front path and felt his heart sink. The front door was hanging off its hinges.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore glanced up and down the street. It seemed quite deserted.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Wand out and follow me, Harry,’ he said quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He opened the gate and walked swiftly and silently up the garden path, Harry at his heels, then pushed the front door very slowly, his wand raised and at the ready.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Lumos.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore’s wand-tip ignited, casting its light up a narrow hallway. To the left, another door stood open. Holding his illuminated wand aloft, Dumbledore walked into the sitting room with Harry right behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A scene of total devastation met their eyes. A grandfather clock lay splintered at their feet, its face cracked, its pendulum lying a little further away like a dropped sword. A piano was on its side, its keys strewn across the floor. The wreckage of a fallen chandelier glittered nearby. Cushions lay deflated, feathers oozing from slashes in their sides; fragments of glass and china lay like powder over everything. Dumbledore raised his wand even higher, so that its light was thrown upon the walls, where something darkly red and glutinous was spattered over the wallpaper. Harry’s small intake of breath made Dumbledore look round.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not pretty, is it,’ he said heavily. ‘Yes, something horrible has happened here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore moved carefully into the middle of the room, scrutinising the wreckage at his feet. Harry followed, gazing around, half-scared of what he might see hidden behind the wreck of the piano or the overturned sofa, but there was no sign of a body.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Maybe there was a fight and – and they dragged him off, Professor?’ Harry suggested, trying not to imagine how badly wounded a man would have to be to leave those stains spattered halfway up the walls.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t think so,’ said Dumbledore quietly, peering behind an overstuffed armchair lying on its side.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You mean he’s –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Still here somewhere? Yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And without warning, Dumbledore swooped, plunging the tip of his wand into the seat of the overstuffed armchair, which yelled, ‘Ouch!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good evening, Horace,’ said Dumbledore, straightening up again.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry’s jaw dropped. Where a split second before there had been an armchair, there now crouched an enormously fat, bald old man who was massaging his lower belly and squinting up at Dumbledore with an aggrieved and watery eye.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘There was no need to stick the wand in that hard,’ he said gruffly, clambering to his feet. ‘It hurt.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The wand-light sparkled on his shiny pate, his prominent eyes, his enormous, silver walrus-like moustache, and the highly polished buttons on the maroon velvet jacket he was wearing over a pair of lilac silk pyjamas. The top of his head barely reached Dumbledore’s chin.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What gave it away?’ he grunted as he staggered to his feet, still rubbing his lower belly. He seemed remarkably unabashed for a man who had just been discovered pretending to be an armchair.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘My dear Horace,’ said Dumbledore, looking amused, ‘if the Death Eaters really had come to call, the Dark Mark would have been set over the house.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The wizard clapped a pudgy hand to his vast forehead.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dark Mark,’ he muttered. ‘Knew there was something … ah well. Wouldn’t have had time, anyway. I’d only just put the finishing touches to my upholstery when you entered the room.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He heaved a great sigh that made the ends of his moustache flutter.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Would you like my assistance clearing up?’ asked Dumbledore politely.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Please,’ said the other.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They stood back to back, the tall thin wizard and the short round one, and waved their wands in one identical sweeping motion.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The furniture flew back to its original place; ornaments re-formed in midair; feathers zoomed into their cushions; torn books repaired themselves as they landed upon their shelves; oil lanterns soared on to side tables and reignited; a vast collection of splintered silver picture frames flew glittering across the room and alighted, whole and untarnished, upon a desk; rips, cracks and holes healed everywhere; and the walls wiped themselves clean.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What kind of blood was that, incidentally?’ asked Dumbledore loudly over the chiming of the newly unsmashed grandfather clock.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘On the walls? Dragon,’ shouted the wizard called Horace as, with a deafening grinding and tinkling, the chandelier screwed itself back into the ceiling.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was a final plunk from the piano, and silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, dragon,’ repeated the wizard conversationally. ‘My last bottle, and prices are sky-high at the moment. Still, it might be reusable.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He stumped over to a small crystal bottle standing on top of a sideboard and held it up to the light, examining the thick liquid within.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hm. Bit dusty.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He set the bottle back on the sideboard and sighed. It was then that his gaze fell upon Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oho,’ he said, his large round eyes flying to Harry’s forehead and the lightning-shaped scar it bore. ‘Oho!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘This,’ said Dumbledore, moving forwards to make the introduction, ‘is Harry Potter. Harry, this is an old friend and colleague of mine, Horace Slughorn.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn turned on Dumbledore, his expression shrewd.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So that’s how you thought you’d persuade me, is it? Well, the answer’s no, Albus.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He pushed past Harry, his face turned resolutely away with the air of a man trying to resist temptation.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I suppose we can have a drink, at least?’ asked Dumbledore. ‘For old times’ sake?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn hesitated.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘All right then, one drink,’ he said ungraciously.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled at Harry and directed him towards a chair not unlike the one that Slughorn had so recently impersonated, which stood right beside the newly burning fire and a brightly glowing oil lamp. Harry took the seat with the distinct impression that Dumbledore, for some reason, wanted to keep him as visible as possible. Certainly when Slughorn, who had been busy with decanters and glasses, turned to face the room again, his eyes fell immediately upon Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Humph,’ he said, looking away quickly as though frightened of hurting his eyes. ‘Here –’ He gave a drink to Dumbledore, who had sat down without invitation, thrust the tray at Harry and then sank into the cushions of the repaired sofa and a disgruntled silence. His legs were so short that they did not touch the floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, how have you been keeping, Horace?’ Dumbledore asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not so well,’ said Slughorn at once. ‘Weak chest. Wheezy. Rheumatism too. Can’t move like I used to. Well, that’s to be expected. Old age. Fatigue.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And yet you must have moved fairly quickly to prepare such a welcome for us at such short notice,’ said Dumbledore. ‘You can’t have had more than three minutes’ warning?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn said, half-irritably, half-proudly, ‘Two. Didn’t hear my Intruder Charm go off, I was taking a bath. Still,’ he added sternly, seeming to pull himself back together again, ‘the fact remains that I’m an old man, Albus. A tired old man who’s earned the right to a quiet life and a few creature comforts.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He certainly had those, thought Harry, looking around the room. It was stuffy and cluttered, yet nobody could say it was uncomfortable; there were soft chairs and footstools, drinks and books, boxes of chocolates and plump cushions. If Harry had not known who lived there, he would have guessed at a rich, fussy old lady.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re not yet as old as I am, Horace,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, maybe you ought to think about retirement yourself,’ said Slughorn bluntly. His pale gooseberry eyes had found Dumbledore’s injured hand. ‘Reactions not what they were, I see.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re quite right,’ said Dumbledore serenely, shaking back his sleeve to reveal the tips of those burned and blackened fingers; the sight of them made the back of Harry’s neck prickle unpleasantly. ‘I am undoubtedly slower than I was. But on the other hand …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He shrugged and spread his hands wide, as though to say that age had its compensations, and Harry noticed a ring on his uninjured hand that he had never seen Dumbledore wear before: it was large, rather clumsily made of what looked like gold, and was set with a heavy black stone that had cracked down the middle. Slughorn’s eyes lingered for a moment on the ring, too, and Harry saw a tiny frown momentarily crease his wide forehead.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So, all these precautions against intruders, Horace … are they for the Death Eaters’ benefit, or mine?’ asked Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What would the Death Eaters want with a poor broken-down old buffer like me?’ demanded Slughorn.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I imagine that they would want you to turn your considerable talents to coercion, torture and murder,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Are you really telling me that they haven’t come recruiting yet?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn eyed Dumbledore balefully for a moment, then muttered, ‘I haven’t given them the chance. I’ve been on the move for a year. Never stay in one place more than a week. Move from Muggle house to Muggle house – the owners of this place are on holiday in the Canary Islands. It’s been very pleasant, I’ll be sorry to leave. It’s quite easy once you know how, one simple Freezing Charm on these absurd burglar alarms they use instead of Sneakoscopes and make sure the neighbours don’t spot you bringing in the piano.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ingenious,’ said Dumbledore. ‘But it sounds a rather tiring existence for a broken-down old buffer in search of a quiet life. Now, if you were to return to Hogwarts –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘If you’re going to tell me my life would be more peaceful at that pestilential school, you can save your breath, Albus! I might have been in hiding, but some funny rumours have reached me since Dolores Umbridge left! If that’s how you treat teachers these days –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Umbridge ran afoul of our centaur herd,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I think you, Horace, would have known better than to stride into the Forest and call a horde of angry centaurs “filthy half-breeds”.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s what she did, did she?’ said Slughorn. ‘Idiotic woman. Never liked her.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry chuckled and both Dumbledore and Slughorn looked round at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry,’ Harry said hastily. ‘It’s just – I didn’t like her, either.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore stood up rather suddenly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you leaving?’ asked Slughorn at once, looking hopeful.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I was wondering whether I might use your bathroom,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh,’ said Slughorn, clearly disappointed. ‘Second on the left down the hall.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore crossed the room. Once the door had closed behind him there was silence. After a few moments Slughorn got to his feet, but seemed uncertain what to do with himself. He shot a furtive look at Harry, then strode to the fire and turned his back on it, warming his wide behind.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t think I don’t know why he’s brought you,’ he said abruptly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry merely looked at Slughorn. Slughorn’s watery eyes slid over Harry’s scar, this time taking in the rest of his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You look very like your father.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I’ve been told,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Except for your eyes. You’ve got –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘My mother’s eyes, yeah.’ Harry had heard it so often he found it a bit wearing.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Humph. Yes, well. You shouldn’t have favourites as a teacher, of course, but she was one of mine. Your mother,’ Slughorn added, in answer to Harry’s questioning look. ‘Lily Evans. One of the brightest I ever taught. Vivacious, you know. Charming girl. I used to tell her she ought to have been in my house. Very cheeky answers I used to get back, too.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Which was your house?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I was Head of Slytherin,’ said Slughorn. ‘Oh, now,’ he went on quickly, seeing the expression on Harry’s face and wagging a stubby finger at him, ‘don’t go holding that against me! You’ll be Gryffindor like her, I suppose? Yes, it usually goes in families. Not always, though. Ever heard of Sirius Black? You must have done – been in the papers for the last couple of years – died a few weeks ago –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It was as though an invisible hand had twisted Harry’s intestines and held them tight.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, anyway, he was a big pal of your father’s at school. The whole Black family had been in my house, but Sirius ended up in Gryffindor! Shame – he was a talented boy. I got his brother Regulus when he came along, but I’d have liked the set.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He sounded like an enthusiastic collector who had been outbid at auction. Apparently lost in memories, he gazed at the opposite wall, turning idly on the spot to ensure an even heat on his backside.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Your mother was Muggle-born, of course. Couldn’t believe it when I found out. Thought she must have been pure-blood, she was so good.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘One of my best friends is Muggle-born,’ said Harry, ‘and she’s the best in our year.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Funny how that sometimes happens, isn’t it?’ said Slughorn.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not really,’ said Harry coldly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn looked down at him in surprise.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You mustn’t think I’m prejudiced!’ he said. ‘No, no, no! Haven’t I just said your mother was one of my all-time favourite students? And there was Dirk Cresswell in the year after her, too – now Head of the Goblin Liaison Office, of course – another Muggle-born, a very gifted student, and still gives me excellent inside information on the goings-on at Gringotts!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He bounced up and down a little, smiling in a self-satisfied way, and pointed at the many glittering photograph frames on the dresser, each peopled with tiny moving occupants.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘All ex-students, all signed. You’ll notice Barnabas Cuffe, editor of the Daily Prophet, he’s always interested to hear my take on the day’s news. And Ambrosius Flume, of Honeydukes – a hamper every birthday, and all because I was able to give him an introduction to Ciceron Harkiss, who gave him his first job! And at the back – you’ll see her if you just crane your neck – that’s Gwenog Jones, who of course captains the Holyhead Harpies … people are always astonished to hear I’m on first-name terms with the Harpies, and free tickets whenever I want them!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: This thought seemed to cheer him up enormously.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And all these people know where to find you, to send you stuff?’ asked Harry, who could not help wondering why the Death Eaters had not yet tracked down Slughorn if hampers of sweets, Quidditch tickets and visitors craving his advice and opinions could find him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The smile slid from Slughorn’s face as quickly as the blood from his walls.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course not,’ he said, looking down at Harry. ‘I have been out of touch with everybody for a year.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry had the impression that the words shocked Slughorn himself; he looked quite unsettled for a moment. Then he shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Still … the prudent wizard keeps his head down in such times. All very well for Dumbledore to talk, but taking up a post at Hogwarts just now would be tantamount to declaring my public allegiance to the Order of the Phoenix! And while I’m sure they’re very admirable and brave and all the rest of it, I don’t personally fancy the mortality rate –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t have to join the Order to teach at Hogwarts,’ said Harry, who could not quite keep a note of derision out of his voice: it was hard to sympathise with Slughorn’s cosseted existence when he remembered Sirius, crouching in a cave and living on rats. ‘Most of the teachers aren’t in it and none of them has ever been killed – well, unless you count Quirrell, and he got what he deserved seeing as he was working with Voldemort.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry had been sure Slughorn would be one of those wizards who could not bear to hear Voldemort’s name spoken aloud, and was not disappointed: Slughorn gave a shudder and a squawk of protest, which Harry ignored.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I reckon the staff are safer than most people while Dumbledore’s headmaster; he’s supposed to be the only one Voldemort ever feared, isn’t he?’ Harry went on.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn gazed into space for a moment or two: he seemed to be thinking over Harry’s words.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, yes, it is true that He Who Must Not Be Named has never sought a fight with Dumbledore,’ he muttered grudgingly. ‘And I suppose one could argue that as I have not joined the Death Eaters, He Who Must Not Be Named can hardly count me a friend … in which case, I might well be safer a little closer to Albus … I cannot pretend that Amelia Bones’s death did not shake me … if she, with all her Ministry contacts and protection …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore re-entered the room and Slughorn jumped as though he had forgotten he was in the house.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, there you are, Albus,’ he said. ‘You’ve been a very long time. Upset stomach?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I was merely reading the Muggle magazines,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I do love knitting patterns. Well, Harry, we have trespassed upon Horace’s hospitality quite long enough; I think it is time for us to leave.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Not at all reluctant to obey, Harry jumped to his feet. Slughorn seemed taken aback.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re leaving?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, indeed. I think I know a lost cause when I see one.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Lost …?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn seemed agitated. He twiddled his fat thumbs and fidgeted as he watched Dumbledore fastening his travelling cloak and Harry zipping up his jacket.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’m sorry you don’t want the job, Horace,’ said Dumbledore, raising his uninjured hand in a farewell salute. ‘Hogwarts would have been glad to see you back again. Our greatly increased security notwithstanding, you will always be welcome to visit, should you wish to.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes … well … very gracious … as I say …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Goodbye, then.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Bye,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They were at the front door when there was a shout from behind them.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘All right, all right, I’ll do it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore turned to see Slughorn standing breathless in the doorway to the sitting room.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You will come out of retirement?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, yes,’ said Slughorn impatiently. ‘I must be mad, but yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Wonderful,’ said Dumbledore, beaming. ‘Then, Horace, we shall see you on the first of September.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I daresay you will,’ grunted Slughorn.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: As they set off down the garden path, Slughorn’s voice floated after them.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll want a pay rise, Dumbledore!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore chuckled. The garden gate swung shut behind them and they set off back down the hill through the dark and the swirling mist.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well done, Harry,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I didn’t do anything,’ said Harry in surprise.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes you did. You showed Horace exactly how much he stands to gain by returning to Hogwarts. Did you like him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Er …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
