book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neville’s childhood had been blighted by Voldemort just as much as Harry’s had, but Neville had no idea how close he had come to having Harry’s destiny. The prophecy could have referred to either of them, yet, for his own inscrutable reasons, Voldemort had chosen to believe that Harry was the one meant.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Had Voldemort chosen Neville, it would be Neville sitting opposite Harry bearing the lightning-shaped scar and the weight of the prophecy … or would it? Would Neville’s mother have died to save him, as Lily had died for Harry? Surely she would … but what if she had been unable to stand between her son and Voldemort? Would there, then, have been no ‘Chosen One’ at all? An empty seat where Neville now sat and a scarless Harry who would have been kissed goodbye by his own mother, not Ron’s?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You all right, Harry? You look funny,’ said Neville.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry started.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry – I –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Wrackspurt got you?’ asked Luna sympathetically, peering at Harry through her enormous coloured spectacles.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I – what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘A Wrackspurt … they’re invisible, they float in through your ears and make your brain go fuzzy,’ she said. ‘I thought I felt one zooming around in here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She flapped her hands at thin air, as though beating off large invisible moths. Harry and Neville caught each other’s eye and hastily began to talk of Quidditch.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The weather beyond the train windows was as patchy as it had been all summer; they passed through stretches of the chilling mist, then out into weak, clear sunlight. It was during one of the clear spells, when the sun was visible almost directly overhead, that Ron and Hermione entered the compartment at last.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Wish the lunch trolley would hurry up, I’m starving,’ said Ron longingly, slumping into the seat beside Harry and rubbing his stomach. ‘Hi, Neville, hi, Luna. Guess what?’ he added, turning to Harry. ‘Malfoy’s not doing prefect duty. He’s just sitting in his compartment with the other Slytherins, we saw him when we passed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry sat up straight, interested. It was not like Malfoy to pass up the chance to demonstrate his power as prefect, which he had happily abused all the previous year.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What did he do when he saw you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The usual,’ said Ron indifferently, demonstrating a rude hand gesture. ‘Not like him, though, is it? Well – that is –’ he did the hand gesture again, ‘but why isn’t he out there bullying first-years?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Dunno,’ said Harry, but his mind was racing. Didn’t this look as though Malfoy had more important things on his mind than bullying younger students?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Maybe he preferred the Inquisitorial Squad,’ said Hermione. ‘Maybe being a prefect seems a bit tame after that.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t think so,’ said Harry, ‘I think he’s –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But before he could expound on his theory, the compartment door slid open again and a breathless third-year girl stepped inside.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m supposed to deliver these to Neville Longbottom and Harry P-Potter,’ she faltered, as her eyes met Harry’s and she turned scarlet. She was holding out two scrolls of parchment tied with violet ribbon. Perplexed, Harry and Neville took the scroll addressed to each of them and the girl stumbled back out of the compartment.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What is it?’ Ron demanded, as Harry unrolled his.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘An invitation,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry, I would be delighted if you would join me for a bite of lunch in compartment C. Sincerely, Professor H.E.F. Slughorn

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Who’s Professor Slughorn?’ asked Neville, looking perplexedly at his own invitation.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘New teacher,’ said Harry. ‘Well, I suppose we’ll have to go, won’t we?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But what does he want me for?’ asked Neville nervously, as though he were expecting detention.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No idea,’ said Harry, which was not entirely true, though he had no proof yet that his hunch was correct. ‘Listen,’ he added, seized by a sudden brainwave, ‘let’s go under the Invisibility Cloak, then we might get a good look at Malfoy on the way, see what he’s up to.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: This idea, however, came to nothing: the corridors, which were packed with people on the lookout for the lunch trolley, were impossible to negotiate while wearing the Cloak. Harry stowed it regretfully back in his bag, reflecting that it would have been nice to wear it just to avoid all the staring, which seemed to have increased in intensity even since he had last walked down the train. Every now and then students would hurtle out of their compartments to get a better look at him. The exception was Cho Chang, who darted into her compartment when she saw Harry coming. As Harry passed the window he saw her deep in determined conversation with her friend Marietta, who was wearing a very thick layer of makeup that did not entirely obscure the odd formation of pimples still etched across her face. Smirking slightly, Harry pushed on.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: When they reached compartment C, they saw at once that they were not Slughorn’s only invitees, although judging by the enthusiasm of Slughorn’s welcome, Harry was the most warmly anticipated.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, m’boy!’ said Slughorn, jumping up at the sight of him so that his great velvet-covered belly seemed to fill all the remaining space in the compartment. His shiny bald head and great silver moustache gleamed as brightly in the sunlight as the golden buttons on his waistcoat. ‘Good to see you, good to see you! And you must be Mr Longbottom!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neville nodded, looking scared. At a gesture from Slughorn, they sat down opposite each other in the only two empty seats, which were nearest the door. Harry glanced around at their fellow guests. He recognised a Slytherin from their year, a tall black boy with high cheekbones and long, slanting eyes; there were also two seventh-year boys Harry did not know and, squashed in the corner beside Slughorn and looking as though she was not entirely sure how she had got there, Ginny.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, do you know everyone?’ Slughorn asked Harry and Neville. ‘Blaise Zabini is in your year, of course –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Zabini did not make any sign of recognition or greeting, and nor did Harry or Neville: Gryffindor and Slytherin students loathed each other on principle.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘This is Cormac McLaggen, perhaps you’ve come across each other –? No?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: McLaggen, a large, wire-haired youth, raised a hand and Harry and Neville nodded back at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– and this is Marcus Belby, I don’t know whether –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Belby, who was thin and nervous-looking, gave a strained smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– and this charming young lady tells me she knows you!’ Slughorn finished.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ginny grimaced at Harry and Neville from behind Slughorn’s back.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well now, this is most pleasant,’ said Slughorn cosily. ‘A chance to get to know you all a little better. Here, take a napkin. I’ve packed my own lunch, the trolley, as I remember it, is heavy on Liquorice Wands, and a poor old man’s digestive system isn’t quite up to such things … pheasant, Belby?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Belby started, and accepted what looked like half a cold pheasant.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I was just telling young Marcus here that I had the pleasure of teaching his Uncle Damocles,’ Slughorn told Harry and Neville, now passing around a basket of rolls. ‘Outstanding wizard, outstanding, and his Order of Merlin most well-deserved. Do you see much of your uncle, Marcus?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Unfortunately, Belby had just taken a large mouthful of pheasant; in his haste to answer Slughorn he swallowed too fast, turned purple and began to choke.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Anapneo,’ said Slughorn calmly, pointing his wand at Belby, whose airway seemed to clear at once.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not … not much of him, no,’ gasped Belby, his eyes streaming.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, of course, I daresay he’s busy,’ said Slughorn, looking questioningly at Belby. ‘I doubt he invented the Wolfsbane Potion without considerable hard work!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I suppose …’ said Belby, who seemed afraid to take another bite of pheasant until he was sure that Slughorn had finished with him. ‘Er … he and my dad don’t get on very well, you see, so I don’t really know much about …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: His voice tailed away as Slughorn gave him a cold smile and turned to McLaggen instead.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, you, Cormac,’ said Slughorn, ‘I happen to know you see a lot of your Uncle Tiberius, because he has a rather splendid picture of the two of you hunting Nogtails in, I think, Norfolk?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yeah, that was fun, that was,’ said McLaggen. ‘We went with Bertie Higgs and Rufus Scrimgeour – this was before he became Minister, obviously –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, you know Bertie and Rufus, too?’ beamed Slughorn, now offering around a small tray of pies; somehow, Belby was missed out. ‘Now tell me …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It was as Harry had suspected. Everyone here seemed to have been invited because they were connected to somebody well-known or influential – everyone except Ginny. Zabini, who was interrogated after McLaggen, turned out to have a famously beautiful witch for a mother (from what Harry could make out, she had been married seven times, each of her husbands dying mysteriously and leaving her mounds of gold). It was Neville’s turn next: this was a very uncomfortable ten minutes, for Neville’s parents, well-known Aurors, had been tortured into insanity by Bellatrix Lestrange and a couple of Death Eater cronies. At the end of Neville’s interview, Harry had the impression that Slughorn was reserving judgement on Neville, yet to see whether he had any of his parents’ flair.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And now,’ said Slughorn, shifting massively in his seat with the air of a compère introducing his star act. ‘Harry Potter! Where to begin? I feel I barely scratched the surface when we met over the summer!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He contemplated Harry for a moment as though he were a particularly large and succulent piece of pheasant, then said, ‘The “Chosen One”, they’re calling you now!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry said nothing. Belby, McLaggen and Zabini were all staring at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course,’ said Slughorn, watching Harry closely, ‘there have been rumours for years … I remember when – well – after that terrible night – Lily – James – and you survived – and the word was that you must have powers beyond the ordinary –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Zabini gave a tiny little cough that was clearly supposed to indicate amused scepticism. An angry voice burst out from behind Slughorn.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, Zabini, because you’re so talented … at posing …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh dear!’ chuckled Slughorn comfortably, looking round at Ginny who was glaring at Zabini around Slughorn’s great belly. ‘You want to be careful, Blaise! I saw this young lady perform the most marvellous Bat-Bogey Hex as I was passing her carriage! I wouldn’t cross her!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Zabini merely looked contemptuous.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway,’ said Slughorn, turning back to Harry. ‘Such rumours this summer. Of course, one doesn’t know what to believe, the Prophet has been known to print inaccuracies, make mistakes – but there seems little doubt, given the number of witnesses, that there was quite a disturbance at the Ministry and that you were there in the thick of it all!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry, who could not see any way out of this without flatly lying, nodded but still said nothing. Slughorn beamed at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So modest, so modest, no wonder Dumbledore is so fond – you were there, then? But the rest of the stories – so sensational, of course, one doesn’t know quite what to believe – this fabled prophecy, for instance –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘We never heard a prophecy,’ said Neville, turning geranium-pink as he said it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s right,’ said Ginny staunchly. ‘Neville and I were both there too, and all this “Chosen One” rubbish is just the Prophet making things up as usual.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You were both there too, were you?’ said Slughorn with great interest, looking from Ginny to Neville, but both of them sat clamlike before his encouraging smile. ‘Yes … well … it is true that the Prophet often exaggerates, of course …’ Slughorn continued, sounding a little disappointed. ‘I remember dear Gwenog telling me – Gwenog Jones, I mean, of course, Captain of the Holyhead Harpies –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He meandered off into a long-winded reminiscence, but Harry had the distinct impression that Slughorn had not finished with him, and that he had not been convinced by Neville and Ginny.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The afternoon wore on with more anecdotes about illustrious wizards Slughorn had taught, all of whom had been delighted to join what he called the ‘Slug Club’ at Hogwarts. Harry could not wait to leave, but couldn’t see how to do so politely. Finally the train emerged from yet another long misty stretch into a red sunset, and Slughorn looked around, blinking in the twilight.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good gracious, it’s getting dark already! I didn’t notice that they’d lit the lamps! You’d better go and change into your robes, all of you. McLaggen, you must drop by and borrow that book on Nogtails. Harry, Blaise – any time you’re passing. Same goes for you, miss,’ he twinkled at Ginny. ‘Well, off you go, off you go!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: As he pushed past Harry into the darkening corridor, Zabini shot him a filthy look that Harry returned with interest. He, Ginny and Neville followed Zabini back along the train.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m glad that’s over,’ muttered Neville. ‘Strange man, isn’t he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, he is a bit,’ said Harry, his eyes on Zabini. ‘How come you ended up in there, Ginny?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He saw me hex Zacharias Smith,’ said Ginny, ‘you remember that idiot from Hufflepuff who was in the DA? He kept on and on asking about what happened at the Ministry and in the end he annoyed me so much I hexed him – when Slughorn came in I thought I was going to get detention, but he just thought it was a really good hex and invited me to lunch! Mad, eh?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Better reason for inviting someone than because their mother’s famous,’ said Harry, scowling at the back of Zabini’s head, ‘or because their uncle –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But he broke off. An idea had just occurred to him, a reckless but potentially wonderful idea … in a minute’s time, Zabini was going to re-enter the Slytherin sixth-year compartment and Malfoy would be sitting there, thinking himself unheard by anybody except fellow Slytherins … if Harry could only enter, unseen, behind him, what might he not see or hear? True, there was little of the journey left – Hogsmeade Station had to be less than half an hour away, judging by the wildness of the scenery flashing by the windows – but nobody else seemed prepared to take Harry’s suspicions seriously, so it was down to him to prove them.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll see you two later,’ said Harry under his breath, pulling out his Invisibility Cloak and flinging it over himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But what’re you – ?’ asked Neville.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Later!’ whispered Harry, darting after Zabini as quietly as possible, though the rattling of the train made such caution almost pointless.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The corridors were almost completely empty now. Nearly everyone had returned to their carriages to change into their school robes and pack up their possessions. Though he was as close as he could get to Zabini without touching him, Harry was not quick enough to slip into the compartment when Zabini opened the door. Zabini was already sliding it shut when Harry hastily stuck out his foot to prevent it closing.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s wrong with this thing?’ said Zabini angrily as he smashed the sliding door repeatedly into Harry’s foot.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry seized the door and pushed it open, hard; Zabini, still clinging on to the handle, toppled over sideways into Gregory Goyle’s lap and, in the ensuing ruckus, Harry darted into the compartment, leapt on to Zabini’s temporarily empty seat and hoisted himself up into the luggage rack. It was fortunate that Goyle and Zabini were snarling at each other, drawing all eyes on to them, for Harry was quite sure his feet and ankles had been revealed as the Cloak had flapped around them; indeed, for one horrible moment he thought he saw Malfoy’s eyes follow his trainer as it whipped upwards out of sight; but then Goyle slammed the door shut and flung Zabini off him, Zabini collapsed into his own seat looking ruffled, Vincent Crabbe returned to his comic and Malfoy, sniggering, lay back down across two seats with his head in Pansy Parkinson’s lap. Harry lay curled uncomfortably under the Cloak to ensure that every inch of him remained hidden, and watched Pansy stroke the sleek blond hair off Malfoy’s forehead, smirking as she did so, as though anyone would have loved to have been in her place. The lanterns swinging from the carriage ceiling cast a bright light over the scene: Harry could read every word of Crabbe’s comic directly below him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So, Zabini,’ said Malfoy, ‘what did Slughorn want?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Just trying to make up to well-connected people,’ said Zabini, who was still glowering at Goyle. ‘Not that he managed to find many.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: This information did not seem to please Malfoy.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Who else had he invited?’ he demanded.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘McLaggen from Gryffindor,’ said Zabini.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yeah, his uncle’s big in the Ministry,’ said Malfoy.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– someone else called Belby, from Ravenclaw –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not him, he’s a prat!’ said Pansy.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– and Longbottom, Potter and that Weasley girl,’ finished Zabini.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Malfoy sat up very suddenly, knocking Pansy’s hand aside.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He invited Longbottom?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I assume so, as Longbottom was there,’ said Zabini indifferently.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s Longbottom got to interest Slughorn?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Zabini shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Potter, precious Potter, obviously he wanted a look at the Chosen One,’ sneered Malfoy, ‘but that Weasley girl! What’s so special about her?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘A lot of boys like her,’ said Pansy, watching Malfoy out of the corner of her eyes for his reaction. ‘Even you think she’s good-looking, don’t you, Blaise, and we all know how hard you are to please!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I wouldn’t touch a filthy little blood traitor like her whatever she looked like,’ said Zabini coldly, and Pansy looked pleased. Malfoy sank back across her lap and allowed her to resume the stroking of his hair.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I pity Slughorn’s taste. Maybe he’s going a bit senile. Shame, my father always said he was a good wizard in his day. My father used to be a bit of a favourite of his. Slughorn probably hasn’t heard I’m on the train, or –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I wouldn’t bank on an invitation,’ said Zabini. ‘He asked me about Nott’s father when I first arrived. They used to be old friends, apparently, but when he heard he’d been caught at the Ministry he didn’t look happy, and Nott didn’t get an invitation, did he? I don’t think Slughorn’s interested in Death Eaters.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Malfoy looked angry, but forced out a singularly humourless laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, who cares what he’s interested in? What is he, when you come down to it? Just some stupid teacher.’ Malfoy yawned ostentatiously. ‘I mean, I might not even be at Hogwarts next year, what’s it matter to me if some fat old has-been likes me or not?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What do you mean, you might not be at Hogwarts next year?’ said Pansy indignantly, ceasing grooming Malfoy at once.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, you never know,’ said Malfoy with the ghost of a smirk. ‘I might have – er – moved on to bigger and better things.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Crouched in the luggage rack under his Cloak, Harry’s heart began to race. What would Ron and Hermione say about this? Crabbe and Goyle were gawping at Malfoy; apparently they had had no inkling of any plans to move on to bigger and better things. Even Zabini had allowed a look of curiosity to mar his haughty features. Pansy resumed the slow stroking of Malfoy’s hair, looking dumbfounded.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Do you mean – Him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Malfoy shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Mother wants me to complete my education, but personally, I don’t see it as that important these days. I mean, think about it … when the Dark Lord takes over, is he going to care how many O.W.L.s or N.E.W.T.s anyone’s got? Of course he isn’t … it’ll be all about the kind of service he received, the level of devotion he was shown.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And you think you’ll be able to do something for him?’ asked Zabini scathingly. ‘Sixteen years old and not even fully qualified yet?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve just said, haven’t I? Maybe he doesn’t care if I’m qualified. Maybe the job he wants me to do isn’t something that you need to be qualified for,’ said Malfoy quietly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Crabbe and Goyle were both sitting with their mouths open like gargoyles. Pansy was gazing down at Malfoy as though she had never seen anything so awe-inspiring.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I can see Hogwarts,’ said Malfoy, clearly relishing the effect he had created as he pointed out of the blackened window. ‘We’d better get our robes on.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry was so busy staring at Malfoy he did not notice Goyle reaching up for his trunk; as he swung it down, it hit Harry hard on the side of the head. He let out an involuntary gasp of pain and Malfoy looked up at the luggage rack, frowning.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry was not afraid of Malfoy, but he still did not much like the idea of being discovered hiding under his Invisibility Cloak by a group of unfriendly Slytherins. Eyes still watering and head still throbbing, he drew his wand, careful not to disarrange the Cloak, and waited, breath held. To his relief, Malfoy seemed to decide that he had imagined the noise; he pulled on his robes like the others, locked his trunk and, as the train slowed to a jerky crawl, fastened a thick new travelling cloak round his neck.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry could see the corridors filling up again and hoped that Hermione and Ron would take his things out on to the platform for him; he was stuck where he was until the compartment had quite emptied. At last, with a final lurch, the train came to a complete halt. Goyle threw the door open and muscled his way out into a crowd of second-years, punching them aside; Crabbe and Zabini followed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You go on,’ Malfoy told Pansy, who was waiting for him with her hand held out as though hoping he would hold it. ‘I just want to check something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Pansy left. Now Harry and Malfoy were alone in the compartment. People were filing past, descending on to the dark platform. Malfoy moved over to the compartment door and let down the blinds, so that people in the corridor beyond could not peer in. He then bent down over his trunk and opened it again.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry peered down over the edge of the luggage rack, his heart pumping a little faster. What had Malfoy wanted to hide from Pansy? Was he about to see the mysterious broken object it was so important to mend?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Petrificus Totalus!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Without warning, Malfoy pointed his wand at Harry, who was instantly paralysed. As though in slow motion, he toppled out of the luggage rack and fell, with an agonising, floor-shaking crash, at Malfoy’s feet, the Invisibility Cloak trapped beneath him, his whole body revealed with his legs still curled absurdly into the cramped kneeling position. He couldn’t move a muscle; he could only gaze up at Malfoy, who smiled broadly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

text_content: With the usual deafening scraping noise, the benches were moved back and the hundreds of students began to file out of the Great Hall towards their dormitories. Harry, who was in no hurry at all to leave with the gawping crowd, nor to get near enough to Malfoy to allow him to retell the story of the nose-stamping, lagged behind, pretending to retie the lace on his trainer, allowing most of the Gryffindors to draw ahead of him. Hermione had darted ahead to fulfil her prefect’s duty of shepherding the first-years, but Ron remained with Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What really happened to your nose?’ he asked, once they were at the very back of the throng pressing out of the Hall, and out of earshot of anyone else.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry told him. It was a mark of the strength of their friendship that Ron did not laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I saw Malfoy miming something to do with a nose,’ he said darkly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, never mind that,’ said Harry bitterly. ‘Listen to what he was saying before he found out I was there …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry had expected Ron to be stunned by Malfoy’s boasts. With what Harry considered pure pigheadedness, however, Ron was unimpressed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Come on, Harry, he was just showing off for Parkinson … what kind of mission would You-Know-Who have given him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘How d’you know Voldemort doesn’t need someone at Hogwarts? It wouldn’t be the first –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I wish yeh’d stop sayin’ tha’ name, Harry,’ said a reproachful voice behind them. Harry looked over his shoulder to see Hagrid shaking his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore uses that name,’ said Harry stubbornly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, tha’s Dumbledore, innit?’ said Hagrid mysteriously. ‘So how come yeh were late, Harry? I was worried.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Got held up on the train,’ said Harry. ‘Why were you late?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I was with Grawp,’ said Hagrid happily. ‘Los’ track o’ the time. He’s got a new home up in the mountains now, Dumbledore fixed it – nice big cave. He’s much happier than he was in the Forest. We were havin’ a good chat.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Really?’ said Harry, taking care not to catch Ron’s eye; the last time he had met Hagrid’s half-brother, a vicious giant with a talent for ripping up trees by the roots, his vocabulary had comprised five words, two of which he was unable to pronounce properly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yeah, he’s really come on,’ said Hagrid proudly. ‘Yeh’ll be amazed. I’m thinkin’ o’ trainin’ him up as me assistant.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ron snorted loudly, but managed to pass it off as a violent sneeze. They were now standing beside the oak front doors.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Anyway, I’ll see yeh tomorrow, firs’ lesson’s straight after lunch. Come early an’ yeh can say hello ter Buck— I mean, Witherwings!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Raising an arm in cheery farewell, he headed out of the front doors into the darkness.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron looked at each other. Harry could tell that Ron was experiencing the same sinking feeling as himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re not taking Care of Magical Creatures, are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ron shook his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And you’re not either, are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry shook his head, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And Hermione,’ said Ron, ‘she’s not, is she?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry shook his head again. Exactly what Hagrid would say when he realised his three favourite students had given up his subject, he did not like to think.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron met Hermione in the common room before breakfast next morning. Hoping for some support for his theory, Harry lost no time in telling Hermione what he had overheard Malfoy saying on the Hogwarts Express.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But he was obviously showing off for Parkinson, wasn’t he?’ interjected Ron quickly, before Hermione could say anything.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ she said uncertainly, ‘I don’t know … it would be like Malfoy to make himself seem more important than he is … but that’s a big lie to tell …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Exactly,’ said Harry, but he could not press the point, because so many people were trying to listen in to his conversation, not to mention staring at him and whispering behind their hands.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s rude to point,’ Ron snapped at a particularly minuscule first-year as they joined the queue to climb out of the portrait hole. The boy, who had been muttering something about Harry behind his hand to his friend, promptly turned scarlet and toppled out of the hole in alarm. Ron sniggered.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I love being a sixth-year. And we’re going to be getting free time this year. Whole periods when we can just sit up here and relax.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re going to need that time for studying, Ron!’ said Hermione, as they set off down the corridor.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, but not today,’ said Ron, ‘today’s going to be a real doss, I reckon.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hold it!’ said Hermione, throwing out an arm and halting a passing fourth-year, who was attempting to push past her with a lime-green disc clutched tightly in his hand. ‘Fanged Frisbees are banned, hand it over,’ she told him sternly. The scowling boy handed over the snarling Frisbee, ducked under Hermione’s arm and took off after his friends. Ron waited for him to vanish, then tugged the Frisbee from Hermione’s grip.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Excellent, I’ve always wanted one of these.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Hermione’s remonstration was drowned by a loud giggle; Lavender Brown had apparently found Ron’s remark highly amusing. She continued to laugh as she passed them, glancing back at Ron over her shoulder. Ron looked rather pleased with himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The ceiling of the Great Hall was serenely blue and streaked with frail, wispy clouds, just like the squares of sky visible through the high mullioned windows. While they tucked into porridge and eggs and bacon, Harry and Ron told Hermione about their embarrassing conversation with Hagrid the previous evening.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But he can’t really think we’d continue Care of Magical Creatures!’ she said, looking distressed. ‘I mean, when has any of us expressed … you know … any enthusiasm?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s it, though, innit?’ said Ron, swallowing an entire fried egg whole. ‘We were the ones who made the most effort in classes because we like Hagrid. But he thinks we liked the stupid subject. D’you reckon anyone’s going to go on to N.E.W.T.?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neither Harry nor Hermione answered; there was no need. They knew perfectly well that nobody in their year would want to continue Care of Magical Creatures. They avoided Hagrid’s eye and returned his cheery wave only half-heartedly when he left the staff table ten minutes later.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: After they had eaten, they remained in their places, awaiting Professor McGonagall’s descent from the staff table. The distribution of timetables was more complicated than usual this year, for Professor McGonagall needed first to confirm that everybody had achieved the necessary O.W.L. grades to continue with their chosen N.E.W.T.s.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Hermione was immediately cleared to continue with Charms, Defence Against the Dark Arts, Transfiguration, Herbology, Arithmancy, Ancient Runes and Potions, and shot off to a first-period Ancient Runes class without further ado. Neville took a little longer to sort out; his round face was anxious as Professor McGonagall looked down his application and then consulted his O.W.L. results.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Herbology, fine,’ she said. ‘Professor Sprout will be delighted to see you back with an “Outstanding” O.W.L. And you qualify for Defence Against the Dark Arts with “Exceeds Expectations”. But the problem is Transfiguration. I’m sorry, Longbottom, but an “Acceptable” really isn’t good enough to continue to N.E.W.T. level, I just don’t think you’d be able to cope with the coursework.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neville hung his head. Professor McGonagall peered at him through her square spectacles.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Why do you want to continue with Transfiguration, anyway? I’ve never had the impression that you particularly enjoyed it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neville looked miserable and muttered something about ‘my grandmother wants’.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Humph,’ snorted Professor McGonagall. ‘It’s high time your grandmother learned to be proud of the grandson she’s got, rather than the one she thinks she ought to have – particularly after what happened at the Ministry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Neville turned very pink and blinked confusedly; Professor McGonagall had never paid him a compliment before.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry, Longbottom, but I cannot let you into my N.E.W.T. class. I see that you have an “Exceeds Expectations” in Charms, however – why not try for a N.E.W.T. in Charms?’ ‘My grandmother thinks Charms is a soft option,’ mumbled Neville.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Take Charms,’ said Professor McGonagall, ‘and I shall drop Augusta a line reminding her that just because she failed her Charms O.W.L., the subject is not necessarily worthless.’ Smiling slightly at the look of delighted incredulity on Neville’s face, Professor McGonagall tapped a blank timetable with the tip of her wand and handed it, now carrying details of his new classes, to Neville.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Professor McGonagall turned next to Parvati Patil, whose first question was whether Firenze, the handsome centaur, was still teaching Divination.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He and Professor Trelawney are dividing classes between them this year,’ said Professor McGonagall, a hint of disapproval in her voice; it was common knowledge that she despised the subject of Divination. ‘The sixth year is being taken by Professor Trelawney.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Parvati set off for Divination five minutes later looking slightly crestfallen.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So, Potter, Potter …’ said Professor McGonagall, consulting her notes as she turned to Harry. ‘Charms, Defence Against the Dark Arts, Herbology, Transfiguration … all fine. I must say, I was pleased with your Transfiguration mark, Potter, very pleased. Now, why haven’t you applied to continue with Potions? I thought it was your ambition to become an Auror?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It was, but you told me I had to get an “Outstanding” in my O.W.L., Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And so you did when Professor Snape was teaching the subject. Professor Slughorn, however, is perfectly happy to accept N.E.W.T. students with “Exceeds Expectations” at O.W.L. Do you wish to proceed with Potions?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry, ‘but I didn’t buy the books or any ingredients or anything –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sure Professor Slughorn will be able to lend you some,’ said Professor McGonagall. ‘Very well, Potter, here is your timetable. Oh, by the way – twenty hopefuls have already put down their names for the Gryffindor Quidditch team. I shall pass the list to you in due course and you can fix up trials at your leisure.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A few minutes later, Ron was cleared to do the same subjects as Harry, and the two of them left the table together.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Look,’ said Ron delightedly, gazing at his timetable, ‘we’ve got a free period now … and a free period after break … and after lunch … excellent!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: They returned to the common room, which was empty apart from half a dozen seventh-years including Katie Bell, the only remaining member of the original Gryffindor Quidditch team that Harry had joined in his first year.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought you’d get that, well done,’ she called over, pointing at the Captain’s badge on Harry’s chest. ‘Tell me when you call trials!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be stupid,’ said Harry, ‘you don’t need to try out, I’ve watched you play for five years …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You mustn’t start off like that,’ she said warningly. ‘For all you know, there’s someone much better than me out there. Good teams have been ruined before now because captains just kept playing the old faces, or letting in their friends …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ron looked a little uncomfortable and began playing with the Fanged Frisbee Hermione had taken from the fourth-year. It zoomed around the common room, snarling and attempting to take bites of the tapestry. Crookshanks’s yellow eyes followed it and he hissed when it came too close.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: An hour later they reluctantly left the sunlit common room for the Defence Against the Dark Arts classroom four floors below. Hermione was already queuing outside, carrying an armful of heavy books and looking put-upon.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘We got so much homework for Runes,’ she said anxiously, when Harry and Ron joined her. ‘A fifteen-inch essay, two translations and I’ve got to read these by Wednesday!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Shame,’ yawned Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You wait,’ she said resentfully. ‘I bet Snape gives us loads.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The classroom door opened as she spoke and Snape stepped into the corridor, his sallow face framed as ever by two curtains of greasy black hair. Silence fell over the queue immediately.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Inside,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around as they entered. Snape had imposed his personality upon the room already; it was gloomier than usual as curtains had been drawn over the windows, and was lit by candlelight. New pictures adorned the walls, many of them showing people who appeared to be in pain, sporting grisly injuries or strangely contorted body parts. Nobody spoke as they settled down, looking around at the shadowy, gruesome pictures.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I have not asked you to take out your books,’ said Snape, closing the door and moving to face the class from behind his desk; Hermione hastily dropped her copy of Confronting the Faceless back into her bag and stowed it under her chair. ‘I wish to speak to you and I want your fullest attention.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: His black eyes roved over their upturned faces, lingering for a fraction of a second longer on Harry’s than anyone else’s.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You have had five teachers in this subject so far, I believe.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: You believe … like you haven’t watched them all come and go, Snape, hoping you’d be next, thought Harry scathingly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Naturally, these teachers will all have had their own methods and priorities. Given this confusion I am surprised so many of you scraped an O.W.L. in this subject. I shall be even more surprised if all of you manage to keep up with the N.E.W.T. work, which will be much more advanced.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Snape set off around the edge of the room, speaking now in a lower voice; the class craned their necks to keep him in view.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dark Arts,’ said Snape, ‘are many, varied, ever-changing and eternal. Fighting them is like fighting a many-headed monster, which, each time a neck is severed, sprouts a head even fiercer and cleverer than before. You are fighting that which is unfixed, mutating, indestructible.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry stared at Snape. It was surely one thing to respect the Dark Arts as a dangerous enemy, another to speak of them, as Snape was doing, with a loving caress in his voice?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Your defences,’ said Snape, a little louder, ‘must therefore be as flexible and inventive as the Arts you seek to undo. These pictures,’ he indicated a few of them as he swept past, ‘give a fair representation of what happens to those who suffer, for instance, the Cruciatus Curse’ (he waved a hand towards a witch who was clearly shrieking in agony) ‘feel the Dementor’s Kiss’ (a wizard lying huddled and blank-eyed slumped against a wall) ‘or provoke the aggression of the Inferius’ (a bloody mass upon the ground).

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Has an Inferius been seen, then?’ said Parvati Patil in a high-pitched voice. ‘Is it definite, is he using them?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dark Lord has used Inferi in the past,’ said Snape, ‘which means you would be well-advised to assume he might use them again. Now …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He set off again around the other side of the classroom towards his desk, and again, the class watched him as he walked, his dark robes billowing behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘… you are, I believe, complete novices in the use of non-verbal spells. What is the advantage of a non-verbal spell?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Hermione’s hand shot into the air. Snape took his time looking around at everybody else, making sure he had no choice, before saying curtly, ‘Very well – Miss Granger?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Your adversary has no warning about what kind of magic you’re about to perform,’ said Hermione, ‘which gives you a split-second advantage.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘An answer copied almost word for word from The Standard Book of Spells, Grade 6,’ said Snape dismissively (over in the corner, Malfoy sniggered), ‘but correct in essentials. Yes, those who progress to using magic without shouting incantations gain an element of surprise in their spell-casting. Not all wizards can do this, of course; it is a question of concentration and mind power which some,’ his gaze lingered maliciously upon Harry once more, ‘lack.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry knew Snape was thinking of their disastrous Occlumency lessons of the previous year. He refused to drop his gaze, but glowered at Snape until Snape looked away.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You will now divide,’ Snape went on, ‘into pairs. One partner will attempt to jinx the other without speaking. The other will attempt to repel the jinx in equal silence. Carry on.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Although Snape did not know it, Harry had taught at least half the class (everyone who had been a member of the DA) how to perform a Shield Charm the previous year. None of them had ever cast the Charm without speaking, however. A reasonable amount of cheating ensued; many people were merely whispering the incantation instead of saying it aloud. Typically, ten minutes into the lesson Hermione managed to repel Neville’s muttered Jelly-Legs Jinx without uttering a single word, a feat that would surely have earned her twenty points for Gryffindor from any reasonable teacher, thought Harry bitterly, but which Snape ignored. He swept between them as they practised, looking just as much like an overgrown bat as ever, lingering to watch Harry and Ron struggling with the task.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ron, who was supposed to be jinxing Harry, was purple in the face, his lips tightly compressed to save himself from the temptation of muttering the incantation. Harry had his wand raised, waiting on tenterhooks to repel a jinx that seemed unlikely ever to come.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Pathetic, Weasley,’ said Snape, after a while. ‘Here – let me show you –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He turned his wand on Harry so fast that Harry reacted instinctively; all thought of non-verbal spells forgotten he yelled, ‘Protego!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: His Shield Charm was so strong Snape was knocked off-balance and hit a desk. The whole class had looked round and now watched as Snape righted himself, scowling.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Do you remember me telling you we are practising non-verbal spells, Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Harry stiffly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes sir.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s no need to call me “sir”, Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The words had escaped him before he knew what he was saying. Several people gasped, including Hermione. Behind Snape, however, Ron, Dean and Seamus grinned appreciatively.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Detention, Saturday night, my office,’ said Snape. ‘I do not take cheek from anyone, Potter … not even the Chosen One.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That was brilliant, Harry!’ chortled Ron, once they were safely on their way to break a short while later.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You really shouldn’t have said it,’ said Hermione, frowning at Ron. ‘What made you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He tried to jinx me, in case you didn’t notice!’ fumed Harry. ‘I had enough of that during those Occlumency lessons! Why doesn’t he use another guinea pig for a change? What’s Dumbledore playing at, anyway, letting him teach Defence? Did you hear him talking about the Dark Arts? He loves them! All that unfixed, indestructible stuff –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Hermione, ‘I thought he sounded a bit like you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Like me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, when you were telling us what it’s like to face Voldemort. You said it wasn’t just memorising a bunch of spells, you said it was just you and your brains and your guts – well, wasn’t that what Snape was saying? That it really comes down to being brave and quick-thinking?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry was so disarmed that she had thought his words as well worth memorising as The Standard Book of Spells that he did not argue.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry! Hey, Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry looked round; Jack Sloper, one of the Beaters on the previous year’s Gryffindor Quidditch team, was hurrying towards him holding a roll of parchment.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘For you,’ panted Sloper. ‘Listen, I heard you’re the new Captain. When’re you holding trials?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not sure yet,’ said Harry, thinking privately that Sloper would be very lucky to get back on the team. ‘I’ll let you know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, right. I was hoping it’d be this weekend –’ But Harry was not listening; he had just recognised the thin, slanting writing on the parchment. Leaving Sloper in mid-sentence, he hurried away with Ron and Hermione, unrolling the parchment as he went.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dear Harry, I would like to start our private lessons this Saturday. Kindly come along to my office at eight p.m. I hope you are enjoying your first day back at school. Yours sincerely Albus Dumbledore P.S. I enjoy Acid Pops.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He enjoys Acid Pops?’ said Ron, who had read the message over Harry’s shoulder and was looking perplexed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s the password to get past the gargoyle outside his study,’ said Harry in a low voice. ‘Ha! Snape’s not going to be pleased … I won’t be able to do his detention!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He, Ron and Hermione spent the whole of break speculating on what Dumbledore would teach Harry. Ron thought it most likely to be spectacular jinxes and hexes of the type the Death Eaters would not know. Hermione said such things were illegal, and thought it much more likely that Dumbledore wanted to teach Harry advanced defensive magic. After break, she went off to Arithmancy while Harry and Ron returned to the common room, where they grudgingly started Snape’s homework. This turned out to be so complex that they still had not finished when Hermione joined them for their after-lunch free period (though she considerably speeded up the process). They had only just finished when the bell rang for the afternoon’s double Potions and they beat the familiar path down to the dungeon classroom that had, for so long, been Snape’s.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: When they arrived in the corridor they saw that there were only a dozen people progressing to N.E.W.T. level. Crabbe and Goyle had evidently failed to achieve the required O.W.L. grade, but four Slytherins had made it through, including Malfoy. Four Ravenclaws were there, and one Hufflepuff, Ernie Macmillan, whom Harry liked despite his rather pompous manner.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry,’ Ernie said portentously, holding out his hand as Harry approached, ‘didn’t get a chance to speak in Defence Against the Dark Arts this morning. Good lesson, I thought, but Shield Charms are old hat, of course, for us old DA lags … and how are you, Ron – Hermione?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Before they could say more than ‘fine’, the dungeon door opened and Slughorn’s belly preceded him out of the door. As they filed into the room, his great walrus moustache curved above his beaming mouth and he greeted Harry and Zabini with particular enthusiasm.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The dungeon was, most unusually, already full of vapours and odd smells. Harry, Ron and Hermione sniffed interestedly as they passed large, bubbling cauldrons. The four Slytherins took a table together, as did the four Ravenclaws. This left Harry, Ron and Hermione to share a table with Ernie.
