text_content: A blinding, sickening pain … a flash of light … distant screams … and the sensation of falling down a long tunnel …

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And the next thing Harry knew, he was lying in a remarkably warm and comfortable bed and looking up at a lamp that was throwing a circle of golden light on to a shadowy ceiling. He raised his head awkwardly. There on his left was a familiar-looking, freckly, red-haired person.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Nice of you to drop in,’ said Ron, grinning.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry blinked and looked around. Of course: he was in the hospital wing. The sky outside was indigo streaked with crimson. The match must have finished hours ago … as had any hope of cornering Malfoy. Harry’s head felt strangely heavy; he raised a hand and felt a stiff turban of bandages.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What happened?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Cracked skull,’ said Madam Pomfrey, bustling up and pushing him back against his pillows. ‘Nothing to worry about, I mended it at once, but I’m keeping you in overnight. You shouldn’t overexert yourself for a few hours.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t want to stay here overnight,’ said Harry angrily, sitting up and throwing back his covers, ‘I want to find McLaggen and kill him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m afraid that would come under the heading of “overexertion”,’ said Madam Pomfrey, pushing him firmly back on to the bed and raising her wand in a threatening manner. ‘You will stay here until I discharge you, Potter, or I shall call the Headmaster.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She bustled back into her office and Harry sank back into his pillows, fuming.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you know how much we lost by?’ he asked Ron through clenched teeth.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, yeah I do,’ said Ron apologetically. ‘Final score was three hundred and twenty to sixty.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Brilliant,’ said Harry savagely. ‘Really brilliant! When I get hold of McLaggen –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t want to get hold of him, he’s the size of a troll,’ said Ron reasonably. ‘Personally I think there’s a lot to be said for hexing him with that toenail thing of the Prince’s. Anyway, the rest of the team might’ve dealt with him before you get out of here, they’re not happy …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was a note of badly suppressed glee in Ron’s voice; Harry could tell he was nothing short of thrilled that McLaggen had messed up so badly. Harry lay there, staring up at the patch of light on the ceiling, his recently mended skull not hurting, precisely, but feeling slightly tender underneath all the bandaging.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I could hear the match commentary from here,’ said Ron, his voice now shaking with laughter. ‘I hope Luna always commentates from now on … Loser’s Lurgy …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But Harry was still too angry to see much humour in the situation, and after a while Ron’s snorts subsided.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ginny came in to visit while you were unconscious,’ he said, after a long pause, and Harry’s imagination zoomed into overdrive, rapidly constructing a scene in which Ginny, weeping over his lifeless form, confessed her feelings of deep attraction to him while Ron gave them his blessing … ‘She reckons you only just arrived in time for the match. How come? You left here early enough.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh …’ said Harry, as the scene in his mind’s eye imploded. ‘Yeah … well, I saw Malfoy sneaking off with a couple of girls who didn’t look like they wanted to be with him, and that’s the second time he’s made sure he isn’t down on the Quidditch pitch with the rest of the school. He skipped the last match too, remember?’ Harry sighed. ‘Wish I’d followed him now, the match was such a fiasco …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be stupid,’ said Ron sharply. ‘You couldn’t have missed a Quidditch match just to follow Malfoy, you’re the Captain!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I want to know what he’s up to,’ said Harry. ‘And don’t tell me it’s all in my head, not after what I overheard between him and Snape –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I never said it was all in your head,’ said Ron, hoisting himself up on an elbow in turn and frowning at Harry, ‘but there’s no rule saying only one person at a time can be plotting anything in this place! You’re getting a bit obsessed with Malfoy, Harry. I mean, thinking about missing a match just to follow him …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I want to catch him at it!’ said Harry in frustration. ‘I mean, where’s he going when he disappears off the map?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I dunno … Hogsmeade?’ suggested Ron, yawning.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve never seen him going along any of the secret passageways on the map. I thought they were being watched now, anyway?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, then, I dunno,’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Silence fell between them. Harry stared up at the circle of lamplight above him, thinking …

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: If only he had Rufus Scrimgeour’s power, he would have been able to set a tail upon Malfoy, but unfortunately Harry did not have an office full of Aurors at his command … he thought fleetingly of trying to set something up with the DA, but there again was the problem that people would be missed from lessons; most of them, after all, still had full timetables …

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was a low, rumbling snore from Ron’s bed. After a while Madam Pomfrey came out of her office, this time wearing a thick dressing-gown. It was easiest to feign sleep; Harry rolled over on to his side and listened to all the curtains closing themselves as she waved her wand. The lamps dimmed, and she returned to her office; he heard the door click behind her, and knew that she was off to bed.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: This was, Harry reflected in the darkness, the third time that he had been brought to the hospital wing because of a Quidditch injury. Last time he had fallen off his broom due to the presence of Dementors around the pitch, and the time before that, all the bones had been removed from his arm by the incurably inept Professor Lockhart … that had been his most painful injury by far … he remembered the agony of regrowing an armful of bones in one night, a discomfort not eased by the arrival of an unexpected visitor in the middle of the –

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry sat bolt upright, his heart pounding, his bandage turban askew. He had the solution at last: there was a way to have Malfoy followed – how could he have forgotten, why hadn’t he thought of it before?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But the question was, how to call him? What did you do?

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Quietly, tentatively, Harry spoke into the darkness.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was a very loud crack and the sounds of scuffling and squeaks filled the silent room. Ron awoke with a yelp.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s going –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry pointed his wand hastily at the door of Madam Pomfrey’s office and muttered ‘Muffliato!’ so that she would not come running. Then he scrambled to the end of his bed for a better look at what was going on.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Two house-elves were rolling around on the floor in the middle of the dormitory, one wearing a shrunken maroon jumper and several woolly hats, the other, a filthy old rag strung over his hips like a loincloth. Then there was another loud bang, and Peeves the poltergeist appeared in midair above the wrestling elves.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I was watching that, Potty!’ he told Harry indignantly, pointing at the fight below, before letting out a loud cackle. ‘Look at the ickle creatures squabbling, bitey bitey, punchy punchy –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher will not insult Harry Potter in front of Dobby, no he won’t, or Dobby will shut Kreacher’s mouth for him!’ cried Dobby in a high-pitched voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– kicky, scratchy!’ cried Peeves happily, now pelting bits of chalk at the elves to enrage them further. ‘Tweaky, pokey!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher will say what he likes about his master, oh yes, and what a master he is, filthy friend of Mudbloods, oh, what would poor Kreacher’s mistress say –?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Exactly what Kreacher’s mistress would have said they did not find out, for at that moment Dobby sank his knobbly little fist into Kreacher’s mouth and knocked out half of his teeth. Harry and Ron both leapt out of their beds and wrenched the two elves apart, though they continued to try to kick and punch each other, egged on by Peeves, who swooped around the lamp squealing, ‘Stick your fingers up his nosey, draw his cork and pull his earsies –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry aimed his wand at Peeves and said, ‘Langlock!’ Peeves clutched at his throat, gulped, then swooped from the room making obscene gestures but unable to speak, owing to the fact that his tongue had just glued itself to the roof of his mouth.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Nice one,’ said Ron appreciatively, lifting Dobby into the air so that his flailing limbs no longer made contact with Kreacher. ‘That was another Prince hex, wasn’t it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, twisting Kreacher’s wizened arm into a half-nelson. ‘Right – I’m forbidding you to fight each other! Well, Kreacher, you’re forbidden to fight Dobby. Dobby, I know I’m not allowed to give you orders –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Dobby is a free house-elf and he can obey anyone he likes and Dobby will do whatever Harry Potter wants him to do!’ said Dobby, tears now streaming down his shrivelled little face on to his jumper.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘OK, then,’ said Harry and he and Ron both released the elves, who fell to the floor, but did not continue fighting.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Master called me?’ croaked Kreacher, sinking into a bow even as he gave Harry a look that plainly wished him a painful death.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I did,’ said Harry, glancing towards Madam Pomfrey’s office door to check that the Muffliato spell was still working; there was no sign that she had heard any of the commotion. ‘I’ve got a job for you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher will do whatever Master wants,’ said Kreacher, sinking so low that his lips almost touched his gnarled toes, ‘because Kreacher has no choice, but Kreacher is ashamed to have such a Master, yes –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Dobby will do it, Harry Potter!’ squeaked Dobby, his tennis-ball-sized eyes still swimming with tears. ‘Dobby would be honoured to help Harry Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Come to think of it, it would be good to have both of you,’ said Harry. ‘OK, then … I want you to tail Draco Malfoy.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ignoring the look of mingled surprise and exasperation on Ron’s face, Harry went on, ‘I want to know where he’s going, who he’s meeting and what he’s doing. I want you to follow him around the clock.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Harry Potter!’ said Dobby at once, his great eyes shining with excitement. ‘And if Dobby does it wrong, Dobby will throw himself off the topmost tower, Harry Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘There won’t be any need for that,’ said Harry hastily.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Master wants me to follow the youngest of the Malfoys?’ croaked Kreacher. ‘Master wants me to spy upon the pureblood great-nephew of my old mistress?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the one,’ said Harry, foreseeing a great danger and determining to prevent it immediately. ‘And you’re forbidden to tip him off, Kreacher, or to show him what you’re up to, or to talk to him at all, or to write him messages, or … or to contact him in any way. Got it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He thought he could see Kreacher struggling to see a loophole in the instructions he had just been given, and waited. After a moment or two, and to Harry’s great satisfaction, Kreacher bowed deeply again and said, with bitter resentment, ‘Master thinks of everything and Kreacher must obey him even though Kreacher would much rather be the servant of the Malfoy boy, oh yes …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s settled, then,’ said Harry. ‘I’ll want regular reports, but make sure I’m not surrounded by people when you turn up. Ron and Hermione are OK. And don’t tell anyone what you’re doing. Just stick to Malfoy like a couple of wart plasters.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron left the hospital wing first thing on Monday morning, restored to full health by the ministrations of Madam Pomfrey and now able to enjoy the benefits of having been knocked out and poisoned, the best of which was that Hermione was friends with Ron again. Hermione even escorted them down to breakfast, bringing with her the news that Ginny had argued with Dean. The drowsing creature in Harry’s chest suddenly raised its head, sniffing the air hopefully.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What did they row about?’ he asked, trying to sound casual as they turned into a seventh-floor corridor which was deserted but for a very small girl who had been examining a tapestry of trolls in tutus. She looked terrified at the sight of the approaching sixth-years and dropped the heavy brass scales she was carrying.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s all right!’ said Hermione kindly, hurrying forwards to help her. ‘Here …’ She tapped the broken scales with her wand and said, ‘Reparo.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The girl did not say thank you, but remained rooted to the spot as they passed and watched them out of sight; Ron glanced back at her.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I swear they’re getting smaller,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Never mind her,’ said Harry, a little impatiently. ‘What did Ginny and Dean row about, Hermione?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Dean was laughing about McLaggen hitting that Bludger at you,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It must’ve looked funny,’ said Ron reasonably.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It didn’t look funny at all!’ said Hermione hotly. ‘It looked terrible, and if Coote and Peakes hadn’t caught Harry he could have been very badly hurt!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, there was no need for Ginny and Dean to split up over it,’ said Harry, still trying to sound casual. ‘Or are they still together?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, they are – but why are you so interested?’ asked Hermione, giving Harry a sharp look.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I just don’t want my Quidditch team messed up again!’ he said hastily, but Hermione continued to look suspicious, and he was most relieved when a voice behind them called, ‘Harry!’, giving him an excuse to turn his back on her.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, hi, Luna.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I went to the hospital wing to find you,’ said Luna, rummaging in her bag. ‘But they said you’d left …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She thrust what appeared to be a green onion, a large spotted toadstool and a considerable amount of what looked like cat litter into Ron’s hands, finally pulling out a rather grubby scroll of parchment that she handed to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘… I’ve been told to give you this.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: It was a small roll of parchment, which Harry recognised at once as another invitation to a lesson with Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Tonight,’ he told Ron and Hermione, once he had unrolled it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Nice commentary last match!’ said Ron to Luna, as she took back the green onion, the toadstool and the cat litter. Luna smiled vaguely.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re making fun of me, aren’t you?’ she said. ‘Everyone says I was dreadful.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I’m serious!’ said Ron earnestly. ‘I can’t remember enjoying commentary more! What is this, by the way?’ he added, holding the onionlike object up to eye-level.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, it’s a Gurdyroot,’ she said, stuffing the cat litter and the toadstool back into her bag. ‘You can keep it if you like, I’ve got a few of them. They’re really excellent for warding off Gulping Plimpies.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And she walked away, leaving Ron chortling, still clutching the Gurdyroot.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You know, she’s grown on me, Luna,’ he said, as they set off again for the Great Hall. ‘I know she’s insane, but it’s in a good –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He stopped talking very suddenly. Lavender Brown was standing at the foot of the marble staircase looking thunderous.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hi,’ said Ron nervously.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘C’mon,’ Harry muttered to Hermione, and they sped past, though not before they had heard Lavender say, ‘Why didn’t you tell me you were getting out today? And why was she with you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Ron looked both sulky and annoyed when he appeared at breakfast half an hour later, and though he sat with Lavender, Harry did not see them exchange a word all the time they were together. Hermione was acting as though she was quite oblivious to all of this, but once or twice Harry saw an inexplicable smirk cross her face. All that day she seemed to be in a particularly good mood, and that evening in the common room she even consented to look over (in other words, finish writing) Harry’s Herbology essay, something she had been resolutely refusing to do up to that point, because she had known that Harry would then let Ron copy his work.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Thanks a lot, Hermione,’ said Harry, giving her a hasty pat on the back as he checked his watch and saw that it was nearly eight o’clock. ‘Listen, I’ve got to hurry or I’ll be late for Dumbledore …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She did not answer, but merely crossed out a few of his feebler sentences in a weary sort of way. Grinning, Harry hurried out through the portrait hole and off to the Headmaster’s office. The gargoyle leapt aside at the mention of toffee eclairs and Harry took the spiral staircase two steps at a time, knocking on the door just as a clock within chimed eight.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Enter,’ called Dumbledore, but as Harry put out a hand to push the door, it was wrenched open from inside. There stood Professor Trelawney.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Aha!’ she cried, pointing dramatically at Harry as she blinked at him through her magnifying spectacles. ‘So this is the reason I am to be thrown unceremoniously from your office, Dumbledore!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘My dear Sybill,’ said Dumbledore in a slightly exasperated voice, ‘there is no question of throwing you unceremoniously from anywhere, but Harry does have an appointment and I really don’t think there is any more to be said –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Very well,’ said Professor Trelawney, in a deeply wounded voice. ‘If you will not banish the usurping nag, so be it … perhaps I shall find a school where my talents are better appreciated …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She pushed past Harry and disappeared down the spiral staircase; they heard her stumble halfway down and Harry guessed that she had tripped over one of her trailing shawls.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Please close the door and sit down, Harry,’ said Dumbledore, sounding rather tired.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry obeyed, noticing as he took his usual seat in front of Dumbledore’s desk that the Pensieve lay between them once more, as did two more tiny crystal bottles full of swirling memory.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Trelawney still isn’t happy Firenze is teaching, then?’ Harry asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Divination is turning out to be much more trouble than I could have foreseen, never having studied the subject myself. I cannot ask Firenze to return to the Forest, where he is now an outcast, nor can I ask Sybill Trelawney to leave. Between ourselves, she has no idea of the danger she would be in outside the castle. She does not know – and I think it would be unwise to enlighten her – that she made the prophecy about you and Voldemort, you see.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore heaved a deep sigh, then said, ‘But never mind my staff problems. We have much more important matters to discuss. Firstly – have you managed the task I set you at the end of our previous lesson?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ said Harry, brought up short. What with Apparition lessons and Quidditch and Ron being poisoned and getting his skull cracked and his determination to find out what Draco Malfoy was up to, Harry had almost forgotten about the memory Dumbledore had asked him to extract from Professor Slughorn … ‘Well, I asked Professor Slughorn about it at the end of Potions, sir, but, er, he wouldn’t give it to me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was a little silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I see,’ said Dumbledore eventually, peering at Harry over the top of his half-moon spectacles and giving Harry the usual sensation that he was being X-rayed. ‘And you feel that you have exerted your very best efforts in this matter, do you? That you have exercised all of your considerable ingenuity? That you have left no depth of cunning unplumbed in your quest to retrieve the memory?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ Harry stalled, at a loss for what to say next. His single attempt to get hold of the memory suddenly seemed embarrassingly feeble. ‘Well … the day Ron swallowed love potion by mistake I took him to Professor Slughorn. I thought maybe if I got Professor Slughorn in a good enough mood –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And did that work?’ asked Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, no, sir, because Ron got poisoned –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– which, naturally, made you forget all about trying to retrieve the memory; I would have expected nothing else, while your best friend was in danger. Once it became clear that Mr Weasley was going to make a full recovery, however, I would have hoped that you returned to the task I set you. I thought I made it clear to you how very important that memory is. Indeed, I did my best to impress upon you that it is the most crucial memory of all and that we will be wasting our time without it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A hot, prickly feeling of shame spread from the top of Harry’s head all the way down his body. Dumbledore had not raised his voice, he did not even sound angry, but Harry would have preferred him to yell; this cold disappointment was worse than anything.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sir,’ he said, a little desperately, ‘it isn’t that I wasn’t bothered or anything, I’ve just had other – other things …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Other things on your mind,’ Dumbledore finished the sentence for him. ‘I see.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Silence fell between them again, the most uncomfortable silence Harry had ever experienced with Dumbledore; it seemed to go on and on, punctuated only by the little grunting snores of the portrait of Armando Dippet over Dumbledore’s head. Harry felt strangely diminished, as though he had shrunk a little since he had entered the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: When he could stand it no longer he said, ‘Professor Dumbledore, I’m really sorry. I should have done more … I should have realised you wouldn’t have asked me to do it if it wasn’t really important.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you for saying that, Harry,’ said Dumbledore quietly. ‘May I hope, then, that you will give this matter higher priority from now on? There will be little point our meeting after tonight unless we have that memory.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll do it, sir, I’ll get it from him,’ Harry said earnestly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Then we shall say no more about it just now,’ said Dumbledore more kindly, ‘but continue with our story where we left off. You remember where that was?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, sir,’ said Harry quickly. ‘Voldemort killed his father and his grandparents and made it look as though his uncle Morfin did it. Then he went back to Hogwarts and he asked … he asked Professor Slughorn about Horcruxes,’ he mumbled shamefacedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Very good,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Now, you will remember, I hope, that I told you at the very outset of these meetings of ours that we would be entering the realms of guesswork and speculation?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, sir.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Thus far, as I hope you agree, I have shown you reasonably firm sources of fact for my deductions as to what Voldemort did until the age of seventeen?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry nodded.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But now, Harry,’ said Dumbledore, ‘now things become murkier and stranger. If it was difficult to find evidence about the boy Riddle, it has been almost impossible to find anyone prepared to reminisce about the man Voldemort. In fact, I doubt whether there is a soul alive, apart from himself, who could give us a full account of his life since he left Hogwarts. However, I have two last memories that I would like to share with you.’ Dumbledore indicated the two little crystal bottles gleaming beside the Pensieve. ‘I shall then be glad of your opinion as to whether the conclusions I have drawn from them seem likely.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The idea that Dumbledore valued his opinion this highly made Harry feel even more deeply ashamed that he had failed in the task of retrieving the Horcrux memory, and he shifted guiltily in his seat as Dumbledore raised the first of the two bottles to the light and examined it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I hope you are not tired of diving into other people’s memories, for they are curious recollections, these two,’ he said. ‘This first one came from a very old house-elf by the name of Hokey. Before we see what Hokey witnessed, I must quickly recount how Lord Voldemort left Hogwarts.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He reached the seventh year of his schooling with, as you might have expected, top grades in every examination he had taken. All around him, his classmates were deciding which jobs they were to pursue once they had left Hogwarts. Nearly everybody expected spectacular things from Tom Riddle, prefect, Head Boy, winner of the Special Award for Services to the School. I know that several teachers, Professor Slughorn amongst them, suggested that he join the Ministry of Magic, offered to set up appointments, put him in touch with useful contacts. He refused all offers. The next thing the staff knew, Voldemort was working at Borgin and Burkes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘At Borgin and Burkes?’ Harry repeated, stunned.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘At Borgin and Burkes,’ repeated Dumbledore calmly. ‘I think you will see what attractions the place held for him when we have entered Hokey’s memory. But this was not Voldemort’s first choice of job. Hardly anyone knew of it at the time – I was one of the few in whom the then Headmaster confided – but Voldemort first approached Professor Dippet and asked whether he could remain at Hogwarts as a teacher.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He wanted to stay here? Why?’ asked Harry, more amazed still.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I believe he had several reasons, though he confided none of them to Professor Dippet,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Firstly, and very importantly, Voldemort was, I believe, more attached to this school than he has ever been to a person. Hogwarts was where he had been happiest; the first and only place he had felt at home.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry felt slightly uncomfortable at these words, for this was exactly how he felt about Hogwarts, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Secondly, the castle is a stronghold of ancient magic. Undoubtedly Voldemort had penetrated many more of its secrets than most of the students who pass through the place, but he may have felt that there were still mysteries to unravel, stores of magic to tap.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And thirdly, as a teacher, he would have had great power and influence over young witches and wizards. Perhaps he had gained the idea from Professor Slughorn, the teacher with whom he was on best terms, who had demonstrated how influential a role a teacher can play. I do not imagine for an instant that Voldemort envisaged spending the rest of his life at Hogwarts, but I do think that he saw it as a useful recruiting ground, and a place where he might begin to build himself an army.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But he didn’t get the job, sir?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No, he did not. Professor Dippet told him that he was too young at eighteen, but invited him to reapply in a few years, if he still wished to teach.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘How did you feel about that, sir?’ asked Harry hesitantly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Deeply uneasy,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I had advised Armando against the appointment – I did not give the reasons I have given you, for Professor Dippet was very fond of Voldemort and convinced of his honesty – but I did not want Lord Voldemort back at this school, and especially not in a position of power.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Which job did he want, sir? What subject did he want to teach?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Somehow, Harry knew the answer even before Dumbledore gave it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Defence Against the Dark Arts. It was being taught at the time by an old Professor by the name of Galatea Merrythought, who had been at Hogwarts for nearly fifty years.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So Voldemort went off to Borgin and Burkes, and all the staff who had admired him said what a waste it was, a brilliant young wizard like that, working in a shop. However, Voldemort was no mere assistant. Polite and handsome and clever, he was soon given particular jobs of the type that only exist in a place like Borgin and Burkes, which specialises, as you know, Harry, in objects with unusual and powerful properties. Voldemort was sent to persuade people to part with their treasures for sale by the partners, and he was, by all accounts, unusually gifted at doing this.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll bet he was,’ said Harry, unable to contain himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, quite,’ said Dumbledore, with a faint smile. ‘And now it is time to hear from Hokey the house-elf, who worked for a very old, very rich witch by the name of Hepzibah Smith.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore tapped a bottle with his wand, the cork flew out and he tipped the swirling memory into the Pensieve, saying as he did so, ‘After you, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry got to his feet and bent once more over the rippling silver contents of the stone basin until his face touched them. He tumbled through dark nothingness and landed in a sitting room in front of an immensely fat old lady wearing an elaborate ginger wig and a brilliant pink set of robes that flowed all around her, giving her the look of a melting iced cake. She was looking into a small jewelled mirror and dabbing rouge on to her already scarlet cheeks with a large powder puff, while the tiniest and oldest house-elf Harry had ever seen laced her fleshy feet into tight satin slippers.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hurry up, Hokey!’ said Hepzibah imperiously. ‘He said he’d come at four, it’s only a couple of minutes to and he’s never been late yet!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She tucked away her powder puff as the house-elf straightened up. The top of the elf ’s head barely reached the seat of Hepzibah’s chair and her papery skin hung off her frame just like the crisp linen sheet she wore draped like a toga.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘How do I look?’ said Hepzibah, turning her head to admire the various angles of her face in the mirror.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Lovely, madam,’ squeaked Hokey.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry could only assume that it was down in Hokey’s contract that she must lie through her teeth when asked this question, because Hepzibah Smith looked a long way from lovely in his opinion.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: A tinkling doorbell rang and both mistress and elf jumped.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Quick, quick, he’s here, Hokey!’ cried Hepzibah and the elf scurried out of the room, which was so crammed with objects that it was difficult to see how anybody could navigate their way across it without knocking over at least a dozen things: there were cabinets full of little lacquered boxes, cases full of gold-embossed books, shelves of orbs and celestial globes and many flourishing pot plants in brass containers: in fact, the room looked like a cross between a magical antique shop and a conservatory.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The house-elf returned within minutes, followed by a tall young man Harry had no difficulty whatsoever in recognising as Voldemort. He was plainly dressed in a black suit; his hair was a little longer than it had been at school and his cheeks were hollowed, but all of this suited him: he looked more handsome than ever. He picked his way through the cramped room with an air that showed he had visited many times before and bowed low over Hepzibah’s fat little hand, brushing it with his lips.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I brought you flowers,’ he said quietly, producing a bunch of roses from nowhere.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You naughty boy, you shouldn’t have!’ squealed old Hepzibah, though Harry noticed that she had an empty vase standing ready on the nearest little table. ‘You do spoil this old lady, Tom … sit down, sit down … where’s Hokey … ah …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The house-elf had come dashing back into the room carrying a tray of little cakes, which she set at her mistress’s elbow.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Help yourself, Tom,’ said Hepzibah, ‘I know how you love my cakes. Now, how are you? You look pale. They overwork you at that shop, I’ve said it a hundred times …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Voldemort smiled mechanically and Hepzibah simpered.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, what’s your excuse for visiting this time?’ she asked, batting her lashes.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Burke would like to make an improved offer for the goblin-made armour,’ said Voldemort. ‘Five hundred Galleons, he feels it is a more than fair –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, now, not so fast, or I’ll think you’re only here for my trinkets!’ pouted Hepzibah.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I am ordered here because of them,’ said Voldemort quietly. ‘I am only a poor assistant, madam, who must do as he is told. Mr Burke wishes me to enquire –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Mr Burke, phooey!’ said Hepzibah, waving a little hand. ‘I’ve something to show you that I’ve never shown Mr Burke! Can you keep a secret, Tom? Will you promise you won’t tell Mr Burke I’ve got it? He’d never let me rest if he knew I’d shown it to you, and I’m not selling, not to Burke, not to anyone! But you, Tom, you’ll appreciate it for its history, not how many Galleons you can get for it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’d be glad to see anything Miss Hepzibah shows me,’ said Voldemort quietly, and Hepzibah gave another girlish giggle.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I had Hokey bring it out for me … Hokey, where are you? I want to show Mr Riddle our finest treasure … in fact, bring both, while you’re at it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Here, madam,’ squeaked the house-elf, and Harry saw two leather boxes, one on top of the other, moving across the room as if of their own volition, though he knew the tiny elf was holding them over her head as she wended her way between tables, pouffes and footstools.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now,’ said Hepzibah happily, taking the boxes from the elf, laying them in her lap and preparing to open the topmost one, ‘I think you’ll like this, Tom … oh, if my family knew I was showing you … they can’t wait to get their hands on this!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She opened the lid. Harry edged forwards a little to get a better view and saw what looked like a small golden cup with two finely wrought handles.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I wonder whether you know what it is, Tom? Pick it up, have a good look!’ whispered Hepzibah, and Voldemort stretched out a long-fingered hand and lifted the cup by one handle out of its snug silken wrappings. Harry thought he saw a red gleam in his dark eyes. His greedy expression was curiously mirrored on Hepzibah’s face, except that her tiny eyes were fixed upon Voldemort’s handsome features.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘A badger,’ murmured Voldemort, examining the engraving upon the cup. ‘Then this was …?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Helga Hufflepuff’s, as you very well know, you clever boy!’ said Hepzibah, leaning forwards with a loud creaking of corsets and actually pinching his hollow cheek. ‘Didn’t I tell you I was distantly descended? This has been handed down in the family for years and years. Lovely, isn’t it? And all sorts of powers it’s supposed to possess, too, but I haven’t tested them thoroughly, I just keep it nice and safe in here …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She hooked the cup back off Voldemort’s long forefinger and restored it gently to its box, too intent upon settling it carefully back into position to notice the shadow that crossed Voldemort’s face as the cup was taken away.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now then,’ said Hepzibah happily, ‘where’s Hokey? Oh yes, there you are – take that away now, Hokey –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The elf obediently took the boxed cup, and Hepzibah turned her attention to the much flatter box in her lap.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I think you’ll like this even more, Tom,’ she whispered. ‘Lean in a little, dear boy, so you can see … of course, Burke knows I’ve got this one, I bought it from him, and I daresay he’d love to get it back when I’m gone …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She slid back the fine, filigree clasp and flipped open the box. There upon the smooth crimson velvet lay a heavy golden locket.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Voldemort reached out his hand without invitation this time and held it up to the light, staring at it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Slytherin’s mark,’ he said quietly, as the light played upon an ornate, serpentine S.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s right!’ said Hepzibah, delighted, apparently, at the sight of Voldemort gazing at her locket, transfixed. ‘I had to pay an arm and a leg for it, but I couldn’t let it pass, not a real treasure like that, had to have it for my collection. Burke bought it, apparently, from a ragged-looking woman who seemed to have stolen it, but had no idea of its true value –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was no mistaking it this time: Voldemort’s eyes flashed scarlet at her words and Harry saw his knuckles whiten on the locket’s chain.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– I daresay Burke paid her a pittance, but there you are … pretty, isn’t it? And again, all kinds of powers attributed to it, though I just keep it nice and safe …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She reached out to take the locket back. For a moment Harry thought Voldemort was not going to let go of it, but then it had slid through his fingers and was back on its red velvet cushion.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So there you are, Tom, dear, and I hope you enjoyed that!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: She looked him full in the face and, for the first time, Harry saw her foolish smile falter.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you all right, dear?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes,’ said Voldemort quietly. ‘Yes, I’m very well …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought – but a trick of the light, I suppose –’ said Hepzibah, looking unnerved, and Harry guessed that she, too, had seen the momentary red gleam in Voldemort’s eyes. ‘Here, Hokey, take these away and lock them up again … the usual enchantments …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Time to leave, Harry,’ said Dumbledore quietly, and as the little elf bobbed away bearing the boxes, Dumbledore grasped Harry once again above the elbow and together they rose up through oblivion and back to Dumbledore’s office.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hepzibah Smith died two days after that little scene,’ said Dumbledore, resuming his seat and indicating that Harry should do the same. ‘Hokey the house-elf was convicted by the Ministry of poisoning her mistress’s evening cocoa by accident.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No way!’ said Harry angrily.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I see we are of one mind,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Certainly, there are many similarities between this death and that of the Riddles. In both cases, somebody else took the blame, someone who had a clear memory of having caused the death –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hokey confessed?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘She remembered putting something in her mistress’s cocoa that turned out not to be sugar, but a lethal and little-known poison,’ said Dumbledore. ‘It was concluded that she had not meant to do it, but being old and confused –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort modified her memory, just like he did with Morfin!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, that is my conclusion, too,’ said Dumbledore. ‘And, just as with Morfin, the Ministry was predisposed to suspect Hokey –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– because she was a house-elf,’ said Harry. He had rarely felt more in sympathy with the society Hermione had set up, S.P.E.W.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Precisely,’ said Dumbledore. ‘She was old, she admitted to having tampered with the drink and nobody at the Ministry bothered to enquire further. As in the case of Morfin, by the time I traced her and managed to extract this memory, her life was almost over – but her memory, of course, proves nothing except that Voldemort knew of the existence of the cup and the locket.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘By the time Hokey was convicted, Hepzibah’s family had realised that two of her greatest treasures were missing. It took them a while to be sure of this, for she had many hiding places, having always guarded her collection most jealously. But before they were sure beyond doubt that the cup and the locket were both gone, the assistant who had worked at Borgin and Burkes, the young man who had visited Hepzibah so regularly and charmed her so well, had resigned his post and vanished. His superiors had no idea where he had gone; they were as surprised as anyone at his disappearance. And that was the last that was seen or heard of Tom Riddle for a very long time.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Now,’ said Dumbledore, ‘if you don’t mind, Harry, I want to pause once more to draw your attention to certain points of our story. Voldemort had committed another murder; whether it was his first since he killed the Riddles, I do not know, but I think it was. This time, as you will have seen, he killed not for revenge, but for gain. He wanted the two fabulous trophies that poor, besotted old woman showed him. Just as he had once robbed the other children at his orphanage, just as he had stolen his uncle Morfin’s ring, so he ran off now with Hepzibah’s cup and locket.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But,’ said Harry, frowning, ‘it seems mad … risking everything, throwing away his job, just for those …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Mad to you, perhaps, but not to Voldemort,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I hope you will understand in due course exactly what those objects meant to him, Harry, but you must admit that it is not difficult to imagine that he saw the locket, at least, as rightfully his.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The locket maybe,’ said Harry, ‘but why take the cup as well?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It had belonged to another of Hogwarts’ founders,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I think he still felt a great pull towards the school and that he could not resist an object so steeped in Hogwarts’ history. There were other reasons, I think … I hope to be able to demonstrate them to you, in due course.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And now for the very last recollection I have to show you, at least until you manage to retrieve Professor Slughorn’s memory for us. Ten years separate Hokey’s memory and this one, ten years during which we can only guess at what Lord Voldemort was doing …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry got to his feet once more as Dumbledore emptied the last memory into the Pensieve.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Whose memory is it?’ he asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Mine,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And Harry dived after Dumbledore through the shifting silver mass, landing in the very office he had just left. There was Fawkes, slumbering happily on his perch, and there, behind the desk, was Dumbledore, who looked very similar to the Dumbledore standing beside Harry, though both hands were whole and undamaged and his face was, perhaps, a little less lined. The one difference between the present-day office and this one was that it was snowing in the past; bluish flecks were drifting past the window in the dark and building up on the outside ledge.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The younger Dumbledore seemed to be waiting for something, and sure enough, moments after their arrival, there was a knock on the door and he said, ‘Enter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry let out a hastily stifled gasp. Voldemort had entered the room. His features were not those Harry had seen emerge from the great stone cauldron almost two years before; they were not as snakelike, the eyes were not yet scarlet, the face not yet masklike, and yet he was no longer handsome Tom Riddle. It was as though his features had been burned and blurred; they were waxy and oddly distorted, and the whites of the eyes now had a permanently bloody look, though the pupils were not yet the slits that Harry knew they would become. He was wearing a long black cloak and his face was as pale as the snow glistening on his shoulders.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The Dumbledore behind the desk showed no sign of surprise. Evidently this visit had been made by appointment.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good evening, Tom,’ said Dumbledore easily. ‘Won’t you sit down?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you,’ said Voldemort, and he took the seat to which Dumbledore had gestured – the very seat, by the looks of it, that Harry had just vacated in the present. ‘I heard that you had become Headmaster,’ he said, and his voice was slightly higher and colder than it had been. ‘A worthy choice.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I am glad you approve,’ said Dumbledore, smiling. ‘May I offer you a drink?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That would be welcome,’ said Voldemort. ‘I have come a long way.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore stood and swept over to the cabinet where he now kept the Pensieve, but which then was full of bottles. Having handed Voldemort a goblet of wine and poured one for himself, he returned to the seat behind his desk.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘So, Tom … to what do I owe the pleasure?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Voldemort did not answer at once, but merely sipped his wine.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘They do not call me “Tom” any more,’ he said. ‘These days, I am known as –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I know what you are known as,’ said Dumbledore, smiling pleasantly. ‘But to me, I’m afraid, you will always be Tom Riddle. It is one of the irritating things about old teachers, I am afraid, that they never quite forget their charges’ youthful beginnings.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He raised his glass as though toasting Voldemort, whose face remained expressionless. Nevertheless, Harry felt the atmosphere in the room change subtly: Dumbledore’s refusal to use Voldemort’s chosen name was a refusal to allow Voldemort to dictate the terms of the meeting, and Harry could tell that Voldemort took it as such.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I am surprised you have remained here so long,’ said Voldemort after a short pause. ‘I always wondered why a wizard such as yourself never wished to leave school.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Dumbledore, still smiling, ‘to a wizard such as myself, there can be nothing more important than passing on ancient skills, helping hone young minds. If I remember correctly, you once saw the attraction of teaching, too.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I see it still,’ said Voldemort. ‘I merely wondered why you – who is so often asked for advice by the Ministry, and who has twice, I think, been offered the post of Minister –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Three times at the last count, actually,’ said Dumbledore. ‘But the Ministry never attracted me as a career. Again, something we have in common, I think.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Voldemort inclined his head, unsmiling, and took another sip of wine. Dumbledore did not break the silence that stretched between them now, but waited, with a look of pleasant expectancy, for Voldemort to talk first.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I have returned,’ he said, after a little while, ‘later, perhaps, than Professor Dippet expected … but I have returned, nevertheless, to request again what he once told me I was too young to have. I have come to you to ask that you permit me to return to this castle, to teach. I think you must know that I have seen and done much since I left this place. I could show and tell your students things they can gain from no other wizard.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore considered Voldemort over the top of his own goblet for a while before speaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I certainly do know that you have seen and done much since leaving us,’ he said quietly. ‘Rumours of your doings have reached your old school, Tom. I should be sorry to believe half of them.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Voldemort’s expression remained impassive as he said, ‘Greatness inspires envy, envy engenders spite, spite spawns lies. You must know this, Dumbledore.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You call it “greatness”, what you have been doing, do you?’ asked Dumbledore delicately.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Certainly,’ said Voldemort, and his eyes seemed to burn red. ‘I have experimented; I have pushed the boundaries of magic further, perhaps, than they have ever been pushed –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Of some kinds of magic,’ Dumbledore corrected him quietly. ‘Of some. Of others, you remain … forgive me … woefully ignorant.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: For the first time, Voldemort smiled. It was a taut leer, an evil thing, more threatening than a look of rage.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘The old argument,’ he said softly. ‘But nothing I have seen in the world has supported your famous pronouncements that love is more powerful than my kind of magic, Dumbledore.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Perhaps you have been looking in the wrong places,’ suggested Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, then, what better place to start my fresh researches than here, at Hogwarts?’ said Voldemort. ‘Will you let me return? Will you let me share my knowledge with your students? I place myself and my talents at your disposal. I am yours to command.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore raised his eyebrows.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What does it feel like?’ whispered Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He got to his feet smiling, brimful of confidence.

text_content: ‘What?’ said Ron and Hermione together, looking aghast.

text_content: ‘No, Harry – you’ve got to go and see Slughorn, remember?’ said Hermione.

text_content: ‘You’ve got a good feeling about burying a giant spider?’ asked Ron, looking stunned.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

text_content: Getting through the portrait hole was simple; as he approached it, Ginny and Dean came through it and Harry was able to slip between them. As he did so, he brushed accidentally against Ginny.

text_content: ‘… I do thank you for taking the time, Pomona,’ Slughorn was saying courteously. ‘Most authorities agree that they are at their most efficacious if picked at twilight.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Professor Sprout headed off into the gathering darkness in the direction of her greenhouses and Slughorn directed his steps to the spot where Harry stood, invisible.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good evening, Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

text_content: ‘Well, I can’t promise that,’ he said gruffly. ‘But I know that Dumbledore trusts Hagrid to the hilt, so I’m sure he can’t be up to anything very dreadful …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘… seems an awful waste not to collect it … might get a hundred Galleons a pint … to be frank, my salary is not large …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)

text_content: ‘I use it fer bindin’ on bandages an’ stuff if a creature gets injured,’ said Hagrid, shrugging. ‘It’s dead useful … very strong, see.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn took another deep draught from his mug, his eyes moving carefully around the cabin now, looking, Harry knew, for more treasures that he might be able to convert into a plentiful supply of oak-matured mead, crystallised pineapple and velvet smoking jackets. He refilled Hagrid’s mug and his own, and questioned him about the creatures that lived in the Forest these days and how Hagrid was able to look after them all. Hagrid, becoming expansive under the influence of the drink and Slughorn’s flattering interest, stopped mopping his eyes and entered happily into a long explanation of Bowtruckle husbandry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: The Felix Felicis gave Harry a little nudge at this point and he noticed that the supply of drink that Slughorn had brought was running out fast. Harry had not yet managed to bring off the Refilling Charm without saying the incantation aloud, but the idea that he might not be able to do it tonight was laughable: indeed, Harry grinned to himself as, unnoticed by either Hagrid or Slughorn (now swapping tales of the illegal trade in dragon eggs), he pointed his wand under the table at the emptying bottles and they immediately began to refill.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: After an hour or so, Hagrid and Slughorn began making extravagant toasts: to Hogwarts, to Dumbledore, to elf-made wine and to –

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry Potter!’ bellowed Hagrid, slopping some of his fourteenth bucket of wine down his chin as he drained it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, indeed,’ cried Slughorn a little thickly, ‘Parry Otter, the Chosen Boy Who – well – something of that sort,’ he mumbled, and drained his mug, too.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Not long after this, Hagrid became tearful again and pressed the whole unicorn tail upon Slughorn, who pocketed it with cries of, ‘To friendship! To generosity! To ten Galleons a hair!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And for a while after that, Hagrid and Slughorn were sitting side by side, arms around each other, singing a slow sad song about a dying wizard called Odo.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Aaargh, the good die young,’ muttered Hagrid, slumping low on to the table, a little cross-eyed, while Slughorn continued to warble the refrain. ‘Me dad was no age ter go … nor were your mum an’ dad, Harry …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Great fat tears oozed out of the corners of Hagrid’s crinkled eyes again; he grasped Harry’s arm and shook it.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘… bes’ wiz and witchard o’ their age I never knew … terrible thing … terrible thing …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn sang plaintively:

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And Odo the hero, they bore him back home To the place that he’d known as a lad, They laid him to rest with his hat inside out And his wand snapped in two, which was sad.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘… terrible,’ Hagrid grunted and his great shaggy head rolled sideways on to his arms and he fell asleep, snoring deeply.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry,’ said Slughorn with a hiccough. ‘Can’t carry a tune to save my life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid wasn’t talking about your singing,’ said Harry quietly. ‘He was talking about my mum and dad dying.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh,’ said Slughorn, repressing a large belch. ‘Oh, dear. Yes, that was – was terrible indeed. Terrible … terrible …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He looked quite at a loss for what to say, and resorted to refilling their mugs.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t – don’t suppose you remember it, Harry?’ he asked awkwardly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘No – well, I was only one when they died,’ said Harry, his eyes on the flame of the candle flickering in Hagrid’s heavy snores. ‘But I’ve found out pretty much what happened since. My dad died first. Did you know that?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I – I didn’t,’ said Slughorn in a hushed voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah … Voldemort murdered him and then stepped over his body towards my mum,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn gave a great shudder, but he did not seem able to tear his horrified gaze away from Harry’s face.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He told her to get out of the way,’ said Harry remorselessly. ‘He told me she needn’t have died. He only wanted me. She could have run.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh dear,’ breathed Slughorn. ‘She could have … she needn’t … that’s awful …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It is, isn’t it?’ said Harry, in a voice barely more than a whisper. ‘But she didn’t move. Dad was already dead, but she didn’t want me to go too. She tried to plead with Voldemort … but he just laughed …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s enough!’ said Slughorn suddenly, raising a shaking hand. ‘Really, my dear boy, enough … I’m an old man … I don’t need to hear … I don’t want to hear …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I forgot,’ lied Harry, Felix Felicis leading him on. ‘You liked her, didn’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Liked her?’ said Slughorn, his eyes brimming with tears once more. ‘I don’t imagine anyone who met her wouldn’t have liked her … very brave … very funny … it was the most horrible thing …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But you won’t help her son,’ said Harry. ‘She gave me her life, but you won’t give me a memory.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Hagrid’s rumbling snores filled the cabin. Harry looked steadily into Slughorn’s tear-filled eyes. The Potions master seemed unable to look away.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t say that,’ he whispered. ‘It isn’t a question … if it were to help you, of course … but no purpose can be served …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘It can,’ said Harry clearly. ‘Dumbledore needs information. I need information.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: He knew he was safe: Felix was telling him that Slughorn would remember nothing of this in the morning. Looking Slughorn straight in the eye, Harry leant forwards a little.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I am the Chosen One. I have to kill him. I need that memory.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn turned paler than ever; his shiny forehead gleamed with sweat.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You are the Chosen One?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course I am,’ said Harry calmly.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘But then … my dear boy … you’re asking a great deal … you’re asking me, in fact, to aid you in your attempt to destroy –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t want to get rid of the wizard who killed Lily Evans?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, Harry, of course I do, but –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re scared he’ll find out you helped me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn said nothing; he looked terrified.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Be brave like my mother, Professor …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Slughorn raised a pudgy hand and pressed his shaking fingers to his mouth; he looked for a moment like an enormously overgrown baby.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I am not proud …’ he whispered through his fingers. ‘I am ashamed of what – of what that memory shows … I think I may have done great damage that day …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’d cancel out anything you did by giving me the memory,’ said Harry. ‘It would be a very brave and noble thing to do.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Hagrid twitched in his sleep and snored on. Slughorn and Harry stared at each other over the guttering candle. There was a long, long silence, but Felix Felicis told Harry not to break it, to wait.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Then, very slowly, Slughorn put his hand in his pocket and pulled out his wand. He put his other hand inside his cloak and took out a small, empty bottle. Still looking into Harry’s eyes, Slughorn touched the tip of his wand to his temple and withdrew it, so that a long, silver thread of memory came away too, clinging to the wand-tip. Longer and longer the memory stretched until it broke and swung, silvery bright, from the wand. Slughorn lowered it into the bottle where it coiled, then spread, swirling like gas. He corked the bottle with a trembling hand and then passed it across the table to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you very much, Professor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re a good boy,’ said Professor Slughorn, tears trickling down his fat cheeks into his walrus moustache. ‘And you’ve got her eyes … just don’t think too badly of me once you’ve seen it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: And he, too, put his head on his arms, gave a deep sigh, and fell asleep.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry could feel the Felix Felicis wearing off as he crept back into the castle. The front door had remained unlocked for him, but on the third floor he met Peeves and only narrowly avoided detection by diving sideways through one of his short cuts. By the time he got up to the portrait of the Fat Lady and pulled off his Invisibility Cloak, he was not surprised to find her in a most unhelpful mood.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What sort of time do you call this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m really sorry – I had to go out for something important –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, the password changed at midnight, so you’ll just have to sleep in the corridor, won’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re joking!’ said Harry. ‘Why did it have to change at midnight?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s the way it is,’ said the Fat Lady. ‘If you’re angry, go and take it up with the Headmaster, he’s the one who’s tightened security.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Fantastic,’ said Harry bitterly, looking around at the hard floor. ‘Really brilliant. Yeah, I would go and take it up with Dumbledore if he was here, because he’s the one who wanted me to –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘He is here,’ said a voice behind Harry. ‘Professor Dumbledore returned to the school an hour ago.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Nearly Headless Nick was gliding towards Harry, his head wobbling as usual upon his ruff.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘I had it from the Bloody Baron, who saw him arrive,’ said Nick. ‘He appeared, according to the Baron, to be in good spirits, though a little tired, of course.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Where is he?’ said Harry, his heart leaping.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, groaning and clanking up on the Astronomy Tower, it’s a favourite pastime of his –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Not the Bloody Baron, Dumbledore!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh – in his office,’ said Nick. ‘I believe, from what the Baron said, that he had business to attend to before turning in –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, he has,’ said Harry, excitement blazing in his chest at the prospect of telling Dumbledore he had secured the memory. He wheeled about and sprinted off again, ignoring the Fat Lady who was calling after him.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Come back! All right, I lied! I was annoyed you woke me up! The password’s still “tapeworm”!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: But Harry was already hurtling back along the corridor, and, within minutes, he was saying ‘toffee eclairs’ to Dumbledore’s gargoyle, which leapt aside, permitting Harry entrance on to the spiral staircase.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Enter,’ said Dumbledore when Harry knocked. He sounded exhausted.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry pushed open the door. There was Dumbledore’s office, looking the same as ever, but with black, star-strewn skies beyond the windows.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Good gracious, Harry,’ said Dumbledore in surprise. ‘To what do I owe this very late pleasure?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Sir – I’ve got it. I’ve got the memory from Slughorn.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry pulled out the tiny glass bottle and showed it to Dumbledore. For a moment or two, the Headmaster looked stunned. Then his face split in a wide smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, this is spectacular news! Very well done indeed! I knew you could do it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: All thought of the lateness of the hour apparently forgotten, he hurried around his desk, took the bottle with Slughorn’s memory in his uninjured hand and strode over to the cabinet where he kept the Pensieve.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘And now,’ said Dumbledore, placing the stone basin upon his desk and emptying the contents of the bottle into it, ‘now, at last, we shall see. Harry, quickly …’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Harry bowed obediently over the Pensieve and felt his feet leave the office floor … once again he fell through darkness and landed in Horace Slughorn’s office many years before.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: There was the much younger Horace Slughorn, with his thick, shiny, straw-coloured hair and his gingery-blond moustache, sitting again in the comfortable winged armchair in his office, his feet resting upon a velvet pouffe, a small glass of wine in one hand, the other rummaging in a box of crystallised pineapple. And there were the half a dozen teenage boys sitting around Slughorn with Tom Riddle in the midst of them, Marvolo’s gold and black ring gleaming on his finger.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore landed beside Harry just as Riddle asked, ‘Sir, is it true that Professor Merrythought is retiring?’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘Tom, Tom, if I knew I couldn’t tell you,’ said Slughorn, wagging his finger reprovingly at Riddle, though winking at the same time. ‘I must say, I’d like to know where you get your information, boy; more knowledgeable than half the staff, you are.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Riddle smiled; the other boys laughed and cast him admiring looks.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘What with your uncanny ability to know things you shouldn’t, and your careful flattery of the people who matter – thank you for the pineapple, by the way, you’re quite right, it is my favourite –’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Several of the boys tittered again.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: ‘– I confidently expect you to rise to Minister for Magic within twenty years. Fifteen, if you keep sending me pineapple. I have excellent contacts at the Ministry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
text_content: Tom Riddle merely smiled as the others laughed again. Harry noticed that he was by no means the eldest of the group of boys, but that they all seemed to look to him as their leader.

book: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (UK)
