book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Uncle Vernon said nothing, but continued to pace up and down. Outside, the sun hung low over the privet hedges. The next-door neighbour’s lawnmower stalled again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought there was a Ministry of Magic?’ asked Vernon Dursley abruptly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There is,’ said Harry, surprised.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, then, why can’t they protect us? It seems to me that, as innocent victims, guilty of nothing more than harbouring a marked man, we ought to qualify for government protection!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry laughed; he could not help himself. It was so very typical of his uncle to put his hopes in the establishment, even within this world that he despised and mistrusted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You heard what Mr Weasley and Kingsley said,’ Harry replied. ‘We think the Ministry has been infiltrated.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Uncle Vernon strode to the fireplace and back, breathing so heavily that his great, black moustache rippled, his face still purple with concentration.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right,’ he said, stopping in front of Harry yet again. ‘All right, let’s say, for the sake of argument, we accept this protection. I still don’t see why we can’t have that Kingsley bloke.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry managed not to roll his eyes, but with difficulty. This question had also been addressed half a dozen times.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘As I’ve told you,’ he said, through gritted teeth, ‘Kingsley is protecting the Mug— I mean, your Prime Minister.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Exactly - he’s the best!’ said Uncle Vernon, pointing at the blank television screen. The Dursleys had spotted Kingsley on the news, walking along discreetly behind the Muggle Prime Minister as he visited a hospital. This, and the fact that Kingsley had mastered the knack of dressing like a Muggle, not to mention a certain reassuring something in his slow, deep voice, had caused the Dursleys to take to Kingsley in a way that they had certainly not done with any other wizard, although it was true that they had never seen him with his earring in.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, he’s taken,’ said Harry. ‘But Hestia Jones and Dedalus Diggle are more than up to the job -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If we’d even seen CVs …’ began Uncle Vernon, but Harry lost patience. Getting to his feet, he advanced on his uncle, now pointing at the TV set himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘These accidents aren’t accidents - the crashes and explosions and derailments and whatever else has happened since we last watched the news. People are disappearing and dying and he’s behind it - Voldemort. I’ve told you this over and over again, he kills Muggles for fun. Even the fogs - they’re caused by Dementors, and if you can’t remember what they are, ask your son!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dudley’s hands jerked upwards to cover his mouth. With his parents’ and Harry’s eyes upon him, he slowly lowered them again and asked, ‘There are … more of them?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘More?’ laughed Harry. ‘More than the two that attacked us, you mean? Of course there are, there are hundreds, maybe thousands by this time, seeing as they feed off fear and despair -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right, all right,’ blustered Vernon Dursley. ‘You’ve made your point -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I hope so,’ said Harry, ‘because once I’m seventeen, all of them - Death Eaters, Dementors, maybe even Inferi, which means dead bodies enchanted by a Dark wizard - will be able to find you and will certainly attack you. And if you remember the last time you tried to outrun wizards, I think you’ll agree you need help.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a brief silence in which the distant echo of Hagrid smashing down a wooden front door seemed to reverberate through the intervening years. Aunt Petunia was looking at Uncle Vernon; Dudley was staring at Harry. Finally Uncle Vernon blurted out, ‘But what about my work? What about Dudley’s school? I don’t suppose those things matter to a bunch of layabout wizards -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t you understand?’ shouted Harry. ‘They will torture and kill you like they did my parents!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dad,’ said Dudley in a loud voice, ‘Dad - I’m going with these Order people.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dudley,’ said Harry, ‘for the first time in your life, you’re talking sense.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He knew that the battle was won. If Dudley was frightened enough to accept the Order’s help, his parents would accompany him: there could be no question of being separated from their Diddykins. Harry glanced at the carriage clock on the mantelpiece.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They’ll be here in about five minutes,’ he said, and when none of the Dursleys replied, he left the room. The prospect of parting - probably forever - from his aunt, uncle and cousin was one that he was able to contemplate quite cheerfully, but there was nevertheless a certain awkwardness in the air. What did you say to one another at the end of sixteen years’ solid dislike?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Back in his bedroom, Harry fiddled aimlessly with his rucksack, then poked a couple of owl nuts through the bars of Hedwig’s cage. They fell with dull thuds to the bottom, where she ignored them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re leaving soon, really soon,’ Harry told her. ‘And then you’ll be able to fly again.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The doorbell rang. Harry hesitated, then headed back out of his room and downstairs: it was too much to expect Hestia and Dedalus to cope with the Dursleys on their own.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry Potter!’ squeaked an excited voice, the moment Harry had opened the door; a small man in a mauve top hat was sweeping him a deep bow. ‘An honour, as ever!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thanks, Dedalus,’ said Harry, bestowing a small and embarrassed smile upon the dark-haired Hestia. ‘It’s really good of you to do this … they’re through here, my aunt and uncle and cousin …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good day to you, Harry Potter’s relatives!’ said Dedalus happily, striding into the living room. The Dursleys did not look at all happy to be addressed thus; Harry half expected another change of mind. Dudley shrank nearer to his mother at the sight of the witch and wizard.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I see you are packed and ready. Excellent! The plan, as Harry has told you, is a simple one,’ said Dedalus, pulling an immense pocket watch out of his waistcoat and examining it. ‘We shall be leaving before Harry does. Due to the danger of using magic in your house - Harry being still under-age, it could provide the Ministry with an excuse to arrest him - we shall be driving, say ten miles or so, before Disapparating to the safe location we have picked out for you. You know how to drive, I take it?’ he asked Uncle Vernon politely.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Know how to -? Of course I ruddy well know how to drive!’ spluttered Uncle Vernon.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Very clever of you, sir, very clever, I personally would be utterly bamboozled by all those buttons and knobs,’ said Dedalus. He was clearly under the impression that he was flattering Vernon Dursley, who was visibly losing confidence in the plan with every word Dedalus spoke.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Can’t even drive,’ he muttered under his breath, his moustache rippling indignantly, but fortunately neither Dedalus nor Hestia seemed to hear him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You, Harry,’ Dedalus continued, ‘will wait here for your guard. There has been a little change in the arrangements -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What d’you mean?’ said Harry at once. ‘I thought Mad-Eye was going to come and take me by Side-Along-Apparition?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Can’t do it,’ said Hestia tersely. ‘Mad-Eye will explain.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The Dursleys, who had listened to all of this with looks of utter incomprehension on their faces, jumped as a loud voice screeched: ‘Hurry up!’ Harry looked all around the room before realising that the voice had issued from Dedalus’s pocket watch.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Quite right, we’re operating to a very tight schedule,’ said Dedalus, nodding at his watch and tucking it back into his waistcoat. ‘We are attempting to time your departure from the house with your family’s Disapparition, Harry; thus, the charm breaks at the moment you all head for safety.’ He turned to the Dursleys. ‘Well, are we all packed and ready to go?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: None of them answered him: Uncle Vernon was still staring, appalled, at the bulge in Dedalus’s waistcoat pocket.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Perhaps we should wait outside in the hall, Dedalus,’ murmured Hestia: she clearly felt that it would be tactless for them to remain in the room while Harry and the Dursleys exchanged loving, possibly tearful farewells.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s no need,’ Harry muttered, but Uncle Vernon made any further explanation unnecessary by saying loudly, ‘Well, this is goodbye, then, boy.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He swung his right arm upwards to shake Harry’s hand, but at the last moment seemed unable to face it, and merely closed his fist and began swinging it backwards and forwards like a metronome.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ready, Diddy?’ asked Aunt Petunia, fussily checking the clasp of her handbag so as to avoid looking at Harry altogether.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dudley did not answer, but stood there with his mouth slightly ajar, reminding Harry a little of the giant, Grawp.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Come along, then,’ said Uncle Vernon.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He had already reached the living-room door when Dudley mumbled, ‘I don’t understand.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What don’t you understand, Popkin?’ asked Aunt Petunia, looking up at her son.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dudley raised a large, ham-like hand to point at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why isn’t he coming with us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia froze where they stood, staring at Dudley as though he had just expressed a desire to become a ballerina.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Uncle Vernon loudly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why isn’t he coming too?’ asked Dudley.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, he - he doesn’t want to,’ said Uncle Vernon, turning to glare at Harry and adding, ‘you don’t want to, do you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not in the slightest,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There you are,’ Uncle Vernon told Dudley. ‘Now come on, we’re off.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He marched out of the room: they heard the front door open, but Dudley did not move and after a few faltering steps Aunt Petunia stopped too.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What now?’ barked Uncle Vernon, reappearing in the doorway.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It seemed that Dudley was struggling with concepts too difficult to put into words. After several moments of apparently painful internal struggle, he said, ‘But where’s he going to go?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon looked at each other. It was clear that Dudley was frightening them. Hestia Jones broke the silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But … surely you know where your nephew is going?’ she asked, looking bewildered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Certainly we know,’ said Vernon Dursley. ‘He’s off with some of your lot, isn’t he? Right, Dudley, let’s get in the car, you heard the man, we’re in a hurry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Again, Vernon Dursley marched as far as the front door, but Dudley did not follow.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Off with some of our lot?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hestia looked outraged. Harry had met this attitude before: witches and wizards seemed stunned that his closest living relatives took so little interest in the famous Harry Potter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s fine,’ Harry assured her. ‘It doesn’t matter, honestly.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Doesn’t matter?’ repeated Hestia, her voice rising ominously. ‘Don’t these people realise what you’ve been through? What danger you are in? The unique position you hold in the hearts of the anti-Voldemort movement?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Er - no, they don’t,’ said Harry. ‘They think I’m a waste of space, actually, but I’m used to -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t think you’re a waste of space.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: If Harry had not seen Dudley’s lips move, he might not have believed it. As it was, he stared at Dudley for several seconds before accepting that it must have been his cousin who had spoken; for one thing, Dudley had turned red. Harry was embarrassed and astonished himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well … er … thanks, Dudley.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Again, Dudley appeared to grapple with thoughts too unwieldy for expression before mumbling, ‘You saved my life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not really,’ said Harry. ‘It was your soul the Dementor would have taken …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He looked curiously at his cousin. They had had virtually no contact during this summer or last, as Harry had come back to Privet Drive so briefly and kept to his room so much. It now dawned on Harry, however, that the cup of cold tea on which he had trodden that morning might not have been a booby trap at all. Although rather touched, he was nevertheless quite relieved that Dudley appeared to have exhausted his ability to express his feelings. After opening his mouth once or twice more, Dudley subsided into scarlet-faced silence.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aunt Petunia burst into tears. Hestia Jones gave her an approving look which changed to outrage as Aunt Petunia ran forwards and embraced Dudley rather than Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘S - So sweet, Dudders …’ she sobbed into his massive chest, ‘s - such a lovely b - boy … s - saying thank you …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But he hasn’t said thank you at all!’ said Hestia indignantly. ‘He only said he didn’t think Harry was a waste of space!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, but coming from Dudley that’s like “I love you”,’ said Harry, torn between annoyance and a desire to laugh as Aunt Petunia continued to clutch at Dudley as if he had just saved Harry from a burning building.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Are we going or not?’ roared Uncle Vernon, reappearing yet again at the living-room door. ‘I thought we were on a tight schedule!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes - yes, we are,’ said Dedalus Diggle, who had been watching these exchanges with an air of bemusement and now seemed to pull himself together. ‘We really must be off. Harry -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He tripped forwards and wrung Harry’s hand with both of his own.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- good luck. I hope we meet again. The hopes of the wizarding world rest upon your shoulders.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh,’ said Harry, ‘right. Thanks.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Farewell, Harry,’ said Hestia, also clasping his hand. ‘Our thoughts go with you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I hope everything’s OK,’ said Harry, with a glance towards Aunt Petunia and Dudley.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I’m sure we shall end up the best of chums,’ said Diggle brightly, waving his hat as he left the room. Hestia followed him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dudley gently released himself from his mother’s clutches and walked towards Harry, who had to repress an urge to threaten him with magic. Then Dudley held out his large, pink hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Blimey, Dudley,’ said Harry, over Aunt Petunia’s renewed sobs, ‘did the Dementors blow a different personality into you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dunno,’ muttered Dudley. ‘See you, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah …’ said Harry, taking Dudley’s hand and shaking it. ‘Maybe. Take care, Big D.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dudley nearly smiled, then lumbered from the room. Harry heard his heavy footfalls on the gravelled drive, and then a car door slammed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aunt Petunia, whose face had been buried in her handkerchief, looked round at the sound. She did not seem to have expected to find herself alone with Harry. Hastily stowing her wet handkerchief into her pocket she said, ‘Well - goodbye,’ and marched towards the door without looking at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Goodbye,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She stopped and looked back. For a moment Harry had the strangest feeling that she wanted to say something to him: she gave him an odd, tremulous look and seemed to teeter on the edge of speech, but then, with a little jerk of her head, she bustled out of the room after her husband and son.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry ran back upstairs to his bedroom, arriving at the window just in time to see the Dursleys’ car swinging out of the drive and off up the road. Dedalus’s top hat was visible between Aunt Petunia and Dudley in the back seat. The car turned right at the end of Privet Drive, its windows burned scarlet for a moment in the now setting sun, and then it was gone.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry picked up Hedwig’s cage, his Firebolt and his rucksack, gave his unnaturally tidy bedroom one last sweeping look and then made his ungainly way back downstairs to the hall, where he deposited cage, broomstick and bag near the foot of the stairs. The light was fading rapidly now, the hall full of shadows in the evening light. It felt most strange to stand here in the silence and know that he was about to leave the house for the last time. Long ago, when he had been left alone while the Dursleys went out to enjoy themselves, the hours of solitude had been a rare treat: pausing only to sneak something tasty from the fridge he had rushed upstairs to play on Dudley’s computer, or put on the television and flicked through the channels to his heart’s content. It gave him an odd, empty feeling to remember those times; it was like remembering a younger brother whom he had lost.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t you want to take a last look at the place?’ he asked Hedwig, who was still sulking with her head under her wing. ‘We’ll never be here again. Don’t you want to remember all the good times? I mean, look at this doormat. What memories … Dudley puked on it after I saved him from the Dementors … Turns out he was grateful after all, can you believe it? … And last summer, Dumbledore walked through that front door …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry lost the thread of his thoughts for a moment and Hedwig did nothing to help him retrieve it, but continued to sit with her head under her wing. Harry turned his back on the front door.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And under here, Hedwig -‘ Harry pulled open a door under the stairs ‘- is where I used to sleep! You never knew me then - blimey, it’s small, I’d forgotten …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around at the stacked shoes and umbrellas, remembering how he used to wake every morning looking up at the underside of the staircase, which was more often than not adorned with a spider or two. Those had been the days before he had known anything about his true identity; before he had found out how his parents had died or why such strange things often happened around him. But Harry could still remember the dreams that had dogged him, even in those days: confused dreams involving flashes of green light and, once - Uncle Vernon had nearly crashed the car when Harry had recounted it - a flying motorbike …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a sudden, deafening roar from somewhere nearby. Harry straightened up with a jerk and smacked the top of his head on the low door frame. Pausing only to employ a few of Uncle Vernon’s choicest swear words, he staggered back into the kitchen, clutching his head and staring out of the window into the back garden.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The darkness seemed to be rippling, the air itself quivering. Then, one by one, figures began to pop into sight as their Disillusionment Charms lifted. Dominating the scene was Hagrid, wearing a helmet and goggles and sitting astride an enormous motorbike with a black sidecar attached. All around him other people were dismounting from brooms and, in two cases, skeletal, black winged horses.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Wrenching open the back door, Harry hurtled into their midst. There was a general cry of greeting as Hermione flung her arms around him, Ron clapped him on the back and Hagrid said, ‘All righ’, Harry? Ready fer the off?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Definitely,’ said Harry, beaming around at them all. ‘But I wasn’t expecting this many of you!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Change of plan,’ growled Mad-Eye, who was holding two enormous, bulging sacks and whose magical eye was spinning from darkening sky to house to garden with dizzying rapidity. ‘Let’s get undercover before we talk you through it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry led them all back into the kitchen where, laughing and chattering, they settled on chairs, sat themselves upon Aunt Petunia’s gleaming work-surfaces or leaned up against her spotless appliances: Ron, long and lanky; Hermione, her bushy hair tied back in a long plait; Fred and George, grinning identically; Bill, badly scarred and long-haired; Mr Weasley, kind-faced, balding, his spectacles a little awry; Mad-Eye, battle-worn, one-legged, his bright blue magical eye whizzing in its socket; Tonks, whose short hair was her favourite shade of bright pink; Lupin, greyer, more lined; Fleur, slender and beautiful, with her long, silvery blonde hair; Kingsley, bald, black, broad-shouldered; Hagrid, with his wild hair and beard, standing hunchbacked to avoid hitting his head on the ceiling, and Mundungus Fletcher, small, dirty and hangdog, with his droopy, basset hound’s eyes and matted hair. Harry’s heart seemed to expand and glow at the sight: he felt incredibly fond of all of them, even Mundungus, whom he had tried to strangle the last time they had met.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kingsley, I thought you were looking after the Muggle Prime Minister?’ he called across the room.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He can get along without me for one night,’ said Kingsley. ‘You’re more important.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, guess what?’ said Tonks from her perch on top of the washing machine, and she wiggled her left hand at him; a ring glittered there.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You got married?’ Harry yelped, looking from her to Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry you couldn’t be there, Harry, it was very quiet.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s brilliant, congrat—’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right, all right, we’ll have time for a cosy catch-up later!’ roared Moody over the hubbub, and silence fell in the kitchen. Moody dropped the sacks at his feet and turned to Harry. ‘As Dedalus probably told you, we had to abandon Plan A. Pius Thicknesse has gone over, which gives us a big problem. He’s made it an imprisonable offence to connect this house to the Floo Network, place a Portkey here or Apparate in or out. All done in the name of your protection, to prevent You-Know-Who getting in at you. Absolutely pointless, seeing as your mother’s charm does that already. What he’s really done is to stop you getting out of here safely.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Second problem: you’re under-age, which means you’ve still got the Trace on you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Trace, the Trace!’ said Mad-Eye impatiently. ‘The charm that detects magical activity around under-seventeens, the way the Ministry finds out about under-age magic! If you, or anyone around you, casts a spell to get you out of here, Thicknesse is going to know about it, and so will the Death Eaters.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We can’t wait for the Trace to break, because the moment you turn seventeen you’ll lose all the protection your mother gave you. In short: Pius Thicknesse thinks he’s got you cornered good and proper.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could not help but agree with the unknown Thicknesse.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So what are we going to do?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re going to use the only means of transport left to us, the only ones the Trace can’t detect, because we don’t need to cast spells to use them: brooms, Thestrals and Hagrid’s motorbike.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could see flaws in this plan; however, he held his tongue to give Mad-Eye the chance to address them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, your mother’s charm will only break under two conditions: when you come of age, or -‘ Moody gestured around the pristine kitchen ‘- you no longer call this place home. You and your aunt and uncle are going your separate ways tonight, in the full understanding that you’re never going to live together again, correct?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry nodded.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So this time, when you leave, there’ll be no going back, and the charm will break the moment you get outside its range. We’re choosing to break it early, because the alternative is waiting for You-Know-Who to come and seize you the moment you turn seventeen.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The one thing we’ve got on our side is that You-Know-Who doesn’t know we’re moving you tonight. We’ve leaked a fake trail to the Ministry: they think you’re not leaving until the thirtieth. However, this is You-Know-Who we’re dealing with, so we can’t just rely on him getting the date wrong; he’s bound to have a couple of Death Eaters patrolling the skies in this general area, just in case. So, we’ve given a dozen different houses every protection we can throw at them. They all look like they could be the place we’re going to hide you, they’ve all got some connection with the Order: my house, Kingsley’s place, Molly’s Auntie Muriel’s - you get the idea.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, not entirely truthfully, because he could still spot a gaping hole in the plan.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You’ll be going to Tonks’s parents’. Once you’re within the boundaries of the protective enchantments we’ve put on their house, you’ll be able to use a Portkey to The Burrow. Any questions?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Er - yes,’ said Harry. ‘Maybe they won’t know which of the twelve secure houses I’m heading for at first, but won’t it be sort of obvious once -‘ he performed a quick headcount ‘- fourteen of us fly off towards Tonks’s parents’?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ said Moody, ‘I forgot to mention the key point. Fourteen of us won’t be flying to Tonks’s parents’. There will be seven Harry Potters moving through the skies tonight, each of them with a companion, each pair heading for a different safe house.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: From inside his cloak Moody now withdrew a flask of what looked like mud. There was no need for him to say another word; Harry understood the rest of the plan immediately.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ he said loudly, his voice ringing through the kitchen. ‘No way!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I told them you’d take it like this,’ said Hermione, with a hint of complacency.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If you think I’m going to let six people risk their lives -!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- because it’s the first time for all of us,’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘This is different, pretending to be me -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, none of us really fancy it, Harry,’ said Fred earnestly. ‘Imagine if something went wrong and we were stuck as specky, scrawny gits forever.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry did not smile.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You can’t do it if I don’t cooperate, you need me to give you some hair.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, that’s that plan scuppered,’ said George. ‘Obviously there’s no chance at all of us getting a bit of your hair unless you cooperate.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, thirteen of us against one bloke who’s not allowed to use magic; we’ve got no chance,’ said Fred.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Funny,’ said Harry. ‘Really amusing.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If it has to come to force, then it will,’ growled Moody, his magical eye now quivering a little in its socket as he glared at Harry. ‘Everyone here’s over-age, Potter, and they’re all prepared to take the risk.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mundungus shrugged and grimaced; the magical eye swerved sideways to glare at him out of the side of Moody’s head.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Let’s have no more arguments. Time’s wearing on. I want a few of your hairs, boy, now.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But this is mad, there’s no need -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No need!’ snarled Moody. ‘With You-Know-Who out there and half the Ministry on his side? Potter, if we’re lucky, he’ll have swallowed the fake bait and he’ll be planning to ambush you on the thirtieth, but he’d be mad not to have a Death Eater or two keeping an eye out, it’s what I’d do. They might not be able to get at you or this house while your mother’s charm holds, but it’s about to break and they know the rough position of the place. Our only chance is to use decoys. Even You-Know-Who can’t split himself into seven.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry caught Hermione’s eye and looked away at once.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So, Potter - some of your hair, if you please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry glanced at Ron, who grimaced at him in a just-do-it sort of way.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Now!’ barked Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: With all of their eyes upon him, Harry reached up to the top of his head, grabbed a hank of hair and pulled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ said Moody, limping forwards as he pulled the stopper out of the flask of Potion. ‘Straight in here, if you please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry dropped the hair into the mud-like liquid. The moment it made contact with its surface the Potion began to froth and smoke then, all at once, it turned a clear, bright gold.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ooh, you look much tastier than Crabbe and Goyle, Harry,’ said Hermione, before catching sight of Ron’s raised eyebrows, blushing slightly and saying, ‘oh, you know what I mean - Goyle’s Potion looked like bogies.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Right then, fake Potters line up over here, please,’ said Moody.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron, Hermione, Fred, George and Fleur lined up in front of Aunt Petunia’s gleaming sink.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re one short,’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Here,’ said Hagrid gruffly, and he lifted Mundungus by the scruff of the neck and dropped him down beside Fleur, who wrinkled her nose pointedly and moved along to stand between Fred and George instead.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve toldjer, I’d sooner be a protector,’ said Mundungus.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Shut it,’ growled Moody. ‘As I’ve already told you, you spineless worm, any Death Eaters we run into will be aiming to capture Potter, not kill him. Dumbledore always said You-Know-Who would want to finish Potter in person. It’ll be the protectors who have got the most to worry about, the Death Eaters’ll want to kill them.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mundungus did not look particularly reassured, but Moody was already pulling half a dozen egg-cup-sized glasses from inside his cloak, which he handed out, before pouring a little Polyjuice Potion into each one.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Altogether, then …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron, Hermione, Fred, George, Fleur and Mundungus drank. All of them gasped and grimaced as the Potion hit their throats: at once, their features began to bubble and distort like hot wax. Hermione and Mundungus were shooting upwards; Ron, Fred and George were shrinking; their hair was darkening, Hermione’s and Fleur’s appearing to shoot backwards into their skulls.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Moody, quite unconcerned, was now loosening the ties of the large sacks he had brought with him: when he straightened up again, there were six Harry Potters gasping and panting in front of him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Fred and George turned to each other and said together, ‘Wow - we’re identical!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I dunno, though, I think I’m still better-looking,’ said Fred, examining his reflection in the kettle.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Bah,’ said Fleur, checking herself in the microwave door, ‘Bill, don’t look at me - I’m ‘ideous.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Those whose clothes are a bit roomy, I’ve got smaller here,’ said Moody, indicating the first sack, ‘and vice versa. Don’t forget the glasses, there’s six pairs in the side pocket. And when you’re dressed, there’s luggage in the other sack.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The real Harry thought that this might just be the most bizarre thing he had ever seen, and he had seen some extremely odd things. He watched as his six doppelgangers rummaged in the sacks, pulling out sets of clothes, putting on glasses, stuffing their own things away. He felt like asking them to show a little more respect for his privacy as they all began stripping off with impunity, clearly much more at ease with displaying his body than they would have been with their own.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew Ginny was lying about that tattoo,’ said Ron, looking down at his bare chest.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, your eyesight really is awful,’ said Hermione, as she put on glasses.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Once dressed, the fake Harrys took rucksacks and owl cages, each containing a stuffed snowy owl, from the second sack.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good,’ said Moody, as at last seven dressed, bespectacled and luggage-laden Harrys faced him. ‘The pairs will be as follows: Mundungus will be travelling with me, by broom -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why’m I with you?’ grunted the Harry nearest the back door.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Because you’re the one that needs watching,’ growled Moody, and sure enough, his magical eye did not waver from Mundungus as he continued, ‘Arthur and Fred -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m George,’ said the twin at whom Moody was pointing. ‘Can’t you even tell us apart when we’re Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry, George -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m only yanking your wand, I’m Fred really -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Enough messing around!’ snarled Moody. ‘The other one - George or Fred or whoever you are - you’re with Remus. Miss Delacour -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m taking Fleur on a Thestral,’ said Bill. ‘She’s not that fond of brooms.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Fleur walked over to stand beside him, giving him a soppy, slavish look that Harry hoped with all his heart would never appear on his face again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Miss Granger with Kingsley, again by Thestral -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked reassured as she answered Kingsley’s smile; Harry knew that Hermione, too, lacked confidence on a broomstick.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Which leaves you and me, Ron!’ said Tonks brightly, knocking over a mug-tree as she waved at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron did not look quite as pleased as Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘An’ you’re with me, Harry. That all righ’?’ said Hagrid, looking a little anxious. ‘We’ll be on the bike, brooms an’ Thestrals can’t take me weight, see. ‘Not a lot o’ room on the seat with me on it, though, so you’ll be in the sidecar.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s great,’ said Harry, not altogether truthfully.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We think the Death Eaters will expect you to be on a broom,’ said Moody, who seemed to guess how Harry was feeling. ‘Snape’s had plenty of time to tell them everything about you he’s never mentioned before, so if we do run into any Death Eaters, we’re betting they’ll choose one of the Potters who look at home on a broomstick. All right then,’ he went on, tying up the sack with the fake Potters’ clothes in it and leading the way back to the door, ‘I make it three minutes until we’re supposed to leave. No point locking the back door, it won’t keep the Death Eaters out when they come looking … Come on …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry hurried into the hall to fetch his rucksack, Firebolt and Hedwig’s cage before joining the others in the dark back garden. On every side broomsticks were leaping into hands; Hermione had already been helped up on to a great, black Thestral by Kingsley; Fleur on to the other by Bill. Hagrid was standing ready beside the motorbike, goggles on.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Is this it? Is this Sirius’s bike?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The very same,’ said Hagrid, beaming down at Harry. ‘An’ the last time you was on it, Harry, I could fit yeh in one hand!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could not help but feel a little humiliated as he got into the sidecar. It placed him several feet below everybody else: Ron smirked at the sight of him sitting there like a child in a bumper car. Harry stuffed his rucksack and broomstick down by his feet and rammed Hedwig’s cage between his knees. It was extremely uncomfortable.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Arthur’s done a bit o’ tinkerin’,’ said Hagrid, quite oblivious to Harry’s discomfort. He settled himself astride the motorcycle, which creaked slightly and sank inches into the ground. ‘It’s got a few tricks up its handlebars now. Tha’ one was my idea.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He pointed a thick finger at a purple button near the speedometer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Please be careful, Hagrid,’ said Mr Weasley, who was standing beside them, holding his broomstick. ‘I’m still not sure that was advisable and it’s certainly only to be used in emergencies.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right then,’ said Moody. ‘Everyone ready, please; I want us all to leave at exactly the same time or the whole point of the diversion’s lost.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Everybody mounted their brooms.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hold tight, now, Ron,’ said Tonks, and Harry saw Ron throw a furtive, guilty look at Lupin before placing his hands on either side of her waist. Hagrid kicked the motorbike into life: it roared like a dragon and the sidecar began to vibrate.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good luck, everyone,’ shouted Moody. ‘See you all in about an hour at The Burrow. On the count of three. One … two … THREE.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a great roar from the motorbike and Harry felt the sidecar give a nasty lurch: he was rising through the air fast, his eyes watering slightly, hair whipped back off his face. Around him brooms were soaring upwards too: the long, black tail of a Thestral flicked past. His legs, jammed into the sidecar by Hedwig’s cage and his rucksack, were already sore and starting to go numb. So great was his discomfort that he almost forgot to take a last glimpse of number four, Privet Drive; by the time he looked over the edge of the sidecar, he could no longer tell which one it was. Higher and higher they climbed into the sky -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And then, out of nowhere, out of nothing, they were surrounded. At least thirty hooded figures, suspended in mid-air, formed a vast circle in the midst of which the Order members had risen, oblivious -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Screams, a blaze of green light on every side: Hagrid gave a yell and the motorbike rolled over. Harry lost any sense of where they were: street lights above him, yells around him, he was clinging to the sidecar for dear life. Hedwig’s cage, the Firebolt and his rucksack slipped from beneath his knees -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No - HEDWIG!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The broomstick spun to earth, but he just managed to seize the strap of his rucksack and the top of the cage as the motorbike swung the right way up again. A second’s relief, and then another burst of green light. The owl screeched and fell to the floor of the cage.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No - NO!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The motorbike zoomed forwards; Harry glimpsed hooded Death Eaters scattering as Hagrid blasted through their circle.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hedwig - Hedwig -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But the owl lay motionless and pathetic as a toy on the floor of her cage. He could not take it in, and his terror for the others was paramount. He glanced over his shoulder and saw a mass of people moving, flares of green light, two pairs of people on brooms soaring off into the distance, but he could not tell who they were -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, we’ve got to go back, we’ve got to go back!’ he yelled over the thunderous roar of the engine, pulling out his wand, ramming Hedwig’s cage on to the floor, refusing to believe that she was dead. ‘Hagrid, TURN ROUND!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My job’s ter get you there safe, Harry!’ bellowed Hagrid, and he opened the throttle.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stop - STOP!’ Harry shouted. But as he looked back again two jets of green light flew past his left ear: four Death Eaters had broken away from the circle and were pursuing them, aiming for Hagrid’s broad back. Hagrid swerved, but the Death Eaters were keeping up with the bike; more curses shot after them, and Harry had to sink low into the sidecar to avoid them. Wriggling round, he cried, ‘Stupefy!’ and a red bolt of light shot from his own wand, cleaving a gap between the four pursuing Death Eaters as they scattered to avoid it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hold on, Harry, this’ll do for ‘em!’ roared Hagrid, and Harry looked up just in time to see Hagrid slamming a thick finger into a green button near the fuel gauge.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A wall, a solid brick wall, erupted out of the exhaust pipe. Craning his neck, Harry saw it expand into being in mid-air. Three of the Death Eaters swerved and avoided it, but the fourth was not so lucky: he vanished from view and then dropped like a boulder from behind it, his broomstick broken into pieces. One of his fellows slowed up to save him, but they and the airborne wall were swallowed by darkness as Hagrid leaned low over the handlebars and sped up.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: More Killing Curses flew past Harry’s head from the two remaining Death Eaters’ wands; they were aiming for Hagrid. Harry responded with further Stunning Spells: red and green collided in mid-air in a shower of multi-coloured sparks and Harry thought wildly of fireworks, and the Muggles below who would have no idea what was happening -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Here we go again, Harry, hold on!’ yelled Hagrid, and he jabbed at a second button. This time a great net burst from the bike’s exhaust, but the Death Eaters were ready for it. Not only did they swerve to avoid it, but the companion who had slowed to save their unconscious friend had caught up: he bloomed suddenly out of the darkness and now three of them were pursuing the motorbike, all shooting curses after it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘This’ll do it, Harry, hold on tight!’ yelled Hagrid, and Harry saw him slam his whole hand on to the purple button beside the speedometer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: With an unmistakable bellowing roar, dragon fire burst from the exhaust, white-hot and blue, and the motorbike shot forwards like a bullet with a sound of wrenching metal. Harry saw the Death Eaters swerve out of sight to avoid the deadly trail of flame, and at the same time felt the sidecar sway ominously: its metal connections to the bike had splintered with the force of acceleration.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s all righ’, Harry!’ bellowed Hagrid, now thrown flat on to his back by the surge of speed; nobody was steering now, and the sidecar was starting to twist violently in the bike’s slipstream.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m on it, Harry, don’ worry!’ Hagrid yelled, and from inside his jacket pocket he pulled his flowery pink umbrella.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid! No! Let me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘REPARO!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a deafening bang and the sidecar broke away from the bike completely: Harry sped forwards, propelled by the impetus of the bike’s flight, then the sidecar began to lose height -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: In desperation Harry pointed his wand at the sidecar and shouted, ‘Wingardium Leviosa!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The sidecar rose like a cork, unsteerable but at least still airborne: he had but a split second’s relief, however, as more curses streaked past him: the three Death Eaters were closing in.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m comin’, Harry!’ Hagrid yelled from out of the darkness, but Harry could feel the sidecar beginning to sink again: crouching as low as he could, he pointed at the middle of the oncoming figures and yelled, ‘Impedimenta!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The jinx hit the middle Death Eater in the chest: for a moment the man was absurdly spread-eagled in mid-air as though he had hit an invisible barrier: one of his fellows almost collided with him -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then the sidecar began to fall in earnest, and the remaining Death Eater shot a curse so close to Harry that he had to duck below the rim of the car, knocking out a tooth on the edge of his seat -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m comin’, Harry, I’m comin’!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A huge hand seized the back of Harry’s robes and hoisted him out of the plummeting sidecar; Harry pulled his rucksack with him as he dragged himself on to the motorbike’s seat and found himself back to back with Hagrid. As they soared upwards, away from the two remaining Death Eaters, Harry spat blood out of his mouth, pointed his wand at the falling sidecar, and yelled, ‘Confringo!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He knew a dreadful, gut-wrenching pang for Hedwig as it exploded; the Death Eater nearest it was blasted off his broom and fell from sight; his companion fell back and vanished.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, I’m sorry, I’m sorry,’ moaned Hagrid, ‘I shouldn’ta tried ter repair it meself - yeh’ve got no room -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not a problem, just keep flying!’ Harry shouted back, as two more Death Eaters emerged out of the darkness, drawing closer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: As the curses came shooting across the intervening space again, Hagrid swerved and zigzagged: Harry knew that Hagrid did not dare use the dragon-fire button again, with Harry seated so insecurely. Harry sent Stunning Spell after Stunning Spell back at their pursuers, barely holding them off. He shot another blocking jinx at them: the closest Death Eater swerved to avoid it and his hood slipped, and by the red light of his next Stunning Spell, Harry saw the strangely blank face of Stanley Shunpike - Stan -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Expelliarmus!’ Harry yelled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s him, it’s him, it’s the real one!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The hooded Death Eater’s shout reached Harry even above the thunder of the motorbike’s engine: next moment, both pursuers had fallen back and disappeared from view.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, what’s happened?’ bellowed Hagrid. ‘Where’ve they gone?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But Harry was afraid: the hooded Death Eater had shouted ‘it’s the real one’; how had he known? He gazed around at the apparently empty darkness and felt its menace. Where were they?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He clambered round on the seat to face forwards and seized hold of the back of Hagrid’s jacket.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid, do the dragon fire thing again, let’s get out of here!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hold on tight, then, Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a deafening, screeching roar again and the white-blue fire shot from the exhaust: Harry felt himself slipping backwards off what little of the seat he had, Hagrid flung backwards upon him, barely maintaining his grip on the handlebars -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I think we’ve lost ‘em Harry, I think we’ve done it!’ yelled Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But Harry was not convinced: fear lapped at him as he looked left and right for pursuers he was sure would come … why had they fallen back? One of them had still had a wand … It’s him, it’s the real one … they had said it right after he had tried to Disarm Stan …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re nearly there, Harry, we’ve nearly made it!’ shouted Hagrid.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt the bike drop a little, though the lights down on the ground still seemed remote as stars.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then the scar on his forehead burned like fire: as a Death Eater appeared on either side of the bike, two Killing Curses missed Harry by millimetres, cast from behind -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And then Harry saw him. Voldemort was flying like smoke on the wind, without broomstick or Thestral to hold him, his snakelike face gleaming out of the blackness, his white fingers raising his wand again -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hagrid let out a bellow of fear and steered the motorbike into a vertical dive. Clinging on for dear life, Harry sent Stunning Spells flying at random into the whirling night. He saw a body fly past him and knew he had hit one of them, but then he heard a bang and saw sparks from the engine; the motorbike spiralled through the air, completely out of control -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Green jets of light shot past them again. Harry had no idea which way was up, which down: his scar was still burning; he expected to die at any second. A hooded figure on a broomstick was feet from him, he saw it raise its arm -

text_content: ‘Hagrid?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid?’

text_content: ‘Easy, now,’ said Ted Tonks, placing a hand on Harry’s shoulder and pushing him back against the cushions. ‘That was a nasty crash you just had. What happened, anyway? Something go wrong with the bike? Arthur Weasley overstretch himself again, him and his Muggle contraptions?’

text_content: As she moved forwards into the room, Mrs Tonks’s resemblance to her sister Bellatrix became much less pronounced: her hair was a light, soft brown and her eyes were wider and kinder. Nevertheless, she looked a little haughty after Harry’s exclamation.

text_content: ‘The Portkey,’ he said, remembering all of a sudden. ‘We’ve got to get back to The Burrow and find out - then we’ll be able to send you word, or - or Tonks will, once she’s -‘

text_content: ‘Dora’ll be OK, Dromeda,’ said Ted. ‘She knows her stuff, she’s been in plenty of tight spots with the Aurors. The Portkey’s through here,’ he added to Harry. ‘It’s supposed to leave in three minutes, if you want to take it.’

text_content: Lupin ignored him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What creature sat in the corner, the first time that Harry Potter visited my office at Hogwarts?’ he said, giving Harry a small shake. ‘Answer me!’

text_content: ‘A - a Grindylow in a tank, wasn’t it?’

text_content: Lupin released Harry and fell back against a kitchen cupboard.

text_content: ‘Wha’ was tha’ about?’ roared Hagrid.

text_content: ‘I’m sorry, Harry, but I had to check,’ said Lupin tersely. ‘We’ve been betrayed. Voldemort knew that you were being moved tonight and the only people who could have told him were directly involved in the plan. You might have been an impostor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So why aren’ you checkin’ me?’ panted Hagrid, still struggling to fit through the door.

text_content: ‘You’re half-giant,’ said Lupin, looking up at Hagrid. ‘The Polyjuice Potion is designed for human use only.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘None of the Order would have told Voldemort we were moving tonight,’ said Harry: the idea was dreadful to him, he could not believe it of any of them. ‘Voldemort only caught up with me towards the end, he didn’t know which one I was in the beginning. If he’d been in on the plan, he’d have known from the start I was the one with Hagrid.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort caught up with you?’ said Lupin sharply. ‘What happened? How did you escape?’

text_content: Harry explained, briefly, how the Death Eaters pursuing them had seemed to recognise him as the true Harry, how they had abandoned the chase, how they must have summoned Voldemort, who had appeared just before he and Hagrid had reached the sanctuary of Tonks’s parents’.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They recognised you? But how? What had you done?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin looked aghast.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, the time for Disarming is past! These people are trying to capture and kill you! At least Stun if you aren’t prepared to kill!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Harry,’ said Lupin with painful restraint, ‘and a great number of Death Eaters witnessed that happening! Forgive me, but it was a very unusual move then, under imminent threat of death. book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So you think I should have killed Stan Shunpike?’ said Harry angrily.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course not,’ said Lupin, ‘but the Death Eaters - frankly, most people! - would have expected you to attack back! Expelliarmus is a useful spell, Harry, but the Death Eaters seem to think it is your signature move, and I urge you not to let it become so!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin was making Harry feel idiotic, and yet there was still a grain of defiance inside him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I won’t blast people out of my way just because they’re there,’ said Harry. ‘That’s Voldemort’s job.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin’s retort was lost: finally succeeding in squeezing through the door, Hagrid staggered to a chair and sat down; it collapsed beneath him. Ignoring his mingled oaths and apologies, Harry addressed Lupin again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Will George be OK?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The last words Albus Dumbledore spoke to the pair of us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right, all right!’ said Kingsley, stowing his wand back beneath his cloak. ‘But somebody betrayed us! They knew, they knew it was tonight!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So it seems,’ replied Lupin, ‘but apparently they did not realise that there would be seven Harrys.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Small comfort!’ snarled Kingsley. ‘Who else is back?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Only Harry, Hagrid, George and me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione stifled a little moan behind her hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What happened to you?’ Lupin asked Kingsley.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Followed by five, injured two, might’ve killed one,’ Kingsley reeled off, ‘and we saw You-Know-Who as well, he joined the chase halfway through, but vanished pretty quickly. Remus, he can -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Fly,’ supplied Harry. ‘I saw him too, he came after Hagrid and me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry behaved a little too kindly to Stan Shunpike,’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stan?’ repeated Hermione. ‘But I thought he was in Azkaban?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kingsley let out a mirthless laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione, there’s obviously been a mass breakout which the Ministry has hushed up. Travers’s hood fell off when I cursed him, he’s supposed to be inside too. But what happened to you, Remus? Where’s George?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He lost an ear,’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Lost an -?’ repeated Hermione in a high voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Silence fell between the four of them as they looked up at the sky. There was no sign of movement; the stars stared back, unblinking, indifferent, unobscured by flying friends. Where was Ron? Where were Fred and Mr Weasley? Where were Bill, Fleur, Tonks, Mad-Eye and Mundungus?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, give us a hand!’ called Hagrid hoarsely from the door, in which he was stuck again. Glad of something to do, Harry pulled him free, then headed through the empty kitchen and back into the sitting room, where Mrs Weasley and Ginny were still tending to George. Mrs Weasley had staunched his bleeding now, and by the lamplight Harry saw a clean, gaping hole where George’s ear had been.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How is he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mrs Weasley looked round and said, ‘I can’t make it grow back, not when it’s been removed by Dark Magic. But it could have been so much worse … he’s alive.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry. ‘Thank God.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Did I hear someone else in the yard?’ Ginny asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione and Kingsley,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank goodness,’ Ginny whispered. They looked at each other; Harry wanted to hug her, hold on to her; he did not even care much that Mrs Weasley was there, but before he could act on the impulse there was a great crash from the kitchen.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll prove who I am, Kingsley, after I’ve seen my son, now back off if you know what’s good for you!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had never heard Mr Weasley shout like that before. He burst into the living room, his bald patch gleaming with sweat, his spectacles askew, Fred right behind him, both pale but uninjured.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Arthur!’ sobbed Mrs Weasley. ‘Oh thank goodness!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How is he?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mr Weasley dropped to his knees beside George. For the first time since Harry had known him, Fred seemed to be lost for words. He gaped over the back of the sofa at his twin’s wound as if he could not believe what he was seeing.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Perhaps roused by the sound of Fred and their father’s arrival, George stirred.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How do you feel, Georgie?’ whispered Mrs Weasley.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: George’s fingers groped for the side of his head.

text_content: ‘Saint-like,’ he murmured.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s wrong with him?’ croaked Fred, looking terrified. ‘Is his mind affected?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mrs Weasley sobbed harder than ever. Colour flooded Fred’s pale face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Pathetic,’ he told George. ‘Pathetic! With the whole wide world of ear-related humour before you, you go for holey?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah well,’ said George, grinning at his tear-soaked mother. ‘You’ll be able to tell us apart now, anyway, Mum.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hi Harry - you are Harry, right?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
