text_content: ‘Smooth,’ said Ron approvingly, as the waiters popped up on all sides, some bearing silver trays of pumpkin juice, Butterbeer and Firewhisky, others tottering piles of tarts and sandwiches.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We should go and congratulate them!’ said Hermione, standing on tiptoe to see the place where Bill and Fleur had vanished amid a crowd of well-wishers.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ll have time later,’ shrugged Ron, snatching three Butterbeers from a passing tray and handing one to Harry. ‘Hermione, cop hold, let’s grab a table … not there! Nowhere near Muriel -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron led the way across the empty dance floor, glancing left and right as he went: Harry felt sure that he was keeping an eye out for Krum. By the time they had reached the other side of the marquee, most of the tables were occupied: the emptiest was the one where Luna sat alone.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right if we join you?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes,’ she said happily. ‘Daddy’s just gone to give Bill and Fleur our present.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What is it, a lifetime’s supply of Gurdyroots?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione aimed a kick at him under the table, but caught Harry instead. Eyes watering in pain, Harry lost track of the conversation for a few moments.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The band had begun to play. Bill and Fleur took to the dance floor first, to great applause; after a while, Mr Weasley led Madame Delacour on to the floor, followed by Mrs Weasley and Fleur’s father.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I like this song,’ said Luna, swaying in time to the waltz-like tune, and a few seconds later she stood up and glided on to the dance floor, where she revolved on the spot, quite alone, eyes closed and waving her arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She’s great, isn’t she?’ said Ron admiringly. ‘Always good value.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But the smile vanished from his face at once: Viktor Krum had dropped into Luna’s vacant seat. Hermione looked pleasurably flustered, but this time Krum had not come to compliment her. With a scowl on his face he said, ‘Who is that man in the yellow?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s Xenophilius Lovegood, he’s the father of a friend of ours,’ said Ron. His pugnacious tone indicated that they were not about to laugh at Xenophilius, despite the clear provocation. ‘Come and dance,’ he added abruptly to Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She looked taken aback, but pleased too, and got up: they vanished together into the growing throng on the dance floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, they are together now?’ asked Krum, momentarily distracted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Er - sort of,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Who are you?’ Krum asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Barny Weasley.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They shook hands.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You, Barny - you know this man Lovegood vell?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No, I only met him today. Why?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum glowered over the top of his drink, watching Xenophilius, who was chatting to several warlocks on the other side of the dance floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Because,’ said Krum, ‘if he vos not a guest of Fleur’s, I vould duel him, here and now, for vearing that filthy sign upon his chest.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sign?’ said Harry, looking over at Xenophilius too. The strange, triangular eye was gleaming on his chest. ‘Why? What’s wrong with it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Grindelvald. That is Grindelvald’s sign.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Grindelwald … the Dark wizard Dumbledore defeated?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Exactly.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum’s jaw muscles worked as if he were chewing, then he said, ‘Grindelvald killed many people, my grandfather, for instance. Of course, he vos never poverful in this country, they said he feared Dumbledore - and rightly, seeing how he vos finished. But this -‘ He pointed a finger at Xenophilius. ‘This is his symbol, I recognised it at vunce: Grindelvald carved it into a vall at Durmstrang ven he vos a pupil there. Some idiots copied it on to their books and clothes, thinking to shock, make themselves impressive - until those of us who had lost family members to Grindelvald taught them better.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum cracked his knuckles menacingly and glowered at Xenophilius. Harry felt perplexed. It seemed incredibly unlikely that Luna’s father was a supporter of the Dark Arts, and nobody else in the tent seemed to have recognised the triangular, rune-like shape.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you - er - quite sure it’s Grindelwald’s -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I am not mistaken,’ said Krum coldly. ‘I valked past that sign for several years, I know it vell.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, there’s a chance,’ said Harry, ‘that Xenophilius doesn’t actually know what the symbol means. The Lovegoods are quite … unusual. He could easily have picked it up somewhere and think it’s a cross-section of the head of a Crumple-Horned Snorkack or something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The cross-section of a vot?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I don’t know what they are, but apparently he and his daughter go on holiday looking for them …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt he was doing a bad job explaining Luna and her father.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s her,’ he said, pointing at Luna, who was still dancing alone, waving her arms around her head like someone attempting to beat off midges.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Vy is she doing that?’ asked Krum.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Probably trying to get rid of a Wrackspurt,’ said Harry, who recognised the symptoms.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum did not seem to know whether or not Harry was making fun of him. He drew his wand from inside his robes and tapped it menacingly on his thigh; sparks flew out of the end.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Gregorovitch!’ said Harry loudly, and Krum started, but Harry was too excited to care: the memory had come back to him at the sight of Krum’s wand: Ollivander taking it and examining it carefully before the Triwizard Tournament.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Vot about him?’ asked Krum suspiciously.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s a wandmaker!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know that,’ said Krum.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He made your wand! That’s why I thought - Quidditch …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum was looking more and more suspicious.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How do you know Gregorovitch made my vand?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I … I read it somewhere, I think,’ said Harry. ‘In a - a fan magazine,’ he improvised wildly and Krum looked mollified.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I had not realised I ever discussed my vand vith fans,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So … er … where is Gregorovitch these days?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum looked puzzled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He retired several years ago. I vos one of the last to purchase a Gregorovitch vand. They are the best - although I know, of course, that you Britons set much store by Ollivander.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry did not answer. He pretended to watch the dancers, like Krum, but he was thinking hard. So Voldemort was looking for a celebrated wandmaker, and Harry did not have to search far for a reason: it was surely because of what Harry’s wand had done on the night that Voldemort had pursued him across the skies. The holly and phoenix feather wand had conquered the borrowed wand, something that Ollivander had not anticipated or understood. Would Gregorovitch know better? Was he truly more skilled than Ollivander, did he know secrets of wands that Ollivander did not?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘This girl is very nice-looking,’ Krum said, recalling Harry to his surroundings. Krum was pointing at Ginny, who had just joined Luna. ‘She is also a relative of yours?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Harry, suddenly irritated, ‘and she’s seeing someone. Jealous type. Big bloke. You wouldn’t want to cross him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Krum grunted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Vot,’ he said, draining his goblet and getting to his feet again, ‘is the point of being an international Quidditch player if all the good-looking girls are taken?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And he strode off, leaving Harry to take a sandwich from a passing waiter and make his way round the edge of the crowded dance floor. He wanted to find Ron, to tell him about Gregorovitch, but Ron was dancing with Hermione out in the middle of the floor. Harry leaned up against one of the golden pillars and watched Ginny, who was now dancing with Fred and George’s friend Lee Jordan, trying not to feel resentful about the promise he had given Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He had never been to a wedding before, so he could not judge how wizarding celebrations differed from Muggle ones, though he was pretty sure that the latter would not involve a wedding cake topped with two model phoenixes that took flight when the cake was cut, or bottles of champagne that floated unsupported through the crowd. As evening drew in and moths began to swoop under the canopy, now lit with floating golden lanterns, the revelry became more and more uncontained. Fred and George had long since disappeared into the darkness with a pair of Fleur’s cousins; Charlie, Hagrid and a squat wizard in a purple pork-pie hat were singing ‘Odo the Hero’ in a corner.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Wandering through the crowd so as to escape a drunken uncle of Ron’s who seemed unsure whether or not Harry was his son, Harry spotted an old wizard sitting alone at a table. His cloud of white hair made him look rather like an aged dandelion clock, and was topped by a moth-eaten fez. He was vaguely familiar: racking his brains Harry suddenly realised that this was Elphias Doge, member of the Order of the Phoenix, and the writer of Dumbledore’s obituary.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry approached him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘May I sit down?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course, of course,’ said Doge; he had a rather high-pitched, wheezy voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry leaned in.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Doge, I’m Harry Potter.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge gasped.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My dear boy! Arthur told me you were here, disguised … I am so glad, so honoured!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: In a flutter of nervous pleasure Doge poured Harry a goblet of champagne.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought of writing to you,’ he whispered, ‘after Dumbledore … the shock … and for you, I am sure …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge’s tiny eyes filled with sudden tears.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I saw the obituary you wrote for the Daily Prophet,’ said Harry. ‘I didn’t realise you knew Professor Dumbledore so well.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘As well as anyone,’ said Doge, dabbing his eyes with a napkin. ‘Certainly I knew him longest, if you don’t count Aberforth - and somehow, people never do seem to count Aberforth.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Speaking of the Daily Prophet … I don’t know whether you saw, Mr Doge -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, please call me Elphias, dear boy.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Elphias, I don’t know whether you saw the interview Rita Skeeter gave about Dumbledore?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge’s face flooded with angry colour.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes, Harry, I saw it. That woman, or vulture might be a more accurate term, positively pestered me to talk to her. I am ashamed to say that I became rather rude, called her an interfering trout, which resulted, as you may have seen, in aspersions cast upon my sanity.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, in that interview,’ Harry went on, ‘Rita Skeeter hinted that Professor Dumbledore was involved in the Dark Arts when he was young.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t believe a word of it!’ said Doge at once. ‘Not a word, Harry! Let nothing tarnish your memories of Albus Dumbledore!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked into Doge’s earnest, pained face and felt not reassured, but frustrated. Did Doge really think it was that easy, that Harry could simply choose not to believe? Didn’t Doge understand Harry’s need to be sure, to know everything?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Perhaps Doge suspected Harry’s feelings, for he looked concerned and hurried on, ‘Harry, Rita Skeeter is a dreadful -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But he was interrupted by a shrill cackle.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Rita Skeeter? Oh, I love her, always read her!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry and Doge looked up to see Auntie Muriel standing there, the plumes dancing on her hat, a goblet of champagne in her hand. ‘She’s written a book about Dumbledore, you know!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello, Muriel,’ said Doge. ‘Yes, we were just discussing -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You there! Give me your chair, I’m a hundred and seven!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Another redheaded Weasley cousin jumped off his seat, looking alarmed, and Auntie Muriel swung it round with surprising strength and plopped herself down upon it between Doge and Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hello again, Barry, or whatever your name is,’ she said to Harry. ‘Now, what were you saying about Rita Skeeter, Elphias? You know she’s written a biography of Dumbledore? I can’t wait to read it, I must remember to place an order at Flourish and Blotts!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge looked stiff and solemn at this, but Auntie Muriel drained her goblet and clicked her bony fingers at a passing waiter for a replacement. She took another large gulp of champagne, belched and then said, ‘There’s no need to look like a pair of stuffed frogs! Before he became so respected and respectable and all that tosh, there were some mighty funny rumours about Albus!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ill-informed sniping,’ said Doge, turning radish-coloured again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You would say that, Elphias,’ cackled Auntie Muriel. ‘I noticed how you skated over the sticky patches in that obituary of yours!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry you think so,’ said Doge, more coldly still. ‘I assure you I was writing from the heart.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, we all know you worshipped Dumbledore; I daresay you’ll still think he was a saint even if it does turn out that he did away with his Squib sister!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Muriel!’ exclaimed Doge.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A chill that had nothing to do with the iced champagne was stealing through Harry’s chest.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What do you mean?’ he asked Muriel. ‘Who said his sister was a Squib? I thought she was ill?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thought wrong, then, didn’t you, Barry!’ said Auntie Muriel, looking delighted at the effect she had produced. ‘Anyway, how could you expect to know anything about it? It all happened years and years before you were even thought of, my dear, and the truth is that those of us who were alive then never knew what really happened. That’s why I can’t wait to find out what Skeeter’s unearthed! Dumbledore kept that sister of his quiet for a long time!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Untrue!’ wheezed Doge. ‘Absolutely untrue!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He never told me his sister was a Squib,’ said Harry, without thinking, still cold inside.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And why on earth would he tell you?’ screeched Muriel, swaying a little in her seat as she attempted to focus upon Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The reason Albus never spoke about Ariana,’ began Elphias, in a voice stiff with emotion, ‘is, I should have thought, quite clear. He was so devastated by her death -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why did nobody ever see her, Elphias?’ squawked Muriel. ‘Why did half of us never even know she existed, until they carried the coffin out of the house and held a funeral for her? Where was saintly Albus, while Ariana was locked in the cellar? Off being brilliant at Hogwarts, and never mind what was going on in his own house!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What d’you mean “locked in the cellar”?’ asked Harry. ‘What is this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge looked wretched. Auntie Muriel cackled again and answered Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore’s mother was a terrifying woman, simply terrifying. Muggle-born, though I heard she pretended otherwise -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She never pretended anything of the sort! Kendra was a fine woman,’ whispered Doge miserably, but Auntie Muriel ignored him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- proud and very domineering, the sort of witch who would have been mortified to produce a Squib -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ariana was not a Squib!’ wheezed Doge.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So you say, Elphias, but explain, then, why she never attended Hogwarts!’ said Auntie Muriel. She turned back to Harry. ‘In our day Squibs were often hushed up. Though to take it to the extreme of actually imprisoning a little girl in the house and pretending she didn’t exist -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I tell you, that’s not what happened!’ said Doge, but Auntie Muriel steamrollered on, still addressing Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Squibs were usually shipped off to Muggle schools and encouraged to integrate into the Muggle community … much kinder than trying to find them a place in the wizarding world, where they must always be second class; but naturally Kendra Dumbledore wouldn’t have dreamed of letting her daughter go to a Muggle school -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ariana was delicate!’ said Doge desperately. ‘Her health was always too poor to permit her -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘To permit her to leave the house?’ cackled Muriel. ‘And yet she was never taken to St Mungo’s and no healer was ever summoned to see her!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Really, Muriel, how you can possibly know whether -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘For your information, Elphias, my cousin Lancelot was a healer at St Mungo’s at the time, and he told my family in strictest confidence that Ariana had never been seen there. All most suspicious, Lancelot thought!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Doge looked to be on the verge of tears. Auntie Muriel, who seemed to be enjoying herself hugely, snapped her fingers for more champagne. Numbly Harry thought of how the Dursleys had once shut him up, locked him away, kept him out of sight, all for the crime of being a wizard. Had Dumbledore’s sister suffered the same fate in reverse: imprisoned for her lack of magic? And had Dumbledore truly left her to her fate while he went off to Hogwarts, to prove himself brilliant and talented?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Now, if Kendra hadn’t died first,’ Muriel resumed, ‘I’d have said that it was she who finished off Ariana -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How can you, Muriel?’ groaned Doge. ‘A mother kill her own daughter? Think what you are saying!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If the mother in question was capable of imprisoning her daughter for years on end, why not?’ shrugged Auntie Muriel. ‘But as I say, it doesn’t fit, because Kendra died before Ariana - of what, nobody ever seemed sure -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, no doubt Ariana murdered her,’ said Doge, with a brave attempt at scorn. ‘Why not?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Ariana might have made a desperate bid for freedom and killed Kendra in the struggle,’ said Auntie Muriel thoughtfully. ‘Shake your head all you like, Elphias! You were at Ariana’s funeral, were you not?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, I was,’ said Doge, through trembling lips. ‘And a more desperately sad occasion I cannot remember. Albus was heartbroken -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘His heart wasn’t the only thing. Didn’t Aberforth break Albus’s nose halfway through the service?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: If Doge had looked horrified before this, it was nothing to how he looked now. Muriel might have stabbed him. She cackled loudly and took another swig of champagne, which dribbled down her chin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How do you -?’ croaked Doge.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My mother was friendly with old Bathilda Bagshot,’ said Auntie Muriel happily. ‘Bathilda described the whole thing to Mother while I was listening at the door. A coffin-side brawl! The way Bathilda told it, Aberforth shouted that it was all Albus’s fault that Ariana was dead and then punched him in the face. According to Bathilda, Albus did not even defend himself, and that’s odd enough in itself, Albus could have destroyed Aberforth in a duel with both hands tied behind his back.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Muriel swigged yet more champagne. The recitation of these old scandals seemed to elate her as much as they horrified Doge. Harry did not know what to think, what to believe: he wanted the truth, and yet all Doge did was sit there and bleat feebly that Ariana had been ill. Harry could hardly believe that Dumbledore would not have intervened if such cruelty was happening inside his own house, and yet there was undoubtedly something odd about the story.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And I’ll tell you something else,’ Muriel said, hiccoughing slightly as she lowered her goblet. ‘I think Bathilda has spilled the beans to Rita Skeeter. All those hints in Skeeter’s interview about an important source close to the Dumbledores - goodness knows she was there all through the Ariana business and it would fit!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Bathilda would never talk to Rita Skeeter!’ whispered Doge.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Bathilda Bagshot?’ Harry said. ‘The author of A History of Magic?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The name was printed on the front of one of Harry’s textbooks, though admittedly not one of the ones he had read most attentively.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Doge, clutching at Harry’s question like a drowning man at a lifebelt. ‘A most gifted magical historian and an old friend of Albus’s.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Quite gaga these days, I’ve heard,’ said Auntie Muriel cheerfully.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If that is so, it is even more dishonourable for Skeeter to have taken advantage of her,’ said Doge, ‘and no reliance can be placed on anything Bathilda may have said!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, there are ways of bringing back memories, and I’m sure Rita Skeeter knows them all,’ said Auntie Muriel. ‘But even if Bathilda’s completely cuckoo, I’m sure she’d still have old photographs, maybe even letters. She knew the Dumbledores for years … well worth a trip to Godric’s Hollow, I’d have thought.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry, who had been taking a sip of Butterbeer, choked. Doge banged him on the back as Harry coughed, looking at Auntie Muriel through streaming eyes. Once he had control of his voice again, he asked, ‘Bathilda Bagshot lives in Godric’s Hollow?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes, she’s been there forever! The Dumbledores moved there after Percival was imprisoned, and she was their neighbour.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dumbledores lived in Godric’s Hollow?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Barry, that’s what I just said,’ said Auntie Muriel testily.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt drained, empty. Never once, in six years, had Dumbledore told Harry that they had both lived and lost loved ones in Godric’s Hollow. Why? Were Lily and James buried close to Dumbledore’s mother and sister? Had Dumbledore visited their graves, perhaps walked past Lily and James’s to do so? And he had never once told Harry … never bothered to say …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And why it was so important, Harry could not explain, even to himself, yet he felt it had been tantamount to a lie not to tell him that they had this place, and these experiences, in common.
