text_content: Excitement trickled through Harry, but he was not immediately sure why. He read the sign again. Hermione was already a flight of stairs below him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione,’ he said, and he was surprised that his voice was so calm. ‘Come back up here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s the matter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘R.A.B. I think I’ve found him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a gasp and then Hermione ran back up the stairs.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In your mum’s letter? But I didn’t see -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry shook his head, pointing at Regulus’s sign. She read it, then clutched Harry’s arm so tightly that he winced.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sirius’s brother?’ she whispered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He was a Death Eater,’ said Harry, ‘Sirius told me about him, he joined up when he was really young and then got cold feet and tried to leave - so they killed him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That fits!’ gasped Hermione. ‘If he was a Death Eater, he had access to Voldemort, and if he became disenchanted then he would have wanted to bring Voldemort down!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She released Harry, leaned over the banister and screamed, ‘Ron! RON! Get up here, quick!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron appeared, panting, a minute later, his wand ready in his hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s up? If it’s massive spiders again, I want breakfast before I -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He frowned at the sign on Regulus’s door, to which Hermione was silently pointing.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What? That was Sirius’s brother, wasn’t it? Regulus Arcturus … Regulus … R.A.B.! The locket - you don’t reckon -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Let’s find out,’ said Harry. He pushed the door: it was locked. Hermione pointed her wand at the handle and said, ‘Alohomora.’ There was a click, and the door swung open.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They moved over the threshold together, gazing around. Regulus’s bedroom was slightly smaller than Sirius’s, though it had the same sense of former grandeur. Whereas Sirius had sought to advertise his difference from the rest of the family, Regulus had striven to emphasise the opposite. The Slytherin colours of emerald and silver were everywhere, draping the bed, the walls and the windows. The Black family crest was painstakingly painted over the bed, along with its motto, Toujours Pur. Beneath this was a collection of yellow newspaper cuttings, all stuck together to make a ragged collage. Hermione crossed the room to examine them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re all about Voldemort,’ she said. ‘Regulus seems to have been a fan for a few years before he joined the Death Eaters …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A little puff of dust rose from the bedcovers as she sat down to read the clippings. Harry, meanwhile, had noticed another photograph; a Hogwarts Quidditch team was smiling and waving out of the frame. He moved closer and saw the snakes emblazoned on their chests: Slytherins. Regulus was instantly recognisable as the boy sitting in the middle of the front row: he had the same dark hair and slightly haughty look of his brother, though he was smaller, slighter and rather less handsome than Sirius had been.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He played Seeker,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Hermione vaguely; she was still immersed in Voldemort’s press clippings.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s sitting in the middle of the front row, that’s where the Seeker … never mind,’ said Harry, realising that nobody was listening: Ron was on his hands and knees, searching under the wardrobe. Harry looked around the room for likely hiding places and approached the desk. Yet again, somebody had searched before them. The drawers’ contents had been turned over recently, the dust disturbed, but there was nothing of value there: old quills, out of date textbooks that bore evidence of being roughly handled, a recently smashed ink bottle, its sticky residue covering the contents of the drawer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s an easier way,’ said Hermione, as Harry wiped his inky fingers on his jeans. She raised her wand and said, ‘Accio locket!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Nothing happened. Ron, who had been searching the folds of the faded curtains, looked disappointed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Is that it, then? It’s not here?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, it could still be here, but under counter-enchantments,’ said Hermione. ‘Charms to prevent it being summoned magically, you know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Like Voldemort put on the stone basin in the cave,’ said Harry, remembering how he had been unable to Summon the fake locket.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How are we supposed to find it, then?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We search manually,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s a good idea,’ said Ron, rolling his eyes, and he resumed his examination of the curtains.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They combed every inch of the room for over an hour, but were forced, finally, to conclude that the locket was not there.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The sun had risen now; its light dazzled them even through the grimy landing windows.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It could be somewhere else in the house, though,’ said Hermione in a rallying tone as they walked back downstairs: as Harry and Ron had become more discouraged, she seemed to have become more determined. ‘Whether he’d managed to destroy it or not, he’d want to keep it hidden from Voldemort, wouldn’t he? Remember all those awful things we had to get rid of when we were here last time? That clock that shot bolts at everyone and those old robes that tried to strangle Ron; Regulus might have put them there to protect the locket’s hiding place, even though we didn’t realise it at … at …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry and Ron looked at her. She was standing with one foot in mid-air, with the dumbstruck look of one who had just been Obliviated; her eyes had even drifted out of focus.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘… at the time,’ she finished in a whisper.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Something wrong?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There was a locket.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Harry and Ron together.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In the cabinet in the drawing room. Nobody could open it. And we … we …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt as though a brick had slid down through his chest into his stomach. He remembered: he had even handled the thing as they passed it round, each trying in turn to prise it open. It had been tossed into a sack of rubbish, along with the snuffbox of Wartcap powder and the music box that had made everyone sleepy …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher nicked loads of things back from us,’ said Harry. It was the only chance, the only slender hope left to them, and he was going to cling to it until forced to let go. ‘He had a whole stash of stuff in his cupboard in the kitchen. C’mon.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He ran down the stairs taking two steps at a time, the other two thundering along in his wake. They made so much noise that they woke the portrait of Sirius’s mother as they passed through the hall.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Filth! Mudbloods! Scum!’ she screamed after them as they dashed down into the basement kitchen and slammed the door behind them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry ran the length of the room, skidded to a halt at the door of Kreacher’s cupboard and wrenched it open. There was the nest of dirty, old blankets in which the house-elf had once slept, but they were no longer glittering with the trinkets Kreacher had salvaged. The only thing there was an old copy of Nature’s Nobility: A Wizarding Genealogy. Refusing to believe his eyes, Harry snatched up the blankets and shook them. A dead mouse fell out and rolled dismally across the floor. Ron groaned as he threw himself into a kitchen chair; Hermione closed her eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not over yet,’ said Harry, and he raised his voice and called, ‘Kreacher!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a loud crack and the house-elf that Harry had so reluctantly inherited from Sirius appeared out of nowhere in front of the cold and empty fireplace: tiny, half-human-sized, his pale skin hanging off him in folds, white hair sprouting copiously from his bat-like ears. He was still wearing the filthy rag in which they had first met him, and the contemptuous look he bent upon Harry showed that his attitude to his change of ownership had altered no more than his outfit.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master,’ croaked Kreacher in his bullfrog’s voice, and he bowed low, muttering to his knees, ‘back in my mistress’s old house with the blood traitor Weasley and the Mudblood -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I forbid you to call anyone “blood traitor” or “Mudblood”,’ growled Harry. He would have found Kreacher, with his snout-like nose and bloodshot eyes, a distinctly unlovable object even if the elf had not betrayed Sirius to Voldemort.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve got a question for you,’ said Harry, his heart beating rather fast as he looked down at the elf, ‘and I order you to answer it truthfully. Understand?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes, Master,’ said Kreacher, bowing low again: Harry saw his lips moving soundlessly, undoubtedly framing the insults he was now forbidden to utter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Two years ago,’ said Harry, his heart now hammering against his ribs, ‘there was a big gold locket in the drawing room upstairs. We threw it out. Did you steal it back?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a moment’s silence, during which Kreacher straightened up to look Harry full in the face. Then he said, ‘Yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Where is it now?’ asked Harry jubilantly, as Ron and Hermione looked gleeful.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher closed his eyes as though he could not bear to see their reactions to his next word.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Gone.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Gone?’ echoed Harry, elation flooding out of him. ‘What do you mean, it’s gone?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The elf shivered. He swayed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher,’ said Harry fiercely, ‘I order you -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Mundungus Fletcher,’ croaked the elf, his eyes still tight shut. ‘Mundungus Fletcher stole it all: Miss Bella and Miss Cissy’s pictures, my mistress’s gloves, the Order of Merlin, First Class, the goblets with the family crest, and, and -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher was gulping for air: his hollow chest was rising and falling rapidly, then his eyes flew open and he uttered a blood-curdling scream.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and the locket, Master Regulus’s locket, Kreacher did wrong, Kreacher failed in his orders!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry reacted instinctively: as Kreacher lunged for the poker standing in the grate, he launched himself upon the elf, flattening him. Hermione’s scream mingled with Kreacher’s, but Harry bellowed louder than both of them: ‘Kreacher, I order you to stay still!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He felt the elf freeze and released him. Kreacher lay flat on the cold stone floor, tears gushing from his sagging eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, let him up!’ Hermione whispered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So he can beat himself up with the poker?’ snorted Harry, kneeling beside the elf. ‘I don’t think so. Right, Kreacher, I want the truth: how do you know Mundungus Fletcher stole the locket?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher saw him!’ gasped the elf, as tears poured over his snout and into his mouth full of greying teeth. ‘Kreacher saw him coming out of Kreacher’s cupboard with his hands full of Kreacher’s treasures. Kreacher told the sneakthief to stop, but Mundungus Fletcher laughed and r - ran …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You called the locket “Master Regulus’s”,’ said Harry. ‘Why? Where did it come from? What did Regulus have to do with it? Kreacher, sit up and tell me everything you know about that locket, and everything Regulus had to do with it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The elf sat up, curled into a ball, placed his wet face between his knees and began to rock backwards and forwards. When he spoke, his voice was muffled but quite distinct in the silent, echoing kitchen.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master Sirius ran away, good riddance, for he was a bad boy and broke my mistress’s heart with his lawless ways. But Master Regulus had proper pride; he knew what was due to the name of Black and the dignity of his pure blood. For years he talked of the Dark Lord, who was going to bring the wizards out of hiding to rule the Muggles and the Muggle-borns … and when he was sixteen years old, Master Regulus joined the Dark Lord. So proud, so proud, so happy to serve …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And one day, a year after he had joined, Master Regulus came down to the kitchen to see Kreacher. Master Regulus always liked Kreacher. And Master Regulus said … he said …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The old elf rocked faster than ever.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘… he said that the Dark Lord required an elf.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort needed an elf ?’ Harry repeated, looking round at Ron and Hermione, who looked just as puzzled as he did.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes,’ moaned Kreacher. ‘And Master Regulus had volunteered Kreacher. It was an honour, said Master Regulus, an honour for him and for Kreacher, who must be sure to do whatever the Dark Lord ordered him to do … and then to c - come home.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher rocked still faster, his breath coming in sobs.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So Kreacher went to the Dark Lord. The Dark Lord did not tell Kreacher what they were to do, but took Kreacher with him to a cave beside the sea. And beyond the cave there was a cavern, and in the cavern was a great, black lake …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The hairs on the back of Harry’s neck stood up. Kreacher’s croaking voice seemed to come to him from across that dark water. He saw what had happened as clearly as though he had been present.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘… there was a boat …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Of course there had been a boat; Harry knew the boat, ghostly green and tiny, bewitched so as to carry one wizard and one victim towards the island in the centre. This, then, was how Voldemort had tested the defences surrounding the Horcrux: by borrowing a disposable creature, a house-elf …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There was a b - basin full of potion on the island. The D - Dark Lord made Kreacher drink it …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The elf quaked from head to foot.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher drank, and as he drank, he saw terrible things … Kreacher’s insides burned … Kreacher cried for Master Regulus to save him, he cried for his Mistress Black, but the Dark Lord only laughed … he made Kreacher drink all the potion … he dropped a locket into the empty basin … he filled it with more potion.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And then the Dark Lord sailed away, leaving Kreacher on the island …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could see it happening. He watched Voldemort’s white, snake-like face vanishing into darkness, those red eyes fixed pitilessly on the thrashing elf whose death would occur within minutes, whenever he succumbed to the desperate thirst that the burning potion caused its victim … but here, Harry’s imagination could go no further, for he could not see how Kreacher had escaped.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher needed water, he crawled to the island’s edge and he drank from the black lake … and hands, dead hands, came out of the water and dragged Kreacher under the surface …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How did you get away?’ Harry asked, and he was not surprised to hear himself whispering.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher raised his ugly head and looked at Harry with his great, bloodshot eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master Regulus told Kreacher to come back,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know - but how did you escape the Inferi?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher did not seem to understand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master Regulus told Kreacher to come back,’ he repeated.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know, but -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, it’s obvious, isn’t it, Harry?’ said Ron. ‘He Disapparated!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But … you couldn’t Apparate in and out of that cave,’ said Harry, ‘otherwise Dumbledore -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Elf magic isn’t like wizard’s magic, is it?’ said Ron. ‘I mean, they can Apparate and Disapparate in and out of Hogwarts when we can’t.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was silence as Harry digested this. How could Voldemort have made such a mistake? But even as he thought this, Hermione spoke, and her voice was icy.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course, Voldemort would have considered the ways of house-elves far beneath his notice, just like all the pure-bloods who treat them like animals … it would never have occurred to him that they might have magic that he didn’t.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The house-elf’s highest law is his master’s bidding,’ intoned Kreacher. ‘Kreacher was told to come home, so Kreacher came home …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, then, you did what you were told, didn’t you?’ said Hermione kindly. ‘You didn’t disobey orders at all!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher shook his head, rocking as fast as ever.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So what happened when you got back?’ Harry asked. ‘What did Regulus say when you told him what had happened?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master Regulus was very worried, very worried,’ croaked Kreacher. ‘Master Regulus told Kreacher to stay hidden, and not to leave the house. And then … it was a little while later … Master Regulus came to find Kreacher in his cupboard one night, and Master Regulus was strange, not as he usually was, disturbed in his mind, Kreacher could tell … and he asked Kreacher to take him to the cave, the cave where Kreacher had gone with the Dark Lord …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And so they had set off. Harry could visualise them quite clearly, the frightened old elf and the thin, dark Seeker who had so resembled Sirius … Kreacher knew how to open the concealed entrance to the underground cavern, knew how to raise the tiny boat; this time it was his beloved Regulus who sailed with him to the island with its basin of poison …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And he made you drink the potion?’ said Harry, disgusted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But Kreacher shook his head and wept. Hermione’s hands leapt to her mouth: she seemed to have understood something.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘M - Master Regulus took from his pocket a locket like the one the Dark Lord had,’ said Kreacher, tears pouring down either side of his snout-like nose. ‘And he told Kreacher to take it and, when the basin was empty, to switch the lockets …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher’s sobs came in great rasps now; Harry had to concentrate hard to understand him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And he ordered - Kreacher to leave - without him. And he told Kreacher - to go home - and never to tell my mistress - what he had done - but to destroy - the first locket. And he drank - all the potion - and Kreacher swapped the lockets - and watched … as Master Regulus … was dragged beneath the water … and …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, Kreacher!’ wailed Hermione, who was crying. She dropped to her knees beside the elf and tried to hug him. At once he was on his feet, cringing away from her, quite obviously repulsed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Mudblood touched Kreacher, he will not allow it, what would his mistress say?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I told you not to call her “Mudblood”!’ snarled Harry, but the elf was already punishing himself: he fell to the ground and banged his forehead on the floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stop him - stop him!’ Hermione cried. ‘Oh, don’t you see, now, how sick it is, the way they’ve got to obey?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher - stop, stop!’ shouted Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The elf lay on the floor, panting and shivering, green mucus glistening around his snout, a bruise already blooming on his pallid forehead where he had struck himself, his eyes swollen and bloodshot and swimming in tears. Harry had never seen anything so pitiful.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So you brought the locket home,’ he said relentlessly, for he was determined to know the full story. ‘And you tried to destroy it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Nothing Kreacher did made any mark upon it,’ moaned the elf. ‘Kreacher tried everything, everything he knew, but nothing, nothing would work … so many powerful spells upon the casing, Kreacher was sure the way to destroy it was to get inside it, but it would not open … Kreacher punished himself, he tried again, he punished himself, he tried again. Kreacher failed to obey orders, Kreacher could not destroy the locket! And his mistress was mad with grief, because Master Regulus had disappeared, and Kreacher could not tell her what had happened, no, because Master Regulus had f - f - forbidden him to tell any of the f - f - family what happened in the c - cave …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher began to sob so hard that there were no more coherent words. Tears flowed down Hermione’s cheeks as she watched Kreacher, but she did not dare touch him again. Even Ron, who was no fan of Kreacher’s, looked troubled. Harry sat back on his heels and shook his head, trying to clear it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t understand you, Kreacher,’ he said finally. ‘Voldemort tried to kill you, Regulus died to bring Voldemort down, but you were still happy to betray Sirius to Voldemort? You were happy to go to Narcissa and Bellatrix, and pass information to Voldemort through them …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, Kreacher doesn’t think like that,’ said Hermione, wiping her eyes on the back of her hand. ‘He’s a slave; house-elves are used to bad, even brutal treatment; what Voldemort did to Kreacher wasn’t that far out of the common way. What do wizard wars mean to an elf like Kreacher? He’s loyal to people who are kind to him, and Mrs Black must have been, and Regulus certainly was, so he served them willingly and parroted their beliefs. I know what you’re going to say,’ she went on, as Harry began to protest, ‘that Regulus changed his mind … but he doesn’t seem to have explained that to Kreacher, does he? And I think I know why. Kreacher and Regulus’s family were all safer if they kept to the old pure-blood line. Regulus was trying to protect them all.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sirius -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sirius was horrible to Kreacher, Harry, and it’s no good looking like that, you know it’s true. Kreacher had been alone for a long time when Sirius came to live here, and he was probably starving for a bit of affection. I’m sure “Miss Cissy” and “Miss Bella” were perfectly lovely to Kreacher when he turned up, so he did them a favour and told them everything they wanted to know. I’ve said all along that wizards would pay for how they treat house-elves. Well, Voldemort did … and so did Sirius.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had no retort. As he watched Kreacher sobbing on the floor, he remembered what Dumbledore had said to him, mere hours after Sirius’s death: I do not think Sirius ever saw Kreacher as a being with feelings as acute as a human’s …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher,’ said Harry, after a while, ‘when you feel up to it, er … please sit up.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was several minutes before Kreacher hiccoughed himself into silence. Then he pushed himself into a sitting position again, rubbing his knuckles into his eyes like a small child.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher, I am going to ask you to do something,’ said Harry. He glanced at Hermione for assistance: he wanted to give the order kindly, but at the same time, he could not pretend that it was not an order. However, the change in his tone seemed to have gained her approval: she smiled encouragingly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher, I want you, please, to go and find Mundungus Fletcher. We need to find out where the locket - where Master Regulus’s locket is. It’s really important. We want to finish the work Master Regulus started, we want to - er - ensure that he didn’t die in vain.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher dropped his fists and looked up at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Find Mundungus Fletcher?’ he croaked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And bring him here, to Grimmauld Place,’ said Harry. ‘Do you think you could do that for us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: As Kreacher nodded and got to his feet, Harry had a sudden inspiration. He pulled out Hagrid’s purse and took out the fake Horcrux, the substitute locket in which Regulus had placed the note to Voldemort.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Kreacher, I’d, er, like you to have this,’ he said, pressing the locket into the elf’s hand. ‘This belonged to Regulus and I’m sure he’d want you to have it as a token of gratitude for what you -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Overkill, mate,’ said Ron, as the elf took one look at the locket, let out a howl of shock and misery and threw himself back on to the ground.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It took them nearly half an hour to calm down Kreacher, who was so overcome to be presented with a Black family heirloom for his very own that he was too weak at the knees to stand properly. When finally he was able to totter a few steps, they all accompanied him to his cupboard, watched him tuck up the locket safely in his dirty blankets, and assured him that they would make its protection their first priority while he was away. He then made two low bows to Harry and Ron, and even gave a funny little spasm in Hermione’s direction that might have been an attempt at a respectful salute, before Disapparating with the usual loud crack.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: If Kreacher could escape a lake full of Inferi, Harry was confident that the capture of Mundungus would take a few hours at most, and he prowled the house all morning in a state of high anticipation. However, Kreacher did not return that morning, or even that afternoon. By nightfall, Harry felt discouraged and anxious, and a supper composed largely of mouldy bread, upon which Hermione had tried a variety of unsuccessful Transfigurations, did nothing to help.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Kreacher did not return the following day, nor the day after that. However, two cloaked men had appeared in the square outside number twelve, and they remained there into the night, gazing in the direction of the house that they could not see.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Death Eaters, for sure,’ said Ron, as he, Harry and Hermione watched from the drawing-room windows. ‘Reckon they know we’re in here?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t think so,’ said Hermione, though she looked frightened, ‘or they’d have sent Snape in after us, wouldn’t they?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘D’you reckon he’s been in here and had his tongue tied by Moody’s curse?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Hermione, ‘otherwise he’d have been able to tell that lot how to get in, wouldn’t he? But they’re probably watching to see whether we turn up. They know that Harry owns the house, after all.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How do they -?’ began Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Wizarding wills are examined by the Ministry, remember? They’ll know Sirius left you the place.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The presence of the Death Eaters outside increased the ominous mood inside number twelve. They had not heard a word from anyone beyond Grimmauld Place since Mr Weasley’s Patronus, and the strain was starting to tell. Restless and irritable, Ron had developed an annoying habit of playing with the Deluminator in his pocket: this particularly infuriated Hermione, who was whiling away the wait for Kreacher by studying The Tales of Beedle the Bard and did not appreciate the way the lights kept flashing on and off.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Will you stop it!’ she cried on the third evening of Kreacher’s absence, as all light was sucked from the drawing room yet again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Sorry, sorry!’ said Ron, clicking the Deluminator and restoring the lights. ‘I don’t know I’m doing it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, can’t you find something useful to occupy yourself?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What, like reading kids’ stories?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore left me this book, Ron -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and he left me the Deluminator, maybe I’m supposed to use it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Unable to stand the bickering, Harry slipped out of the room unnoticed by either of them. He headed downstairs towards the kitchen, which he kept visiting because he was sure that was where Kreacher was most likely to reappear. Halfway down the flight of stairs into the hall, however, he heard a tap on the front door, then metallic clicks and the grinding of the chain.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Every nerve in his body seemed to tauten: he pulled out his wand, moved into the shadows beside the decapitated elf-heads and waited. The door opened: he saw a glimpse of the lamplit square outside, and a cloaked figure edged into the hall and closed the door behind it. The intruder took a step forwards and Moody’s voice asked, ‘Severus Snape?’ Then the dust figure rose from the end of the hall and rushed him, raising its dead hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It was not I who killed you, Albus,’ said a quiet voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The jinx broke: the dust figure exploded again, and it was impossible to make out the newcomer through the dense grey cloud it left behind.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry pointed his wand into the middle of it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t move!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He had forgotten the portrait of Mrs Black: at the sound of his yell the curtains hiding her flew open and she began to scream, ‘Mudbloods and filth dishonouring my house -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione came crashing down the stairs behind Harry, wands pointing, like his, at the unknown man now standing with his arms raised in the hall below.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hold your fire, it’s me, Remus!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, thank goodness,’ said Hermione weakly, pointing her wand at Mrs Black instead; with a bang, the curtains swished shut again and silence fell. Ron, too, lowered his wand, but Harry did not.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Show yourself!’ he called back.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin moved forwards into the lamplight, hands still held high in a gesture of surrender.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I am Remus John Lupin, werewolf, sometimes known as Moony, one of the four creators of the Marauder’s Map, married to Nymphadora, usually known as Tonks, and I taught you how to produce a Patronus, Harry, which takes the form of a stag.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, all right,’ said Harry, lowering his wand, ‘but I had to check, didn’t I?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Speaking as your ex-Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher, I quite agree that you had to check. Ron, Hermione, you shouldn’t be quite so quick to lower your defences.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They ran down the stairs towards him. Wrapped in a thick, black travelling cloak, he looked exhausted, but pleased to see them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No sign of Severus, then?’ he asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry. ‘What’s going on? Is everyone OK?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Lupin, ‘but we’re all being watched. There are a couple of Death Eaters in the square outside -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- we know -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- I had to Apparate very precisely on to the top step outside the front door to be sure that they would not see me. They can’t know you’re in here or I’m sure they’d have more people out there; they’re staking out everywhere that’s got any connection with you, Harry. Let’s go downstairs, there’s a lot to tell you and I want to know what happened after you left The Burrow.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They descended into the kitchen, where Hermione pointed her wand at the grate. A fire sprang up instantly: it gave the illusion of cosiness to the stark stone walls and glistened off the long wooden table. Lupin pulled a few Butterbeers from beneath his travelling cloak and they sat down.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’d have been here three days ago but I needed to shake off the Death Eater tailing me,’ said Lupin. ‘So, you came straight here after the wedding?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry, ‘only after we ran into a couple of Death Eaters in a cafe on Tottenham Court Road.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin slopped most of his Butterbeer down his front.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They explained what had happened; when they had finished, Lupin looked aghast.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But how did they find you so quickly? It’s impossible to track anyone who Apparates, unless you grab hold of them as they disappear!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And it doesn’t seem likely they were just strolling down Tottenham Court Road at the time, does it?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We wondered,’ said Hermione tentatively, ‘whether Harry could still have the Trace on him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Impossible,’ said Lupin. Ron looked smug, and Harry felt hugely relieved. ‘Apart from anything else, they’d know for sure Harry was here if he still had the Trace on him, wouldn’t they? But I can’t see how they could have tracked you to Tottenham Court Road, that’s worrying, really worrying.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He looked disturbed, but as far as Harry was concerned, that question could wait.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell us what happened after we left, we haven’t heard a thing since Ron’s dad told us the family were safe.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Kingsley saved us,’ said Lupin. ‘Thanks to his warning most of the wedding guests were able to Disapparate before they arrived.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Were they Death Eaters or Ministry people?’ interjected Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘A mixture; but to all intents and purposes they’re the same thing now,’ said Lupin. ‘There were about a dozen of them, but they didn’t know you were there, Harry. Arthur heard a rumour that they tried to torture your whereabouts out of Scrimgeour before they killed him; if it’s true, he didn’t give you away.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked at Ron and Hermione; their expressions reflected the mingled shock and gratitude he felt. He had never liked Scrimgeour much, but if what Lupin said was true, the man’s final act had been to try to protect Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Death Eaters searched The Burrow from top to bottom,’ Lupin went on. ‘They found the ghoul, but didn’t want to get too close - and then they interrogated those of us who remained for hours. They were trying to get information on you, Harry, but, of course, nobody apart from the Order knew that you had been there.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘At the same time that they were smashing up the wedding, more Death Eaters were forcing their way into every Order-connected house in the country. No deaths,’ he added quickly, forestalling the question, ‘but they were rough. They burned down Dedalus Diggle’s house, but as you know he wasn’t there, and they used the Cruciatus Curse on Tonks’s family. Again, trying to find out where you went after you visited them. They’re all right - shaken, obviously, but otherwise OK.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Death Eaters got through all those protective charms?’ Harry asked, remembering how effective these had been on the night he had crashed in Tonks’s parents’ garden.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What you’ve got to realise, Harry, is that the Death Eaters have got the full might of the Ministry on their side now,’ said Lupin. ‘They’ve got the power to perform brutal spells without fear of identification or arrest. They managed to penetrate every defensive spell we’d cast against them, and once inside, they were completely open about why they’d come.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And are they bothering to give an excuse for torturing Harry’s whereabouts out of people?’ asked Hermione, an edge to her voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Lupin. He hesitated, then pulled out a folded copy of the Daily Prophet.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Here,’ he said, pushing it across the table to Harry, ‘you’ll know sooner or later anyway. That’s their pretext for going after you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry smoothed out the paper. A huge photograph of his own face filled the front page. He read the headline over it:

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: WANTED FOR QUESTIONING ABOUT THE DEATH OF ALBUS DUMBLEDORE

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione gave roars of outrage, but Harry said nothing. He pushed the newspaper away; he did not want to read any more: he knew what it would say. Nobody but those who had been on top of the tower when Dumbledore died knew who had really killed him and, as Rita Skeeter had already told the wizarding world, Harry had been seen running from the place moments after Dumbledore had fallen.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry, Harry,’ Lupin said.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So Death Eaters have taken over the Daily Prophet too?’ asked Hermione furiously.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin nodded.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But surely people realise what’s going on?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The coup has been smooth and virtually silent,’ said Lupin. ‘The official version of Scrimgeour’s murder is that he resigned; he has been replaced by Pius Thicknesse, who is under the Imperius Curse.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why didn’t Voldemort declare himself Minister for Magic?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin laughed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He doesn’t need to, Ron. Effectively he is the Minister, but why should he sit behind a desk at the Ministry? His puppet, Thicknesse, is taking care of everyday business, leaving Voldemort free to extend his power beyond the Ministry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Naturally many people have deduced what has happened: there has been such a dramatic change in Ministry policy in the last few days, and many are whispering that Voldemort must be behind it. However, that is the point: they whisper. They daren’t confide in each other, not knowing whom to trust; they are scared to speak out, in case their suspicions are true and their families are targeted. Yes, Voldemort is playing a very clever game. Declaring himself might have provoked open rebellion: remaining masked has created confusion, uncertainty and fear.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And this dramatic change in Ministry policy,’ said Harry, ‘involves warning the wizarding world against me instead of Voldemort?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That’s certainly part of it,’ said Lupin, ‘and it is a masterstroke. Now that Dumbledore is dead, you - the Boy Who Lived - were sure to be the symbol and rallying point for any resistance to Voldemort. But by suggesting that you had a hand in the old hero’s death, Voldemort has not only set a price upon your head, but sown doubt and fear amongst many who would have defended you.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Meanwhile, the Ministry has started moving against Muggleborns.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin pointed at the Daily Prophet.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Look at page two.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione turned the pages with much the same expression of distaste she had worn when handling Secrets of The Darkest Art.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“Muggle-born Register”,’ she read aloud. ‘“The Ministry of Magic is undertaking a survey of so-called ‘Muggle-borns’, the better to understand how they came to possess magical secrets.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“Recent research undertaken by the Department of Mysteries reveals that magic can only be passed from person to person when wizards reproduce. Where no proven wizarding ancestry exists, therefore, the so-called Muggle-born is likely to have obtained magical power by theft or force.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“The Ministry is determined to root out such usurpers of magical power, and to this end has issued an invitation to every so-called Muggle-born to present themselves for interview by the newly appointed Muggle-born Registration Commission.”’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘People won’t let this happen,’ said Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It is happening, Ron,’ said Lupin. ‘Muggle-borns are being rounded up as we speak.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But how are they supposed to have “stolen” magic?’ said Ron. ‘It’s mental, if you could steal magic there wouldn’t be any Squibs, would there?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know,’ said Lupin. ‘Nevertheless, unless you can prove that you have at least one close wizarding relative, you are now deemed to have obtained your magical power illegally and must suffer the punishment.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron glanced at Hermione, then said, ‘What if pure-bloods and half-bloods swear a Muggle-born’s part of their family? I’ll tell everyone Hermione’s my cousin -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione covered Ron’s hand with hers and squeezed it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you, Ron, but I couldn’t let you -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You won’t have a choice,’ said Ron fiercely, gripping her hand back. ‘I’ll teach you my family tree so you can answer questions on it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione gave a shaky laugh.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron, as we’re on the run with Harry Potter, the most wanted person in the country, I don’t think it matters. If I was going back to school, it would be different. What’s Voldemort planning for Hogwarts?’ she asked Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Attendance is now compulsory for every young witch and wizard,’ he replied. ‘That was announced yesterday. It’s a change, because it was never obligatory before. Of course, nearly every witch and wizard in Britain has been educated at Hogwarts, but their parents had the right to teach them at home or send them abroad if they preferred. This way, Voldemort will have the whole wizarding population under his eye from a young age. And it’s also another way of weeding out Muggle-borns, because students must be given Blood Status - meaning that they have proven to the Ministry that they are of wizard descent - before they are allowed to attend.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt sickened and angry: at this moment excited eleven-year-olds would be poring over stacks of newly purchased spellbooks, unaware that they would never see Hogwarts, perhaps never see their families again, either.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s … it’s …’ he muttered, struggling to find words that did justice to the horror of his thoughts, but Lupin said quietly, ‘I know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin hesitated.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ll understand if you can’t confirm this, Harry, but the Order is under the impression that Dumbledore left you a mission.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He did,’ Harry replied, ‘and Ron and Hermione are in on it and they’re coming with me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Can you confide in me what the mission is?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked into the prematurely lined face, framed in thick but greying hair, and wished that he could return a different answer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t, Remus, I’m sorry. If Dumbledore didn’t tell you, I don’t think I can.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought you’d say that,’ said Lupin, looking disappointed. ‘But I might still be of some use to you. You know what I am and what I can do. I could come with you to provide protection. There would be no need to tell me exactly what you were up to.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry hesitated. It was a very tempting offer, though how they would be able to keep their mission secret from Lupin if he were with them all the time he could not imagine.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione, however, looked puzzled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But what about Tonks?’ she asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What about her?’ said Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Hermione, frowning, ‘you’re married! How does she feel about you going away with us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tonks will be perfectly safe,’ said Lupin. ‘She’ll be at her parents’ house.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was something strange in Lupin’s tone; it was almost cold. There was also something odd in the idea of Tonks remaining hidden at her parents’ house; she was, after all, a member of the Order and, as far as Harry knew, was likely to want to be in the thick of the action.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Remus,’ said Hermione tentatively, ‘is everything all right … you know … between you and -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Everything is fine, thank you,’ said Lupin pointedly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione turned pink. There was another pause, an awkward and embarrassed one, and then Lupin said, with an air of forcing himself to admit something unpleasant, ‘Tonks is going to have a baby.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, how wonderful!’ squealed Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Excellent!’ said Ron enthusiastically.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Congratulations,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin gave an artificial smile that was more like a grimace, then said, ‘So … do you accept my offer? Will three become four? I cannot believe that Dumbledore would have disapproved, he appointed me your Defence Against the Dark Arts teacher, after all. And I must tell you that I believe that we are facing magic many of us have never encountered or imagined.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione both looked at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Just - just to be clear,’ he said. ‘You want to leave Tonks at her parents’ house and come away with us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She’ll be perfectly safe there, they’ll look after her,’ said Lupin. He spoke with a finality bordering on indifference. ‘Harry, I’m sure James would have wanted me to stick with you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ said Harry slowly, ‘I’m not. I’m pretty sure my father would have wanted to know why you aren’t sticking with your own kid, actually.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin’s face drained of colour. The temperature in the kitchen might have dropped ten degrees. Ron stared around the room as though he had been bidden to memorise it, while Hermione’s eyes swivelled backwards and forwards from Harry to Lupin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t understand,’ said Lupin at last.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Explain, then,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin swallowed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I - I made a grave mistake in marrying Tonks. I did it against my better judgement and I have regretted it very much ever since.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I see,’ said Harry, ‘so you’re just going to dump her and the kid and run off with us?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin sprang to his feet: his chair toppled over backwards, and he glared at them so fiercely that Harry saw, for the first time ever, the shadow of the wolf upon his human face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t you understand what I’ve done to my wife and my unborn child? I should never have married her, I’ve made her an outcast!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin kicked aside the chair he had overturned.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You have only ever seen me amongst the Order, or under Dumbledore’s protection at Hogwarts! You don’t know how most of the wizarding world sees creatures like me! When they know of my affliction, they can barely talk to me! Don’t you see what I’ve done? Even her own family is disgusted by our marriage, what parents want their only daughter to marry a werewolf? And the child - the child -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Lupin actually seized handfuls of his own hair; he looked quite deranged.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My kind don’t usually breed! It will be like me, I am convinced of it - how can I forgive myself, when I knowingly risked passing on my own condition to an innocent child? And if, by some miracle, it is not like me, then it will be better off, a hundred times so, without a father of whom it must always be ashamed!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Remus!’ whispered Hermione, tears in her eyes. ‘Don’t say that - how could any child be ashamed of you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I don’t know, Hermione,’ said Harry. ‘I’d be pretty ashamed of him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry did not know where his rage was coming from, but it had propelled him to his feet too. Lupin looked as though Harry had hit him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
