book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There were several distinct splashes and then the slapping sounds of fish against flesh. Somebody grunted appreciatively. Harry pressed the Extendable Ear deeper into his own: over the murmur of the river he could make out more voices, but they were not speaking English or any human language he had ever heard. It was a rough and unmelodious tongue, a string of rattling, guttural noises, and there seemed to be two speakers, one with a slightly lower, slower voice than the other.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A fire danced into life on the other side of the canvas; large shadows passed between tent and flames. The delicious smell of baking salmon wafted tantalisingly in their direction. Then came the clinking of cutlery on plates, and the first man spoke again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Here, Griphook, Gornuk.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Goblins! Hermione mouthed at Harry, who nodded.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you,’ said the goblins together in English.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So, you three have been on the run, how long?’ asked a new, mellow and pleasant voice; it was vaguely familiar to Harry, who pictured a round-bellied, cheerful-faced man.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Six weeks … seven … I forget,’ said the tired man. ‘Met up with Griphook in the first couple of days and joined forces with Gornuk not long after. Nice to have a bit of company.’ There was a pause, while knives scraped plates and tin mugs were picked up and replaced on the ground. ‘What made you leave, Ted?’ continued the man.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Knew they were coming for me,’ replied mellow-voiced Ted, and Harry suddenly knew who he was: Tonks’s father. ‘Heard Death Eaters were in the area last week and decided I’d better run for it. Refused to register as a Muggle-born on principle, see, so I knew it was a matter of time, knew I’d have to leave in the end. My wife should be OK, she’s pure-blood. And then I met Dean here, what, a few days ago, son?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said another voice, and Harry, Ron and Hermione stared at each other, silent but beside themselves with excitement, sure they recognised the voice of Dean Thomas, their fellow Gryffindor.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Muggle-born, eh?’ asked the first man.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not sure,’ said Dean. ‘My dad left my mum when I was a kid. I’ve got no proof he was a wizard, though.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was silence for a while, except for the sounds of munching; then Ted spoke again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’ve got to say, Dirk, I’m surprised to run into you. Pleased, but surprised. Word was you’d been caught.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was,’ said Dirk. ‘I was halfway to Azkaban when I made a break for it, Stunned Dawlish and nicked his broom. It was easier than you’d think; I don’t reckon he’s quite right at the moment. Might be Confunded. If so, I’d like to shake the hand of the witch or wizard who did it, probably saved my life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was another pause, in which the fire crackled and the river rushed on. Then Ted said, ‘And where do you two fit in? I, er, had the impression the goblins were for You-Know-Who, on the whole.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You had a false impression,’ said the higher-voiced of the goblins. ‘We take no sides. This is a wizards’ war.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How come you’re in hiding, then?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I deemed it prudent,’ said the deeper-voiced goblin. ‘Having refused what I considered an impertinent request, I could see that my personal safety was in jeopardy.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What did they ask you to do?’ asked Ted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Duties ill-befitting the dignity of my race,’ replied the goblin, his voice rougher and less human as he said it. ‘I am not a house-elf.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What about you, Griphook?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Similar reasons,’ said the higher-voiced goblin. ‘Gringotts is no longer under the sole control of my race. I recognise no wizarding master.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He added something under his breath in Gobbledegook and Gornuk laughed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s the joke?’ asked Dean.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He said,’ replied Dirk, ‘that there are things wizards don’t recognise, either.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a short pause.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t get it,’ said Dean.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I had my small revenge before I left,’ said Griphook in English.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good man - goblin, I should say,’ amended Ted hastily. ‘Didn’t manage to lock a Death Eater up in one of the old high-security vaults, I suppose?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If I had, the sword would not have helped him break out,’ replied Griphook. Gornuk laughed again and even Dirk gave a dry chuckle.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dean and I are still missing something here,’ said Ted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So is Severus Snape, though he does not know it,’ said Griphook, and the two goblins roared with malicious laughter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Inside the tent Harry’s breathing was shallow with excitement: he and Hermione stared at each other, listening as hard as they could.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Didn’t you hear about that, Ted?’ asked Dirk. ‘About the kids who tried to steal Gryffindor’s sword out of Snape’s office at Hogwarts?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: An electric current seemed to course through Harry, jangling his every nerve as he stood rooted to the spot.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Never heard a word,’ said Ted. ‘Not in the Prophet, was it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hardly,’ chortled Dirk. ‘Griphook here told me, he heard about it from Bill Weasley who works for the bank. One of the kids who tried to take the sword was Bill’s younger sister.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry glanced towards Hermione and Ron, both of whom were clutching the Extendable Ears as tightly as lifelines.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She and a couple of friends got into Snape’s office and smashed open the glass case where he was apparently keeping the sword. Snape caught them as they were trying to smuggle it down the staircase.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, God bless ‘em,’ said Ted. ‘What did they think, that they’d be able to use the sword on You-Know-Who? Or on Snape himself?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, whatever they thought they were going to do with it, Snape decided the sword wasn’t safe where it was,’ said Dirk. ‘Couple of days later, once he’d got the say so from You-Know-Who, I imagine, he sent it down to London to be kept in Gringotts instead.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The goblins started to laugh again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m still not seeing the joke,’ said Ted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s a fake,’ rasped Griphook.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The sword of Gryffindor!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes. It is a copy - an excellent copy, it is true - but it was wizard-made. The original was forged centuries ago by goblins and had certain properties only goblin-made armour possesses. Wherever the genuine sword of Gryffindor is, it is not in a vault at Gringotts Bank.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I see,’ said Ted. ‘And I take it you didn’t bother telling the Death Eaters this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I saw no reason to trouble them with the information,’ said Griphook smugly, and now Ted and Dean joined in Gornuk and Dirk’s laughter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Inside the tent, Harry closed his eyes, willing someone to ask the question he needed answered, and after a minute that seemed ten, Dean obliged; he was (Harry remembered with a jolt) an ex-boyfriend of Ginny’s too.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What happened to Ginny and the others? The ones who tried to steal it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, they were punished, and cruelly,’ said Griphook indifferently.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They’re OK, though?’ asked Ted quickly. ‘I mean, the Weasleys don’t need any more of their kids injured, do they?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They suffered no serious injury, as far as I am aware,’ said Griphook.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Lucky for them,’ said Ted. ‘With Snape’s track record, I suppose we should just be glad they’re still alive.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You believe that story, then, do you, Ted?’ asked Dirk. ‘You believe Snape killed Dumbledore?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ”Course I do,’ said Ted. ‘You’re not going to sit there and tell me you think Potter had anything to do with it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hard to know what to believe these days,’ muttered Dirk.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know Harry Potter,’ said Dean. ‘And I reckon he’s the real thing - the Chosen One, or whatever you want to call it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, there’s a lot would like to believe he’s that, son,’ said Dirk, ‘me included. But where is he? Run for it, by the looks of things. You’d think, if he knew anything we don’t, or had anything special going for him, he’d be out there now fighting, rallying resistance, instead of hiding. And you know, the Prophet made a pretty good case against him -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Prophet?’ scoffed Ted. ‘You deserve to be lied to if you’re still reading that muck, Dirk. You want the facts, try The Quibbler.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a sudden explosion of choking and retching, plus a good deal of thumping; by the sound of it, Dirk had swallowed a fishbone. At last he spluttered, ‘The Quibbler? That lunatic rag of Xeno Lovegood’s?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not so lunatic these days,’ said Ted. ‘You want to give it a look. Xeno is printing all the stuff the Prophet‘s ignoring, not a single mention of Crumple-Horned Snorkacks in the last issue. How long they’ll let him get away with it, mind, I don’t know. But Xeno says, front page of every issue, that any wizard who’s against You-Know-Who ought to make helping Harry Potter their number one priority.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hard to help a boy who’s vanished off the face of the earth,’ said Dirk.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Listen, the fact that they haven’t caught him yet’s one hell of an achievement,’ said Ted. ‘I’d take tips from him gladly. It’s what we’re trying to do, stay free, isn’t it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, you’ve got a point there,’ said Dirk heavily. ‘With the whole of the Ministry and all their informers looking for him, I’d have expected him to be caught by now. Mind, who’s to say they haven’t already caught and killed him without publicising it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, don’t say that, Dirk,’ murmured Ted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a long pause filled with more clattering of knives and forks. When they spoke again, it was to discuss whether they ought to sleep on the bank or retreat back up the wooded slope. Deciding the trees would give better cover, they extinguished their fire, then clambered back up the incline, their voices fading away.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione reeled in the Extendable Ears. Harry, who had found the need to remain silent increasingly difficult the longer they eavesdropped, now found himself unable to say more than, ‘Ginny - the sword -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know!’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She lunged for the tiny beaded bag, this time sinking her arm in it right up to the armpit.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Here … we … are …’ she said between gritted teeth, and she pulled at something that was evidently in the depths of the bag. Slowly, the edge of an ornate picture frame came into sight. Harry hurried to help her. As they lifted the empty portrait of Phineas Nigellus free of Hermione’s bag, she kept her wand pointing at it, ready to cast a spell at any moment.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If somebody swapped the real sword for the fake while it was in Dumbledore’s office,’ she panted, as they propped the painting against the side of the tent, ‘Phineas Nigellus would have seen it happen, he hangs right beside the case!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Unless he was asleep,’ said Harry, but he still held his breath as Hermione knelt down in front of the empty canvas, her wand directed at its centre, cleared her throat, then said, ‘Er - Phineas? Phineas Nigellus?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Nothing happened.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Phineas Nigellus?’ said Hermione again. ‘Professor Black? Please could we talk to you? Please?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“Please” always helps,’ said a cold, snide voice, and Phineas Nigellus slid into his portrait. At once, Hermione cried, ‘Obscuro!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A black blindfold appeared over Phineas Nigellus’s clever, dark eyes, causing him to bump into the frame and shriek with pain.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What - how dare - what are you -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m very sorry, Professor Black,’ said Hermione, ‘but it’s a necessary precaution!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Remove this foul addition at once! Remove it, I say! You are ruining a great work of art! Where am I? What is going on?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Never mind where we are,’ said Harry, and Phineas Nigellus froze, abandoning his attempts to peel off the painted blindfold.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Can that possibly be the voice of the elusive Mr Potter?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Maybe,’ said Harry, knowing that this would keep Phineas Nigellus’s interest. ‘We’ve got a couple of questions to ask you - about the sword of Gryffindor.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ said Phineas Nigellus, now turning his head this way and that in an effort to catch sight of Harry, ‘yes. That silly girl acted most unwisely there -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Shut up about my sister,’ said Ron roughly. Phineas Nigellus raised supercilious eyebrows.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Who else is here?’ he asked, turning his head from side to side. ‘Your tone displeases me! The girl and her friends were foolhardy in the extreme. Thieving from the Headmaster!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They weren’t thieving,’ said Harry. ‘That sword isn’t Snape’s.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It belongs to Professor Snape’s school,’ said Phineas Nigellus. ‘Exactly what claim did the Weasley girl have upon it? She deserved her punishment, as did the idiot Longbottom and the Lovegood oddity!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville is not an idiot and Luna is not an oddity!’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Where am I?’ repeated Phineas Nigellus, starting to wrestle with the blindfold again. ‘Where have you brought me? Why have you removed me from the house of my forebears?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Never mind that! How did Snape punish Ginny, Neville and Luna?’ asked Harry urgently.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Snape sent them into the Forbidden Forest, to do some work for the oaf, Hagrid.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hagrid’s not an oaf!’ said Hermione shrilly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And Snape might’ve thought that was a punishment,’ said Harry, ‘but Ginny, Neville and Luna probably had a good laugh with Hagrid. The Forbidden Forest … they’ve faced plenty worse than the Forbidden Forest, big deal!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He felt relieved; he had been imagining horrors, the Cruciatus Curse at the very least.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What we really wanted to know, Professor Black, is whether anyone else has, um, taken out the sword at all? Maybe it’s been taken away for cleaning or - or something?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Phineas Nigellus paused again in his struggles to free his eyes and sniggered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Muggle-borns,’ he said. ‘Goblin-made armour does not require cleaning, simple girl. Goblins’ silver repels mundane dirt, imbibing only that which strengthens it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t call Hermione simple,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I grow weary of contradiction,’ said Phineas Nigellus. ‘Perhaps it is time for me to return to the Headmaster’s office?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Still blindfolded, he began groping the side of his frame, trying to feel his way out of his picture and back into the one at Hogwarts. Harry had a sudden inspiration.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore! Can’t you bring us Dumbledore?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I beg your pardon?’ asked Phineas Nigellus.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Dumbledore’s portrait - couldn’t you bring him along, here, into yours?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Phineas Nigellus turned his face in the direction of Harry’s voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Evidently it is not only Muggle-borns who are ignorant, Potter. The portraits of Hogwarts may commune with each other, but they cannot travel outside the castle except to visit a painting of themselves hanging elsewhere. Dumbledore cannot come here with me, and after the treatment I have received at your hands, I can assure you that I shall not be making a return visit!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Slightly crestfallen, Harry watched Phineas redouble his attempts to leave his frame.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Black,’ said Hermione, ‘couldn’t you just tell us, please, when was the last time the sword was taken out of its case? Before Ginny took it out, I mean?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Phineas snorted impatiently.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I believe that the last time I saw the sword of Gryffindor leave its case was when Professor Dumbledore used it to break open a ring.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione whipped round to look at Harry. Neither of them dared say more in front of Phineas Nigellus, who had at last managed to locate the exit.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, goodnight to you,’ he said, a little waspishly, and he began to move out of sight again. Only the edge of his hat brim remained in view when Harry gave a sudden shout.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Wait! Have you told Snape you saw this?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Phineas Nigellus stuck his blindfolded head back into the picture.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Snape has more important things on his mind than the many eccentricities of Albus Dumbledore. Goodbye, Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And with that, he vanished completely, leaving behind him nothing but his murky backdrop.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry!’ Hermione cried.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know!’ Harry shouted. Unable to contain himself, he punched the air: it was more than he had dared to hope for. He strode up and down the tent, feeling that he could have run a mile; he did not even feel hungry any more. Hermione was squashing Phineas Nigellus’s portrait back into the beaded bag; when she had fastened the clasp, she threw the bag aside and raised a shining face to Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The sword can destroy Horcruxes! Goblin-made blades imbibe only that which strengthens them - Harry, that sword’s impregnated with Basilisk venom!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And Dumbledore didn’t give it to me because he still needed it, he wanted to use it on the locket -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and he must have realised they wouldn’t let you have it if he put it in his will -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- so he made a copy -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and put a fake in the glass case -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and he left the real one … where?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They gazed at each other; Harry felt that the answer was dangling invisibly in the air above them, tantalisingly close. Why hadn’t Dumbledore told him? Or had he, in fact, told Harry, but Harry had not realised it at the time?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Think!’ whispered Hermione. ‘Think! Where would he have left it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not at Hogwarts,’ said Harry, resuming his pacing.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Somewhere in Hogsmeade?’ suggested Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Shrieking Shack?’ said Harry. ‘Nobody ever goes in there.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But Snape knows how to get in, wouldn’t that be a bit risky?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Dumbledore trusted Snape,’ Harry reminded her.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not enough to tell him that he had swapped the swords,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, you’re right!’ said Harry; and he felt even more cheered at the thought that Dumbledore had had some reservations, however faint, about Snape’s trustworthiness. ‘So, would he have hidden the sword well away from Hogsmeade, then? What d’you reckon, Ron? Ron?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked around. For one bewildered moment he thought that Ron had left the tent, then realised that Ron was lying in the shadow of a lower bunk, looking stony.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, remembered me, have you?’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron snorted as he stared up at the underside of the upper bunk.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You two carry on. Don’t let me spoil your fun.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Perplexed, Harry looked to Hermione for help, but she shook her head, apparently as nonplussed as he was.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s the problem?’ asked Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Problem? There’s no problem,’ said Ron, still refusing to look at Harry. ‘Not according to you, anyway.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There were several plunks on the canvas over their heads. It had started to rain.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, you’ve obviously got a problem,’ said Harry. ‘Spit it out, will you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron swung his long legs off the bed and sat up. He looked mean, unlike himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All right, I’ll spit it out. Don’t expect me to skip up and down the tent because there’s some other damn thing we’ve got to find. Just add it to the list of stuff you don’t know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know?’ repeated Harry. ‘I don’t know?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Plunk, plunk, plunk: the rain was falling harder and heavier; it pattered on the leaf-strewn bank all around them and into the river chattering through the dark. Dread doused Harry’s jubilation: Ron was saying exactly what he had suspected and feared him to be thinking.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not like I’m not having the time of my life here,’ said Ron, ‘you know, with my arm mangled and nothing to eat and freezing my backside off every night. I just hoped, you know, after we’d been running round a few weeks, we’d have achieved something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron,’ Hermione said, but in such a quiet voice that Ron could pretend not to have heard it over the loud tattoo the rain was now beating on the tent.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought you knew what you’d signed up for,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: The muddy river beside them was rising rapidly and would soon spill over on to their bank. They had lingered a good hour after they would usually have departed their campsite. Everything inside him felt cold and tight: again he saw the contemptuous expression on Ron’s face. Harry strode off through the heather, walking in a large circle with the distraught Hermione at its centre, casting the spells she usually performed to ensure their protection.

text_content: They did not discuss Ron at all over the next few days. Harry was determined never to mention his name again, and Hermione seemed to know that it was no use forcing the issue, although sometimes at night when she thought he was sleeping, he would hear her crying. Meanwhile, Harry had started bringing out the Marauder’s Map and examining it by wandlight. He was waiting for the moment when Ron’s labelled dot would reappear in the corridors of Hogwarts, proving that he had returned to the comfortable castle, protected by his status of pure-blood. However, Ron did not appear on the map, and after a while Harry found himself taking it out simply to stare at Ginny’s name in the girls’ dormitory, wondering whether the intensity with which he gazed at it might break into her sleep, that she would somehow know he was thinking about her, hoping that she was all right.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: By day, they devoted themselves to trying to determine the possible locations of Gryffindor’s sword, but the more they talked about the places in which Dumbledore might have hidden it, the more desperate and far-fetched their speculation became. Cudgel his brains though he might, Harry could not remember Dumbledore ever mentioning a place in which he might hide something. There were moments when he did not know whether he was angrier with Ron or with Dumbledore. We thought you knew what you were doing … we thought Dumbledore had told you what to do … we thought you had a real plan!

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He could not hide it from himself: Ron had been right. Dumbledore had left him with virtually nothing. They had discovered one Horcrux, but they had no means of destroying it: the others were as unattainable as they had ever been. Hopelessness threatened to engulf him. He was staggered, now, to think of his own presumption in accepting his friends’ offers to accompany him on this meandering, pointless journey. He knew nothing, he had no ideas, and he was constantly, painfully on the alert for any indication that Hermione, too, was about to tell him that she had had enough, that she was leaving.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They were spending many evenings in near silence, and Hermione took to bringing out Phineas Nigellus’s portrait and propping it up in a chair, as though he might fill part of the gaping hole left by Ron’s departure. Despite his previous assertion that he would never visit them again, Phineas Nigellus did not seem able to resist the chance to find out more about what Harry was up to, and consented to reappear, blindfolded, every few days or so. Harry was even glad to see him, because he was company, albeit of a snide and taunting kind. They relished any news about what was happening at Hogwarts, though Phineas Nigellus was not an ideal informer. He venerated Snape, the first Slytherin Headmaster since he himself had controlled the school, and they had to be careful not to criticise, or ask impertinent questions about Snape, or Phineas Nigellus would instantly leave his painting.

text_content: However, he did let drop certain snippets. Snape seemed to be facing a constant, low-level of mutiny from a hard core of students. Ginny had been banned from going into Hogsmeade. book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: From all of these things, Harry deduced that Ginny, and probably Neville and Luna along with her, had been doing their best to continue Dumbledore’s Army. This scant news made Harry want to see Ginny so badly it felt like stomach ache; but it also made him think of Ron again, and of Dumbledore, and of Hogwarts itself, which he missed nearly as much as his ex-girlfriend. Indeed, as Phineas Nigellus talked about Snape’s crackdown, Harry experienced a split second of madness when he imagined simply going back to school to join the destabilisation of Snape’s regime: being fed, and having a soft bed, and other people being in charge seemed the most wonderful prospect in the world at that moment. But then he remembered that he was Undesirable Number One, that there was a ten thousand Galleon price on his head, and that to walk into Hogwarts these days was just as dangerous as walking into the Ministry of Magic. Indeed, Phineas Nigellus inadvertently emphasised this fact by slipping in leading questions about Harry and Hermione’s whereabouts. Hermione shoved him back inside the beaded bag every time he did this, and Phineas Nigellus invariably refused to reappear for several days after these unceremonious goodbyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

They did not dare remain in any one area too long, so rather than staying in the south of England, where a hard ground frost was the worst of their worries, they continued to meander up and down the country, braving a mountainside, where sleet pounded the tent, a wide flat marsh, where the tent was flooded with chill water, and a tiny island in the middle of a Scottish loch, where snow half buried the tent in the night.

text_content: ‘“Upon the signature of the International Statute of Secrecy in 1689, wizards went into hiding for good. The villages of Tinworth in Cornwall, Upper Flagley in Yorkshire and Ottery St Catchpole on the south coast of England were notable homes to knots of wizarding families who lived alongside tolerant and sometimes Confunded Muggles. Most celebrated of these half-magical dwelling places is, perhaps, Godric’s Hollow, the West Country village where the great wizard Godric Gryffindor was born, and where Bowman Wright, wizarding smith, forged the first Golden Snitch. The graveyard is full of the names of ancient magical families, and this accounts, no doubt, for the stories of hauntings that have dogged the little church for many centuries.”

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He was about to go home, about to return to the place where he had had a family. It was in Godric’s Hollow that, but for Voldemort, he would have grown up and spent every school holiday. He could have invited friends to his house … he might even have had brothers and sisters … it would have been his mother who had made his seventeenth birthday cake. The life he had lost had hardly ever seemed so real to him as at this moment when he knew he was about to see the place where it had been taken from him. After Hermione had gone to bed that night, Harry quietly extracted his rucksack from her beaded bag, and from inside it, the photograph album Hagrid had given him so long ago. For the first time in months, he perused the old pictures of his parents, smiling and waving up at him from the images, which were all he had left of them now.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry would gladly have set out for Godric’s Hollow the following day, but Hermione had other ideas. Convinced as she was that Voldemort would expect Harry to return to the scene of his parents’ deaths, she was determined that they would set off only after they had ensured that they had the best disguises possible. It was therefore a full week later - once they had surreptitiously obtained hairs from innocent Muggles who were Christmas shopping, and had practised Apparating and Disapparating while underneath the Invisibility Cloak together - that Hermione agreed to make the journey.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They were to Apparate to the village under cover of darkness, so it was late afternoon when they finally swallowed Polyjuice Potion, Harry transforming into a balding, middle-aged Muggle man, Hermione into his small and rather mousy wife. The beaded bag containing all of their possessions (apart from the Horcrux, which Harry was wearing around his neck) was tucked into an inside pocket of Hermione’s buttoned-up coat. Harry lowered the Invisibility Cloak over them, then they turned into the suffocating darkness once again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: Then something closed tight around his neck. He thought of water weeds, though nothing had brushed him as he dived, and raised his empty hand to free himself. It was not weed: the chain of the Horcrux had tightened and was slowly constricting his wind pipe.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry kicked out wildly, trying to push himself back to the surface, but merely propelled himself into the rocky side of the pool. Thrashing, suffocating, he scrabbled at the strangling chain, his frozen fingers unable to loosen it, and now little lights were popping inside his head, and he was going to drown, there was nothing left, nothing he could do, and the arms that closed around his chest were surely Death’s …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Choking and retching, soaking and colder than he had ever been in his life, he came to, face down in the snow. Somewhere close by, another person was panting and coughing and staggering around. Hermione had come again, as she had come when the snake attacked … yet it did not sound like her, not with those deep coughs, not judging by the weight of the footsteps …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had no strength to lift his head and see his saviour’s identity. All he could do was raise a shaking hand to his throat and feel the place where the locket had cut tightly into his flesh. It was gone: someone had cut him free. Then a panting voice spoke from over his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Are - you - mental?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Nothing but the shock of hearing that voice could have given Harry the strength to get up. Shivering violently, he staggered to his feet. There before him stood Ron, fully dressed but drenched to the skin, his hair plastered to his face, the sword of Gryffindor in one hand and the Horcrux dangling from its broken chain in the other.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why the hell,’ panted Ron, holding up the Horcrux, which swung backwards and forwards on its shortened chain in some parody of hypnosis, ‘didn’t you take this thing off before you dived?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could not answer. The silver doe was nothing, nothing compared with Ron’s reappearance, he could not believe it. Shuddering with cold, he caught up the pile of clothes still lying at the water’s edge and began to pull them on. As he dragged sweater after sweater over his head, Harry stared at Ron, half expecting him to have disappeared every time he lost sight of him, and yet he had to be real: he had just dived into the pool, he had saved Harry’s life.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It was y - you?’ Harry said at last, his teeth chattering, his voice weaker than usual due to his near-strangulation.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, yeah,’ said Ron, looking slightly confused.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Y - you cast that doe?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What? No, of course not! I thought it was you doing it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My Patronus is a stag.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yeah. I thought it looked different. No antlers.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry put Hagrid’s pouch back around his neck, pulled on a final sweater, stooped to pick up Hermione’s wand and faced Ron again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How come you’re here?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Apparently Ron had hoped that this point would come up later, if at all.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I’ve - you know - I’ve come back. If -‘ He cleared his throat. ‘You know. You still want me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a pause, in which the subject of Ron’s departure seemed to rise like a wall between them. Yet he was here. He had returned. He had just saved Harry’s life.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron looked down at his hands. He seemed momentarily surprised to see the things he was holding.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yeah; I got it out,’ he said, rather unnecessarily, holding up the sword for Harry’s inspection. ‘That’s why you jumped in, right?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry was already hurrying to the place Ron had indicated. The two oaks grew close together; there was a gap of only a few inches between the trunks at eye-level, an ideal place to see, but not be seen. The ground around the roots, however, was free of snow and Harry could see no sign of footprints. He walked back to where Ron stood waiting, still holding the sword and the Horcrux.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Anything there?’ Ron asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They both looked at the ornate silver sword, its rubied hilt glinting a little in the light from Hermione’s wand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You reckon this is the real one?’ asked Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘One way to find out, isn’t there?’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The Horcrux was still swinging from Ron’s hand. The locket was twitching slightly. Harry knew that the thing inside it was agitated again. Harry looked around, holding Hermione’s wand high, and saw the place: a flattish rock lying in the shadow of a sycamore tree.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Come here,’ he said, and he led the way, brushed snow from the rock’s surface and held out his hand for the Horcrux. When Ron offered the sword, however, Harry shook his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: ‘I’m going to open it,’ said Harry, ‘and you stab it. Straight away, OK? Because whatever’s in there will put up a fight. The bit of Riddle in the diary tried to kill me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No!’ said Ron, ‘no, don’t open it! I’m serious!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t, Harry, I’m serious - you do it -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But why?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Because that thing’s bad for me!’ said Ron, backing away from the locket on the rock. ‘I can’t handle it! book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He had backed away, the sword dragging at his side, shaking his head.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You can do it,’ said Harry, ‘you can! You’ve just got the sword, I know it’s supposed to be you who uses it. Please, just get rid of it, Ron.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The sound of his name seemed to act like a stimulant. Ron swallowed, then, still breathing hard through his long nose, moved back towards the rock.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell me when,’ he croaked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘On three,’ said Harry, looking back down at the locket and narrowing his eyes, concentrating on the letter ‘S’, imagining a serpent, while the contents of the locket rattled like a trapped cockroach. book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘One … two … three … open.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron raised the sword in his shaking hands: the point dangled over the frantically swivelling eyes, and Harry gripped the locket tightly, bracing himself, already imagining blood pouring from the empty windows.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then a voice hissed from out of the Horcrux.

text_content: ‘I have seen your heart, and it is mine.’

text_content: ‘Don’t listen to it!’ Harry said harshly. ‘Stab it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I have seen your dreams, Ronald Weasley, and I have seen your fears. All you desire is possible, but all that you dread is also possible …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stab!’ shouted Harry; his voice echoed off the surrounding trees, the sword point trembled, and Ron gazed down into Riddle’s eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Least loved, always, by the mother who craved a daughter … least loved, now, by the girl who prefers your friend … second best, always, eternally overshadowed …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Out of the locket’s two windows, out of the eyes, there bloomed, like two grotesque bubbles, the heads of Harry and Hermione, weirdly distorted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Your mother confessed,’ sneered Riddle-Harry, while Riddle-Hermione jeered, ‘that she would have preferred me as a son, would be glad to exchange …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: On the ground in front of them, Ron’s face filled with anguish: he raised the sword high, his arms shaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Do it, Ron!’ Harry yelled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron looked towards him and Harry thought he saw a trace of scarlet in his eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ron -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The sword flashed, plunged: Harry threw himself out of the way, there was a clang of metal and a long, drawn-out scream. Harry whirled round, slipping in the snow, wand held ready to defend himself: but there was nothing to fight.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The monstrous versions of himself and Hermione were gone: there was only Ron, standing there with the sword held slackly in his hand, looking down at the shattered remains of the locket on the flat rock.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Slowly, Harry walked back to him, hardly knowing what to say or do. Ron was breathing heavily. His eyes were no longer red at all, but their normal blue; they were also wet.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry stooped, pretending he had not seen, and picked up the broken Horcrux. Ron had pierced the glass in both windows: Riddle’s eyes were gone, and the stained silk lining of the locket was smoking slightly. The thing that had lived in the Horcrux had vanished; torturing Ron had been its final act.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The sword clanged as Ron dropped it. He had sunk to his knees, his head in his arms. He was shaking, but not, Harry realised, from cold. Harry crammed the broken locket into his pocket, knelt down beside Ron and placed a hand, cautiously, on his shoulder. He took it as a good sign that Ron did not throw it off.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘After you left,’ he said in a low voice, grateful for the fact that Ron’s face was hidden, ‘she cried for a week. Probably longer, only she didn’t want me to see. There were loads of nights when we never even spoke to each other. With you gone …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He could not finish; it was only now that Ron was here again that Harry fully realised how much his absence had cost them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She’s like my sister,’ he went on. ‘I love her like a sister and I reckon she feels the same way about me. It’s always been like that. I thought you knew.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron did not respond, but turned his face away from Harry and wiped his nose noisily on his sleeve. Harry got to his feet again and walked to where Ron’s enormous rucksack lay, yards away, discarded as Ron had run towards the pool to save Harry from drowning. He hoisted it on to his own back and walked back to Ron, who clambered to his feet as Harry approached, eyes bloodshot but otherwise composed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry,’ he said in a thick voice. ‘I’m sorry I left. I know I was a - a -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He looked around at the darkness, as if hoping a bad enough word would swoop down upon him and claim him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You’ve sort of made up for it tonight,’ said Harry. ‘Getting the sword. Finishing off the Horcrux. Saving my life.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That makes me sound a lot cooler than I was,’ Ron mumbled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stuff like that always sounds cooler than it really was,’ said Harry. ‘I’ve been trying to tell you that for years.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Simultaneously they walked forwards and hugged, Harry gripping the still sopping back of Ron’s jacket.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And now,’ said Harry, as they broke apart, ‘all we’ve got to do is find the tent again.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But it was not difficult. Though the walk through the dark forest with the doe had seemed lengthy, with Ron by his side the journey back seemed to take a surprisingly short time. Harry could not wait to wake Hermione, and it was with quickening excitement that he entered the tent, Ron lagging a little behind him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was gloriously warm after the pool and the forest, the only illumination the bluebell flames still shimmering in a bowl on the floor. Hermione was fast asleep, curled up under her blankets, and did not move until Harry had said her name several times.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She stirred, then sat up quickly, pushing her hair out of her face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What’s wrong? Harry? Are you all right?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s OK, everything’s fine. More than fine. I’m great. There’s someone here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What do you mean? Who -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She saw Ron, who stood there holding the sword and dripping on to the threadbare carpet. Harry backed into a shadowy corner, slipped off Ron’s rucksack and attempted to blend in with the canvas.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione slid out of her bunk and moved like a sleepwalker towards Ron, her eyes upon his pale face. She stopped right in front of him, her lips slightly parted, her eyes wide. Ron gave a weak, hopeful smile and half-raised his arms.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione launched herself forwards and started punching every inch of him that she could reach.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ouch - ow - gerroff! What the -? Hermione - OW!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You - complete - arse - Ronald - Weasley!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She punctuated every word with a blow: Ron backed away, shielding his head as Hermione advanced.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You - crawl - back - here - after - weeks - and - weeks - oh, where’s my wand?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She looked as though ready to wrestle it out of Harry’s hands and he reacted instinctively.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Protego!’

text_content: The invisible shield erupted between Ron and Hermione: the force of it knocked her backwards on to the floor. Spitting hair out of her mouth, she leapt up again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Give me back my wand! Give it back to me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hermione, will you please -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t you tell me what to do, Harry Potter!’ she screeched. ‘Don’t you dare! Give it back now! And YOU!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She was pointing at Ron in dire accusation: it was like a malediction and Harry could not blame Ron for retreating several steps.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I came running after you! I called you! I begged you to come back!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know,’ Ron said. ‘Hermione, I’m sorry, I’m really -‘

text_content: ‘Oh, you’re sorry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You come back after weeks - weeks - and you think it’s all going to be all right if you just say sorry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew you weren’t dead!’ bellowed Ron, drowning her voice for the first time, and approaching as close as he could with the Shield Charm between them. ‘Harry’s all over the Prophet, all over the radio, they’re looking for you everywhere, all these rumours and mental stories, I knew I’d hear straight off if you were dead, you don’t know what it’s been like -‘

text_content: ‘What it’s been like for you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I wanted to come back the minute I’d Disapparated, but I walked straight into a gang of Snatchers, Hermione, and I couldn’t go anywhere!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: ‘What did you say to them?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
