book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But if it was bought -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- then they would consider it rented by the one who had paid the money. They have, however, great difficulty with the idea of goblin-made objects passing from wizard to wizard. You saw Griphook’s face when the tiara passed under his eyes. He disapproves. I believe he thinks, as do the fiercest of his kind, that it ought to have been returned to the goblins once the original purchaser died. They consider our habit of keeping goblin-made objects, passing them from wizard to wizard without further payment, little more than theft.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had an ominous feeling now; he wondered whether Bill guessed more than he was letting on.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All I am saying,’ said Bill, setting his hand on the door back into the sitting room, ‘is to be very careful what you promise goblins, Harry. It would be less dangerous to break into Gringotts than to renege on a promise to a goblin.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Right,’ said Harry, as Bill opened the door, ‘yeah. Thanks. I’ll bear that in mind.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: As he followed Bill back to the others, a wry thought came to him, born no doubt of the wine he had drunk. He seemed set on course to become just as reckless a godfather to Teddy Lupin as Sirius Black had been to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Their plans were made, their preparations complete; in the smallest bedroom a single long, coarse, black hair (plucked from the sweater Hermione had been wearing at Malfoy Manor) lay curled in a small glass phial on the mantelpiece.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And you’ll be using her actual wand,’ said Harry, nodding towards the walnut wand, ‘so I reckon you’ll be pretty convincing.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked frightened that the wand might sting or bite her as she picked it up.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I hate this thing,’ she said in a low voice. ‘I really hate it. It feels all wrong, it doesn’t work properly for me … it’s like a bit of her.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could not help but remember how Hermione had dismissed his loathing of the blackthorn wand, insisting that he was imagining things when it did not work as well as his own, telling him to simply practise. He chose not to repeat her own advice back to her, however; the eve of their attempted assault on Gringotts felt like the wrong moment to antagonise her.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’ll probably help you get in character, though,’ said Ron. ‘Think what that wand’s done!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But that’s my point!’ said Hermione. ‘This is the wand that tortured Neville’s mum and dad, and who knows how many other people? This is the wand that killed Sirius!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had not thought of that: he looked down at the wand and was visited by a brutal urge to snap it, to slice it in half with Gryffindor’s sword, which was propped against the wall beside him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I miss my wand,’ Hermione said miserably. ‘I wish Mr Ollivander could have made me another one too.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Mr Ollivander had sent Luna a new wand that morning. She was out on the back lawn at that moment, testing its capabilities in the late afternoon sun. Dean, who had lost his wand to the Snatchers, was watching rather gloomily.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry looked down at the hawthorn wand that had once belonged to Draco Malfoy. He had been surprised, but pleased, to discover that it worked for him at least as well as Hermione’s had done. Remembering what Ollivander had told them of the secret workings of wands, Harry thought he knew what Hermione’s problem was: she had not won the walnut wand’s allegiance by taking it personally from Bellatrix.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The door of the bedroom opened and Griphook entered. Harry reached instinctively for the hilt of the sword and drew it close to him, but regretted his action at once: he could tell that the goblin had noticed. Seeking to gloss over the sticky moment he said, ‘We’ve just been checking the last-minute stuff, Griphook. We’ve told Bill and Fleur we’re leaving tomorrow, and we’ve told them not to get up to see us off.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They had been firm on this point, because Hermione would need to transform into Bellatrix before they left, and the less that Bill and Fleur knew or suspected about what they were about to do, the better. They had also explained that they would not be returning. As they had lost Perkins’s old tent on the night that the Snatchers caught them, Bill had lent them another one. It was now packed inside the beaded bag, which, Harry was impressed to learn, Hermione had protected from the Snatchers by the simple expedient of stuffing it down her sock.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Though he would miss Bill, Fleur, Luna and Dean, not to mention the home comforts they had enjoyed over the last few weeks, Harry was looking forward to escaping the confinement of Shell Cottage. He was tired of trying to make sure that they were not overheard, tired of being shut in the tiny, dark bedroom. Most of all, he longed to be rid of Griphook. However, precisely how and when they were to part from the goblin without handing over Gryffindor’s sword remained a question to which Harry had no answer. It had been impossible to decide how they were going to do it, because the goblin rarely left Harry, Ron and Hermione alone together for more than five minutes at a time; ‘He could give my mother lessons,’ growled Ron, as the goblin’s long fingers kept appearing around the edges of doors. With Bill’s warning in mind, Harry could not help suspecting that Griphook was on the watch for possible skulduggery. Hermione disapproved so heartily of the planned double-cross that Harry had given up attempting to pick her brains on how best to do it; Ron, on the rare occasions that they had been able to snatch a few Griphook-free moments, had come up with nothing better than ‘We’ll just have to wing it, mate.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry slept badly that night. Lying awake in the early hours, he thought back to the way he had felt the night before they had infiltrated the Ministry of Magic and remembered a determination, almost an excitement. Now he was experiencing jolts of anxiety, nagging doubts: he could not shake off the fear that it was all going to go wrong. He kept telling himself that their plan was good, that Griphook knew what they were facing, that they were well-prepared for all the difficulties they were likely to encounter; yet still he felt uneasy. Once or twice he heard Ron stir, and was sure that he, too, was awake, but they were sharing the sitting room with Dean, so Harry did not speak.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was a relief when six o’clock arrived and they could slip out of their sleeping bags, dress in the semi-darkness, then creep out into the garden, where they were to meet Hermione and Griphook. The dawn was chilly, but there was little wind now that it was May. Harry looked up at the stars still glimmering palely in the dark sky and listened to the sea washing backwards and forwards against the cliff: he was going to miss the sound.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Small green shoots were forcing their way up through the red earth of Dobby’s grave now; in a year’s time the mound would be covered in flowers. The white stone that bore the elf’s name had already acquired a weathered look. He realised now that they could hardly have laid Dobby to rest in a more beautiful place, but Harry ached with sadness to think of leaving him behind. Looking down on the grave, he wondered yet again how the elf had known where to come to rescue them. His fingers moved absent-mindedly to the little pouch still strung around his neck, through which he could feel the jagged mirror fragment in which he had been sure he had seen Dumbledore’s eye. Then the sound of a door opening made him look round.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Bellatrix Lestrange was striding across the lawn towards them, accompanied by Griphook. As she walked, she was tucking the small beaded bag into the inside pocket of another set of the old robes they had taken from Grimmauld Place. Though Harry knew perfectly well that it was really Hermione, he could not suppress a shiver of loathing. She was taller than he was, her long, black hair rippling down her back, her heavily lidded eyes disdainful as they rested upon him; but then she spoke, and he heard Hermione through Bellatrix’s low voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She tasted disgusting, worse than Gurdyroots! OK, Ron, come here so I can do you …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Right, but remember, I don’t like the beard too long -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, for heaven’s sake, this isn’t about looking handsome -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s not that, it gets in the way! But I liked my nose a bit shorter, try and do it the way you did last time.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione sighed and set to work, muttering under her breath as she transformed various aspects of Ron’s appearance. He was to be given a completely fake identity, and they were trusting to the malevolent aura cast by Bellatrix to protect him. Meanwhile, Harry and Griphook were to be concealed under the Invisibility Cloak.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There,’ said Hermione, ‘how does he look, Harry?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was just possible to discern Ron under his disguise, but only, Harry thought, because he knew him so well. Ron’s hair was now long and wavy, he had a thick, brown beard and moustache, no freckles, a short, broad nose and heavy eyebrows.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, he’s not my type, but he’ll do,’ said Harry. ‘Shall we go, then?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: All three of them glanced back at Shell Cottage, lying dark and silent under the fading stars, then turned and began to walk towards the point, just beyond the boundary wall, where the Fidelius Charm stopped working and they would be able to Disapparate. Once past the gate, Griphook spoke.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I should climb up now, Harry Potter, I think?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry bent down and the goblin clambered on to his back, his hands linked in front of Harry’s throat. He was not heavy, but Harry disliked the feeling of the goblin and the surprising strength with which he clung on. Hermione pulled the Invisibility Cloak out of the beaded bag and threw it over them both.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Perfect,’ she said, bending down to check Harry’s feet. ‘I can’t see a thing. Let’s go.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry turned on the spot with Griphook on his shoulders, concentrating with all his might on the Leaky Cauldron, the inn that was the entrance to Diagon Alley. The goblin clung even tighter as they moved into the compressing darkness, and seconds later Harry’s feet found pavement and he opened his eyes on Charing Cross Road. Muggles bustled past wearing the hangdog expressions of early morning, quite unconscious of the little inn’s existence.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The bar of the Leaky Cauldron was nearly deserted. Tom, the stooped and toothless landlord, was polishing glasses behind the bar counter; a couple of warlocks having a muttered conversation in the far corner glanced at Hermione and drew back into the shadows.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Madam Lestrange,’ murmured Tom, and as Hermione passed he inclined his head subserviently.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good morning,’ said Hermione, and as Harry crept past, still carrying Griphook piggyback under the Cloak, he saw Tom look surprised.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Too polite,’ Harry whispered in Hermione’s ear as they passed out of the inn into the tiny backyard. ‘You need to treat people like they’re scum!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘OK, OK!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione drew out Bellatrix’s wand and tapped a brick in the nondescript wall in front of them. At once the bricks began to whirl and spin: a hole appeared in the middle of them, which grew wider and wider, finally forming an archway on to the narrow cobbled street that was Diagon Alley.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was quiet, barely time for the shops to open, and there were hardly any shoppers abroad. The crooked, cobbled street was much altered, now, from the bustling place Harry had visited before his first term at Hogwarts so many years before. More shops than ever were boarded-up, though several new establishments dedicated to the Dark Arts had been created since his last visit. Harry’s own face glared down at him from posters plastered over many windows, always captioned with the words Undesirable Number One.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A number of ragged people sat huddled in doorways. He heard them moaning to the few passers-by, pleading for gold, insisting that they were really wizards. One man had a bloody bandage over his eye.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: As they set off along the street, the beggars glimpsed Hermione. They seemed to melt away before her, drawing hoods over their faces and fleeing as fast as they could. Hermione looked after them curiously, until the man with the bloodied bandage came staggering right across her path.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My children!’ he bellowed, pointing at her. His voice was cracked, high-pitched, he sounded distraught. ‘Where are my children? What has he done with them? You know, you know!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I - I really -‘ stammered Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The man lunged at her, reaching for her throat: then, with a bang and a burst of red light he was thrown backwards on to the ground, unconscious. Ron stood there, his wand still outstretched and a look of shock visible behind his beard. Faces appeared at the windows on either side of the street, while a little knot of prosperous-looking passers-by gathered their robes about them and broke into gentle trots, keen to vacate the scene.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Their entrance into Diagon Alley could hardly have been more conspicuous; for a moment Harry wondered whether it might not be better to leave, now, and try to think of a different plan. Before they could move or consult one another, however, they heard a cry from behind them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why, Madam Lestrange!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry whirled round and Griphook tightened his hold around Harry’s neck: a tall, thin wizard with a crown of bushy, grey hair and a long, sharp nose was striding towards them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s Travers,’ hissed the goblin into Harry’s ear, but at that moment Harry could not think who Travers was. Hermione had drawn herself up to her fullest height and said, with as much contempt as she could muster, ‘and what do you want?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Travers stopped in his tracks, clearly affronted.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He’s another Death Eater!’ breathed Griphook, and Harry sidled sideways to repeat the information into Hermione’s ear.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I merely sought to greet you,’ said Travers coolly, ‘but if my presence is not welcome …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry recognised his voice now; Travers was one of the Death Eaters who had been summoned to Xenophilius’s house.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No, no, not at all, Travers,’ said Hermione quickly, trying to cover up her mistake. ‘How are you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I confess I am surprised to see you out and about, Bellatrix.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Really? Why?’ asked Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well,’ Travers coughed, ‘I heard that the inhabitants of Malfoy Manor were confined to the house, after the … ah … escape.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry willed Hermione to keep her head. If this was true, and Bellatrix was not supposed to be out in public -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Dark Lord forgives those who have served him most faithfully in the past,’ said Hermione, in a magnificent imitation of Bellatrix’s most contemptuous manner. ‘Perhaps your credit is not as good with him as mine is, Travers.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Though the Death Eater looked offended, he also seemed less suspicious. He glanced down at the man Ron had just Stunned.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How did it offend you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It does not matter, it will not do so again,’ said Hermione coolly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Some of these Wandless can be troublesome,’ said Travers. ‘While they do nothing but beg I have no objection, but one of them actually asked me to plead her case at the Ministry last week. “I’m a witch, sir, I’m a witch, let me prove it to you!” ‘ he said, in a squeaky impersonation. ‘As if I was going to give her my wand - but whose wand,’ said Travers curiously, ‘are you using at the moment, Bellatrix? I heard that your own was -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I have my wand here,’ said Hermione coldly, holding up Bellatrix’s wand. ‘I don’t know what rumours you have been listening to, Travers, but you seem sadly misinformed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Travers seemed a little taken aback at that, and he turned instead to Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Who is your friend? I do not recognise him.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘This is Dragomir Despard,’ said Hermione; they had decided that a fictional foreigner was the safest cover for Ron to assume. ‘He speaks very little English, but he is in sympathy with the Dark Lord’s aims. He has travelled here from Transylvania to see our new regime.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Indeed? How do you do, Dragomir?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ”Ow you?’ said Ron, holding out his hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Travers extended two fingers and shook Ron’s hand as though frightened of dirtying himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So what brings you and your - ah - sympathetic friend to Diagon Alley this early?’ asked Travers.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I need to visit Gringotts,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Alas, I also,’ said Travers. ‘Gold, filthy gold! We cannot live without it, yet I confess I deplore the necessity of consorting with our long-fingered friends.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt Griphook’s clasped hands tighten momentarily around his neck.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Shall we?’ said Travers, gesturing Hermione forwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione had no choice but to fall into step beside him and head along the crooked, cobbled street towards the place where the snowy-white Gringotts stood towering over the other little shops. Ron sloped along beside them, and Harry and Griphook followed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A watchful Death Eater was the very last thing they needed, and the worst of it was, with Travers marching at what he believed to be Bellatrix’s side, there was no means for Harry to communicate with Hermione or Ron. All too soon they arrived at the foot of the marble steps leading up to the great bronze doors. As Griphook had already warned them, the liveried goblins who usually flanked the entrance had been replaced by two wizards, both of whom were clutching long, thin golden rods.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, Probity Probes,’ sighed Travers theatrically, ‘so crude - but effective!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And he set off up the steps, nodding left and right to the wizards, who raised the golden rods and passed them up and down his body. The Probes, Harry knew, detected spells of concealment and hidden magical objects. Knowing that he had only seconds, Harry pointed Draco’s wand at each of the guards in turn and murmured, ‘Confundo,’ twice. Unnoticed by Travers, who was looking through the bronze doors at the inner hall, each of the guards gave a little start as the spells hit them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione’s long, black hair rippled behind her as she climbed the steps.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘One moment, Madam,’ said the guard, raising his Probe.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But you’ve just done that!’ said Hermione, in Bellatrix’s commanding, arrogant voice. Travers looked round, eyebrows raised. The guard was confused. He stared down at the thin, golden Probe and then at his companion, who said in a slightly dazed voice, ‘Yeah, you’ve just checked them, Marius.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione swept forwards, Ron by her side, Harry and Griphook trotting invisibly behind them. Harry glanced back as they crossed the threshold: the wizards were both scratching their heads.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Two goblins stood before the inner doors, which were made of silver and which carried the poem warning of dire retribution to potential thieves. Harry looked up at it, and all of a sudden a knife-sharp memory came to him: standing on this very spot on the day that he had turned eleven, the most wonderful birthday of his life, and Hagrid standing beside him saying, ‘Like I said, yeh’d be mad ter try an’ rob it.’ Gringotts had seemed a place of wonder that day, the enchanted repository of a trove of gold he had never known he possessed, and never for an instant could he have dreamed that he would return to steal … But within seconds they were standing in the vast marble hall of the bank.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The long counter was manned by goblins sitting on high stools, serving the first customers of the day. Hermione, Ron and Travers headed towards an old goblin who was examining a thick gold coin through an eyeglass. Hermione allowed Travers to step ahead of her on the pretext of explaining features of the hall to Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The goblin tossed the coin he was holding aside, said to nobody in particular, ‘Leprechaun,’ and then greeted Travers, who passed over a tiny golden key, which was examined and given back to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione stepped forwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Madam Lestrange!’ said the goblin, evidently startled. ‘Dear me! How - how may I help you today?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I wish to enter my vault,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The old goblin seemed to recoil a little. Harry glanced around. Not only was Travers hanging back, watching, but several other goblins had looked up from their work to stare at Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You have … identification?’ asked the goblin.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Identification? I - I have never been asked for identification before!’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They know!’ whispered Griphook in Harry’s ear. ‘They must have been warned there might be an impostor!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Your wand will do, Madam,’ said the goblin. He held out a slightly trembling hand, and in a dreadful blast of realisation Harry knew that the goblins of Gringotts were aware that Bellatrix’s wand had been stolen.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Act now, act now,’ whispered Griphook in Harry’s ear, ‘the Imperius Curse!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry raised the hawthorn wand beneath the Cloak, pointed it at the old goblin and whispered, for the first time in his life, ‘Imperio!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A curious sensation shot down Harry’s arm, a feeling of tingling warmth that seemed to flow from his mind, down the sinews and veins connecting him to the wand and the curse it had just cast. The goblin took Bellatrix’s wand, examined it closely and then said, ‘Ah, you have had a new wand made, Madam Lestrange!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’ said Hermione, ‘no, no, that’s mine -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘A new wand?’ said Travers, approaching the counter again; still the goblins all around were watching. ‘But how could you have done, which wandmaker did you use?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry acted without thinking: pointing his wand at Travers, he muttered, ‘Imperio!’ once more.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes, I see,’ said Travers, looking down at Bellatrix’s wand, ‘yes, very handsome. And is it working well? I always think wands require a little breaking in, don’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione looked utterly bewildered, but to Harry’s enormous relief she accepted the bizarre turn of events without comment.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The old goblin behind the counter clapped his hands and a younger goblin approached.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I shall need the Clankers,’ he told the goblin, who dashed away and returned a moment later with a leather bag that seemed to be full of jangling metal, which he handed to his senior. ‘Good, good! So, if you will follow me, Madam Lestrange,’ said the old goblin, hopping down off his stool and vanishing from sight, ‘I shall take you to your vault.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He appeared around the end of the counter, jogging happily towards them, the contents of the leather bag still jingling. Travers was now standing quite still with his mouth hanging wide open. Ron was drawing attention to this odd phenomenon by regarding Travers with confusion.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Wait - Bogrod!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Another goblin came scurrying around the counter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We have instructions,’ he said, with a bow to Hermione, ‘forgive me, Madam Lestrange, but there have been special orders regarding the vault of Lestrange.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He whispered urgently in Bogrod’s ear, but the Imperiused goblin shook him off.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I am aware of the instructions. Madam Lestrange wishes to visit her vault … very old family … old clients … this way, please …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And, still clanking, he hurried towards one of the many doors leading off the hall. Harry looked back at Travers, who was still rooted to the spot looking abnormally vacant, and made his decision: with a flick of his wand he made Travers come with them, walking meekly in their wake as they reached the door and passed into the rough stone passageway beyond, which was lit with flaming torches.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’re in trouble, they suspect,’ said Harry, as the door slammed behind them and he pulled off the Invisibility Cloak. Griphook jumped down from his shoulders; neither Travers nor Bogrod showed the slightest surprise at the sudden appearance of Harry Potter in their midst. ‘They’re Imperiused,’ he added, in response to Hermione and Ron’s confused queries about Travers and Bogrod, who were both now standing there looking blank. ‘I don’t think I did it strongly enough, I don’t know …’

text_content: And another memory darted through his mind, of the real Bellatrix Lestrange shrieking at him when he had first tried to use an Unforgivable Curse: ‘You need to mean them, Potter!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: ‘What are you making him do?’

text_content: ‘Hide,’ said Harry, as he pointed his wand at Bogrod, who whistled to summon a little cart which came trundling along the tracks towards them out of the darkness. text_content: With a jerk the cart moved off, gathering speed: they hurtled past Travers, who was wriggling into a crack in the wall, then the cart began twisting and turning through the labyrinthine passages, sloping downwards all the time. Harry could not hear anything over the rattling of the cart on the tracks: his hair flew behind him as they swerved between stalactites, flying ever deeper into the earth, but he kept glancing back. They might as well have left enormous footprints behind them; the more he thought about it, the more foolish it seemed to have disguised Hermione as Bellatrix, to have brought along Bellatrix’s wand, when the Death Eaters knew who had stolen it -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They were deeper than Harry had ever penetrated within Gringotts; they took a hairpin bend at speed and saw ahead of them, with seconds to spare, a waterfall pounding over the track. Harry heard Griphook shout, ‘No!’ but there was no braking: they zoomed through it. Water filled Harry’s eyes and mouth: he could not see or breathe: then, with an awful lurch, the cart flipped over and they were all thrown out of it. Harry heard the cart smash into pieces against the passage wall, heard Hermione shriek something and felt himself glide back towards the ground as though weightless, landing painlessly on the rocky passage floor.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘C - Cushioning Charm,’ Hermione spluttered, as Ron pulled her to her feet: but to Harry’s horror he saw that she was no longer Bellatrix; instead she stood there in overlarge robes, sopping wet and completely herself; Ron was red-haired and beardless again. They were realising it as they looked at each other, feeling their own faces.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Thief’s Downfall!’ said Griphook, clambering to his feet and looking back at the deluge on to the tracks, which Harry knew, now, had been more than water. ‘It washes away all enchantment, all magical concealment! book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry saw Hermione checking that she still had the beaded bag, and hurriedly thrust his own hand under his jacket to make sure he had not lost the Invisibility Cloak. book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We need him,’ said Griphook, ‘we cannot enter the vault without a Gringotts goblin. And we need the Clankers!’

Bogrod submitted once more to his will, his befuddled expression changing to one of polite indifference, as Ron hurried to pick up the leather bag of metal tools.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, I think I can hear people coming!’ said Hermione, and she pointed Bellatrix’s wand at the waterfall and cried, ‘Protego!’ They saw the Shield Charm break the flow of enchanted water as it flew up the passageway.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good thinking,’ said Harry, ‘lead the way, Griphook!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How are we going to get out again?’ Ron asked, as they hurried on foot into the darkness after the goblin, Bogrod panting in their wake like an old dog.

text_content: ‘Let’s worry about that when we have to,’ said Harry. He was trying to listen: he thought he could hear something clanking and moving around nearby. ‘Griphook, how much further?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not far, Harry Potter, not far …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And they turned a corner and saw the thing for which Harry had been prepared, but which still brought all of them to a halt.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A gigantic dragon was tethered to the ground in front of them, barring access to four or five of the deepest vaults in the place. The beast’s scales had turned pale and flaky during its long incarceration under the ground; its eyes were milkily pink: both rear legs bore heavy cuffs from which chains led to enormous pegs driven deep into the rocky floor. Its great, spiked wings, folded close to its body, would have filled the chamber if it spread them, and when it turned its ugly head towards them, it roared with a noise that made the rock tremble, opened its mouth and spat a jet of fire that sent them running back up the passageway.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It is partially blind,’ panted Griphook, ‘but even more savage for that. However, we have the means to control it. It has learned what to expect when the Clankers come. Give them to me.’

text_content: Ron passed the bag to Griphook and the goblin pulled out a number of small metal instruments that when shaken made a loud, ringing noise like miniature hammers on anvils. Griphook handed them out: Bogrod accepted his meekly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You know what to do,’ Griphook told Harry, Ron and Hermione. ‘It will expect pain when it hears the noise: it will retreat, and Bogrod must place his palm upon the door of the vault.’

text_content: They advanced round the corner again, shaking the Clankers and the noise echoed off the rocky walls, grossly magnified, so that the inside of Harry’s skull seemed to vibrate with the din. book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Search, fast!’ said Harry, as they all hurried inside the vault.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: ‘No matter, Bogrod will be able to release us!’ said Griphook, as Ron gave a shout of surprise. ‘Light your wands, can’t you? And hurry, we have very little time!’

text_content: ‘Lumos!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry, could this be -? Aargh!’

text_content: ‘It burned me!’ moaned Hermione, sucking her blistered fingers.

text_content: ‘It’s there, it’s up there!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

text_content: They were truly trapped now: there was no way out except through the door, and a horde of goblins seemed to be approaching on the other side. Harry looked at Ron and Hermione and saw terror in their faces.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hardly aware of the pain from the burns covering his body, and still borne along on the swell of replicating treasure, Harry shoved the cup into his pocket and reached up to retrieve the sword, but Griphook was gone. Sliding from Harry’s shoulders the moment he could, he had sprinted for cover amongst the surrounding goblins, brandishing the sword and crying, ‘Thieves! Thieves! Help! Thieves!’ He vanished into the midst of the advancing crowd, all of whom were holding daggers and who accepted him without question.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Slipping on the hot metal, Harry struggled to his feet and knew that the only way out was through.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Stupefy!’ he bellowed, and Ron and Hermione joined in: jets of red light flew into the crowd of goblins and some toppled over, but others advanced, and Harry saw several wizard guards running round the corner.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The tethered dragon let out a roar, and a gush of flame flew over the goblins: the wizards fled, doubled-up, back the way they had come, and inspiration, or madness, came to Harry. Pointing his wand at the thick cuffs chaining the beast to the floor he yelled, ‘Relashio!’

text_content: The cuffs broke open with loud bangs.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘This way!’ Harry yelled, and still shooting Stunning Spells at the advancing goblins he sprinted towards the blind dragon.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry - Harry - what are you doing?’ cried Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Get up, climb up, come on -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The dragon had not realised that it was free: Harry’s foot found the crook of its hind leg and he pulled himself up on to its back. The scales were hard as steel: it did not even seem to feel him. He stretched out an arm; Hermione hoisted herself up; Ron climbed on behind them, and a second later the dragon became aware that it was untethered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: With a roar it reared: Harry dug in his knees, clutching as tightly as he could to the jagged scales as the wings opened, knocking the shrieking goblins aside like skittles, and it soared into the air. Harry, Ron and Hermione, flat on its back, scraped against the ceiling as it dived towards the passage opening, while the pursuing goblins hurled daggers that glanced off its flanks.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We’ll never get out, it’s too big!’ Hermione screamed, but the dragon opened its mouth and belched flame again, blasting the tunnel, whose floors and ceiling cracked and crumbled. By sheer force the dragon clawed and fought its way through. Harry’s eyes were tight shut against the heat and dust: deafened by the crashing of rock and the dragon’s roars, he could only cling to its back, expecting to be shaken off at any moment; then he heard Hermione yelling, ‘Defodio!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She was helping the dragon enlarge the passageway, carving out the ceiling as it struggled upwards, towards the fresher air, away from the shrieking and clanking goblins: Harry and Ron copied her, blasting the ceiling apart with more gouging spells. They passed the underground lake, and the great crawling, snarling beast seemed to sense freedom and space ahead of it, and behind them the passage was full of the dragon’s thrashing, spiked tail, of great lumps of rock, gigantic, fractured stalactites, and the clanking of the goblins seemed to be growing more muffled, while ahead, the dragon’s fire kept their progress clear -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And then at last, by the combined force of their spells and the dragon’s brute strength, they had blasted their way out of the passage into the marble hallway. Goblins and wizards shrieked and ran for cover, and finally the dragon had room to stretch its wings: turning its horned head towards the cool outside air it could smell beyond the entrance, it took off, and with Harry, Ron and Hermione still clinging to its back, it forced its way through the metal doors, leaving them buckled and hanging from their hinges as it staggered into Diagon Alley and launched itself into the sky.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: There was no means of steering; the dragon could not see where it was going, and Harry knew that if it turned sharply or rolled in mid-air they would find it impossible to cling on to its broad back. Nevertheless, as they climbed higher and higher, London unfurling below them like a grey and green map, Harry’s overwhelming feeling was of gratitude for an escape that had seemed impossible. Crouching low over the beast’s neck, he clung tight to the metallic scales, and the cool breeze was soothing on his burned and blistered skin, the dragon’s wings beating the air like the sails of a windmill. Behind him, whether from delight or fear he could not tell, Ron kept swearing at the top of his voice, and Hermione seemed to be sobbing.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: After five minutes or so, Harry lost some of his immediate dread that the dragon was going to throw them off, for it seemed intent on nothing but getting as far away from its underground prison as possible, but the question of how and when they were to dismount remained rather frightening. He had no idea how long dragons could fly without landing, nor how this particular dragon, which could barely see, would locate a good place to put down. He glanced around constantly, imagining that he could feel his scar prickling …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: How long would it be before Voldemort knew that they had broken into the Lestranges’ vault? How soon would the goblins of Gringotts notify Bellatrix? How quickly would they realise what had been taken? And then, when they discovered that the golden cup was missing? Voldemort would know, at last, that they were hunting Horcruxes …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: The dragon seemed to crave cooler and fresher air: it climbed steadily until they were flying through wisps of chilly cloud and Harry could no longer make out the little coloured dots which were cars pouring in and out of the capital. On and on they flew, over countryside parcelled out in patches of green and brown, over roads and rivers winding through the landscape like strips of matt and glossy ribbon.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: ‘What do you reckon it’s looking for?’ Ron yelled, as they flew further and further north.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: ‘No idea,’ Harry bellowed back. His hands were numb with cold but he did not dare attempt to shift his grip. He had been wondering for some time what they would do if they saw the coast sail beneath them, if the dragon headed for open sea: he was cold and numb, not to mention desperately hungry and thirsty. When, he wondered, had the beast itself last eaten? Surely it would need sustenance before long? And what if, at that point, it realised it had three highly edible humans sitting on its back?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: The sun slipped lower in the sky, which was turning indigo; and still the dragon flew, cities and towns gliding out of sight beneath them, its enormous shadow sliding over the earth like a great, dark cloud. Every part of Harry ached with the effort of holding on to the dragon’s back.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: ‘Is it my imagination,’ shouted Ron, after a considerable stretch of silence, ‘or are we losing height?’

chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: Harry looked down and saw deep-green mountains and lakes, coppery in the sunset. The landscape seemed to grow larger and more detailed as he squinted over the side of the dragon and he wondered whether it had divined the presence of fresh water by the flashes of reflected sunlight.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: Lower and lower the dragon flew, in great, spiralling circles, honing in, it seemed, upon one of the smaller lakes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: ‘I say we jump when it gets low enough!’ Harry called back to the others. ‘Straight into the water before it realises we’re here!’

chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: They agreed, Hermione a little faintly: and now Harry could see the dragon’s wide, yellow underbelly rippling in the surface of the water.

text_content: He slithered over the side of the dragon and plummeted, feet first, towards the surface of the lake; the drop was greater than he had estimated and he hit the water hard, plunging like a stone into a freezing, green, reed-filled world. He kicked towards the surface and emerged, panting, to see enormous ripples emanating in circles from the places where Ron and Hermione had fallen. The dragon did not seem to have noticed anything: it was already fifty feet away, swooping low over the lake to scoop up water in its scarred snout. As Ron and Hermione emerged, spluttering and gasping from the depths of the lake, the dragon flew on, its wings beating hard, and landed at last on a distant bank.

text_content: Hermione collapsed, coughing and shuddering. Though Harry could have happily lain down and slept, he staggered to his feet, drew out his wand and started casting the usual protective spells around them.

chapter: Chapter Twenty-Seven - The Final Hiding Place
text_content: When he had finished, he joined the others. It was the first time that he had seen them properly since escaping from the vault. Hermione handed Harry the bottle, then pulled out three bottles of pumpkin juice she had brought from Shell Cottage and clean, dry robes for all of them. They changed and then gulped down the juice.

text_content: ‘No sword,’ repeated Ron. ‘That double-crossing little scab …’

text_content: ‘At least we can’t wear it this time, that’d look a bit weird hanging round our necks,’ said Ron, wiping his mouth on the back of his hand.

You get away from this school, Potter, and out of the country if you can. Forget my brother and his clever schemes. He’s gone where none of this can hurt him, and you don’t owe him anything.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You don’t understand,’ said Harry again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, don’t I?’ said Aberforth quietly. ‘You don’t think I understood my own brother? Think you knew Albus better than I did?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I didn’t mean that,’ said Harry, whose brain felt sluggish with exhaustion and from the surfeit of food and wine. ‘It’s … he left me a job.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Did he, now?’ said Aberforth. ‘Nice job, I hope? Pleasant? Easy? Sort of thing you’d expect an unqualified wizard kid to be able to do without overstretching themselves?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron gave a rather grim laugh. Hermione was looking strained.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I - it’s not easy, no,’ said Harry. ‘But I’ve got to -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“Got to”? Why “got to”? He’s dead, isn’t he?’ said Aberforth roughly. ‘Let it go, boy, before you follow him! Save yourself!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why not?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I -‘ Harry felt overwhelmed; he could not explain, so he took the offensive instead. ‘But you’re fighting too, you’re in the Order of the Phoenix -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was,’ said Aberforth. ‘The Order of the Phoenix is finished. You-Know-Who’s won, it’s over, and anyone who’s pretending different’s kidding themselves. It’ll never be safe for you here, Potter, he wants you too badly. So go abroad, go into hiding, save yourself. Best take these two with you.’ He jerked a thumb at Ron and Hermione. ‘They’ll be in danger long as they live now everyone knows they’ve been working with you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t leave,’ said Harry. ‘I’ve got a job -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Give it to someone else!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t. It’s got to be me, Dumbledore explained it all -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, did he, now? And did he tell you everything, was he honest with you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry wanted with all his heart to say ‘yes’, but somehow the simple word would not rise to his lips. Aberforth seemed to know what he was thinking.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I knew my brother, Potter. He learned secrecy at our mother’s knee. Secrets and lies, that’s how we grew up, and Albus … he was a natural.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The old man’s eyes travelled to the painting of the girl over the mantelpiece. It was, now Harry looked around properly, the only picture in the room. There was no photograph of Albus Dumbledore, nor of anyone else.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Mr Dumbledore?’ said Hermione rather timidly. ‘Is that your sister? Ariana?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yes,’ said Aberforth tersely. ‘Been reading Rita Skeeter, have you, missy?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Even by the rosy light of the fire it was clear that Hermione had turned red.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Elphias Doge mentioned her to us,’ said Harry, trying to spare Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That old berk,’ muttered Aberforth, taking another swig of mead. ‘Thought the sun shone out of my brother’s every orifice, he did. Well, so did plenty of people, you three included, by the looks of it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry kept quiet. He did not want to express the doubts and uncertainties about Dumbledore that had riddled him for months now. He had made his choice while he dug Dobby’s grave; he had decided to continue along the winding, dangerous path indicated for him by Albus Dumbledore, to accept that he had not been told everything that he wanted to know, but simply to trust. He had no desire to doubt again, he did not want to hear anything that would deflect him from his purpose. He met Aberforth’s gaze, which was so strikingly like his brother’s: the bright blue eyes gave the same impression that they were X-raying the object of their scrutiny, and Harry thought that Aberforth knew what he was thinking, and despised him for it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Professor Dumbledore cared about Harry, very much,’ said Hermione in a low voice.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Did he, now?’ said Aberforth. ‘Funny thing, how many of the people my brother cared about very much, ended up in a worse state than if he’d left ‘em well alone.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What do you mean?’ asked Hermione breathlessly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Never you mind,’ said Aberforth.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But that’s a really serious thing to say!’ said Hermione. ‘Are you - are you talking about your sister?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aberforth glared at her: his lips moved as if he were chewing the words he was holding back. Then he burst into speech.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘When my sister was six years old, she was attacked, set upon, by three Muggle boys. They’d seen her doing magic, spying through the back garden hedge: she was a kid, she couldn’t control it, no witch or wizard can at that age. What they saw scared them, I expect. They forced their way through the hedge, and when she couldn’t show them the trick, they got a bit carried away trying to stop the little freak doing it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Hermione’s eyes were huge in the firelight: Ron looked slightly sick. Aberforth stood up, tall as Albus, and suddenly terrible in his anger and the intensity of his pain.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It destroyed her, what they did: she was never right again. She wouldn’t use magic, but she couldn’t get rid of it: it turned inwards and drove her mad, it exploded out of her when she couldn’t control it, and at times she was strange and dangerous. But mostly she was sweet, and scared, and harmless.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And my father went after the bastards that did it,’ said Aberforth, ‘and attacked them. And they locked him up in Azkaban for it. He never said why he’d done it, because if the Ministry had known what Ariana had become, she’d have been locked up in St Mungo’s for good. They’d have seen her as a serious threat to the International Statute of Secrecy, unbalanced like she was, with magic exploding out of her at moments when she couldn’t keep it in any longer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We had to keep her safe, and quiet. We moved house, put it about she was ill, and my mother looked after her, and tried to keep her calm and happy.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was her favourite,’ he said, and as he said it, a grubby schoolboy seemed to look out through Aberforth’s wrinkles and tangled beard. ‘Not Albus, he was always up in his bedroom when he was home, reading his books and counting his prizes, keeping up with his correspondence with “the most notable magical names of the day”,’ Aberforth sneered, ‘he didn’t want to be bothered with her. She liked me best. I could get her to eat when she wouldn’t do it for my mother, I could get her to calm down when she was in one of her rages, and when she was quiet, she used to help me feed the goats.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Then, when she was fourteen … see, I wasn’t there,’ said Aberforth. ‘If I’d been there, I could have calmed her down. She had one of her rages, and my mother wasn’t as young as she was, and … it was an accident. Ariana couldn’t control it. But my mother was killed.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry felt a horrible mixture of pity and repulsion; he did not want to hear any more, but Aberforth kept talking and Harry wondered how long it had been since he had spoken about this; whether, in fact, he had ever spoken about it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So that put paid to Albus’s trip round the world with little Doge. The pair of ‘em came home for my mother’s funeral and then Doge went off on his own, and Albus settled down as head of the family. Ha!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aberforth spat into the fire.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’d have looked after her, I told him so, I didn’t care about school, I’d have stayed home and done it. He told me I had to finish my education and he’d take over from my mother. Bit of a comedown for Mr Brilliant, there’s no prizes for looking after your half-mad sister, stopping her blowing up the house every other day. But he did all right for a few weeks … ‘til he came.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And now a positively dangerous look crept over Aberforth’s face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Grindelwald. And at last, my brother had an equal to talk to, someone just as bright and talented as he was. And looking after Ariana took a back seat then, while they were hatching all their plans for a new wizarding order, and looking for Hallows, and whatever else it was they were so interested in. Grand plans for the benefit of all wizardkind, and if one young girl got neglected, what did that matter, when Albus was working for the greater good?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But after a few weeks of it, I’d had enough, I had. It was nearly time for me to go back to Hogwarts, so I told ‘em, both of ‘em, face to face, like I am to you, now,’ and Aberforth looked down at Harry, and it took little imagination to see him as a teenager, wiry and angry, confronting his elder brother. ‘I told him, you’d better give it up, now. You can’t move her, she’s in no fit state, you can’t take her with you, wherever it is you’re planning to go, when you’re making your clever speeches, trying to whip yourselves up a following. He didn’t like that,’ said Aberforth, and his eyes were briefly occluded by the firelight on the lenses of his glasses: they shone white and blind again. ‘Grindelwald didn’t like that at all. He got angry. He told me what a stupid little boy I was, trying to stand in the way of him and my brilliant brother … didn’t I understand, my poor sister wouldn’t have to be hidden once they’d changed the world, and led the wizards out of hiding, and taught the Muggles their place?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And there was an argument … and I pulled out my wand, and he pulled out his, and I had the Cruciatus Curse used on me by my brother’s best friend - and Albus was trying to stop him, and then all three of us were duelling, and the flashing lights and the bangs set her off, she couldn’t stand it -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The colour was draining from Aberforth’s face as though he had suffered a mortal wound.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- and I think she wanted to help, but she didn’t really know what she was doing, and I don’t know which of us did it, it could have been any of us - and she was dead.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: His voice broke on the last word and he dropped down into the nearest chair. Hermione’s face was wet with tears and Ron was almost as pale as Aberforth. Harry felt nothing but revulsion: he wished he had not heard it, wished he could wash his mind clean of it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m so … I’m so sorry,’ Hermione whispered.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Gone,’ croaked Aberforth. ‘Gone forever.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He wiped his nose on his cuff, and cleared his throat.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ”Course, Grindelwald scarpered. He had a bit of a track record already, back in his own country, and he didn’t want Ariana set to his account too. And Albus was free, wasn’t he? Free of the burden of his sister, free to become the greatest wizard of the -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He was never free,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I beg your pardon?’ said Aberforth.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Never,’ said Harry. ‘The night that your brother died he drank a potion that drove him out of his mind. He started screaming, pleading with someone who wasn’t there. “Don’t hurt them, please … hurt me instead.” ‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Ron and Hermione were staring at Harry. He had never gone into details about what had happened on the island on the lake: the events that had taken place after he and Dumbledore had returned to Hogwarts had eclipsed it so thoroughly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He thought he was back there with you and Grindelwald, I know he did,’ said Harry, remembering Dumbledore whimpering, pleading. ‘He thought he was watching Grindelwald hurting you and Ariana … it was torture to him, if you’d seen him then, you wouldn’t say he was free.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aberforth seemed lost in contemplation of his own knotted and veined hands. After a long pause, he said, ‘How can you be sure, Potter, that my brother wasn’t more interested in the greater good than in you? How can you be sure you aren’t dispensable, just like my little sister?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A shard of ice seemed to pierce Harry’s heart.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t believe it. Dumbledore loved Harry,’ said Hermione.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why didn’t he tell him to hide, then?’ shot back Aberforth. ‘Why didn’t he say to him, take care of yourself, here’s how to survive?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Because,’ said Harry, before Hermione could answer, ‘sometimes you’ve got to think about more than your own safety! Sometimes you’ve got to think about the greater good! This is war!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re seventeen, boy!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m of age, and I’m going to keep fighting even if you’ve given up!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Who says I’ve given up?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘“The Order of the Phoenix is finished,”’ Harry repeated. ‘“You-Know-Who’s won, it’s over, and anyone who’s pretending different’s kidding themselves.”’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t say I like it, but it’s the truth!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No, it isn’t,’ said Harry. ‘Your brother knew how to finish You-Know-Who and he passed the knowledge on to me. I’m going to keep going until I succeed - or I die. Don’t think I don’t know how this might end. I’ve known it for years.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He waited for Aberforth to jeer or to argue, but he did not. He merely scowled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We need to get into Hogwarts,’ said Harry again. ‘If you can’t help us, we’ll wait ‘til daybreak, leave you in peace and try to find a way in ourselves. If you can help us - well, now would be a great time to mention it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Aberforth remained fixed in his chair, gazing at Harry with the eyes that were so extraordinarily like his brother’s. At last he cleared his throat, got to his feet, walked around the little table and approached the portrait of Ariana.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You know what to do,’ he said.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: She smiled, turned and walked away, not as people in portraits usually did, out of the sides of their frames, but along what seemed to be a long tunnel painted behind her. They watched her slight figure retreating until finally she was swallowed by the darkness.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Er - what -?’ began Ron.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s only one way in, now,’ said Aberforth. ‘You must know they’ve got all the old secret passageways covered at both ends, Dementors all around the boundary walls, regular patrols inside the school from what my sources tell me. The place has never been so heavily guarded. How you expect to do anything once you get inside it, with Snape in charge and the Carrows as his Deputies … well, that’s your lookout, isn’t it? You say you’re prepared to die.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But what …?’ said Hermione, frowning at Ariana’s picture.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A tiny white dot had reappeared at the end of the painted tunnel, and now Ariana was walking back towards them, growing bigger and bigger as she came. But there was somebody else with her now, someone taller than she was, who was limping along looking excited. His hair was longer than Harry had ever seen it: he appeared to have suffered several gashes to his face and his clothes were ripped and torn. Larger and larger the two figures grew, until only their heads and shoulders filled the portrait. Then the whole thing swung forwards on the wall like a little door, and the entrance to a real tunnel was revealed. And out of it, his hair overgrown, his face cut, his robes ripped, clambered the real Neville Longbottom, who gave a roar of delight, leapt down from the mantelpiece and yelled, ‘I knew you’d come! I knew it, Harry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville - what the - how -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: But Neville had spotted Ron and Hermione, and with yells of delight was hugging them too. The longer Harry looked at Neville, the worse he appeared: one of his eyes was swollen, yellow and purple, there were gouge marks on his face, and his general air of unkemptness suggested that he had been living rough. Nevertheless, his battered visage shone with happiness as he let go of Hermione and said again, ‘I knew you’d come! Kept telling Seamus it was a matter of time!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville, what’s happened to you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What? This?’ Neville dismissed his injuries with a shake of the head. ‘This is nothing. Seamus is worse. You’ll see. Shall we get going, then? Oh,’ he turned to Aberforth, ‘Ab, there might be a couple more people on the way.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Couple more?’ repeated Aberforth ominously. ‘What d’you mean, a couple more, Longbottom? There’s a curfew and a Caterwauling Charm on the whole village!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know, that’s why they’ll be Apparating directly into the bar,’ said Neville. ‘Just send them down the passage when they get here, will you? Thanks a lot.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Neville held out his hand to Hermione and helped her to climb up on to the mantelpiece and into the tunnel; Ron followed, then Neville. Harry addressed Aberforth.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t know how to thank you. You’ve saved our lives, twice.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Look after ‘em, then,’ said Aberforth gruffly. ‘I might not be able to save ‘em a third time.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry clambered up on to the mantelpiece and through the hole behind Ariana’s portrait. There were smooth stone steps on the other side: it looked as though the passageway had been there for years. Brass lamps hung from the walls and the earthy floor was worn and smooth; as they walked, their shadows rippled, fan-like, across the wall.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘How long’s this been here?’ Ron asked, as they set off. ‘It isn’t on the Marauder’s Map, is it, Harry? I thought there were only seven passages in and out of school?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They sealed off all of those before the start of the year,’ said Neville. ‘There’s no chance of getting through any of them now, not with curses over the entrances and Death Eaters and Dementors waiting at the exits.’ He started walking backwards, beaming, drinking them in. ‘Never mind that stuff … is it true? Did you break into Gringotts? Did you escape on a dragon? It’s everywhere, everyone’s talking about it, Terry Boot got beaten up by Carrow for yelling about it in the Great Hall at dinner!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, it’s true,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Neville laughed gleefully.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What did you do with the dragon?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Released it into the wild,’ said Ron. ‘Hermione was all for keeping it as a pet -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t exaggerate, Ron -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But what have you been doing? People have been saying you’ve just been on the run, Harry, but I don’t think so. I think you’ve been up to something.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You’re right,’ said Harry, ‘but tell us about Hogwarts, Neville, we haven’t heard anything.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It’s been … well, it’s not really like Hogwarts any more,’ said Neville, the smile fading from his face as he spoke. ‘Do you know about the Carrows?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Those two Death Eaters who teach here?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They do more than teach,’ said Neville. ‘They’re in charge of all discipline. They like punishment, the Carrows.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Like Umbridge?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Nah, they make her look tame. The other teachers are all supposed to refer us to the Carrows if we do anything wrong. They don’t, though, if they can avoid it. You can tell they all hate them as much as we do.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Amycus, the bloke, he teaches what used to be Defence Against the Dark Arts, except now it’s just the Dark Arts. We’re supposed to practise the Cruciatus Curse on people who’ve earned detentions -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry, Ron and Hermione’s united voices echoed up and down the passage.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah,’ said Neville. ‘That’s how I got this one,’ he pointed at a particularly deep gash in his cheek, ‘I refused to do it. Some people are into it, though; Crabbe and Goyle love it. First time they’ve ever been top in anything, I expect.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Alecto, Amycus’s sister, teaches Muggle Studies, which is compulsory for everyone. We’ve all got to listen to her explain how Muggles are like animals, stupid and dirty, and how they drove wizards into hiding by being vicious towards them, and how the natural order is being re-established. I got this one,’ he indicated another slash to his face, ‘for asking her how much Muggle blood she and her brother have got.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Blimey, Neville,’ said Ron, ‘there’s a time and a place for getting a smart mouth.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You didn’t hear her,’ said Neville. ‘You wouldn’t have stood it either. The thing is, it helps when people stand up to them, it gives everyone hope. I used to notice that when you did it, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But they’ve used you as a knife sharpener,’ said Ron, wincing slightly as they passed a lamp and Neville’s injuries were thrown into even greater relief.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Neville shrugged.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Doesn’t matter. They don’t want to spill too much pure blood, so they’ll torture us a bit if we’re mouthy but they won’t actually kill us.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry did not know what was worse, the things that Neville was saying or the matter-of-fact tone in which he said them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The only people in real danger are the ones whose friends and relatives on the outside are giving trouble. They get taken hostage. Old Xeno Lovegood was getting a bit too outspoken in The Quibbler, so they dragged Luna off the train on the way back for Christmas.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Neville, she’s all right, we’ve seen her -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, I know, she managed to get a message to me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: From his pocket he pulled a golden coin, and Harry recognised it as one of the fake Galleons that Dumbledore’s Army had used to send one another messages.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘These have been great,’ said Neville, beaming at Hermione. ‘The Carrows never rumbled how we were communicating, it drove them mad. We used to sneak out at night and put graffiti on the walls: Dumbledore’s Army, Still Recruiting, stuff like that. Snape hated it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You used to?’ said Harry, who had noticed the past tense.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, it got more difficult as time went on,’ said Neville. ‘We lost Luna at Christmas and Ginny never came back after Easter, and the three of us were sort of the leaders. The Carrows seemed to know I was behind a lot of it, so they started coming down on me hard, and then Michael Corner went and got caught releasing a first-year they’d chained up, and they tortured him pretty badly. That scared people off.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No kidding,’ muttered Ron, as the passage began to slope upwards.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yeah, well, I couldn’t ask people to go through what Michael did, so we dropped those kinds of stunts. But we were still fighting, doing underground stuff, right up until a couple of weeks ago. That’s when they decided there was only one way to stop me, I suppose, and they went for Gran.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘They what?’ said Harry, Ron and Hermione together.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)

To escape into someone else’s head would be a blessed relief … nothing that even Snape had left him could be worse than his own thoughts. The memories swirled, silver-white and strange, and without hesitating, with a feeling of reckless abandonment, as though this would assuage his torturing grief, Harry dived.
