book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry watched, again, as Snape left from the Great Hall, after sitting his O.W.L. in Defence Against the Dark Arts, watched as he wandered away from the castle and strayed, inadvertently, close to the place beneath the beech tree where James, Sirius, Lupin and Pettigrew sat together. But Harry kept his distance this time, because he knew what happened after James had hoisted Severus into the air and taunted him; he knew what had been done and said, and it gave him no pleasure to hear it again. He watched, as Lily joined the group and went to Snape’s defence. Distantly he heard Snape shout at her in his humiliation and his fury, the unforgivable word: ‘Mudblood.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The scene changed …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m not interested.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I’m sorry!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Save your breath.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: It was night-time. Lily, who was wearing a dressing gown, stood with her arms folded in front of the portrait of the Fat Lady, at the entrance to Gryffindor Tower.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I only came out because Mary told me you were threatening to sleep here.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was. I would have done. I never meant to call you Mudblood, it just -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Slipped out?’ There was no pity in Lily’s voice. ‘It’s too late. I’ve made excuses for you for years. None of my friends can understand why I even talk to you. You and your precious little Death Eater friends - you see, you don’t even deny it! You don’t even deny that’s what you’re all aiming to be! You can’t wait to join You-Know-Who, can you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He opened his mouth, but closed it without speaking.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I can’t pretend any more. You’ve chosen your way, I’ve chosen mine.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No - listen, I didn’t mean -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- to call me Mudblood? But you call everyone of my birth Mudblood, Severus. Why should I be any different?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He struggled on the verge of speech, but with a contemptuous look she turned and climbed back through the portrait hole …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The corridor dissolved, and the scene took a little longer to reform: Harry seemed to fly through shifting shapes and colours until his surroundings solidified again and he stood on a hilltop, forlorn and cold in the darkness, the wind whistling through the branches of a few leafless trees. The adult Snape was panting, turning on the spot, his wand gripped tightly in his hand, waiting for something or for someone … his fear infected Harry, too, even though he knew that he could not be harmed, and he looked over his shoulder, wondering what it was that Snape was waiting for -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then a blinding, jagged jet of white light flew through the air: Harry thought of lightning, but Snape had dropped to his knees and his wand had flown out of his hand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t kill me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That was not my intention.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Any sound of Dumbledore Apparating had been drowned by the sound of the wind in the branches. He stood before Snape with his robes whipping around him, and his face was illuminated from below in the light cast by his wand.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, Severus? What message does Lord Voldemort have for me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No - no message - I’m here on my own account!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape was wringing his hands: he looked a little mad, with his straggling, black hair flying around him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I - I come with a warning - no, a request - please -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore flicked his wand. Though leaves and branches still flew through the night air around them, silence fell on the spot where he and Snape faced each other.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What request could a Death Eater make of me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The - the prophecy … the prediction … Trelawney …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, yes,’ said Dumbledore. ‘How much did you relay to Lord Voldemort?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Everything - everything I heard!’ said Snape. ‘That is why - it is for that reason - he thinks it means Lily Evans!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The prophecy did not refer to a woman,’ said Dumbledore. ‘It spoke of a boy born at the end of July -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You know what I mean! He thinks it means her son, he is going to hunt her down - kill them all -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If she means so much to you,’ said Dumbledore, ‘surely Lord Voldemort will spare her? Could you not ask for mercy for the mother, in exchange for the son?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I have - I have asked him -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You disgust me,’ said Dumbledore, and Harry had never heard so much contempt in his voice. Snape seemed to shrink a little.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You do not care, then, about the deaths of her husband and child?

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They can die, as long as you have what you want?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape said nothing, but merely looked up at Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hide them all, then,’ he croaked. ‘Keep her - them - safe. Please.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And what will you give me in return, Severus?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In - in return?’ Snape gaped at Dumbledore, and Harry expected him to protest, but after a long moment he said, ‘Anything.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The hilltop faded, and Harry stood in Dumbledore’s office, and something was making a terrible sound, like a wounded animal. Snape was slumped forwards in a chair and Dumbledore was standing over him, looking grim. After a moment or two, Snape raised his face, and he looked like a man who had lived a hundred years of misery since leaving the wild hilltop.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought … you were going … to keep her … safe …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘She and James put their faith in the wrong person,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Rather like you, Severus. Weren’t you hoping that Lord Voldemort would spare her?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape’s breathing was shallow.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Her boy survives,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: With a tiny jerk of the head, Snape seemed to flick off an irksome fly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Her son lives. He has her eyes, precisely her eyes. You remember the shape and colour of Lily Evans’s eyes, I am sure?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘DON’T!’ bellowed Snape. ‘Gone … Dead …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Is this remorse, Severus?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I wish … I wish I were dead …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And what use would that be to anyone?’ said Dumbledore coldly. ‘If you loved Lily Evans, if you truly loved her, then your way forward is clear.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape seemed to peer through a haze of pain, and Dumbledore’s words appeared to take a long time to reach him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What - what do you mean?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You know how and why she died. Make sure it was not in vain. Help me protect Lily’s son.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He does not need protection. The Dark Lord has gone -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- the Dark Lord will return, and Harry Potter will be in terrible danger when he does.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a long pause, and slowly Snape regained control of himself, mastered his own breathing. At last he said, ‘Very well. Very well. But never - never tell, Dumbledore! This must be between us! Swear it! I cannot bear … especially Potter’s son … I want your word!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My word, Severus, that I shall never reveal the best of you?’ Dumbledore sighed, looking down into Snape’s ferocious, anguished face. ‘If you insist …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The office dissolved but re-formed instantly. Snape was pacing up and down in front of Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- mediocre, arrogant as his father, a determined rule-breaker, delighted to find himself famous, attention-seeking and impertinent -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You see what you expect to see, Severus,’ said Dumbledore, without raising his eyes from a copy of Transfiguration Today. ‘Other teachers report that the boy is modest, likeable and reasonably talented. Personally, I find him an engaging child.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore turned a page, and said, without looking up, ‘Keep an eye on Quirrell, won’t you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A whirl of colour, and now everything darkened, and Snape and Dumbledore stood a little apart in the Entrance Hall, while the last stragglers from the Yule Ball passed them on their way to bed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well?’ murmured Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Karkaroff’s Mark is becoming darker too. He is panicking, he fears retribution; you know how much help he gave the Ministry after the Dark Lord fell.’ Snape looked sideways at Dumbledore’s crooked-nosed profile. ‘Karkaroff intends to flee if the Mark burns.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Does he?’ said Dumbledore softly, as Fleur Delacour and Roger Davies came giggling in from the grounds. ‘And are you tempted to join him?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ said Snape, his black eyes on Fleur and Roger’s retreating figures. ‘I am not such a coward.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘No,’ agreed Dumbledore. ‘You are a braver man by far than Igor Karkaroff. You know, I sometimes think we Sort too soon …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He walked away, leaving Snape looking stricken …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: And now Harry stood in the Headmaster’s office yet again. It was night-time, and Dumbledore sagged sideways in the throne-like chair behind the desk, apparently semi-conscious. His right hand dangled over the side, blackened and burned. Snape was muttering incantations, pointing his wand at the wrist of the hand, while with his left hand he tipped a goblet full of thick golden potion down Dumbledore’s throat. After a moment or two, Dumbledore’s eyelids fluttered and opened.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why,’ said Snape, without preamble, ‘why did you put on that ring? It carries a curse, surely you realised that. Why even touch it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Marvolo Gaunt’s ring lay on the desk before Dumbledore. It was cracked; the sword of Gryffindor lay beside it.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore grimaced.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I … was a fool. Sorely tempted …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tempted by what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore did not answer.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It is a miracle you managed to return here!’ Snape sounded furious. ‘That ring carried a curse of extraordinary power, to contain it is all we can hope for; I have trapped the curse in one hand for the time being -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore raised his blackened, useless hand, and examined it with the expression of one being shown an interesting curio.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You have done very well, Severus. How long do you think I have?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore’s tone was conversational; he might have been asking for a weather forecast. Snape hesitated, and then said, ‘I cannot tell. Maybe a year. There is no halting such a spell forever. It will spread, eventually, it is the sort of curse that strengthens over time.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled. The news that he had less than a year to live seemed a matter of little or no concern to him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I am fortunate, extremely fortunate, that I have you, Severus.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If you had only summoned me a little earlier, I might have been able to do more, buy you more time!’ said Snape furiously. He looked down at the broken ring and the sword. ‘Did you think that breaking the ring would break the curse?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Something like that … I was delirious, no doubt …’ said Dumbledore. With an effort, he straightened himself in his chair. ‘Well, really, this makes matters much more straightforward.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape looked utterly perplexed. Dumbledore smiled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I refer to the plan Lord Voldemort is revolving around me. His plan to have the poor Malfoy boy murder me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape sat down in the chair Harry had so often occupied, across the desk from Dumbledore. Harry could tell that he wanted to say more on the subject of Dumbledore’s cursed hand, but the other held it up in polite refusal to discuss the matter further. Scowling, Snape said, ‘The Dark Lord does not expect Draco to succeed. This is merely punishment for Lucius’s recent failures. Slow torture for Draco’s parents, while they watch him fail and pay the price.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In short, the boy has had a death sentence pronounced upon him as surely as I have,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Now, I should have thought the natural successor to the job, once Draco fails, is yourself?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a short pause.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That, I think, is the Dark Lord’s plan.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Lord Voldemort foresees a moment in the near future when he will not need a spy at Hogwarts?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He believes the school will soon be in his grasp, yes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And if it does fall into his grasp,’ said Dumbledore, almost, it seemed, as an aside, ‘I have your word that you will do all in your power to protect the students of Hogwarts?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape gave a stiff nod.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Good. Now then. Your first priority will be to discover what Draco is up to. A frightened teenage boy is a danger to others as well as to himself. Offer him help and guidance, he ought to accept, he likes you -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- much less since his father has lost favour. Draco blames me, he thinks I have usurped Lucius’s position.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘All the same, try. I am concerned less for myself than for accidental victims of whatever schemes might occur to the boy. Ultimately, of course, there is only one thing to be done if we are to save him from Lord Voldemort’s wrath.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape raised his eyebrows and his tone was sardonic as he asked, ‘Are you intending to let him kill you?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Certainly not. You must kill me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a long silence, broken only by an odd clicking noise. Fawkes the phoenix was gnawing a bit of cuttlebone.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Would you like me to do it now?’ asked Snape, his voice heavy with irony. ‘Or would you like a few moments to compose an epitaph?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, not quite yet,’ said Dumbledore, smiling. ‘I daresay the moment will present itself in due course. Given what has happened tonight,’ he indicated his withered hand, ‘we can be sure that it will happen within a year.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘If you don’t mind dying,’ said Snape roughly, ‘why not let Draco do it?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That boy’s soul is not yet so damaged,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I would not have it ripped apart on my account.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And my soul, Dumbledore? Mine?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You alone know whether it will harm your soul to help an old man avoid pain and humiliation,’ said Dumbledore. ‘I ask this one, great favour of you, Severus, because death is coming for me as surely as the Chudley Cannons will finish bottom of this year’s league. I confess I should prefer a quick, painless exit to the protracted and messy affair it will be if, for instance, Greyback is involved - I hear Voldemort has recruited him? Or dear Bellatrix, who likes to play with her food before she eats it.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: His tone was light but his blue eyes pierced Snape as they had frequently pierced Harry, as though the soul they discussed was visible to him. At last Snape gave another curt nod.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore seemed satisfied.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Thank you, Severus …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The office disappeared, and now Snape and Dumbledore were strolling together in the deserted castle grounds by twilight.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What are you doing with Potter, all these evenings you are closeted together?’ Snape asked abruptly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore looked weary.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why? You aren’t trying to give him more detentions, Severus? The boy will soon have spent more time in detention than out.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He is his father over again -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In looks, perhaps, but his deepest nature is much more like his mother’s. I spend time with Harry because I have things to discuss with him, information I must give him before it is too late.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Information,’ repeated Snape. ‘You trust him … you do not trust me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It is not a question of trust. I have, as we both know, limited time. It is essential that I give the boy enough information for him to do what he needs to do.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And why may I not have the same information?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I prefer not to put all of my secrets in one basket, particularly not a basket that spends so much time dangling on the arm of Lord Voldemort.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Which I do on your orders!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And you do it extremely well. Do not think that I underestimate the constant danger in which you place yourself, Severus. To give Voldemort what appears to be valuable information while withholding the essentials is a job I would entrust to nobody but you.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Yet you confide much more in a boy who is incapable of Occlumency, whose magic is mediocre and who has a direct connection into the Dark Lord’s mind!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Voldemort fears that connection,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Not so long ago he had one, small taste of what truly sharing Harry’s mind means to him. It was pain such as he has never experienced. He will not try to possess Harry again, I am sure of it. Not in that way.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I don’t understand.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Lord Voldemort’s soul, maimed as it is, cannot bear close contact with a soul like Harry’s. Like a tongue on frozen steel, like flesh in flame -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Souls? We were talking of minds!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘In the case of Harry and Lord Voldemort, to speak of one is to speak of the other.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore glanced around to make sure that they were alone. They were close by the Forbidden Forest, now, but there was no sign of anyone near them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘After you have killed me, Severus -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You refuse to tell me everything, yet you expect that small service of me!’ snarled Snape, and real anger flared in the thin face now. ‘You take a great deal for granted, Dumbledore! Perhaps I have changed my mind!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You gave me your word, Severus. And while we are talking about services you owe me, I thought you agreed to keep a close eye on our young Slytherin friend?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Snape looked angry, mutinous. Dumbledore sighed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Come to my office tonight, Severus, at eleven, and you shall not complain that I have no confidence in you …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They were back in Dumbledore’s office, the windows dark, and Fawkes sat silent as Snape sat quite still, as Dumbledore walked around him, talking.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry must not know, not until the last moment, not until it is necessary, otherwise how could he have the strength to do what must be done?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But what must he do?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘That is between Harry and me. Now, listen closely, Severus. There will come a time - after my death - do not argue, do not interrupt! There will come a time when Lord Voldemort will seem to fear for the life of his snake.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘For Nagini?’ Snape looked astonished.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Precisely. If there comes a time when Lord Voldemort stops sending that snake forth to do his bidding, but keeps it safe beside him, under magical protection, then, I think, it will be safe to tell Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell him what?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore took a deep breath and closed his eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Tell him that on the night Lord Voldemort tried to kill him, when Lily cast her own life between them as a shield, the Killing Curse rebounded upon Lord Voldemort, and a fragment of Voldemort’s soul was blasted apart from the whole, and latched itself on to the only living soul left in that collapsing building. Part of Lord Voldemort lives inside Harry, and it is that which gives him the power of speech with snakes, and a connection with Lord Voldemort’s mind that he has never understood. And while that fragment of soul, unmissed by Voldemort, remains attached to, and protected by Harry, Lord Voldemort cannot die.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry seemed to be watching the two men from one end of a long tunnel, they were so far away from him, their voices echoing strangely in his ears.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So the boy … the boy must die?’ asked Snape, quite calmly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And Voldemort himself must do it, Severus. That is essential.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Another long silence. Then Snape said, ‘I thought … all these years … that we were protecting him for her. For Lily.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘We have protected him because it has been essential to teach him, to raise him, to let him try his strength,’ said Dumbledore, his eyes still tight shut. ‘Meanwhile, the connection between them grows ever stronger, a parasitic growth: sometimes I have thought he suspects it himself. If I know him, he will have arranged matters so that when he does set out to meet his death, it will, truly, mean the end of Voldemort.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore opened his eyes. Snape looked horrified.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You have kept him alive so that he can die at the right moment?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t be shocked, Severus. How many men and women have you watched die?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Lately, only those whom I could not save,’ said Snape. He stood up. ‘You have used me.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Meaning?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I have spied for you, and lied for you, put myself in mortal danger for you. Everything was supposed to be to keep Lily Potter’s son safe. Now you tell me you have been raising him like a pig for slaughter -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But this is touching, Severus,’ said Dumbledore seriously. ‘Have you grown to care for the boy, after all?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘For him?’ shouted Snape. ‘Expecto patronum!’

text_content: Bellatrix had spoken: she sat closest to Voldemort, dishevelled, her face a little bloody but otherwise unharmed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Voldemort raised his hand to silence her, and she did not speak another word, but eyed him in worshipful fascination.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I thought he would come,’ said Voldemort in his high, clear voice, his eyes on the leaping flames. ‘I expected him to come.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Nobody spoke. They seemed as scared as Harry, whose heart was now throwing itself against his ribs as though determined to escape the body he was about to cast aside. His hands were sweating as he pulled off the Invisibility Cloak and stuffed it beneath his robes, with his wand. He did not want to be tempted to fight.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was, it seems … mistaken,’ said Voldemort.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You weren’t.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry said it as loudly as he could, with all the force he could muster: he did not want to sound afraid. The Resurrection Stone slipped from between his numb fingers and out of the corner of his eyes he saw his parents, Sirius and Lupin vanish as he stepped forwards into the firelight. At that moment he felt that nobody mattered but Voldemort. It was just the two of them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The illusion was gone as soon as it had come. The giants roared as the Death Eaters rose together, and there were many cries, gasps, even laughter. Voldemort had frozen where he stood, but his red eyes had found Harry, and he stared as Harry moved towards him, with nothing but the fire between them.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then a voice yelled -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘HARRY! NO!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He turned: Hagrid was bound and trussed, tied to a tree nearby. His massive body shook the branches overhead as he struggled, desperate.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘NO! NO! HARRY, WHAT’RE YEH -?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘QUIET!’ shouted Rowle, and with a flick of his wand Hagrid was silenced.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Bellatrix, who had leapt to her feet, was looking eagerly from Voldemort to Harry, her breast heaving. The only things that moved were the flames and the snake, coiling and uncoiling in the glittering cage behind Voldemort’s head.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry could feel his wand against his chest, but he made no attempt to draw it. He knew that the snake was too well protected, knew that if he managed to point the wand at Nagini, fifty curses would hit him first. And still, Voldemort and Harry looked at each other, and now Voldemort tilted his head a little to the side, considering the boy standing before him, and a singularly mirthless smile curled the lipless mouth.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry Potter,’ he said, very softly. His voice might have been part of the spitting fire. ‘The boy who lived.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: None of the Death Eaters moved. They were waiting: everything was waiting. Hagrid was struggling, and Bellatrix was panting, and Harry thought inexplicably of Ginny, and her blazing look, and the feel of her lips on his -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Voldemort had raised his wand. His head was still tilted to one side, like a curious child, wondering what would happen if he proceeded. Harry looked back into the red eyes, and wanted it to happen now, quickly, while he could still stand, before he lost control, before he betrayed fear -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He saw the mouth move and a flash of green light, and everything was gone.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He lay face down, listening to the silence. He was perfectly alone. Nobody was watching. Nobody else was there. He was not perfectly sure that he was there himself.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: A long time later, or maybe no time at all, it came to him that he must exist, must be more than disembodied thought, because he was lying, definitely lying, on some surface. Therefore, he had a sense of a touch, and the thing against which he lay existed too.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Almost as soon as he had reached this conclusion, Harry became conscious that he was naked. Convinced as he was of his total solitude, this did not concern him, but it did intrigue him slightly. He wondered whether, as he could feel, he would be able to see. In opening them, he discovered that he had eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He lay in a bright mist, though it was not like mist he had ever experienced before. His surroundings were not hidden by cloudy vapour; rather the cloudy vapour had not yet formed into surroundings. The floor on which he lay seemed to be white, neither warm nor cold, but simply there, a flat, blank something on which to be.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He sat up. His body appeared unscathed. He touched his face. He was not wearing glasses any more.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Then a noise reached him through the unformed nothingness that surrounded him: the small, soft thumpings of something that flapped, flailed and struggled. It was a pitiful noise, yet also slightly indecent. He had the uncomfortable feeling that he was eavesdropping on something furtive, shameful.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: For the first time, he wished he were clothed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Barely had the wish formed in his head, than robes appeared a short distance away. He took them and pulled them on: they were soft, clean and warm. It was extraordinary how they had appeared, just like that, the moment he had wanted them …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He stood up, looking around. Was he in some great Room of Requirement? The longer he looked, the more there was to see. A great, domed glass roof glittered high above him in sunlight. Perhaps it was a palace. All was hushed and still, except for those odd thumping and whimpering noises coming from somewhere close by in the mist …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry turned slowly on the spot, and his surroundings seemed to invent themselves before his eyes. A wide open space, bright and clean, a hall larger by far than the Great Hall, with that clear, domed glass ceiling. It was quite empty. He was the only person there, except for -

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He recoiled. He had spotted the thing that was making the noises. It had the form of a small, naked child, curled on the ground, its skin raw and rough, flayed-looking, and it lay shuddering under a seat where it had been left, unwanted, stuffed out of sight, struggling for breath.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He was afraid of it. Small and fragile and wounded though it was, he did not want to approach it. Nevertheless, he drew slowly nearer, ready to jump back at any moment. Soon he stood near enough to touch it, yet he could not bring himself to do it. He felt like a coward. He ought to comfort it, but it repulsed him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You cannot help.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He spun round. Albus Dumbledore was walking towards him, sprightly and upright, wearing sweeping robes of midnight blue.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Harry.’ He spread his arms wide, and his hands were both whole and white and undamaged. ‘You wonderful boy. You brave, brave man. Let us walk.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Stunned, Harry followed as Dumbledore strode away from where the flayed child lay whimpering, leading him to two seats that Harry had not previously noticed, set some distance away under that high, sparkling ceiling. Dumbledore sat down in one of them, and Harry fell into the other, staring at his old Headmaster’s face. Dumbledore’s long, silver hair and beard, the piercingly blue eyes behind half-moon spectacles, the crooked nose: everything was as he had remembered it. And yet …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But you’re dead,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes,’ said Dumbledore matter-of-factly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Then … I’m dead too?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah,’ said Dumbledore, smiling still more broadly. ‘That is the question, isn’t it? On the whole, dear boy, I think not.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: They looked at each other, the old man still beaming.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not?’ repeated Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But …’ Harry raised his hand instinctively towards the lightning scar. It did not seem to be there. ‘But I should have died - I didn’t defend myself! I meant to let him kill me!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And that,’ said Dumbledore, ‘will, I think, have made all the difference.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Happiness seemed to radiate from Dumbledore like light, like fire: Harry had never seen the man so utterly, so palpably content.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Explain,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But you already know,’ said Dumbledore. He twiddled his thumbs together.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I let him kill me,’ said Harry. ‘Didn’t I?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You did,’ said Dumbledore, nodding. ‘Go on!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So the part of his soul that was in me …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore nodded still more enthusiastically, urging Harry onwards, a broad smile of encouragement on his face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘… has it gone?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, yes!’ said Dumbledore. ‘Yes, he destroyed it. Your soul is whole, and completely your own, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But then …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry glanced over his shoulder, to where the small, maimed creature trembled under the chair.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What is that, Professor?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Something that is beyond either of our help,’ said Dumbledore.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But if Voldemort used the Killing Curse,’ Harry started again, ‘and nobody died for me this time - how can I be alive?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I think you know,’ said Dumbledore. ‘Think back. Remember what he did, in his ignorance, in his greed and his cruelty.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry thought. He let his gaze drift over his surroundings. If it was indeed a palace in which they sat, it was an odd one, with chairs set in little rows and bits of railing here and there, and still, he and Dumbledore and the stunted creature under the chair were the only beings there. Then the answer rose to his lips easily, without effort.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He took my blood,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Precisely!’ said Dumbledore. ‘He took your blood and rebuilt his living body with it! Your blood in his veins, Harry, Lily’s protection inside both of you! He tethered you to life while he lives!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I live … while he lives? But I thought … I thought it was the other way round! I thought we both had to die? Or is it the same thing?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He was distracted by the whimpering and thumping of the agonised creature behind them and glanced back at it yet again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Are you sure we can’t do anything?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There is no help possible.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Then explain … more,’ said Harry, and Dumbledore smiled.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You were the seventh Horcrux, Harry, the Horcrux he never meant to make. He had rendered his soul so unstable that it broke apart when he committed those acts of unspeakable evil, the murder of your parents, the attempted killing of a child. But what escaped from that room was even less than he knew. He left more than his body behind. He left part of himself latched to you, the would-be victim who had survived.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And his knowledge remained woefully incomplete, Harry! That which Voldemort does not value, he takes no trouble to comprehend. Of house-elves and children’s tales, of love, loyalty and innocence, Voldemort knows and understands nothing. Nothing. That they all have a power beyond his own, a power beyond the reach of any magic, is a truth he has never grasped.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He took your blood believing it would strengthen him. He took into his body a tiny part of the enchantment your mother laid upon you when she died for you. His body keeps her sacrifice alive, and while that enchantment survives, so do you and so does Voldemort’s one last hope for himself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled at Harry, and Harry stared at him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And you knew this? You knew - all along?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I guessed. But my guesses have, usually, been good,’ said Dumbledore happily, and they sat in silence for what seemed like a long time, while the creature behind them continued to whimper and tremble.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘There’s more,’ said Harry. ‘There’s more to it. Why did my wand break the wand he borrowed?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘As to that, I cannot be sure.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Have a guess, then,’ said Harry, and Dumbledore laughed.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What you must understand, Harry, is that you and Lord Voldemort have journeyed together into realms of magic hitherto unknown and untested. But here is what I think happened, and it is unprecedented, and no wandmaker could, I think, ever have predicted it or explained it to Voldemort.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Without meaning to, as you now know, Lord Voldemort doubled the bond between you when he returned to a human form. A part of his soul was still attached to yours, and, thinking to strengthen himself, he took a part of your mother’s sacrifice into himself. If he could only have understood the precise and terrible power of that sacrifice, he would not, perhaps, have dared to touch your blood … but then, if he had been able to understand, he could not be Lord Voldemort, and might never have murdered at all.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Having ensured this two-fold connection, having wrapped your destinies together more securely than ever two wizards were joined in history, Voldemort proceeded to attack you with a wand that shared a core with yours. And now something very strange happened, as we know. The cores reacted in a way that Lord Voldemort, who never knew that your wand was twin of his, had never expected.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He was more afraid than you were that night, Harry. You had accepted, even embraced, the possibility of death, something Lord Voldemort has never been able to do. Your courage won, your wand overpowered his. And in doing so, something happened between those wands, something that echoed the relationship between their masters.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I believe that your wand imbibed some of the power and qualities of Voldemort’s wand that night, which is to say that it contained a little of Voldemort himself. So your wand recognised him when he pursued you, recognised a man who was both kin and mortal enemy, and it regurgitated some of his own magic against him, magic much more powerful than anything Lucius’s wand had ever performed. Your wand now contained the power of your enormous courage and of Voldemort’s own deadly skill: what chance did that poor stick of Lucius Malfoy’s stand?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But if my wand was so powerful, how come Hermione was able to break it?’ asked Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My dear boy, its remarkable effects were directed only at Voldemort, who had tampered so ill-advisedly with the deepest laws of magic. Only towards him was that wand abnormally powerful. Otherwise it was a wand like any other … though a good one, I am sure,’ Dumbledore finished kindly.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry sat in thought for a long time, or perhaps seconds. It was very hard to be sure of things like time, here.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He killed me with your wand.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He failed to kill you with my wand,’ Dumbledore corrected Harry. ‘I think we can agree that you are not dead - though, of course,’ he added, as if fearing he had been discourteous, ‘I do not minimise your sufferings, which I am sure were severe.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I feel great at the moment, though,’ said Harry, looking down at his clean, unblemished hands. ‘Where are we, exactly?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, I was going to ask you that,’ said Dumbledore, looking around. ‘Where would you say that we are?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Until Dumbledore had asked, Harry had not known. Now, however, he found that he had an answer ready to give.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It looks,’ he said slowly, ‘like King’s Cross station. Except a lot cleaner, and empty, and there are no trains as far as I can see.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘King’s Cross station!’ Dumbledore was chuckling immoderately. ‘Good gracious, really?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well, where do you think we are?’ asked Harry, a little defensively.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘My dear boy, I have no idea. This is, as they say, your party.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry had no idea what this meant; Dumbledore was being infuriating. He glared at him, then remembered a much more pressing question than that of their current location.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Deathly Hallows,’ he said, and he was glad to see that the words wiped the smile from Dumbledore’s face.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Ah, yes,’ he said. He even looked a little worried.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Well?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: For the first time since Harry had met Dumbledore, he looked less than an old man, much less. He looked, fleetingly, like a small boy caught in wrongdoing.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Can you forgive me?’ he said. ‘Can you forgive me for not trusting you? For not telling you? Harry, I only feared that you would fail as I had failed. I only dreaded that you would make my mistakes. I crave your pardon, Harry. I have known, for some time now, that you are the better man.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What are you talking about?’ asked Harry, startled by Dumbledore’s tone, by the sudden tears in his eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Hallows, the Hallows,’ murmured Dumbledore. ‘A desperate man’s dream!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But they’re real!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Real, and dangerous, and a lure for fools,’ said Dumbledore. ‘And I was such a fool. But you know, don’t you? I have no secrets from you any more. You know.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘What do I know?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore turned his whole body to face Harry, and tears still sparkled in the brilliantly blue eyes.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Master of death, Harry, master of Death! Was I better, ultimately, than Voldemort?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Of course you were,’ said Harry. ‘Of course - how can you ask that? You never killed if you could avoid it!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘True, true,’ said Dumbledore, and he was like a child seeking reassurance. ‘Yet I, too, sought a way to conquer death, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Not the way he did,’ said Harry. After all his anger at Dumbledore, how odd it was to sit here, beneath the high vaulted ceiling, and defend Dumbledore from himself. ‘Hallows, not Horcruxes.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Hallows,’ murmured Dumbledore, ‘not Horcruxes. Precisely.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: There was a pause. The creature behind them whimpered, but Harry no longer looked round.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Grindelwald was looking for them too?’ he asked.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore closed his eyes for a moment, and nodded.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It was the thing, above all, that drew us together,’ he said quietly. ‘Two clever, arrogant boys with a shared obsession. He wanted to come to Godric’s Hollow, as I am sure you have guessed, because of the grave of Ignotus Peverell. He wanted to explore the place the third brother had died.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So it’s true?’ asked Harry. ‘All of it? The Peverell brothers -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘- were the three brothers of the tale,’ said Dumbledore, nodding. ‘Oh yes, I think so. Whether they met Death on a lonely road … I think it more likely that the Peverell brothers were simply gifted, dangerous wizards who succeeded in creating those powerful objects. The story of them being Death’s own Hallows seems to me the sort of legend that might have sprung up around such creations.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Cloak, as you know now, travelled down through the ages, father to son, mother to daughter, right down to Ignotus’s last living descendant, who was born, as Ignotus was, in the village of Godric’s Hollow.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore smiled at Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Me?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘You. You have guessed, I know, why the Cloak was in my possession on the night your parents died. James had showed it to me just a few days previously. It explained much of his undetected wrongdoing at school! I could hardly believe what I was seeing. I asked to borrow it, to examine it. I had long since given up my dream of uniting the Hallows, but I could not resist, could not help taking a closer look … It was a Cloak the likes of which I had never seen, immensely old, perfect in every respect … and then your father died, and I had two Hallows at last, all to myself!’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: His tone was unbearably bitter.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘The Cloak wouldn’t have helped them survive, though,’ Harry said quickly. ‘Voldemort knew where my mum and dad were. The Cloak couldn’t have made them curse-proof.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘True,’ sighed Dumbledore. ‘True.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Harry waited, but Dumbledore did not speak, so he prompted him.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So you’d given up looking for the Hallows when you saw the Cloak?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh yes,’ said Dumbledore faintly. It seemed that he forced himself to meet Harry’s eyes. ‘You know what happened. You know. You cannot despise me more than I despise myself.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘But I don’t despise you -‘

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Then you should,’ said Dumbledore. He drew a deep breath. ‘You know the secret of my sister’s ill-health, what those Muggles did, what she became. You know how my poor father sought revenge, and paid the price, died in Azkaban. You know how my mother gave up her own life to care for Ariana.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I resented it, Harry.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore stated it baldly, coldly. He was looking, now, over the top of Harry’s head, into the distance.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I was gifted, I was brilliant. I wanted to escape. I wanted to shine. I wanted glory.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Do not misunderstand me,’ he said, and pain crossed the face so that he looked ancient again. ‘I loved them. I loved my parents, I loved my brother and my sister, but I was selfish, Harry, more selfish than you, who are a remarkably selfless person, could possibly imagine.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘So that, when my mother died, and I was left the responsibility of a damaged sister and a wayward brother, I returned to my village in anger and bitterness. Trapped and wasted, I thought! And then, of course, he came …’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Dumbledore looked directly into Harry’s eyes again.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Grindelwald. You cannot imagine how his ideas caught me, Harry, inflamed me. Muggles forced into subservience. We wizards triumphant. Grindelwald and I, the glorious young leaders of the revolution.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Oh, I had a few scruples. I assuaged my conscience with empty words. It would all be for the greater good, and any harm done would be repaid a hundredfold in benefits for wizards. Did I know, in my heart of hearts, what Gellert Grindelwald was? I think I did, but I closed my eyes. If the plans we were making came to fruition, all my dreams would come true.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And at the heart of our schemes, the Deathly Hallows! How they fascinated him, how they fascinated both of us! The unbeatable wand, the weapon that would lead us to power! The Resurrection Stone - to him, though I pretended not to know it, it meant an army of Inferi! To me, I confess, it meant the return of my parents, and the lifting of all responsibility from my shoulders.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘And the Cloak … somehow, we never discussed the Cloak much, Harry. Both of us could conceal ourselves well enough without the Cloak, the true magic of which, of course, is that it can be used to protect and shield others as well as its owner. text_content: ‘- then Slytherin house will have gained an excellent student, won’t it? It doesn’t matter to us, Al. But if it matters to you, you’ll be able to choose Gryffindor over Slytherin. The Sorting Hat takes your choice into account.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Really?’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘It did for me,’ said Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: He had never told any of his children that before, and he saw the wonder in Albus’s face when he said it. But now the doors were slamming all along the scarlet train, and the blurred outlines of parents were swarming forwards for final kisses, last-minute reminders. Albus jumped into the carriage and Ginny closed the door behind him. Students were hanging from the windows nearest them. A great number of faces, both on the train and off, seemed to be turned towards Harry.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Why are they all staring?’ demanded Albus, as he and Rose craned round to look at the other students.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘Don’t let it worry you,’ said Ron. ‘It’s me. I’m extremely famous.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: Albus, Rose, Hugo and Lily laughed. The train began to move, and Harry walked alongside it, watching his son’s thin face, already ablaze with excitement. Harry kept smiling, and waving, even though it was like a little bereavement, watching his son glide away from him …

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The last trace of steam evaporated in the autumn air. The train rounded a corner. Harry’s hand was still raised in farewell.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘He’ll be all right,’ murmured Ginny.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: As Harry looked at her, he lowered his hand absent-mindedly and touched the lightning scar on his forehead.

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: ‘I know he will.’

book: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (UK)
text_content: The scar had not pained Harry for nineteen years. All was well.
